Armed men take hostages in Cartagena, one of Colombia's top tourist destinations
Colombian police say that a group of armed men have seized a super market in the city of Cartagena and taken an unknown number of people hostage
BOGOTA, Colombia -- A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding an unknown number of hostages, Colombian police said.
Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the Exito supermarket in Cartagena’s La Castellana neighborhood Tuesday, while local media have shown footage of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff appears between the armed men and police.
Cartagena is one of Colombia's main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well preserved 18th century architecture, and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.
Cartagena’s airport temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday following the incident. But it later said in an X message that operations were slowly returning to normal.

In November, a claim circulated that U.S. banks warned customers they could be liable for money lost to mistakes made by artificial intelligence agents acting on their behalf.
An AI agent is a tool that can act as a digital assistant and carry out tasks such as writing and sending emails or planning and booking travel. In October, Axios reported that major U.S. banks had found "unauthorized third-party AI agents" logging into banking services using details that belonged to real customers.
Some AI agents, such as X's Grok Bot and Meta's Muse, advertise their reported ability to manage a person's money. Bank executives who spoke to Axios reportedly feared the risks of giving such agents permission to move or manage real people's funds.
By November, social media users claimed banks had taken action to discourage customers from using AI agents to manage their finances. For example, one X user wrote (archived):
BREAKING:
🇺🇸 If an AI agent empties your account, your bank won't refund your money anymore
U.S. banks like Citi, PNC and Citizens changed their terms this week.
If you give your credentials to an external AI agent, everything it does counts as if you had done it yourself, even if it gets hacked or ignores your instructions.
Similar claims also circulated on Facebook and Reddit (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
The claims appeared to come from reporting by Tech Crunch and Business Insider that claimed major banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citi, Wells Fargo, Ally, PNC and Citizens (which included five of the Federal Reserve Board's 10 largest banks in the U.S.) had warned their customers they could be held liable for mistakes third-party AI agents made on their accounts if they gave them permission to use their log in details.
Based on Tech Crunch and Business Insider's reporting and our own verification, we find claims that major banks like the ones listed above warned customers they could be liable for money lost to mistakes made by AI agents acting on their behalf to be true.
Emails sent to customers and the various banks' own terms and conditions suggested that they either advised against or outright prohibited users from allowing third-party AI agents to access their accounts. If users did allow third-party agents to access their accounts, several of the banks listed above said they would treat any transactions that agent carried out as if it were approved by the customer themselves, meaning it might not always be possible to recover funds an AI agent had mistakenly spent on a customer's behalf.
What major US banks say about AI agents
JPMorgan Chase
Jamie Dimon, chief executive officer of JPMorgan Chase & Co., said on a company earnings call on Oct. 13 that the bank was "not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company," describing fears of "rogue" agents causing a threat to customers.
The bank was reportedly developing tools to find and defend against outside AI agents acting on behalf of its customers.
Business Insider reported that Chase bank warned customers in an email that, "authorized transactions may not be reversible if your information is misused," where AI agents were involved.
One Snopes reporter who is also a Chase customer received this email, which asked customers to "Keep your sign-in information private, including when using AI tools." The email continued (emphasis ours):
As AI tools evolve, it's important to understand how your financial information is being used. Always verify who you're sharing with, as authorized transactions may not be reversible if your information is misused.
The bank's "Digital Services Agreement," updated in October, outright prohibits sharing login credentials with third parties "including External AI, automated tools, or data aggregators" (Page 14).
Bank of America
At least three Snopes reporters recieved an email that also circulated online (archived) in October about Bank of America's stance on third-party AI agents. It read (emphasis ours):
Please remember that your username and password should never be shared with another person or provided to an outside service, including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf. If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access.
Citi
The bank updated its "Online User Agreement" in November to include a policy on third-party AI agents. It wrote:
You are cautioned against using any third-party AI Agent to access your accounts or use any digital services including, but not limited to, use of such agent to provide any information or instruction to Citi or perform any transaction through Citi Online or Citi Mobile.
It continued (emphasis ours):
If you disregard this caution and provide your Online Credentials to any third-party AI Agent or otherwise permit such agent access to your accounts or allow such agent to use any digital service and to perform any transactions on your behalf, Citi will consider any access and actions taken by the agent as authorized by You.
Wells Fargo
The bank updated its "Online Access Agreement," effective Nov. 24, to outline the customer's responsibilities if they allowed a third-party AI agent to access their account. It wrote (emphasis ours):
Unless otherwise provided by law or regulation, if you provide an AI Agent with access to the Service or any Eligible Account using your login credentials, or otherwise authorize an AI Agent to act on your behalf, you agree that:
- Any instructions, actions, or transactions initiated by the AI Agent are deemed to have been initiated and authorized directly by you, without further verification, and we have no obligation to investigate the validity or scope of such authority;
- We may rely on any such instructions, actions, or transactions as valid and binding and as evidence of your authorization; and
- We have no obligation to investigate, verify, or confirm the authority, authenticity, or validity of any instruction or action taken by an AI Agent.
Ally
Business Insider reported that Ally emailed its customers in November to warn against the dangers of using an AI agent for managing accounts. One Snopes reporter received this email, which read (emphasis ours):
When you use an Al service, you're responsible for any actions that the Al takes. Al can make mistakes, hallucinate, misunderstand your instructions, or follow them in ways you didn't intend, which could lead to significant loss.
PNC
The bank's "Digital Services Agreement," which becomes effective in December, included the following language on third-party AI agents (Page 9):
Unless PNC expressly permits otherwise for a particular Service, you may not authorize or permit a Third-Party AI Agent to initiate, request, submit, or complete a payment, transfer, or other transaction on your behalf.
It added:
To the extent permitted by applicable law, you are responsible for access and activities you authorize or permit in violation of these restrictions, including unintended activities or activities exceeding the authority you intended to provide.
Citizens
Tech Crunch reported that the Citizens bank sent an email to customers warning that they were "on the hook" for any actions a third-party AI agent might take on their behalf. Snopes contacted Citizens to verify the authenticity of this reported email and await a reply.
Industry group calls banks' precautions 'reasonable'
Though the major banks we investigated expressed in emails or policies that they did not approve of customers using AI agents, some banks were simultaneously developing their own alternatives.
Dimon's statement to investors that he would not allow "just any" AI agents access to the company suggested that some might still be allowed. CNBC reported in November that JPMorgan, which Dimon heads, was working on AI agents that could carry out foreign exchange transactions and aimed to test these in the first half of 2027.
Similarly, PNC said in its "Digital Services Agreement" (Page 9) that customers could "sometimes" be permitted to connect an AI agent to their account if the bank approved of the agent and its use.
Sucharita Kodali, a financial analyst whose specialisms include e-commerce and consumer behavior, reportedly told the technology publication Wired that banks were "fundamentally risk-averse," suggesting that any hesitation they had about AI agents at this early stage in their development might not remain forever.
The Bank Policy Institute, an industry trade group where Dimon sits on the board, predicted in November that "eventually, externally developed agents will be conducting financial transactions at banks and other financial institutions" but that, until the agents had shown they could safely manage people's money, banks that were disallowing their use were engaging in "reasonable risk management practices designed to protect their customers from fraud or mistaken transactions."
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated other rumors surrounding banks.

SC defers Asaram’s rape conviction appeal hearing to January 19, 2027
A bench of justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said, “Four more weeks’ time is granted to the high court to transmit the record to this court
The Supreme Court has deferred till January the hearing on self-styled godman Asaram’s appeal challenging his conviction in a rape case after the Rajasthan High Court sought additional time to transmit the voluminous case record.
The order was passed by the top court on November 17 while hearing Asaram’s appeal against the May 27 order of the Rajasthan high court upholding his conviction and life sentence in the 2013 rape case at Jodhpur.
A bench of justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said, “Four more weeks’ time is granted to the high court to transmit the record to this court.” The matter was posted on January 19, 2027 for final hearing on the appeal.
October 14, the top court had set the hearing date on November 17 to hear the appeal and directed the high court to supply the trial court records along with all necessary documents considered for deciding the appeal.
Pursuant to this, the high court sent a communication to the Supreme Court registry seeking extension of time for compliance. It said that the record is voluminous and the process of preparing translations, scanned or photocopies of documents is under process.
Asaram is currently in jail in connection with this case after he surrendered on October 27 following a 20-day parole. He was convicted in 2018 by a Pocso court in Jodhpur for raping a minor girl at his ashram. The conviction was upheld by the Rajasthan High Court against which he approached the top court. He has also been convicted in another rape case in Gujarat against which his appeal is pending before the Gujarat high court.
The lawyers representing Asaram have informed the court about his multiple health ailments. They have further argued that the Rajasthan High Court upheld his conviction for rape under section 376 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) but did not hold him guilty for offences under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (Pocso). According to them, the material on record suggests that even the charge of rape is not proved.
The bench, on October 14 indicated that it will only examine any question of law or any lapse by the high court that has vitiated the case against him.
The Rajasthan government has maintained that Asaram has rightly been convicted by the trial court and high court. The state had further pointed out that during the trial, three prime witnesses were murdered.
The Rajasthan high court’s May 27 order upheld the conviction and life sentence awarded to Asaram by the trial court on April 25, 2018 that found him guilty of sexually assaulting a minor student at his ashram.

This helpful Apple Watch feature works seamlessly with Apple CarPlay
Some drivers swear by this Apple Watch feature, and it's probably already switched on.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
If you're deep into the Apple ecosystem, the choice between Apple Maps and Google Maps isn't as clear-cut as it used to be. The first was initially a disaster, even threatening the lives of Australian drivers due to inaccuracies. Since then, however, Apple has totally overhauled the app, and these days there's often little to no practical difference — speaking as someone who recently drove cross-country to move to a new city.
I did prefer Apple Maps for that drive for one big reason: my Apple Watch. I knew that I'd be driving for hours at a time, and it was essential to exploit anything and everything to stay alert. Linked with CarPlay, the Apple Watch offers a distinct advantage in the form of haptic feedback.
Most likely this option will already be on once you've configured your watch. But you can double-check this on your iPhone and turn off the feature if it becomes more of an annoyance than a benefit.
How your Apple Watch integrates with CarPlay
With haptic feedback active, your Apple Watch taps your wrist whenever a turn is imminent. These vibrations coincide with CarPlay's audio and visual alerts, so it's always clear what you're supposed to do. You can even choose different vibration patterns depending on whether you need to turn left or right. This makes it virtually impossible to miss a turnoff; the feature might even be lifesaving if you're prone to nodding off on long drives.
As mentioned, these alerts should be on by default. If you want to verify that or disable them, open the Watch app on your iPhone. On the My Watch tab, select Apps, then Maps. If you like, you can toggle alerts for Driving with CarPlay, plus any other driving, walking or cycling.
Whether or not you disable CarPlay integration, you'll probably want to leave cycling alerts on. Apple Maps can be handy while riding a bike or a personal electric vehicle such as a scooter or electric unicycle, but it's sometimes difficult to check your screen and ride at the same time. Audio and haptics may be your only practical cues to make a turn.
Can you drive with just your Apple Watch?
Unfortunately, it's impossible to run CarPlay exclusively from your Apple Watch. Even the Apple Watch Ultra 4 lacks the necessary horsepower, and CarPlay would be an immense battery drain regardless. Since Apple Watches also lack USB ports, they'd be restricted to wireless CarPlay at best.
You can get driving directions directly from the watchOS version of Apple Maps. You'll get the same sort of haptics we've been talking about, plus audio and visual guidance. If you don't have your iPhone, you'll need to download offline maps or use a watch with an active cellular plan. Many carriers charge extra for smartwatch coverage, even though you're rarely going to use your watch and phone data at the same time.
While you can get Google Maps on an Apple Watch, directions won't work without your iPhone. There's no watchOS option for offline maps, and Apple Watches are largely restricted to first-party apps while on cellular. These issues may be solved someday, but neither Apple nor Google seems that eager to tackle them.

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

An Amazon delivery drone that clipped a fiber-optic line before crashing onto a garage roof is now the subject of an investigation by the US Federal Aviation Administration. It’s the latest delivery drone mishap caught on video as Amazon and other companies are ramping up such aerial delivery operations across the United States.
The November 20 incident began with Jim Brennan and his wife, residents of Huntington Woods, Michigan, placing an order for shampoo and being surprised by a notification about the package arriving by drone within seven minutes, according to WXYZ 7 News Detroit. After the drone dropped the package into Brennan’s backyard, it lost a propeller when it caught on fiber-optic cable and floundered sideways before getting pinned between the neighbor’s garage roof and some power lines.
“Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan told WXYZ 7.
Amazon Prime Air currently operates a fleet of battery-powered MK30 drones that can deliver packages weighing up to five pounds and have onboard sense-and-avoid technology to avoid obstacles. However, the drone clearly failed to avoid the thin fiber-optic cable in this case—so hopefully the FAA investigation would take that into account along with Amazon delivery drone procedures.
The FAA preliminary accident and incident notification briefly describes the incident as “UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff.” That notice was posted on November 23.
The National Transportation Safety Board is also gathering information about the incident but has not yet decided whether to open its own probe, according to CNBC. That US government agency holds primary responsibility for investigating aviation accidents and other transportation incidents.

This article is part of a new First Opinion series on the future of medical school.
By this time of year, the sky is black when I step outside. The day has carried me from lectures on gastrointestinal cancer disparities to TAing microbiology, from student government debates to helping free-clinic patients complete paperwork for expensive medications. With the cold nipping at my skin, I look back at the Stanford medical school building, its windows glowing. There is still so much to do, and even more to feel. I call my mother, my home base in human form. Three thousand miles away, she is preparing for bed. Circumstances beyond her control have kept her from taking a domestic flight for decades, let alone visit me in California. Her first question is always, “Did you remember to eat dinner?” Her second: “How were your classes today?”
I am a class-goer. Most of my classmates are, too, though preclinical lecture attendance among medical schools has been declining nationally since the pandemic and the Step 1 exam’s transition to pass/fail. Given the flexibility of recordings and the time students devote to service, research, and other commitments, I understand why some choose to study independently and firmly believe in preserving students’ freedom to make that choice.
For me, though, attending lectures in person has become an important part of feeling at home. It is the most powerful way I take care of my mental health and the classmates I have come to see as my newfound family. I would like to make the case why it could for other medical students, too.
Part of that happiness comes from my daily calls with my immigrant mother. What I learn gives me something to share with the woman who gave up her dream of becoming a clinician so I could pursue mine: dissecting a cadaver for the first time, suturing, administering flu vaccines for undocumented folks, wrapping wound dressing around an unhoused man’s arm. Putting these experiences into words is an exercise of understanding the unmistakably human profession I am entering.
I once worried that telling her the good parts of my day would make the distance between us more painful. Her unconditional love for me throughout the years has taught me otherwise. There are many students like me who left the comfort of our communities to pursue higher education. We should not have to compromise on maintaining relationships with loved ones, which influences medical student well-being and belonging.
In graduate school, where life is more independent, class also gives us a place to come together. During lecture breaks, I learn about friends advocating against the medical bloodletting of horseshoe crabs, making spaces more accessible to people with disabilities, and bringing care to under-resourced youth through mobile vans. We ask to become involved in one another’s work. Other days, happiness is resting my head on a friend’s shoulder, sharing my next bucket-list read — Bryant Lin’s “Sunshine: An Exploration of Living When You Are Dying” — or suggesting that we try the new cafe with robot baristas. It is remembering I am not walking this road alone.
Just as importantly, being physically present gives me opportunities to check in with others. As smartphones and artificial intelligence mediate more of our lives, I worry how easily we can grow used to being alone. Hard workers are remarkable at hiding stress. Intelligent people are good at forgetting to be kind to themselves. Class gives us a place, an excuse, not only to struggle through challenging coursework in real time together, but be part of one another’s lives. In between lectures, I am giving a friend a relationship pep talk as we complain about dating in the Bay Area. The next moment, I am making plans to cheer on another friend at a marathon. After lab, I am curled up on the reading room couch beside a peer whose mother has just been diagnosed with cancer. Our parents are getting older and sicker. It is infuriating. You would think learning medicine would brace us for inevitable losses. False. But knowing there is an abundance of people here to catch you is a peace in its own form.
In the classroom, I have also come to see my education as one I help shape. Conversations with professors following lectures have allowed me to successfully advocate to integrate various topics in our curriculum: sex differences in aortic stenosis pathophysiology, the relationship between ALDH2*2 deficiency and esophageal cancer, overdose response training. Medicine is evolving by the day, and these exchanges make education a collaboration between learners and teachers, showing students that our voices matter.
I think often of watching Celine Song’s “Past Lives” with my mother in December 2024, when I was still in New York. The film introduces in-yun, the idea that an encounter between two people is the result of countless threads from their past lives intertwining. Today, I still wonder if this, too, is a past life, and we are already something else to each other in the next. Perhaps in the next, I am the uninsured one who needs translation, and she is the medical student sitting across from me at the free clinic. In this life, it is 2 a.m. Eastern, and she is calling to ask about my day. It is 11 p.m. in California, and I am at the beach with friends, squinting into the Pacific because someone yelled that they spotted a whale. I imagine the animal’s song, sung at a frequency so low it travels for thousands of miles underwater, enough to carry me home.
I crave a big future, expansive in experience and generosity. For others, that may mean studying independently to make room for research, paid work, service, or rest. Those choices deserve grace.
For me, it begins with being physically present during these four brief years. Honoring my mother means doing good when her familiar applause is far away and nurturing the classmates who will become tomorrow’s doctors. Here is my chance to find where I fit, then widen that space for the next person. I don’t plan to squander a second of it.
Brian Zhang is a second-year M.D. student at Stanford University School of Medicine, where he currently serves as student body president.
The First Opinion series on the future of medical school will run through the end of 2026. Have an idea for a big or small way to change medical school? Email us.

A video showing a white airbag emerging from the helmet of a biker who appears to crash is being widely shared on social media (here, here). The video claims that China has developed helmets equipped with airbags to prevent head injuries in the event of a motorcycle accident. The video has also been shared by several prominent media outlets (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the viral post.
Claim: A video shows a helmet equipped with airbags developed in China.
Fact: The viral video is AI-generated. While some companies are developing airbag helmets, the airbags shown in the video are exaggerated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, upon examining the viral video, we noticed that the bike and the biker are not visible in the phone recording of the fall for a few moments. After the airbags deploy, the biker suddenly disappears. Moreover, the way the bike loses control and the biker falls onto the road appears unnatural. Such visual inconsistencies are commonly seen in AI-generated videos.
Further, we verified the viral video using AI content detection tools Hive Moderation and Sightengine. Both tools indicated that the video was AI-generated, confirming that it is not a genuine video.
Moreover, a reverse image search of the viral video led us to the original video, which was uploaded on Facebook (archived) by a page named Zero Gravity Gang. We found that this page regularly uploads AI-generated videos depicting various vehicle-related experiments.
While it is true that a few companies are experimenting with airbag technology for helmets (here, here, here). However, these designs are not as large as the airbag shown in the viral video. They are designed to provide protection to the head and neck rather than inflate into a large structure around the rider.
To sum up, this viral video of the airbag helmet developed in China is AI-generated, not real.

Rosemary Nyirumbe became a nun when she was just in her mid-teens – and she felt her true vocation lay in rehabilitating children who had been through some of the worst trauma imaginable. So that’s what she did. In this episode Mike Wooldridge hears Sr Rosemary’s astonishing story. The feared rebel group, the Lord’s Resistance Army, started to terrorise the north of Uganda in the 1980s. Many children, girls as well as boys, were abducted and forced to become child soldiers. In many cases, the LRA forced them to commit atrocities, leaving them deeply traumatised. Many of the girls also bore the children of rebel leaders. As they started to return home, these children were often rejected by their families and communities, says Sr Rosemary. So she set about giving them a future and a hope: through enabling them to acquire skills like sewing, and by helping them see that God had not rejected them for the atrocities they had been forced to commit. More than once, Sr Rosemary put herself in enormous danger in order to fulfil her mission. But, she says, she also learnt that small acts of kindness can touch the hearts of even battle-hardened rebels.

NEW DELHI: Eight months after it launched a probe on alleged excess industrial capacity in 16 countries, including India, China and the European Union, the US Trade Representative is all set to unveil its findings in the case and propose tariffs.
The Wall Street Journal said the US is preparing to raise tariffs this week, with Bloomberg reporting that it may come in as early as Tuesday. Indian officials are keeping a close watch on the outcome of the probe, which is likely to be followed by a set of hearings, before final tariffs are announced, in around 45 days.
After the setback in the US Supreme Court over the use of emergency powers to impose "reciprocal tariffs", the Trump administration had launched two probes under Section 301.
Section 301 probe: Govt doesn’t expect any negative impact
While additional tariffs of 10-12.5 per cent were imposed on imports from over 50 countries, including India, for their alleged failure to prohibit the import of goods with forced labour, which harmed American exports, the outcome of the second investigation is awaited.
Going by the mood here, the government does not expect any negative impact, although it maintains that there is no structural excess capacity in India and the surplus is in anticipation of higher demand in the world’s fastest-growing major economy. 
In fact, during deliberations with the US government too, officials have made it clear that the government has not provided subsidy or other support to create capacity, while underlining that any country which has surplus domestic production is engaged in exports.
The report by USTR will be followed by hearings before the final tariff is announced. In the first probe, India had managed to get concessions with the final levy of 10 per cent imposed, against 12.5 per cent, proposed initially. The outcome of the investigation will provide clarity on Trump’s new tariff framework, although the final levy will be known in around 45 days. Based on the final tariff, governments will engage in negotiations for “trade deals”. India is confident of negotiating a deal where its exports enjoy “comparative advantage” over rivals from the region.
While the first set of tariffs related to forced labour have been challenged in US courts, even the second one is expected to face litigation, especially because USTR findings are similar for almost all countries. In the case of structural excess capacity, among the top 20 trading partners for the US, all except Canada, the UK, Brazil and Australia are facing action, with the large European countries being part of the EU. The list also includes Norway, Indonesia, Cambodia and Bangladesh, which are not among the top 20 partners for goods and services trade.

An incorrect or outdated spectacles prescription can leave a child’s vision inadequately corrected, affecting classroom activities and learning. Regular eye examinations are important because children’s eyesight can change as they grow, and wearing spectacles alone does not ensure that their vision is being corrected properly.
A study of 5,268 school-going children in north India found that only 23.03% of those prescribed spectacles were using the correct prescription. Inaccurate spectacle power was common, with younger age and longer duration of spectacle use among the associated factors.

WASHINGTON — A new website launched by the Trump administration provides centralized access to more than 92,000 public records from the Department of Health and Human Services and the agencies it oversees — including partially redacted entries from health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendar.
While many of the records were previously available, the health department heralded the launch of the site as a sign of its “radical transparency.”
In June, after a New York Times report referred to him as disengaged with the job, Kennedy said on social media that his calendar was publicly available, though no such calendar had been made available for the media or the public before Tuesday. A number of Freedom of Information Act requests filed by STAT reporters had previously gone unanswered and even unacknowledged and do not appear to be included in the Tuesday release.
Much of the secretary’s partial calendar, which reflects his activities from Feb. 13, 2025, to June 19, 2026, is redacted, including some private calls taken by the secretary. Federal officials have warned pregnant women and children to evacuate the area amid fears of lead exposure

The Army has issued new maps hours before it detonates nearly 70 barrels of lead azide in Iowa, showing a toxic cloud spreading toward northern Missouri.
The maps showed lead dust from Wednesday morning’s blast traveling southwest from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown into northeastern Missouri between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. Central Time. Officials chose Wednesday because they said it had the most favorable weather conditions.
Federal officials also warned Tuesday that vulnerable individuals such as pregnant women and children should evacuate the area.
“If they are women who are pregnant, children under the age of 6, or children in general, and individuals who may have chronic disease, you definitely want to be out of that area,” Sean Kaufman, the principal deputy assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Department of Health and Human Services, said at a press conference in Iowa, The Washington Sun reported.
“I would evacuate that area that’s signaled in the model. Outside of that area, if you’re close to that proximity and you’re uncomfortable, I think you need to do what you need to do to take care of your family.”
Iowa residents have received an alert from federal emergency officials who said some people within five miles southwest of the detonation site may be evacuated before the controlled detonation and that people living five to 20 miles away should stay indoors with windows shut.
Locals are spending their Thanksgiving week taping up windows in their homes and buying supplies like masks and gloves instead of preparing for the holiday on Thursday.
Resident Bob Kemp was supposed to travel down south for Thanksgiving, but was compelled to stay and watch over his and his sister’s homes.
“I’m going to stay here and see how things go,” Kemp told WQAD News 8. “If they would have blown it today, I probably would have went to Texas for Thanksgiving, but since that’s not happening, it’s going to happen on Wednesday, that changed all our plans.”
The blast was initially scheduled for last Friday, but the Army was held up in court over health and environmental concerns. A federal appeals court ultimately ruled that the Environmental Protection Agency had adequate protections to minimize the spread of lead dust.
But residents are still worried about the potential effects of lead exposure, which is especially harmful for children. Even low levels of lead in a child’s blood can seriously harm their health, including brain damage and slowed growth and development, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
“I’m really angry about this. I feel like we’re guinea pigs,” Krys Plate, a retired second-grade teacher who lives with her husband and their two teenage daughters two miles south of the fence line of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, told The New York Times.
The Army has advised everyone in the affected areas — but especially pregnant women, children and people with chronic diseases — to avoid outdoor activities until further notice. State health officials in neighboring Illinois have warned residents to stay inside for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation.
People may be exposed to lead, not just from breathing it in but also from surfaces where the dust lands, the Army notes. Once it’s safe to leave their homes, the Army advised people to clean surfaces that may be touched by children, including play equipment, tables and chairs and handrails.
As the public becomes more concerned about lead dust filling the air, President Donald Trump has insisted that the detonation is necessary — even calling on Governor-elect Rob Sand to agree to it if he doesn’t want blood on his hands, despite the Democrat not taking office until January.

“If [Sand] or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” the president added.
Later Monday, Sand wrote on X that the Trump administration “should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks.”

Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?
- Published
Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'big six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.
Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it raises the question: are United this season's Spurs?
While Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points last term, they actually started the season better than United have this season. After 11 games in 2025-26, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.
But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.
While the table prompted talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.
United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.
But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.
While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.
Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.
But what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement quickly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.
And it is not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are currently taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.
As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.
By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the percentage chance of each club finishing in each position.
While the above means it is more likely United will survive, it is worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.
There is a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.
History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.
Of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.
A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.
Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.
Having said that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there would not be entirely unprecedented.
It is a big ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they have played than they did last season.
Even if they were to repeat the results that led to them finishing third from now on, they would still only reach 52 points, the number Chelsea narrowly finished 10th with last term.
Though United are without a win in nine Premier League matches, their remaining fixtures of 2026 do offer some hope.
While they have a tough home game against Brentford this weekend and a trip to champions Arsenal just before Christmas, their other five games are against teams currently in the bottom seven - sides we must, at this point, call relegation rivals.
So despite suffering the worst first game by a Manchester United manager for 100 years in the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool, Pochettino will hope to quickly quash any concerns his new club will be embroiled in the same fight as his former one last season.

Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe has warned consumers, particularly students and young people, against relying on protein supplements and nutraceutical products marketed with misleading claims about muscle growth and health benefits. Addressing reporters in Pune, Mundhe said several products, including whey protein supplements, were being promoted through questionable branding and marketing practices. He urged consumers to verify whether the benefits advertised by manufacturers were genuine and whether the products actually contained the ingredients and nutritional components mentioned on their labels. He also stressed that only businesses holding the necessary licences are legally permitted to sell such products. Munde said that those operating without the required authorisation cannot sell them. Mundhe cautioned young people who consume protein supplements to improve their fitness or build muscle, saying such products cannot, on their own, deliver the results manufacturers promise. He emphasised that muscle development requires regular exercise and adequate nutrition, including protein from natural food sources. "These health supplements, be it protein or the claimed nutraceutical items, are being presented in a very wrong way and are being used in a very wrong way. The branding, marketing or the kind of claims being made are wrong. It is important to check whether the claims are true or not," Mundhe said. He further warned that consumers may not always know whether the protein content advertised on a supplement's packaging accurately reflects the product's actual protein content. "To build muscle, you will have to exercise. You will have to eat the natural protein it contains. The FDA chief said consumers should not automatically trust promotional claims made by supplement brands and sellers, particularly when products are advertised as providing specific health or muscle-building benefits. He reiterated that businesses must possess the appropriate licences to sell protein supplements and nutraceutical products. Selling these products without the necessary permissions is illegal. Mundhe also cautioned consumers against depending solely on recommendations from gyms and health clubs when choosing supplements, particularly where guidance may not come from qualified professionals. Mundhe advised consumers to read product labels carefully and check whether the ingredients and nutritional information match the claims made by manufacturers. He also recommended consulting a doctor before taking supplements, especially when consumers are uncertain about a product's suitability or potential health benefits. The commissioner highlighted that muscle development and overall fitness should be supported by a combination of regular physical activity, natural protein intake, adequate sleep and a healthy lifestyle, rather than relying on supplements marketed as quick solutions. North Korea reviews Switzerland relations after sanctions on youth camp linked to war
North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea threatened Tuesday to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, condemning Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a youth camp in eastern North Korea over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russia-occupied areas of Ukraine.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, described the Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan as an “open hostile act” and a “serious infringement” of the North’s sovereignty, according to a statement carried by state media.
Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials, said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia. She didn't directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated.
North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for economic assistance and military technology transfers.
Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he positions North Korea as part of a united front against the United States.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” North Korean state media said at the time.
Kim Yo Jong said that North Korea would need to “comprehensively reconsider the relations with unreliable Switzerland” following the sanctions on the camp and called on North Korean diplomats to take unspecified “corresponding” countermeasures.
“It is my view that the Swiss diplomatic office has spontaneously lost justification for its existence, which was opened in Pyongyang under the pretext of improving the relations, given that the Swiss Confederation has clarified its stand not to respect the sovereignty of the DPRK,” she said, using the initials of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
In adding the Songdowon camp earlier this month to its broader sanctions related to Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine, Swiss authorities held the camp responsible for the “forced assimilation, including indoctrination, and militarized education of Ukrainian minors,” according to a document by Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs.
It said the camp participates in programs involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from Russia-occupied territories to North Korea and exposes them to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.
The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the Songdowon camp, freezing its assets and prohibiting financial transactions with the facility, although the practical impact of such measures is unclear given North Korea’s limited financial ties with European countries.
Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country, which has aggressively expanded its nuclear weapons program since Kim Jong Un took power in 2011.
The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in Pyongyang in 1997 that mostly focused on humanitarian programs, but the office closed in March 2020 as North Korea shut its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Swiss government has said that the new diplomatic office in Pyongyang, which reports to the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, would help strengthen direct contacts with North Korean officials and promote dialogue.
In a statement to The Associated Press, the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said that it had taken note of North Korean statements. But it said that neither the Swiss Embassy in Beijing nor its diplomatic office in Pyongyang had been officially contacted about the matter. It said that Switzerland aims to “maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues.”
Kim Yo Jong's statement came a day after North Korean state media reported that Kim Jong Un received credentials from the newly appointed ambassadors from several countries, including Russia, Sweden, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil and India, in Pyongyang on Sunday.
During the ceremony, Kim Jong Un defended his efforts to strengthen his nuclear-armed military as necessary to protect the North’s security amid what he described as an “unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe,” Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency said.

My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
- Published
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.
They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.
"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.
But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.
This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.
Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.
Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.
After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.
"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.
The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.
The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.
After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.
Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.
This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.
After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.
This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.
"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.
Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.
He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.
In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.
Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.
"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.
Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.
The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.
However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.
"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.
For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.
He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.
Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.
"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.
They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.
Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.
After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.
"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."
During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.
But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.
Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.
"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".
He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.
But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.
Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.
He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."
He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.
"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.
"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

“We buried her under that tree,” says Rani, pointing to a coconut tree near their house at Vechapathi hamlet in Sholayur panchayat of Attappadi, Palakkad district.

In October and November, several posts claimed advertisements in Times Square featuring Jesus Christ left New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani "furious."
A Facebook post shared a video of the advertisement, which reads "Jesus Is Coming." Another post said:
Jesus Christ is taking center stage in Times Square, New York City!
Images of Jesus appearing on massive digital billboards in the heart of Manhattan are drawing attention, with posts circulating online claiming that Zohran Mamdani is furious over the displays.
Regardless of the political controversy surrounding New York City, seeing the image of Christ displayed so prominently in one of the world's most recognizable locations is certainly making a statement.
Perhaps New York City isn't as far gone as some people believe!
(Facebook user "Robin Martyr")
There is no evidence Mamdani, who is Muslim, was "furious" over advertisements of Jesus on Times Square billboards. Mamdani has made no such public statement or criticized the promotion of images of Jesus. On the contrary, Mamdani has frequently spoken in favor of religious freedom and diversity. As such, we rate this claim as false.
We searched through Mamdani's recent statements and found no such expression of anger. In fact, in April, Mamdani posted a message for Easter Sunday (archived): "Happy Easter, New York! Today, millions of New Yorkers celebrate the resurrection of Jesus Christ and the victory of hope over despair and faith over fear."
A spokesperson for Mamdani told us over email, "There is no truth to this claim."
The footage of the advertisement of Jesus Christ in Times Square previously appeared online (archived) in December 2025 — before Mamdani took office — if not earlier.
The claim that Mamdani was furious spread via social media accounts that frequently share unverified information unsupported by reliable media coverage. One such Facebook page, Robyn Martyr, is devoted to pro-Christianity content.
Any company or organization can rent advertising space and time on a Times Square billboard. After Mamdani became mayor, we reported on how the Florida Chamber of Commerce paid for an advertisement in Times Square that appeared to mock him, calling him Florida's "Economic Developer of the Year."
Snopes has covered numerous false rumors about Mamdani.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Monday said that the federal government will save $9.2 billion on drugs purchased through Medicare next year as a result of price negotiations, a net savings of 45% compared to what it would’ve paid last year had the negotiated prices been in effect.
This is the third time the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has negotiated drug prices following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act, but it’s the first time those drugs have included treatments administered in doctors’ offices, which are covered by Part B. Only retail drugs covered by Part D were eligible during the first two years.
The estimated $9.2 billion in savings does not account for discounts the drugmakers pay to the Part D Manufacturer Discount Program. That program was created by the same law that created the price negotiation program. If those discounts were included, the estimated savings would be about $5.5 billion, or 33% in lower net aggregate spending.

Racketeering is traditionally reserved for organized criminal acts — the kind often associated with the Mafia, for example — but the AP writes US prosecutors thought the charge could apply to what they described as Huawei's repeated theft of intellectual property and trade secrets. The company has been accused of copying or outright stealing from competitors in the past, and the DOJ pointed to Huawei's sale of routers with code copied from a competitor as evidence. Prosecutors also accused Huawei of violating US sanctions by selling equipment to Iran and North Korea, and misleading banks and officials to hide it.
In a statement, Huawei welcomed its acquittal on the racketeering charge, saying it lacked "factual basis."
"We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit," the company continued. "The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades. No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation. We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests." Huawei attorney Brian Heberlig told AP the company planned to appeal its convictions.
Huawei isn't allowed to sell its products in the US due to its placement on the Federal Communications Commission's Covered List, so outside of the possibility of paying "billions of dollars in penalties," per the AP, it's not clear how these charges will impact its business. In 2025, the FCC opened an investigation into whether Huawei and fellow Chinese companies ZTE and China Telecom were circumventing those restrictions, so the company could face even more scrutiny in the US soon.
