Thirty-four-year-old Sundar lives in Tappal village in Khair tehsil of Aligarh district, Uttar Pradesh. His name was absent from the state’s draft voter list published on January 6, 2026. However, in the final list published on April 10, his name appears four times, at serial numbers 730, 738, 739 and 757 in booth 19. Each entry carries a different Elector Photo Identity Card (EPIC) number.
The official list of Form 6 applications, used for voter registration, records only two applications from Sundar, dated January 9 and 14. The office of the Uttar Pradesh chief electoral officer (CEO), however, said that he had filed four. The discrepancy aside, the CEO’s office’s response confirms a crucial point: Multiple applications by the same person resulted in the issuance of multiple voter IDs.
The Election Commission launched the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Uttar Pradesh in November 2025, with the removal of duplicate and incorrect entries among its stated objectives. Alt News compared the draft and final electoral rolls across 69 booths in 20 districts, covering 60,558 voters, and cross-checked newly added names against the corresponding Form 6 application lists. The analysis found 230 people whose names appeared at least twice in the final rolls, with some listed three or four times, each against a separate voter ID. Such duplicate entries were found in booths across the political spectrum.
On October 27, 2025, the Election Commission announced the second phase of the SIR across 12 states and Union Territories, including Uttar Pradesh. The exercise, covering approximately 51 crore voters, began on November 4.
The schedule for Uttar Pradesh was subsequently extended four times. The draft electoral roll was published on January 6, 2026. Those whose names were missing from the draft had to submit Form 6 to seek inclusion. Following the fourth extension, the deadline for filing claims and objections was March 6, while the final electoral roll was published on April 10.
At present a special summary revision (SSR) of electoral rolls is going on in the state. The draft roll was published on November 17.
The Methodology
For each of 69 booths in UP, Alt News read the draft list (January 6, 2026) and the final list (April 10, 2026) entry by entry, and matched the count with the totals on each list’s cover page. We treated two entries as the same person only if the name, father’s or husband’s name, age and house number all matched.
We checked every case against the scanned entry. We then looked up Form 6 applications in the Form 9 lists. The latter is a public list of every Form 6 application an election office received, with the applicant’s name, relative and address. The lists we examined cover 13 assembly constituencies. The 69 booths that we chose fall into the three following groups:
One Form, Several Voter IDs
Listed below are 11 voters (chosen randomly from the 230 to explain the nature of the anomalies) whose names did not appear on the January 6 draft list but were all added to the final list. In each of these cases, the entries share the same name, relative, age and house number, but carry different EPIC numbers. We use first names because they are private citizens.
Our findings revealed two patterns: For Ishlok, Najmeen, Himanshu, Pinki, Saurabh and Aakash, every form became a voter ID, and the entries sit next to each other on the list. Saurabh’s are serial numbers 1004 and 1005.
From Sundar to Sunita, the list has more entries than the published Form 6 list has forms. Married couple Vijay Lakshmi and Dharmendra have a cumulative total of five voter IDs. Vijay Lakshmi has three, while her husband has two.
Anushree Verma, whose husband is Akshay Verma, had filled Form 6 twice and received three voter IDs.
Sundar, mentioned at the beginning, had filled the form twice (According to Form 9) and in return got four voter IDs.
The biggest single cluster of duplicate voters is booth 449 in Chachoi, Sikandrabad (Bulandshahr), where the BJP won 94% of the votes in 2022. The final list adds 69 names to this booth.
Of these, 34 entries are for 17 people, each listed twice with a new EPIC. None of the 17 names are on the January 6 draft list. Fifteen of the 17 filed one Form 6 each on the published lists. For two, Hasmuddin and Heema Devi, we found none. Six of the 17 live at house 91. One of them, Vikas, is listed once as female and once as male.
Some duplicates were already there before the revision and were not removed. In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), two brothers appear twice each, at serials 108 and 109 and at 110 and 111 respectively, on both the draft and final lists.
In booth 1044 of Sahibabad, a father and son already on the list at house number 306 were added again with new IDs at house number 840. We found no Form 6 for either.
The published Form 9 lists for Khair village show one applicant, Bhuvnesh, son of Sanjeev Kumar of Simrauthi village, ten times between January 31 and March 6, 2026.
Across the Form 9 lists of the 13 constituencies, 3,369 people were found to have filed Form 6 between two to 10 times.
Missing Addresses, Renamed IDs, Suspicious Deletions
In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), 20 of the 64 new voters have no house number. The field holds a place name, Oramha, for unrelated families.
Across the 37 city booths, 62 new voters were added with house “0” or a blank. In booth 354 of Kairana (Shamli), 48 voters were already listed at “house 3” on the draft list, and eight more were added from at least seven different families.
In Khair constituency, house number 658, under which all four of Sundar’s entries are listed, is associated with 36 voters from approximately 19 families.
A shared or missing house number is not, in itself, evidence of electoral irregularity, as most villages do not have a system of house numbering. The concern, however, is how entries without a verifiable address could be physically checked during field visits.
Moreover, in booth 351 of Sidhauli (Sitapur), three women’s names appeared changed between the draft and final lists, while the EPIC number, husband’s name, house number and age stayed the same. Rekharani became Lakshmi Devi, Gayashri became Meena Devi and Shivrani became Neelam.
We found 15 such cases across 20 rural booths. These changes could be legitimate corrections. However, only the corresponding Form 8 applications, used to request corrections to electoral roll entries, can establish the basis for the changes.
The most striking example of renamed entries is in booth 327 of Gorakhpur Rural. Serial 799 was Bhathwa, male, 53, house 156, on the draft list. On the final list, the same EPIC belongs to Rusha Devi, female, 50, house 56. Rusha Devi, husband Parmeshwar, also appears at serial numbers 924 and 930 of the addition list under two new EPICs. We found no Form 6 for her among the 23,136 applications in the Gorakhpur Rural lists.
In booth 943 of Sahibabad, 298 entries from one part of the 2025 electoral roll were deleted, 280 of them marked as “absent”. The deletions occurred in consecutive chunks of 23, 17, 14 and 10 names (shown in the plot below). Since electoral rolls are arranged by house and lane, such clusters could simply indicate that an entire building or group of homes had been vacated. A door-to-door verification would establish this. Whether such visits were conducted is something the Election Commission can clarify.
It is worth noting how many voters in every 1,000 appear twice or more on the final roll. See the chart below:
Questions for the Poll Panel
The analysis above poses several significant questions for the election commission vis-a-vis the SIR exercise in Uttar Pradesh. Some of them are the following:
- How did one Form 6 become two or three voter IDs – and how many times did this happen across UP?
- Why are repeat applications from the same person, at the same address, not merged before an ID is issued?
- How did officials verify new voters at house ‘0’, blank addresses and catch-all house numbers?
- How to explain the long runs of consecutive ‘Absent’ deletions – were these homes actually visited?
UP CEO’s Response
The Uttar Pradesh CEO initially denied findings by Alt News co-founder Mohammed Zubair, who flagged Sundar’s case of four different EPIC IDs on X. The office responded with the following post:
Mr Fact-checker please fact-check your own facts.
There is no such scheme as “Buy one Get one free” scheme by Election Commission.
As per your post, the voter had submitted only two applications and he got 4 EPIC cards.
This statement is false.
The voter had submitted 4 applications.
If you want to dispute our facts then you post the reference numbers of two applications that you claim he had submitted and we will post the reference number of the remaining two.
The problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long standing one. We do deduplication through ECINET periodically. We are on path to achieving the objective of catching multiple forms submitted by an individual at the submission stage only. We will achieve our objective very soon.
Please do not incite people by making patently false statements about ECI and thereby trying to create disaffection among the citizens towards a Constitutional Body.
You are advised to rectify your mistake by amending or deleting your post after completing your own due diligence now that you have been informed by us about your wrong information.
— CEO Uttar Pradesh (@ceoup) October 17, 2026
The CEO claimed that Sundar had submitted four Form 6 applications, resulting in four separate entries on the final electoral roll. This contradicted the official Form 6 application list, which recorded only two applications from Sundar. However, the CEO’s response also acknowledged that “the problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long-standing one”.
The discrepancy over whether Sundar submitted two or four applications does not alter the central issue: the Commission itself acknowledges that multiple applications by the same voter can result in the generation of multiple EPIC numbers. Its response also indicates that the system does not consistently prevent such duplication at the application stage, necessitating periodic deduplication through ECINET.
On October 19, the CEO directed election officials to expedite the removal of duplicate entries ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections and identify cases in which individual voters had submitted multiple applications during the SIR.
Readers should note that some of the errors documented in this article were rectified by the Election Commission in the intervening period between our initial identification of these anomalies and the publication of this report.

United sources say they have conclusive proof it was impossible for Isak to reach the ball after he took a heavy touch, that it would have run on to goalkeeper Senne Lammens and Yoro should not have been punished for denying a goalscoring opportunity.
Pochettino said he had some sympathy with referee Sam Barrott but he is livid at how the situation played out.
"I am very disappointed," the Argentine said. "This type of thing can never happen.

"We have an unbelievable car, but we need to be at the level to drive [it]. We accept that the technology is there but what are they doing?"
United are furious at both the nature of the audio of the incident, and referees' chief Howard Webb defending referee Barrott's decision and the VAR John Brooks' reinforcing it on the Mic'd Up programme, which was shown on Sky Sports.
They intend to take the matter up with both the Premier League and ProRef.
It is the second time this season United been on the wrong end of a major VAR error.

There has been no apology from Webb on this occasion.

United sources claim this interpretation is wrong.
The club are unhappy at the speed the on-field decision was confirmed. It is thought United used data around Isak's top speed and his chances of reaching the ball in their defence of Yoro to the FA. They claim this could have been done "within minutes" of the incident occurring.
This is not the only bone of contention at Old Trafford around the incident.
Pochettino also pointed out Liverpool forward Bradley Barcola was too close to the United wall from the resulting free-kick and Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal should have been disallowed.
"No-one talked about [the fact] that the goal wasn't legal," said Pochettino. "Barcola was touching our wall. It must be disallowed.

What referee's chief Webb said about the incident on the Mic'd Up programme.
"There's a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would.

United's fury over Yoro and the way the situation has been handled cannot completely obscure the fact they lost 4-0 in Pochettino's first game in charge.

Skipper Bruno Fernandes revealed at the weekend talks over a new United contract were on hold.

Speaking alongside Pochettino at a media conference before his first meeting with Sporting since he left to join United in a £47m deal in January 2020, Fernandes said his sole focus at present is to drag United out of the mire.

Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war
- Published
Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.
"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.
Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.
Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.
The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).
The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.
Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.
But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.
"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.
The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.
A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.
Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.
The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.
"When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said.
More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.
"They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation."
Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.
They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.
But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.
For many of those who survive, the consequences are devastating and permanent.
Majid Abdul Rahman, 27, was travelling in a car in the Ghouta region on the outskirts of Damascus in March 2025 when it struck an explosive device. The vehicle filled with smoke and he felt a pain in his leg.
More than a year later, Majid has difficulty walking and has been unable to return to work, leaving him struggling to provide for his family.
The danger has continued into this month, with at least 20 people killed and more than 40 injured by explosive ordnance in November.
In one of the worst recorded incidents, an explosion in a school courtyard in Hasakah on 4 November killed a 12-year-old and injured 19 others. And on Monday, a 13-year-old boy was killed when an unexploded cluster munition detonated in southern Daraa province.
The threat is also holding back Syria's economic recovery. Contaminated farmland cannot be safely cultivated, while people collecting scrap metal or trying to salvage materials from abandoned areas also risk triggering explosions.
The Syrian Ministry of Defence says since the end of 2024 its teams have found and dealt with more than 315,000 mines and unexploded munitions.
But no nationwide survey has established how much land remains contaminated, making it difficult to assess the full scale of the problem.
"We're in a bit of a black hole," Atkins said.
And with the extent of contamination still largely unknown, the war continues to claim victims two years after it ended.

Australia to pass safety bill that could result in massive fines for tech platforms
The amendment would give the country a similar ability to fine tech companies as the EU’s Digital Services Act from 2022.
Australian lawmakers are close to passing the Digital Duty of Care Bill, the Associated Press reports, an amendment to the country's Online Safety Act of 2021 that would set minimum safety standards for online platforms and provide ways to fine tech companies that don't comply. The bill follows Australia's recent social media ban for children under 16, an attempt to protect younger internet users with limited success so far.
If passed, the Digital Duty of Care Bill would require online platforms and services like games, social media apps and AI chatbots to protect Australians from harmful content and conduct, according to the AP, including protecting children from exposure to content that promotes eating disorders and pornography. It would also guarantee users the ability to opt out of algorithmic feeds and empower the country's eSafety Commissioner to remove "nudify" websites and apps that use AI to generate and spread nonconsensual nude images. As with the European Union's Digital Services Act, the bill's real teeth come from its possible fines. In this case, Australian regulators could fine tech companies up to five percent of their global revenue, a cap that was raised this week from 109 million AUD, or about $72 million in the US, to help the bill pass the Senate.
"Vaguely defined 'harms,' backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech," US Ambassador to Australia David Brat posted on X. "As Australia's largest foreign investor, the US is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors."
Similar concerns have been raised about the UK's Online Safety Act, which also applies safety standards to online platforms, and helped encourage a wave of new age verification systems across US apps and services in the last year. The Wikimedia Foundation, the owner of Wikipedia, has challenged the ways the UK's law categorizes platforms as one example of how these laws can be ill-defined or overly broad. Australia's bill is expected to clear Parliament and become law by the end of the week, according to the AP.

Made for defenders, but attackers like it too
Cairn is an open source AI problem-solving engine whose first validated domain is autonomous penetration testing. Users give it a task or goal and, optionally, hints for achieving it. A server maintains a shared graph containing facts and hints. A dispatcher reads the graph, schedules tasks, manages containers, and writes the protocol. The dispatcher can then assign each project to a dedicated worker container, each of which runs multiple agents concurrently. Cairn is model-agnostic and can be used on worker backends including Claude Code, Codex, and Pi. Bleeding, birth defects: Congo residents sue over alleged mining pollution
KOLWEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In a small cinderblock home in the scrub beside a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine in Kolwezi, a mother shares a story of devastating loss.
She believes pollution from the neighboring mine is responsible for her family's suffering.
She has lost three children. Two died at birth. A third suffered repeated nosebleeds before dying. One of her two surviving children has stunted growth.
Now she and 26 other residents are taking the company to court in a rare attempt to hold alleged polluters accountable in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They are also suing the government, accusing it of failing to enforce environmental regulations.
Like other plaintiffs, she asked NPR not to identify her, fearing retribution from the company or government. Although the claimants' names are public in court documents, they want to avoid further exposure. Their lawyers also fear the plaintiffs could face intimidation from other locals.
"Our children are the first victims," she said, as the sun set over a nearby mound of mine tailings. "What we're hoping for is to see justice done."
The plaintiffs, whose case began Nov. 3, describe similar problems: contaminated water, nosebleeds, skin rashes, miscarriages and birth defects, which they blame on mining pollution.
The mine, known as COMMUS, is owned by Chinese multinational Zijin and lies in Kolwezi, a city of more than 500,000 people in the heart of Congo's copper belt, a southern region with vast mineral reserves.
Congo is the world's second-largest producer of copper, and also the source of over 70% of the world's cobalt, a metal that is critical to the electric-vehicle revolution because of its use in rechargeable batteries.
Last year, the U.S. signed a sweeping economic partnership with Congo aimed at attracting American investment and challenging the dominance of Chinese companies in the country's mining industry
Despite the global importance of Congo's copper and cobalt mines, however, environmental pollution from the industry has received comparatively little scrutiny.
In Kolwezi, pollution is severe. Neighborhoods near mines are often filled with an acrid smell that residents attribute to the sulfuric acid used to process minerals. A study published in June by environmental research organization Source International — carried out with the advocacy groups RAID and Afrewatch, and scientists from Congo's University of Lubumbashi — also highlighted the scale of the contamination.
Researchers found that levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, in Kolwezi were three to six times the World Health Organization's air quality guideline. The highest concentrations were recorded near the COMMUS mine.
These tiny particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure poses health risks generally, but is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and young children.
The researchers also tested dust samples and found residue of copper, cobalt and manganese, which they said pointed to mining waste as the main source. When the study was released, Source International's executive director, Flaviano Bianchini, said that "these are among the most concerning air quality results we have documented in years of monitoring pollution at industrial mining sites around the world."
The study did not examine health impacts directly, and the authors recommended formal epidemiological research. Residents and health workers in Kolwezi nonetheless point to a string of ailments that they blame on a polluted environment.
In a dilapidated health clinic in the shadow of a mountain of waste from the COMMUS mine, nurse Héritier Bukassa said that people routinely break out in itchy hives. "Some sick people scratch themselves with knives to relieve itching," he explained.
Bukassa added that women in the area also suffer from high rates of miscarriage, and that he had referred four babies born with congenital malformations — mostly cleft palates — to hospitals this year alone.
Respiratory illnesses are common too, Bukassa said, especially in otherwise healthy babies who develop breathing problems a few weeks after birth. "No one from the [mining] company has ever come to talk to us about this," the nurse said.
Zijin, the owner of COMMUS, did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Neither did Congo's mining and environment ministries.
The Cobalt Institute, an industry lobby, said that understanding environmental pollution requires "an evidence-based approach that considers all potential sources and contributors." It added that companies perform environmental monitoring and carry out mitigation measures.
RAID, which is supporting the plaintiffs alongside Afrewatch, described the case this month as one of "the most ambitious legal challenges yet brought by Congolese residents over industrial mining pollution."
The suit is an important test case that could lead to communities challenging other mines in the future, it added.
The plaintiffs are seeking $1.3 million in compensation for health problems and medical expenses, as well as $5 million to restore the environment. Their lawyers say they worry their clients might come under pressure or intimidation to withdraw their testimony.
The mother, however, said she had no such fears. "We have a right to a clean environment," she said, "and to health."

A video showing a woman holding a weapon and trying to protect her house and child as a mob attacks and vandalises the house is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it depicts an attack on Hindu homes in Bangladesh. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a mob attacking Hindu homes in Bangladesh, while a woman tries to protect her house and child.
Fact: The video shows a mob attacking the houses of two men accused of cattle theft in Dakshin Kurshi village, Sunamganj District, Bangladesh, on 25 March 2026. The woman seen holding a child and a sharp weapon while trying to protect her house is the wife of one of the accused. Police confirmed that theft cases had been registered against the accused but condemned the mob attack. Bangladeshi fact-checkers also clarified that the woman is Muslim and that the incident stemmed from allegations of cattle theft, not communal violence. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) from March 2026, which identified the incident as one involving allegations of cattle theft in Dakshin Kurshi village, Dolar Bazar Union, Chhatak Upazila, Sunamganj District, Bangladesh.
According to these reports, villagers were angered by repeated cattle theft. A man named Saifur Rahman was reportedly caught stealing cattle in neighbouring North Kurshi village. During questioning, he allegedly named Ali Hussain, his son-in-law Tarek Mia, and several others as being involved in the thefts. Following this, an agitated mob attacked the houses of Ali Hussain and Tarek Mia in South Kurshi village on 25 March 2026.
The reports stated that more than a hundred people gathered following the allegations and vandalised and looted the houses of the accused. The mob threw bricks and stones, damaged tin walls and household belongings, and attacked women and children. The viral video shows Tarek Mia’s wife, who is also Ali Hussain’s daughter, holding a child and a sharp weapon as she attempts to protect her house from the mob. She tries to fend off the attackers, but they continue to vandalise the house.
Reports further stated that Ali Hussain and Tarek Mia had previously faced theft allegations. Sub-Inspector Abdur Rahman of the Zahidpur Police Investigation Centre reportedly said that police had registered multiple theft cases against the accused and filed a case in connection with the latest incident. However, the officer condemned the mob attack, stating that vandalising someone’s house was unjustified, despite the villagers’ frustration over repeated thefts. The viral video, therefore, depicts an incident arising from allegations of cattle theft in Bangladesh and has no communal angle.
We also found an X post by Bangladeshi fact-checker Shohanur Rahman dated 1 November 2026, stating that the woman is Muslim and the wife of Mohammad Tarek. He clarified that she was trying to protect her father’s house during an attack triggered by allegations of theft.
To sum up, the video of a mob attacking houses in Bangladesh over cattle theft allegations is falsely shared with a communal spin.

Nagaland gets 20-day PAP waiver for Hornbill Festival; stakeholders say not enough
A Protected Area Permit (PAP) is a mandatory travel document required by all foreign nationals wishing to visit or stay in certain areas, including parts of the northeast
The Centre has relaxed a rule barring foreign tourists from entering Nagaland without a special permit for 20 days starting November 26 every year to boost tourism around its famed Hornbill Festival, though local officials and tour operators insist the restrictions must be lifted year-round to revive the state’s tourism sector.
A Protected Area Permit (PAP) is a mandatory travel document required by all foreign nationals wishing to visit or stay in certain areas, including parts of the northeast. The PAP regime was lifted from Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram in 2011 to encourage tourism. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), however, reimposed the restrictions in December 2024, citing regional security concerns.
PAP regime
Under the rules, most foreign travelers must secure permits from the Foreigners Registration Officer (FRO) before entering Nagaland. Citizens or people of origin from Afghanistan, China and Pakistan require prior approval of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) in New Delhi before their visit to the state.
This restriction has been relaxed for 20 days, between November 26 and December 15, for foreign tourists coinciding with the state’s premier cultural tourism event- the Hornbill Festival. The annual festival celebrating the rich traditional and cultural heritage of the Naga tribes has drawn over 2,000 foreign tourists in 2023, 2024 and 2025.
The Union home ministry informed the Nagaland government about its decision on November 14. “The matter regarding relaxation in Protected Area Permit Regime in the State of Nagaland has been considered in this Ministry and exercising the powers conferred under para 14 (2) of the Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025, and after the approval of Competent Authority, it has been decided to relax the Protected Area Regime in the State of Nagaland for a brief period of 20 days i.e., 26 November to 15 December of every year for tourism purpose only,” the MHA’s Foreigners-I Division said.
The home ministry also decided to provide PAP with the validity co-terminus with the project, to the foreign nationals associated with certain projects in the state.
The Neiphiu Rio government has been asking the central government to revisit its decision to reimpose the PAP regime since January 2025.
After MHA indicated on November 4 that it would give a 10-day relaxation, Rio wrote to Union home minister Amit Shah to complain that the 10-day exemption created practical difficulties for tourists, tour operators, travel agencies and hospitality establishments, restricting the potential benefits that tourism can generate for the state’s economy.
Rio said he wanted the Centre to grant a year-round exemption from the PAP regime for foreign visitors to the state. If this was not feasible, he said MHA should at least grant exemption from PAP for one month for the 2026 edition of the festival.
On September 3, the state assembly had also passed a resolution asking the central government to withdraw the PAP regime from the state since it was negatively impacting the growth of international tourism, investment, business engagement, cultural exchange and international partnerships in the state.
Tourism sector
Kovi Meyase, the state commissioner and tourism secretary, said PAP had impacted tourism in the state. “Yes, the re-imposition of the PAP regime has impacted tourism in Nagaland, particularly in terms of accessibility and the overall number of foreign tourist arrivals. Prior to its re-imposition, Nagaland attracted a diverse range of international visitors, including high-end tourists, organized tour groups, independent travelers and backpackers. The mandatory permit requirement, additional documentation, processing time and associated costs have discouraged some independent and budget-conscious travelers,” Meyase said.
The official said overall year-round foreign tourist arrivals have significantly declined following the re-imposition of PAP.
“The additional documentation, uncertainty surrounding the processing timelines and the need for advance coordination have made travel planning comparatively more complicated. This is particularly significant because Nagaland is often part of a larger Northeast India itinerary,” Meyase said.
He said international tour operators may reconsider including Nagaland if the permit process creates uncertainty for their clients.
Nagaland Tourism Association president Vimeto Vakha, agreed, calling PAP a procedural hassle that creates harassment to foreign tourists wanting to visit the state.
“People want to travel to Nagaland for tribal and cultural experiences. But when they are required to be put through the difficulty of extra documentation processes, they will definitely opt to visit other places where such hurdles are not required,” said Nino Zhasa, a Kohima-based tour operator.
Meyase suggested that the permit system could encourage more planned and organised travel, attracting visitors who are prepared to make advance arrangements and engage established accommodation and transport services. “The challenge is to strike a balance between national security considerations and the state’s tourism development objectives,” he added.

This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026
Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

NVIDIA has reinstated cofounder Jensen Huang as its president and chief executive officer (CEO). The reappointment comes 11 days after he resigned from the company amid reports of a foreign intelligence effort targeting him. In a statement today, the company informed that its board of directors unanimously approved the reinstatement, effective immediately, following a series of discussions and meetings with him. The board said it was satisfied with Huang's candour and ability to lead the company moving forward. Pertinent to mention that the company also took into account inputs from senior US government officials, based on which it felt confident that the reinstatement won’t pose any threat to the country’s security risk. The development reverses the leadership transition announced on November 12, when Huang resigned as president, CEO and a member of the board with immediate effect. Huang’s exit came after the revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which involved a woman accused of spying for China. In a letter written to NVIDIA employees, Huang apologised for the issue. Before the allegations of the third affair came to light, the company’s board met on November 12, and voted to oust Jensen Huang. At the time, Nvidia appointed its executive vice president and chief financial officer (CFO) Colette Kress as interim CEO. "Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in a post on November 17. Post his return, Kress will transition back to the role of CFO, while Harvey Jones will remain chair of the board. Nvidia said its board had formed a committee comprising only independent directors to investigate the matter. The committee has retained independent legal counsel, and the investigation will continue to its conclusion. Huang has agreed to cooperate with the probe. The company has also constituted a separate National Security and Export Control Committee, comprising independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. Additionally, NVIDIA is beginning a search for a chief compliance officer (CCO), who will oversee compliance across the company and report to its Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. The company said it would continue cooperating with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

Just as GTA 6 has left fans around the world amazed by its expansive world and detailed storyline, the upcoming game has also impressed industry professionals. Developers are reportedly in awe of the scale and technological advancements showcased by Rockstar Games' latest offering.
Cyberpunk 2 creative director Igor Sarzynski recently took to social media to share his apprehensions about releasing the next CD Projekt Red title in a world where GTA 6 has set such high expectations. Sarzynski jokingly announced that the game, currently codenamed Project Orion, had been cancelled.
Calling GTA 6 the 'single greatest artistic achievement', Sarzynski described its development as nothing short of a miracle. He also joked that the game's extraordinary scale had left developers such as himself struggling with 'depression'.
"GTA 6-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real. Probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history, I mean it. Scale, density, coherence, thoughtfulness of it all, just a technological and creative miracle," wrote Sarzynski in a post on BlueSky. He added: "Cyberpunk 2 is cancelled, imma go sweep autumn leaves in my backyard now."
Although Sarzynski used humour and exaggeration to express his admiration for GTA 6, he also acknowledged that the game's achievements could make other developers nervous about how their upcoming projects would be received.
However, he maintained that Cyberpunk 2 would offer something different rather than attempting to compete directly with Rockstar's latest title.
"Seriously though, I think we're doing something of our own, with a different unique flavour," he said. "GTA is impressive in a way all great art is: It expands what is possible, a captivating vision flawlessly executed."
Sarzynski is not the only gaming industry professional to have expressed amazement at GTA 6. Michael Barclay, world design director at Naughty Dog, has also shared his thoughts on the technological advancements demonstrated by the upcoming title.
Barclay, who has previously worked on acclaimed titles such as Uncharted and The Last of Us Part 2, used an unusual comparison to convey how significant the game's technological leap appeared to him.
"I've made video games for 19 years, and GTA VI appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child," Barclay wrote in a post on X (formerly Twitter).
GTA 6 has also generated remarkable commercial expectations. According to figures released by its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, the game recorded estimated worldwide retail sales of $3.79 billion (approximately ₹35,126 crore) within its first 24 hours of release.
The company said the estimate was based on worldwide sales and noted that 32.5 million units had been sold before launch, setting a new record across platforms.

(Bloomberg) -- The US Department of Health and Human Services launched a website hosting more than 92,000 documents including Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendars and agency correspondence during the Covid-19 pandemic, in what HHS called a push for greater transparency.
The documents span agencies across the health department and include records previously released under the Freedom of Information Act and other public documents, HHS said in a news release. The department will update the site as more documents are made public.
About a quarter of the documents on the new site have not been previously made public, a spokesperson for HHS said.
Though Kennedy has been a frequent and vocal critic of corporate influence in medicine and agriculture, his calendars show many meetings with business leaders in healthcare, food and other industries.
The calendars list a meeting with Eli Lilly & Co. Chief Executive Dave Ricks in April 2025, a pull-aside during a visit to Indiana when he also met with Governor Mike Braun. A separate entry for February 2026 shows a meeting with Novo Nordisk A/S. A May 2026 entry shows a call with George Yancopoulos of Regeneron Pharmaceuticals Inc.
A meeting with the CEO of Tylenol-maker Kenvue Inc. preceded the administration’s White House news conference in which President Donald Trump told pregnant women to avoid the painkiller, citing unproven theories of a link to autism. The meeting occurred three days after the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was expected to link the drug to autism.
Other entries show meetings with CEOs of infant formula makers, a roundtable with hospital executives and a session with insurance CEOs.
Kennedy, who has also criticized the food industry, met in March 2025 with Donnie King, CEO of Tyson Foods Inc. at the time. He has also met with leaders from Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc., Starbucks Corp, and In-N-Out Burgers.
Kennedy also met Stacey Kennedy, the US CEO of tobacco company Philip Morris International Inc., the listings show.
A June 2026 entry shows a meeting with SoftBank Group Chairman Masayoshi Son along with Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
Kennedy has had regular meetings with Louisiana Senator Bill Cassidy, a key vote for his confirmation.
Three Centuries
The documents appear to range from as early as 1840 (a handwritten catalog of the surgeon general’s library) through the first half of 2026. More than 10,000 records were from previous centuries, according to search results returned by the site.
The site is searchable and offers some initial “collections,” prominently featuring a batch of documents on Covid-19. Other collections include records on infant formula, the opioid crisis and several batches related to FOIA litigation.
Kennedy’s calendars show meetings with other cabinet officials and media appearances, including briefings on the ongoing measles outbreak starting in February 2025, when cases were increasing in Texas.
HHS said it’s also using artificial intelligence to process public records requests and propose redactions for trade secrets or other information subject to withholding. Thousands of documents have been requested under FOIA and the use of AI will allow quicker searches and reviews, the agency said.
The transparency website replaces an online reading room that previously aggregated records released under FOIA and other documents.
Last year, the Department of Government Efficiency led by Elon Musk cut thousands of staff across HHS, including in the FOIA departments, impairing the agency’s ability to respond to records requests quickly.
The Food and Drug Administration has previously published the agency’s response letters for new drug and biologic applications.

Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling
- Published
Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.
With the game goalless, Senegal left the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them. The match in Rabat was delayed by over 15 minutes before Morocco's Brahim Diaz had his spot-kick saved.
Senegal then triumphed 1-0 after extra time, with Pape Gueye scoring the winner.
That result was overturned almost two months later when a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board decreed the Teranga Lions had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play after the penalty was awarded.
Senegal's football federation (FSF) subsequently appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), sport's highest legal authority, with a three-man panel hearing its case behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.
In a unanimous verdict, the Cas panel has effectively backed the decision by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala to restart the game after Senegal returned to the field and the match was played to a conclusion. The result of the final stands and Senegal are now confirmed as Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) 2025 winners.
A statement issued by Cas said the court considered that "the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority".
"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume."
The FSF immediately reacted with a social media post featuring a picture of the side lifting the trophy in January captioned with the phrase "again and always champions of Africa".
"The FSF welcomes this ruling with deep satisfaction," it later said in a statement.
"This decision affirms, above all, the triumph of sporting fairness and reaffirms a fundamental principle: the true outcome of a match is determined exclusively on the field of play, under the protection of sports law."
Meanwhile, Morocco's football federation (FRMF) expressed "surprise" at the ruling and added that it would "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".
Caf says it respects the Cas award and "will take all the necessary measures to implement it".
The full grounds for the decision will be published by Cas in due course unless the parties request confidentiality.
- 'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Afcon 2025 final 
  - Published19 January
Senegal's walk-off during the final in Rabat has already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at a referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.
"This new rule will also apply to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Morocco and Senegal have both changed coach since the Afcon 2025 final and earlier this month secured their places at the 2027 edition of the tournament with two rounds of qualification remaining.
What happened in the Afcon final?
A tightly contested final between the continent's top-ranked sides produced two moments of controversy in second-half stoppage time, with referee Ndala at the centre of the drama.
First the Congolese official denied Senegal a near-certain goal, blowing his whistle for a challenge by Abdoulaye Seck on Morocco right-back Achraf Hakimi moments before Ismaila Sarr nodded in.
The free-kick looked soft, but the video assistant referee (VAR) was unable to get involved because Ndala had awarded the foul before the ball crossed the line.
Three minutes later came a flashpoint in the Senegal box, when El Hadji Malick Diouf tugged Morocco playmaker Diaz back before heading a corner clear.
Diaz vehemently claimed a penalty and Ndala eventually awarded a spot-kick after being sent to consult his pitchside monitor by the VAR.
Senegal coach Pape Thiaw called his players over to the touchline, and Thiaw subsequently headed down the tunnel to the changing room in protest against the decision - accompanied by several players.
They eventually returned, but over 15 minutes had elapsed since the award of the penalty by the time Real Madrid's Diaz failed to convert, with his Panenka-style attempt easily saved by goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Meanwhile, there was unrest inside the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium as a small contingent of Senegal supporters clashed with security staff.
The game went into extra time, with midfielder Gueye scoring the goal which settled the contest in Senegal's favour.
Off the pitch, another match involving disciplinary boards and lawyers would soon begin.
What was the fallout?
Senegal celebrated their second continental title but the FRMF quickly lodged an appeal with Caf, arguing their opponents had breached Article 82 of Afcon regulations, which covers withdrawals.
It states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".
A disciplinary board from the continental game's governing body rejected the FRMF's appeal days after the final as it sanctioned and fined those found guilty of unsporting conduct during the match.
Yet in March, almost two months on from the final, a Caf appeals board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.
The FSF described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and swiftly lodged its case with Cas.
The director general of the Switzerland-based court said arbitration proceedings would be conducted "as swiftly as possible", but it was over five months until all parties descended on Lausanne for a one-day hearing.
The Cas panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
Both the FRMF and FSF were able to nominate an arbitrator to exercise an independent judicial function once their appointment was confirmed.
The FRMF nominated Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli, while the FSF nominated Hamburg-based attorney and professor of law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas. Those two men completed the Cas panel.
Over six weeks on from that hearing - and 10 months since the Afcon 2025 final - Senegal have been proclaimed champions once again.
But the debate and damage done to the reputation of African football is likely to linger for some time yet.
The arguments and the 'field of play' doctrine
In its appeal, the FSF argued that the decision of referee Ndala to resume the match in the 19th minute of added time - and to allow it to be concluded with a sporting result - could not be reviewed, pursuant to the 'field of play' doctrine.
Cas has a long-standing practice where it refrains from "reviewing decisions taken on the playing field by referees for applying the rules of the game, unless there is evidence that those rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith".
The FRMF argued, on the contrary, that the referee's decision did not fall under the field of play doctrine because Senegal should have faced disciplinary consequences for walking off the pitch.
The Moroccan federation went on to argue that, according to Afcon tournament rules, the referee should have brought the match to an early conclusion.
It added that Ndala "erred in law" and that his decision was "arbitrary".
However, in the view of the panel, the referee's decisions were limited to the pitch and the relevant Afcon regulations regarding withdrawals were not applicable.
"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," the Cas statement added.
"However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary'. On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."
Is this decision final?
Despite Cas being the highest authority in sport, and its decision coming 10 months on from the final, there could yet be a further twist.
The FRMF raised a grievance with the process before the panel's judgement was announced on Tuesday.
It alleged that German attorney Haas, the arbitrator on the panel nominated by the Senegalese, held a telephone call with FSF president Abdoulaye Fall on Sunday.
Fall "categorically" denies that any such phone call ever took place.
The FRMF says that any unauthorised communication between a member of the panel and one of the interested parties would constitute a serious breach of Cas regulations.
It has demanded that "appropriate legal consequences be applied to actions that compromise the integrity and credibility of the arbitration process".
The Moroccans could appeal against the ruling by taking the case to the Swiss Federal Tribunal, and the country's highest court could set Cas' judgement aside.
The case would then likely be heard again at Cas, with a different panel in place.
A precedent would be the case of Chinese swimmer Sun Yang, who had an appeal against the decision by Cas to impose an eight-year doping ban upheld by the Swiss Federal Tribunal.
A new panel heard his case at Cas, and his ban was reduced to four years and three months.

As summer draws to a close, the theatrical release of Children of Blood and Bone draws nearer.
The film adaptation of Tomi Adeyemi’s YA fantasy is directed by Gina Prince-Bythewood, and it stars quite a stacked cast of actors and characters.
For everything we know about the Children of Blood and Bone movie, read on.
When will Gina Prince-Bythewood’s Children of Blood and Bone come out?

Russia backs tax rises as 2027 budget sees military spending soar
Russia’s lower house of parliament has approved a 2027-2029 state budget and passed tax increases to fund the war in Ukraine
Russia’s lower house of parliament approved a 2027-2029 state budget Tuesday and separately passed a series of tax increases to fund Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
The budget allocates approximately 17.15 trillion rubles ($208.9 billion) for national defense in 2027, up from the 12.93 trillion rubles ($157.5 billion) in 2026. The amount is also a marked increase from the 13.6 trillion rubles ($165.7 billion) forecast for expenditure in 2027 in last year’s budget.
The government seeks to help cover rising military costs with additional taxes on mining companies and income from citizens’ investments.
Deputies approved the bill with 396 votes in favor and 37 abstentions. It now goes to the Federation Council, Russia’s upper house of parliament, for approval.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has increasingly sought to squeeze tax revenue out of businesses and consumers to support his nearly five-year war in Ukraine, even as the country’s economy increasingly skews toward military spending at the expense of civilian needs.
Russia’s budget deficit has swelled beyond forecast this year because of heavy military spending and sluggish economic growth. The economy has also been strained by sanctions, high interest rates for nonmilitary companies, labor shortages and Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and export terminals.
Dmitry Kobylkin, head of the parliamentary faction for the ruling United Russia party, hailed the bill as a “victory budget,” writing in a statement that it included spending on national defense and care for veterans and their families, as well as state social support.
Additional funding for veterans' programs was added before the bill’s second reading, Russian state news agency Tass reported. The programs include Time of Heroes, a Kremlin-backed program that seeks to prepare former soldiers for careers in government.
Russia has previously implemented broad tax increases that proved unpopular among small businesses. The new hikes, part of the 2027-2029 budget bill, are more selective in scope, including a 20% to 30% windfall profits tax on mining companies that have benefited from rising prices in iron ore, nickel and gold.
Another measure imposes higher rates of 13% to 22% on income from interest, dividends and proceeds from selling property. Such income is currently taxed at 13% for amounts under 2.4 million rubles ($29,800) and 15% above that.
Other proposals taking effect Jan. 1 include a 100-ruble per parcel charge and a 22% value-added tax on online purchases of foreign goods worth less than 200 euros ($219), which are currently tax-exempt.
The changes will allow the Kremlin to raise more revenue from its domestic financial resources as sanctions continue to bar Moscow from international bond markets, foreign banks and investors.
Russia has enough financing to cover its budget deficit in 2027 and probably 2028, Chris Weafer, CEO of consultancy Macro-Advisory Ltd, told the Associated Press in October. “But that is at the expense of raising taxes, of increasing costs for households as well as businesses,” he said.
Weafer said that the Russian budget now prioritizes the military over normal economic development or infrastructure, creating an image of growth only by boosting state-linked defense industries.
On the streets of Moscow, most people linked rising taxes and other economic pressures to Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Homemaker Oksana Savitskaya said she believed the situation would worsen until the end of the “special military operation,” the Kremlin’s preferred term for the invasion.
“It seems to me that the economic instability right now and the rise in taxes is bad for development, for small businesses, for example. It’s bad for the everyday person,” she said.
Retired journalist Boris Khizhnyak said that Russia’s economic situation in the upcoming year would be “complicated.”
“You know that we have a “special military operation” underway, and that first and foremost will bring economic adjustments,” he said.

Akhilesh asks Congress to send list of winnable seats beyond 26 discussed, urges to fight UP polls as INDIA bloc
The SP chief said discussions between senior leaders should focus on candidates representing the INDIA bloc rather than individual parties.
Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, in a lengthy post on X, reached out to Congress leaders, urging them to jointly choose candidates as INDIA bloc nominees rather than as representatives of two separate parties while discussing seat-sharing for the 2027 UP elections.
He said the common objective of both parties should be to oust the BJP from power, adding that changing circumstances and political equations would require both allies to adjust and accommodate certain candidates to achieve this goal.
