Suresh Mittal is 87. According to Uttar Pradesh’s latest draft electoral roll, his father, Vansh Mittal, is 23. Both are registered at house number 869 in booth 111 of the Dholana constituency in Hapur. The same roll lists Vansh as the son of Ajay, a 56-year-old in the same house.
Suresh is not an exception. Alt News found 1,10,875 voters in the Special Summary Revision (SSR) draft roll whose father or mother, registered in the same booth and the same house, is recorded as the same age as them or younger. The draft was published on November 17.
A Year of Revisions: First SIR, Now SSR
The draft comes at the end of a long year for UP’s voter list. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the rolls began on October 27, 2025 and ended with the final roll on April 10, 2026. In those 166 days the state’s electorate shrank from 15.44 crore to 13.39 crore.
As per the process of SIR, every voter was supposed to be issued an enumeration form, which was supposed to be collected by booth-level officers (BLOs). The Election Commission’s software then allegedly went through the data looking for what it called logical discrepancies. One of these was a parent less than 15 years older than the voter. About 2.22 crore voters in UP were sent notices for such discrepancies, and the Commission says hearings were completed on all of them.
On October 15, six months after the SIR’s final roll, the Election Commission ordered a Special Summary Revision (SSR) in 17 states and Union territories, including UP. The SSR draft roll, which merges the SIR roll with all supplementary lists, has 13.58 crore electors. Claims and objections can be filed till December 16, and the final roll is due on January 4, 2027.
What We Found and How
The SSR draft rolls are machine readable. We took every voter whose entry names a father or a mother, and looked in the same booth for a voter with that name living in the same house. If that ‘parent’ turned out to be the same age as the voter, or younger, we flagged the entry.
We found 1,10,875 such cases spread across all 75 districts and 403 constituencies.
In 35,523 of these cases, parent and child are the same age. In the other 75,352, the parent is younger, and in 6,860 of them by 20 years or more.
Some of the cases are shown below for representation:
What did SIR Actually Achieve?
The SIR was designed to weed out exactly this kind of error. It had enumeration forms, BLO visits, software flags and hearings. A parent who is younger than their own child is perhaps the most basic inconsistency a voter list can have. This raises a larger question: if a process this elaborate left the most basic errors untouched, what did the SIR actually achieve?
Moreover, spotting these anomalous entries is no rocket science. Each one is a contradiction between two lines of the same booth’s roll, often on the same page: An 87-year-old whose father is 23, a 123-year-old woman whose mother is 45, two women who are each other’s mother. A simple check on the roll itself would have thrown them up. Either no such check was run, or nobody acted on what it found.
As of now, all 1,10,875 are in the draft, and the window for corrections closes on December 16.
The district-wise and constituency-wise count of such cases is given below. Kushinagar district has the most cases (3,646), and Fazilnagar has the most for a single assembly constituency (711).
Skip to PDF content
In a related report published on November 21, Alt News showed several glaring anomalies that the final SIR list for Uttar Pradesh had, including at least 230 voters listed multiple times across 69 booths, missing addresses, unexplained name and gender changes, and suspicious deletions. The report can be read here.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

MEERUT: A 24-year-old woman allegedly escaped from a hotel room in Meerut on Tuesday but was caught by her former boyfriend, who tried to drag her back. The incident, which took place in the busy Abu Lane market, was captured on CCTV.
The accused, identified as Mohd Salman, allegedly chased the woman, caught hold of her and attempted to take her back to the hotel. He fled across the rooftop after police reached the spot following alerts from passersby.
According to police, the woman, a resident of Vasundhara in Ghaziabad, had known Salman, a resident of Jainpur village in Meerut's Rohta area, for around two-and-a-half years. The two were previously in a relationship. Her family has recently arranged her marriage elsewhere.
The woman told police that she had visited a friend in Mohkampur on Monday. While she was returning to Ghaziabad later that night, Salman allegedly took her to a hotel on Abu Lane, assaulted her and confined her to a room overnight. He also snatched her phone, which he returned later, she alleged.
In her FIR, registered on Tuesday night, the woman stated: "Salman was my boyfriend a year ago. 
On Monday, I came to meet a friend in Mohkampur. While I was returning to Ghaziabad at night, Salman took me from my friend's place to a hotel, thrashed me and confined me there. He even snatched away my phone, though he returned it later. I escaped on Tuesday afternoon, but he caught hold of me, threatened me and then fled."
Salman has been booked under sections 115(2), 127(2) and 351(3) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), relating to voluntarily causing hurt, wrongful confinement and criminal intimidation.
"A man and a woman had checked into a hotel. Following an argument, violence broke out between them. The woman told us that she had known the youth for the past two-and-a-half years and clarified that she had not been abducted. Teams have been constituted based on her complaint, and strict action will be taken against the accused," said Circle Officer (Sadar) Sanjay Gupta.
Police have sealed the hotel and formed two teams, including the SWAT unit, to conduct raids and apprehend Salman.

Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.
The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.
Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.
The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".
Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."
"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.
The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.
French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.
In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.
"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.
Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.
French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".
"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.
Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".
Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.
Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.
After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.
Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.

Virginia reported its first measles-associated death of 2026 on Friday, November 20, 2026, involving a child who tested positive for measles, the state health department said.
The department said the child was between 0 and 4 years old. It did not disclose additional details, including the child's vaccination status, citing the family's privacy.
Measles can cause serious complications, including pneumonia, brain inflammation, complications during pregnancy and death.
Virginia has reported 220 measles cases so far in 2026, including 40 among children aged 0 to 4 and 75 among those aged 5 to 12, state health department data showed as of November 19. Of those cases, 179 were in unvaccinated individuals, 39 were in people whose vaccination status was unknown and two were in vaccinated individuals.
Virginia health officials have reported increased measles activity driven largely by outbreaks in central region. Buckingham County has reported 127 cases, the highest in the state, while neighbouring Charlotte County has recorded 34 cases.
The death adds to a worsening national measles outbreak that this week cost the United States its measles elimination status after 26 years.
Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit U.S. state, reported an eighth measles-related death and confirmed 1,631 measles cases, as of November 20. Wisconsin has also reported two deaths, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated death, involving a child.
The CDC has confirmed six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not specify the states where the deaths were recorded.
A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after the CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.
The sharp increase in U.S. measles cases has coincided with declining immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under Kennedy, who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines.

A jury has found Huawei guilty of stealing US trade secrets, as reported earlier by NBC News and Bloomberg. The verdict, handed down in a federal court in New York, concludes a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of stealing source code and proprietary technology from several companies, including T-Mobile, Cisco, and Motorola.
Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets
The Chinese telecom giant was also found guilty of bank fraud.
The Department of Justice’s 2018 criminal indictment against Huawei came to light following the arrest of the company’s CFO, Wanzhou Meng, whom the agency accused of fraud. Though the indictment against Meng was eventually dismissed, she admitted to misleading banks over Huawei’s operations in Iran as part of a deferred prosecution agreement. The US government blacklisted Huawei in 2019 over national security concerns.
In total, the jury found Huawei guilty of 10 of 12 criminal counts, including money laundering, violating US sanctions, bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to defraud the US. The company was acquitted of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. Huawei’s sentencing is set for September 14th, 2027, where it may face “financial penalties including criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution,” according to the DOJ.
“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception,” Tysen A. Duva, the assistant attorney general of the DOJ’s criminal division, says in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.”
In a statement to NBC News, a Huawei spokesperson said the charges are “without legal or factual merit” and that it plans to appeal the decision. Huawei didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

An experimental monoclonal antibody showed 70% to 90% protection against symptomatic Covid-19, Invivyd, a small biotech firm, said Monday.
The result, from a 2,359-volunteer clinical trial called DECLARATION, included three arms: a single 250-mg dose of the antibody, VYD2311; monthly doses of VYD2311; or a saline placebo. Results were released by press release. Invivyd said that it plans to file for accelerated approval for VYD2311 for preventing symptomatic Covid.
During the pandemic, monoclonal antibodies were employed both as treatments and preventatives for Covid. The technology, however, fell into disuse as the market shrank and people gained protection against the infection. Still, Covid causes tens of thousands of deaths in the U.S., and Invivyd executives argued that there is a need for a monoclonal antibody. Moreover, they say, for some patients the monoclonal could be more effective than existing Covid vaccines. Covid vaccines reduced symptomatic infection by about 30%.
“Clinically, I really do believe that most Americans who are interested in using a pharmacological agent to protect themselves from Covid would probably move over to a monoclonal if given the option,” said Michael Mina, the former Harvard University infectious disease expert who is Invivyd’s chief medical officer. “And I think we’re going to aim to have volumes that can accommodate that over the coming couple of years.”

In November, Robert Pattinson was announced as the seventh actor hired to play the titular British assassin and spy, James Bond. Pattinson, who is 40 years old, is older than some of the other actors who have played the role before.
A popular meme on Instagram captured all the previous Bond actors and the purported ages they were hired to play Bond:
Sean Connery: 31, cast in 1961 (Dr. No)
George Lazenby: 29, cast in 1968 (On Her Majesty's Secret Service)
Roger Moore: 44, cast in 1972 (Live and Let Die)
Timothy Dalton: 42, cast in 1986 (The Living Daylights)
Pierce Brosnan: 41, cast in 1994 (GoldenEye)
Daniel Craig: 37, cast in 2005 (Casino Royale)
Robert Pattinson: 40, cast in 2026 (Bond 26)
(Instagram user "thefilmthusiasts")
The meme is largely accurate, notwithstanding conflicting accounts about Dalton's exact age when he got the part. Below, we break down the ages of each actor cast to play Bond.
Sean Connery, according to "James Bond, Dr. No" a book about the making of the first Bond film, was cast in 1961 and the movie came out in 1962. Connery, who was born in 1930, was 31 years old at the time of his casting.
George Lazenby, an Australian actor, played Bond only once, in the 1969 film "On Her Majesty's Secret Service." Lazenby was born in 1939. In 1968, newspapers announced he was cast as the new Bond. He would have been 29 years old at the time, and 30 years old when the movie was released.
Roger Moore was born on Oct. 14, 1927. His first Bond film was the 1973 film "Live and Let Die." Moore was announced as the new Bond at the Dorchester Hotel in London on Aug. 2, 1972. He was 44 years old, just a few months shy of turning 45.
Timothy Dalton first played the role in 1987's "The Living Daylights" and was announced as the next Bond on Aug. 7, 1986, according to Reuters. If we go by the date of birth given on his IMDb page, March 21, 1946, Dalton was 40 years old when cast. If we go by the age stated in the Reuters announcement, he was 38 years old when cast and 39 when the film was released. In an interview on the official website for the Bond films, 007.com, Dalton said he was first approached for the role (which he turned down at that time) in 1968, when he was only "about 25 years old," which would make his year of birth 1943, while IMDb lists it as 1946. Dalton, who was much older when he gave the interview to 007.com, may have misremembered at what age he was first approached.
Pierce Brosnan was announced as Bond on June 8, 1994. He was born on May 16, 1953, making him 41 years old when he was cast.
Daniel Craig was announced as Bond in October 2005 and "Casino Royale" was released in November 2006. Craig was 37 years old when cast. He was born on March 2, 1968.
Robert Pattinson was born on May 13, 1986, making him 40 years old when cast.
In sum, while the meme is mostly accurate, there are conflicting accounts about Dalton's exact age when he was hired to play Bond.
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous rumors about Bond and the actors who have played the character, including the true claim that Connery condoned slapping women and a fake Bond movie trailer.

Early backer and hedge fund Steadview Capital has sold 1.27 Cr shares of omnichannel eyewear giant Lenskart via multiple block deals for ₹920.6 Cr. As per NSE data, Steadview Capital, via two funds - Steadview Capital Mauritius Ltd and LTR Focus Fund, sold the shares at ₹725 apiece to rake in the amount. The shares that flooded the market were lapped up by Goldman Sachs and Societe Generale. While Goldman Sachs, via two affiliates, picked up 65.2 Lakh shares for a sum of ₹472.8 Cr, Societe Generale bought the remaining 61.8 Lakh shares for ₹447.8 Cr. Steadview Capital Mauritius Ltd held a 3.31% stake, or 5.8 Cr shares, in the eyewear giant at the end of September 2026. With the latest block deals, the hedge fund has offloaded nearly a fifth (22% to be precise) of its shareholding in Lenskart. The latest move adds to a series of stake sales by Lenskart’s early investors in recent months. Just last month, Alpha Wave Ventures sold Lenskart shares worth ₹1,704.8 Cr. Prior to this in August, the VC firm also offloaded 2.94 Cr shares of the omnichannel eyewear giant in multiple block deals for ₹1,856.8 Cr. Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) also sold Lenskart shares worth ₹2,390.6 Cr in September, while SoftBank offloaded 4.5 Cr shares of the eyewear giant, worth ₹2,887.9 Cr, in August. An extended bull run for the stock has provided a fertile ground for investors to cash in. The company’s stock touched an all-time high of ₹767.40 on November 5, and has zoomed over 58.5% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. This surge has come on the back of robust financial performance. Lenskart saw its consolidated net profit zoom 124.7% to ₹232.5 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) compared to ₹103.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue also rose 35.7% to ₹2,845 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹2,096.1 Cr in Q2 FY26.

Cops flee, doors shut as man goes on stabbing spree at Delhi police station; CCTV captures horror
The footage shows cops fleeing and trying to overpower Mohd Nabeel as he stabbed five personnel inside Jama Masjid police station before injuring four more.
As a 30-year-old man went on a stabbing spree at the Jama Masjid police station on Monday, CCTV footage of the incident seen by HT captured the pandemonium – several cops running for cover as the knife-wielding attacker walked around the police station, others trying to shut doors to lock him inside, and a handful attempting to subdue him with sticks, all in vain. Throughout, the video shows, the knifeman continuously swung his weapon, stabbing anyone within reach.
The shocking incident took place on Monday when the man, identified by police as Mohd Nabeel, wounded nine police officers – five at the police station and four during an encounter where he was shot six times. He then stole a two-wheeler at knifepoint but was caught two hours later. Police fired eight rounds at him, six of which hit his legs. They said they fired after he injured four more personnel at Chitli Qabar.
According to police officers, Nabeel was summoned to the police station after his mother and sister complained about his aggressive behaviour. He was aggressive from the moment he arrived and, without provocation, attacked the officer he thought had phoned him.
Deep Dive
Nabeel has been ordered to judicial custody by court. He will lodged in custody after treatment.
On Tuesday, HT saw parts of the footage showing the accused entering the police station and heading straight towards two personnel, including a female official sitting on chairs. The footage shows the man apparently shouting.
“When the female official identified herself and the sub-inspector next to her, the man got angry and charged at sub-inspector Aravind,” a senior officer part of the investigation said.
The footage shows the man slashing Aravind’s neck and face. As soon as he attacked the SI, the female official screamed while Nabeel’s mother and sister – sitting in the same room – ducked under a desk. A second officer then arrived and tried to confront Nabeel. The SI is stabbed in his neck and arm and and he goes to hide himself in a corner.
By this time, panic broke out inside the police station.
At least three personnel were seen running for cover. Nabeel then moved towards a room and tried to force his way inside, but personnel shut the door. He then walked near the lock-up area, where panicked cops tried to pick up weapons.
Three cops attacked him with sticks in an attempt to subdue him, but he slashed away, stabbing two of them. One was identified as head-constable Harender, who suffered injuries on his face, neck, and chest.
Another policeman, a head-constable in his 50s, tried to shut the main door but Nabeel pushed it and kicked it, causing him to fall. Another policeman followed with a stick, but Nabeel stabbed the fifth cop. He walks out of the station in front of an armed sentry.
The incident took place around 2:30 pm. Nabeel then went outside and snatched a two-wheeler at knifepoint.
“It all happened in five minutes. Even when this was happening, his mother and sister were inside the station. They then left. Since they had only interacted with SI Ajay, who was also injured, nobody knew who Nabeel was and why he had come. Amid the panic, all five policemen were rushed to a nearby hospital. After 15-20 minutes, Ajay said two women had come to complain about Nabeel. We then traced the women, took details and photos, and started a probe,” a senior officer said.

DCP (Central) Rohit Rajbir Singh said the team managed to catch him within two hours. “There was no time to scan footage and analyse technical information. We had seen his photo and forwarded it to informers and public persons. People on the street outside the station helped trace the route.”
DCP Singh said the injured – SI Ajay, SI Aravind, and HC Harender – suffered 2-3-inch-deep injuries on their faces, neck, chest, and arms. “They will undergo plastic surgery as well as critical surgery for damaged arteries. I tend to favor devices that let technology do much of the work and don't make you join a cult of engineers before your first cup. Frequently Asked Questions
How Do I Test Espresso Machines?
Over the past decade, WIRED has tested dozens of espresso makers to find our favorites. The process, in part, is simple. We brew a whole lot of coffee. I’ve written about coffee for more than a decade on both the East and West Coasts, including my hometown coffee mecca of Portland, Oregon. Other current and past WIRED espresso testers—who include former baristas and longtime coffee writers—include Jaina Grey, Jeffrey Van Camp, Kat Merck, Tyler Shane, Pete Cottell, and Scott Gilbertson.
On each machine that’s capable, I make and assess at least four styles of drink, on multiple roasts and beans: a basic 2:1 espresso, an Americano, a latte, and a cappuccino. On machines that advertise a wacky array of drinks, I test each one. This includes any newfangled coldspresso and head-scratching variations on a “long.” It also includes, if science dictates, espresso martinis. And I test to see whether a machine can be dialed to both dark roasts and lighter roasts.
I might make many dozens of coffees to dial in a machine and truly understand it, and on any of my top picks I've made at least fifty drinks. Sometimes, alas, you understand a machine’s shortcomings far sooner—and so some of our less-recommended devices are dismissed a bit earlier.
What I’m looking for is nuance, aromatics, beauty, sensitivity to the characteristics of each bean, and the satisfying texture of fully integrated milk. But also, I’m looking for ease, the thoughtful touches that make an espresso maker something you can fall in love with.
I test whether the hot water spout splatters, whether descaling requires a degree in hydrology, whether the brewing temperature is consistent, and whether the latte milk gets silked. I’m truly terrible at latte art, but whether it’s possible is a straightforward test of the body of the frothed milk. I test the airier foam of cappuccinos and compare manual and automatic milk frothing on machines that try to froth milk for you. I test how fast the wand steams and whether it’s easy to fully integrate milk before the dang thing starts to burn your milk.
On machines with built-in grinders, I both assess the grind and weigh the dose—and then weigh it again. And then again. Consistency is the hobgoblin of little cups. I also test multiple grind settings to make sure the grind is consistent.
On any semiautomatic machine that decides the shot size for you, I test this to see whether you're getting a ristretto or a lungo by default. Then I resolve never to say the word “lungo” again.
I don’t generally take apart the machines I’m sent, but I do quite often look up videos of people who do—and look at how the thing’s constructed under the hood.
How I Select Espresso Machines to Review
In part, we select machines to test by looking at the espresso makers with long track records of making good espresso machines—people with long tails in the industry and good track records of customer support. Names like Breville, De'Longhi, La Marzocco, and Rancilio. But also, I listen. I read. I ask every coffee-obsessive in my life. I pay attention to the newest releases, follow trade shows, watch Youtube videos, and spend a lot of time tracking down not just the obious big names but the unexpected recommendations.
I often also look at how accessible each machine will be to most users. Espresso isn’t just a finicky process: It’s finicky by design. The most sensitive and sophisticated traditional machines are responsive to every tiny variation in the coffee grind and every fluctuation in the water temperature. The deepest bean geeks want this: They want the control, the frustration, the vision quest.
But I also know that most of you out there aren’t looking to be in an abusive relationship with your coffee machine. Few want to wake up to feelings of inadequacy, brought on by a machine that costs as much as a used car. And so what I look for is the espresso machines that can pull lovely character from each bean, but also make this easy on you.
This means that our top picks, the ones I recommend to most people, tend to fall in the semiautomatic camp: They’re the ones that offer the best coffee with the least effort. Finding this balance is delicate and often rewarding. It used to be that a built-in grinder was a recipe for blown shots, sadness, or pressurized portafilters with less character. But year by year, espresso machine makers get better at this goal.
The lowest-cost machines I recommend tend to offer more forgiving pressurized filter baskets as options, even though these sacrifice a bit of nuance for forgiveness, because I don’t want to assume you’re pairing a $200 espresso machine with a $2,000 coffee grinder. Although I know some of you do this, especially with our beloved Breville Bambino.
But hey, if you’re a tinkerer for life, and want to join modding groups? We recommend a machine for you, too. Mostly so you can disagree on Reddit, and explain why your favorite is better.
What Beans Are Best for Espresso?
First off, there's no such thing as “espresso beans,” whatever it says on the bag you buy. Espresso beans are coffee beans, ground finely enough to be pressed into service as espresso.
But traditionally, espresso is made with darker-roast beans that best elicit the deep, chocolatey notes of classic Italian espresso. In fact, most machines you use are probably designed with dark-roast beans in mind: Darker beans grind easier, extract easier, and are a bit more homogeneous across the market. And so when someone writes “espresso roast” or “espresso blend” on their grind, that's often what they mean.
Does that mean dark roast is the only espresso? Of course not. Modern craft and premium coffee roasters in the United States have begun trending toward medium and medium-dark roasts that offer a bit more balance, character, and even a little acidity—beans that have more aromatics, and more individuality. Some, including me, love experimenting with truly light roasts, including the lightest of natural-processed beans that let me brew up espresso that tastes like strawberries.
It's up to you. But note that the lighter the roast, the more you'll need to adjust grind and temperature to accommodate—and sometimes even go off-script entirely. (See here for an explainer on light-roast espresso.) But the classic recommendations for espresso? Pulling a 25- to 30-second shot, at a steady 9 bars of pressure, at a 2:1 ratio for a standard shot? These were all designed for traditional dark-roast beans.
One thing that's true, however, is that you should use fresh beans. They'll taste better and more aromatic, sure. But stale beans exposed to oxygen also make it technically difficult to make good espresso: they've begun to break down, often allow channeling, and are more likely to lead to a less evenly extracted shot with funny off-flavors.
Obviously, fresh beans are easiest to obtain from a local roaster, and on the plus side you'll be able to ask the baristas there how best to make espresso from their beans. But when in doubt in a supermarket, look for a roast date on the bag. If you can't find it, or if your beans were roasted in Italy and sent on a ship? Chances are they're not fresh. And your espresso will be worse. For fresh beans delivered to your house, check out WIRED's guide to the best coffee subscriptions.
Espresso Accessories That Make for Great Cups
If you're spending this much on an espresso machine, you'll want to invest in a good grinder and even a scale, as well as a few other devices that make your shots better, and your life a little easier.
An espresso-capable grinder: If your espresso machine doesn't come with a grinder, you'll need one. Preground bag beans are especially difficult to use when making espresso, and will likely lead to off-flavors or channeling. But not just any grinder will do. You'll need a good grinder that can grind consistent beans finely enough for espresso. WIRED's top-pick Baratza Encore ESP is always a good choice—positioned squarely at the fulcrum where more expensive grinders begin to offer diminishing returns.
An accurate scale with a timer: Most grinders, and a goodly portion of espresso machines, do not offer a precise scale. But a precise scale is what you need to get espresso ratios right. WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu loved the Acaia brew-by-weight scale ($400) that automatically connects to the La Marzocco Linea Mini and a few other devices via its companion app. But a far less sophisticated scale can still help you measure your shot size and control the dose you want on each espresso shot. If you're not precious about beauty, there's always this low-cost, little no-name scale. It's accurate to a 10th of a gram, and has a timer to boot.
The best knockbox: When you're done with that portafilter filled with coffee grounds, what do you do with it? Beat it against the side of a trashcan? Dig out those grounds into the sink? Nah. You need a good knock box. And somehow this jobby-job from Breville is the best one I've ever found. It's sturdy, the cross bar is in the right spot so that the grinds dump cleanly into the bin, and the bottom has enough grip that the box doesn't scoot around on the counter. Simplicity is competence.
Not all steaming pitchers are created equal, notes WIRED contributing reviewer (and former barista) Pete Cottell. As opposed to the sad piece of aluminum that probably came with your espresso maker, this Brewista offers thick walls for heat retention, a precision tip for expert latte pours, and a thermometer sticker on its side so you can get a rough gauge of milk temperature without hunting down an actual thermometer. It can also take a beating. This is your new frothing pitcher.
Other Machines We Like
Breville Oracle Jet for $2,000: The Breville Oracle Jet is my previous top pick for threading that delicate needle between ease and deliciousness, before getting displaced by my new top-pick Fellow device. The Oracle Jet remains a powerful and frankly beautiful stainless-steel machine, with sterling temperature control and a solid built-in grinder that uses the same conical burrs as the excellent Baratza Encore ESP ($200). This Oracle Jet will pull beautiful nuances from beans ranging from berry-light to chocolate dark, on drinks ranging from an Americano to a flat white to “cold espresso” best placed in a martini. And yet the Jet's easily accessible for anyone who can figure out an iPhone, with a touchscreen tutorial, digital guidance on finding the right grind for each bean, and automatic tamping and steaming. You'll be nose-deep in a cappuccino within 20 minutes of pulling this thing out of the box. Note that manual milk steaming with the Jet's powerful wand is still better than the automatic version.
Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro for $750: Tradition is the opposite of what Ninja does. This is the company that made the soft-serve Swirl, the Slushi, and the portable air fryer. Ninja is all about the extras. And Ninja doesn't judge. And so of course Ninja jumped in with both feet on cold-foam coldspresso. In fact, the new Luxe Cafe Pro makes the best cold foam out of any espresso machine I've tried, with a whisk that whips up plant milk or cow milk into thick, creamy, dense, beautiful froth—ready for your ridiculously complicated cold caramel-vanilla latte TikTok recipe. What I didn't expect was that Ninja would also nail the fundamentals so well, on only its second entry into the espresso market. The relatively accurate by-weight dosing is nice. So is the excellent steam wand that also outpaces most contenders on automatic hot foaming, adjustable to multiple densities of foam. The Pro clears up some oversights in the previous-model Premier, including an easy tamping lever, and a hot water spout. Maintenance, whether descaling or purging, is also as easy as it gets. Just don't use this grinder with light roast beans. Medium or dark only.
Breville Oracle Dual Boiler for $3,000: This update to the previous Breville Dual Boiler espresso machine is a powerful, truly impressive machine in many regards. It combines the easy touchscreen operation and automatic dosing and tamping of WIRED's previous top-pick Oracle Jet with a welcome “manual” mode that lets you play with pre-infusion and bloom while monitoring a digital pressure gauge on the touchscreen. I kinda love this as an exercise in future-retro design—or whatever the inverse of steampunk is—but also as a means of really controlling my shot, and getting a lot more crema and body out of it. The dual boiler heats up very fast—like four minutes fast—and gives you the wonderful temperature stability and consistency you expect from a dual boiler, plus the ability to steam milk and make espresso simultaneously. The production model I received had a very tight portafilter fit, which loosened up after the first 30 shots or so but initially required some muscle. I also haven't been able to get good results with lighter-roast beans, which led to the occasional under-filled portafilter that had to be retamped manually. We'll update as we resolve those quirks, but can attest that for medium to dark beans, this Dual Boiler is an absolute beast.
Meraki Espresso Machine for $1,999: Meraki is a young Hong Kong–based company. Last year, it was still Kickstarting funds for its debut Meraki Espresso Machine. But the company started off with a bang, with a premium semiautomatic double-boiler machine offering features you don't find even in machines that cost hundreds more. This means a Timemore grinder that'll grind by weight within two-tenths of a gram precision. PID temperature control. Easy pre-infusion. A quiet rotary pump. Another scale under the brewer that lets you control output. A powerful steam wand that regulates the temperature of froth within about 3 degrees for whatever milk drinks strike your fancy. A tamper with satisfying heft, and a tamping station that feels like luxury. Frankly, despite having to overrotate the portafilter for proper fit, its wondrous aesthetics and ease made it a contender for our top picks. But service is always a worry among newer, direct-to-consumer entrants, and the wackily complicated descaling procedure makes maintenance a concern.
Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier for $600: Ninja has already released an upgraded Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro version ($750) after its espresso machine debut. But its first device, the Luxe Cafe Premier, is already a corker, a low-priced all-in-one with cold brew, coffee, espresso, excellent milk frothing, and unexpected luxury features like a built-in scale so the grinder can dose by weight. The device can feel either overstuffed or generous, depending on who you are. Either way this damn near unseated the Breville Barista Express as WIRED's mid-tier top pick, aside from a few leaks and sensible caution about its durability.
De'Longhi La Specialista Opera for $900: Speaking of espresso makers that came running at Breville, this Opera is a beautifully forgiving semiautomatic machine that makes excellent espresso in the medium- to dark-roast range, with non-pressurized portafilter baskets that make for a nice and surprisingly subtle cup. It's the best De'Longhi espresso machine I've tested, in many ways, among the semiautomatic camp. The Opera sports a lot of options—including dose and temperature control—while remaining refreshingly analog with its satisfying metal frame, metal buttons, and prominent pressure gauge. Cold brew is a perk for those who like milk. The grinder is decent, though its 15 settings might not offer enough sensitivity to pull the best from each roast. One could wish for a removable hopper and a sturdier tamping lever. But if you or your partner love cold coffee drinks or espresso martinis, this gives comparable Brevilles a strong run for the money.
De'Longhi La Specialista Touch for $1,000: De'Longhi's new Touch, released this year, isn't merely a touchscreen version of the very analog Opera—though it is just as handsome as the Opera. Instead, it offers a very specific set of trade-offs. Like De'Longhi's Rivelia, there's a bean-assist function that you can save for each bean you like. It's also got a better steam wand, with the ability to read the temperature of the milk you're steaming, as you steam it. In fact, it's maybe more intuitive overall. But it doesn't quite offer the easy customization on temperature, shot time, or ratios. The cold brew is not quite as well-dialed as the Opera. The Touch is an Italian machine on training wheels, designed for Italian-style medium to dark shots. This should work for most people, but minus a pressure bar or a shot timer, it can also feel like a bit of a black box.
La Marzocco Linea Mini for $6,600: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu spent two weeks with La Marzocco's Linea Mini, a home version of the fancy espresso machines you'll see in coffee shops around the world. The price may be eye-searing, but Chokkattu did find the resulting elixir to be absolutely fantastic—and the same went for La Marzocco's customer service while Chokkattu was dialing in his machine. It offers a lot of room for experimentation, and sports a killer cool-touch steam wand that froths milk in seconds.
De'Longhi Stilosa for $150: The Stilosa was our top budget pick for years. It's still a good budget pick, and it often goes on sale for less than $100. You're not going to get high-end features like a pressure gauge or built-in grinder, and it's a little plasticky. But what the Stilosa does provide is everything you need to make great espresso at home: a solid portafilter, a reliable steam pump, and a steaming wand. It is a little light, so you'll want to brace it when you mount and dismount the portafilter (or it might slide around on you). After brewing cup after cup of espresso, the Stilosa never showed signs of slowing or breaking down the way many inexpensive machines can. In fact, we're now revisiting the Stilosa as our budget pick, after catching a few tips on how to use the Stilosa for light roast espresso.
Breville Barista Express Impress for $800: This espresso machine is the more tricked-out sibling of the Breville Barista Express. It includes more grind and dosing settings and automates some of the more complicated parts of brewing consistently good espresso, like getting just the right amount of beans ground per shot.
Breville Dual Boiler for $1,600: The previous-generation Breville Dual Boiler is an absolute tank of an espresso machine. It's huge. It's heavy. It makes amazing espresso. But while its size makes brewing espresso feel luxurious, it does eat up a lot of space and needs a little time to heat up, versus newer Brevilles like the Oracle Jet that favor thermoblock-style heaters. But a dual boiler does mean you can brew shot after shot, with steamed milk and hot water at the same time, without having to wait in between shots. The new Breville Oracle Dual Boiler ($3,000) is already on the market, but you can still pick up the previous generation for half the price.
Cuisinart EM-160 Slim for $250: The lowest-cost espresso maker from Cuisinart's new espresso line is among the slimmer espresso machines out there, less than 7 inches across. This makes it a treasure for certain kitchens. The espresso quality is about what you'd expect from a pressurized portafilter: smoother, less nuanced, but also pretty forgiving for beginners trying to dial in a bean. This'll be best for those who mix milk with their espresso. Same goes for the fast-dripped “cold espresso” option, which takes a couple minutes to complete and comes out a bit tannic, but mixes well with cold milk or a lot of ice. You'll need a grinder if you don't want sad supermarket beans.
Superkop Manual Espresso Maker for $600: This manual espresso machine is technically not a Jackie Chan movie. The Superkop is instead a quite finely engineered espresso device. It looks pretty, and unlike other manual espresso machines, you don't need a strong arm to use it. So if you want to pull espresso, but not pull it hard, the Superkop is your huckleberry. That said, $600 is a lot of money for a manual device. Buy it if you know you'll love it.
Also Tried
Gevi Espresso Machine With Grinder and Milk Frother for $350: WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell prized the pressure control and built-in grinder on this Gevi espresso machine, when you take into account the near-unfathomable low price for a machine with this functionality. Alas, a somewhat erratic steam wand makes it hard to recommend.
Cuisinart EM-640 Espresso Bar for $650: Cuisinart rolled in with some ambition on this semiautomatic espresso machine, with a built-in grinder and a non-pressurized, bottomless portafilter meant to play in the same sandbox as Breville's top devices. Alas, I really couldn't get consistency on either dosing or grinding from the device's built-in grinder—and the system for customizing the dose in particular was mostly wild guesswork. This all added up to botched shots, wild spray from the portafilter, and none of the ease one wants from a semiautomatic.
De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $675: This semiautomatic De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo comes with a built-in burr grinder makes great espresso right out of the box, and is slimmer than other espresso machines in its category, It does have quirks: It includes a little plastic adapter needed to attach the portafilter to the grinder spout, and a little stepstool for your espresso cup to keep the coffee from splashing. It's a good machine, but I'd upgrade to the Opera any day of the week.

Every time I called my cousin Arun* around 9 a.m., his voice would echo, as though he were in a bathroom. “I’m on the throne, I’ll call you in 20 minutes,” he would say. The first time I heard this, it took me a while to understand what ‘the throne’ was, and as if that was not confusing enough, what was he doing there for 20 minutes. Perplexed, I asked him why he had the phone in the bathroom when he was doing his morning business, to which he casually replied that he would sit on the throne solving Wordle, crosswords and reading the news until he ‘downloaded’. A couple of months ago he told me that he was diagnosed with early stages of haemorrhoids and was on treatment. I advised him on this matter, stressing how his morning ritual could be contributing to his condition. This ultimately led to his ‘conscious reduction of phone time in the bathroom’. His words, not mine. Recently, he proudly announced that his scheduled ‘throne time’ was now down to six minutes, every morning after breakfast.
Bathroom humour is universal. Cinema is no exception — it has found humour and dependable plotlines from this predictable ritual. Just one instance is in Lokesh Kanagaraj’s Vikram, where a character pulling the flush coincides with the house exploding. Thankfully, the consequences of spending 20 minutes on the toilet are far less dramatic.

After nearly two decades, Emraan Hashmi and filmmaker Aditya Datt are reuniting for Gunmaaster G9. The upcoming action film marks another collaboration between the two, who previously worked together on Dil Diya Hai and Aashiq Banaya Aapne. In the film, Emraan will be seen playing a secret operative navigating the dangerous world of firearms, espionage and personal conflicts. Ahead of its release, Aditya spoke exclusively to News18 about reuniting with the actor, the projects that failed to take off over the years and the expectations surrounding their latest collaboration.
Gunmaaster G9 director Aditya Datt reveals why three films with Emraan Hashmi never materialised; says, “Aashiq Banaya Aapne came with ‘huge baggage’”
Speaking about how Gunmaaster G9 could have been their sixth collaboration had their previous attempts materialised, Aditya revealed that they had explored several projects after their earlier films but could not take them forward.
“After Aashiq Banaya Aapne and Dil Diya Hai, we tried coming together a few times. For one reason or the other, things fell apart at the last minute. In fact, we tried locking three scripts. We were about to take them on floors but none of them worked out," he said.
The filmmaker further explained that their professional commitments also contributed to the delays. While he got occupied with Commando 3 and Table No 21, Emraan had his own busy schedule. However, Aditya felt that the right opportunity eventually came along with Gunmaaster G9.
“I then got busy with Commando 3 and Table No 21. Emraan, anyway, is super busy. So, each time, we locked a script and were about to shoot, some mess would crop up. But like they say, there’s a time for everything. So, we waited for the right time," he added.
Aditya also revealed that he was keen on exploring the masala action genre with Emraan instead of returning to the romantic thriller space they had previously worked in. He wanted to present the actor in a larger-than-life avatar, particularly after his recent inclination towards realistic cinema.
“When Emraan and I were thinking about what to do, I told him I can’t do normal anymore. I like portraying my leads as stars. I don’t want to do slice-of-life. If you look at Emraan’s career graph in the last couple of years, he was trying to do realistic cinema. I wanted to present him as a larger-than-life action hero. Interestingly, we connected on this genre and this time around, things fell into place," Aditya remarked.
The film also reunites Emraan, Aditya and music composer Himesh Reshammiya after 20 years. Interestingly, Aditya revealed that bringing Himesh on board was not part of his initial plan. He had shortlisted songs by other composers after completing the script, but a chance encounter eventually led to their reunion.
Another aspect of the collaboration was dealing with expectations surrounding the music of Aashiq Banaya Aapne, which had made a strong impact upon its release. Aditya admitted that the previous film's success came with considerable expectations but said he did not want the team to feel pressured while working on the new album.
“Yes, it comes with huge baggage. I told Emraan and Himesh that let’s just have fun without getting trapped into that pressure of expectations. The only thing we stuck to was bringing that freshness and spark that we had during Aashiq Banaya Aapne. We sat on each song for 2-3 months," he shared.
He further explained that the team consciously avoided recreating or rehashing the earlier film's popular tracks, despite knowing that comparisons were inevitable.
“The music of Aashiq Banaya Aapne created history and we knew there would be comparison. We wanted to give audiences the same feeling without copying the music of Aashiq Banaya Aapne. The easiest thing would be to pick up songs from that film, rehash and release them. That temptation could’ve been there. But then I said that we aren’t going to take that route," Aditya told News18.
Gunmaaster G9 also features Genelia Deshmukh and Aparshakti Khurana. The film is scheduled to release theatrically on November 27.

There will be a new president at the helm of a new-look Indian Olympic Association, but who it might be remains unclear.
Incumbent P.T. Usha did not turn up on the final day of filing nominations for the upcoming Executive Council elections, effectively marking the end of her innings as the first woman IOA president, even as Tuesday saw more activity at the IOA Bhawan here than in a long time.
While former Secretary General and Fencing Association of India secretary Rajeev Mehta set the ball rolling with his nomination for the top spot on Monday, the final hours saw most of the prospective contestants rolling in to file their nominations. Current vice-president and Olympic medalist shooter Gagan Narang has emerged as a frontrunner, but Archery Association of India’s secretary and Delhi BJP leader Virender Sachdeva is also in the fray, making it a three-way contest.
Sachdeva, however, has also filed for the male vice-president’s spot, along with boxer Vijender Singh, while Anju Bobby George is being challenged by Bhavneet Handoo of wushu and Suman Kaushik from netball for the female VP post. Former table tennis player Kamlesh Mehta is set to be the next treasurer as the lone candidate.
Senior VP Ajay Patel is seeking another term, with Mona Shah (swimming) and netball’s Vagish Pathak challenging him. Sunaina Kumari and Amitabh Sharma are among those fighting to be joint secretaries, along with archer Purnima Mahato and ice hockey’s Harjinder Singh. The nominations also present interesting permutations with Vijender and Harjinder being proposed by Usha.
With some of the big names from the present EC missing out, including treasurer and weightlifting boss Sahdev Yadav, football chief Kalyan Choubey – who, incidentally, is the proposer for Narang -- and shuttler Saina Nehwal, one of the four elected Sportsperson of Outstanding Merit (SOM), the next leadership of the IOA is expected to have a new look, leading India’s sporting organisation for the next four years.
Rani Rampal and Yogeshwar Dutt have filed for the SOM quota of EC and are set to be nominated unopposed, while Dola Banerjee, Bhupinder Singh Bajwa, R.N. Jayaprakash, Prashant Kushwaha, Vitthal Shirgaonkar, Mona and Suman Kaushik are in the fray for the remaining four EC spots.
Elections are scheduled for December 5 for 13 positions – President, senior vice-president and treasurer (one each), vice-presidents and joint secretaries (two each, one male and one female) and six EC members including two from among the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) elected earlier.
However, with the sports ministry and political circles keen on unanimous choices and the last date of withdrawal of names being December 2 till 5 pm, the next week is set to see more action in the corridors of sporting power than on the field. It also remains to be seen if Usha presents India’s bid to the IOC’s Future Hosts Commission for the 2036 Olympics, scheduled for Thursday.

Alberta government plans Sovereignty Act pushback against federal hate speech law
Federal act removed Criminal Code defence for expressing religious beliefs or opinions in good faith
Alberta’s government plans to introduce a motion under the province’s Sovereignty Act targeting the federal government’s recent anti-hate legislation.
Bill C-9, the Combatting Hate Act, came into force this summer. The Alberta government’s motion specifically targets its removal of a religious exemption from Canada’s hate speech laws.
“This motion protects lawful political and religious expression, and it would ensure Albertans remain free to read and quote sacred religious texts without fear of prosecution,” said Premier Danielle Smith at a news conference on Tuesday.
A news release from the province says the motion, if passed, will "urge cabinet to consider lawful steps to protect Albertans from the effects of the federal Combatting Hate Act."
I don't think anyone wants to see their pastor or their rabbi or their imam monitored in their sermons or arrested and prosecuted.Alberta Premier Danielle Smith
The Criminal Code previously included an exemption for hate speech, "if, in good faith, the person expressed or attempted to establish by an argument an opinion on a religious subject or an opinion based on a belief in a religious text." That was removed when C-9 came into effect.
“We will not always agree on matters of beliefs, but it is our government's responsibility to preserve the space in which people with different convictions can live alongside one another with dignity, security and mutual respect,” said Smith.
Smith said the province's opposition to the federal legislation does not lessen its commitment to combatting hate-motivated crime.
She noted Justice Minister Mickey Amery previously told prosecutors to not pursue charges when someone simply “expresses controversial or unpopular political or religious beliefs.”
Joannie Fogue, spokesperson for the federal Minister of Justice Sean Fraser, said in a statement that the Combatting Hate Act was a response to calls for stronger protections against hate crimes.
"We agree with Alberta that Canadians should be free to practice their faith, read scripture, and express their religious beliefs. Those freedoms are protected by the Charter. The law strengthens the Criminal Code by giving law enforcement stronger tools to respond to hate-motivated crime and protect our communities.
"As threats evolve, our government will keep moving with urgency to strengthen Canada’s laws and keep Canadians safe.”
A Department of Justice website says the federal bill "does not limit anyone's ability to express religious beliefs in good faith."
"The repeal of this defence does not criminalize religious expression, which is protected under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms," the site states.
Smith said her government had hoped Ottawa would change course.
"I don't think anyone wants to see their pastor or their rabbi or their imam monitored in their sermons or arrested and prosecuted," said Smith.
The UCP government passed the Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act in 2022. It allows the province to push back on federal laws or policies that the legislature deems unconstitutional, violate Albertans' rights or negatively impact the province.
One Edmonton religious leader said he supports the general idea behind the federal legislation, but that there has to be a balance.
Rabbi Ari Drelich, executive director of Chabad Lubavitch in Edmonton, said disagreement can be healthy, as long as the dialogue is free and open.
"If, however, the expression of those views has a sinister motive behind it and it's potentially going to lead to violence, whether it be verbal violence or certainly anything beyond that, then we have a very big problem," he said.
Constitutional law expert Gerard Kennedy, associate professor in the faculty of law at the University of Alberta, said the federal and provincial governments have shared jurisdiction over the justice system.
He said the province's motion will likely take the form of guidance to police and prosecutors, not an order, which he said would go too far.
"The province can refuse to enforce federal law if it doesn't think it's a priority, but then the federal government would be able to enforce it if it was so inclined," Kennedy said.
Naheed Nenshi, leader of Alberta's Official Opposition NDP, said the motivation behind the motion was political.
He said Smith is trying to shore up support ahead of this weekend's UCP annual general meeting.
“They need to throw some red meat to the base," Nenshi said. "So they're trying to open yet another chapter in the culture wars.”
With files from Julia Wong and Michelle Bellefontaine

Jenna Ushkowitz doesn’t want to remember when Glee did a tribute to Cory Monteith after his death.
In a new interview, the star of the musical comedy explains why it was difficult to film the episode and why she felt they shouldn’t have done it.
“To shoot ‘The Quarterback’ [tribute episode]… I think it wasn’t the right thing,” Ushkowitz said on the We Need to Talk podcast. “And I think everybody collectively agrees that it’s maybe not the thing that we should have done, because we were grieving both privately and publicly.”
Monteith played Finn Hudson in the Ryan Murphy series until his death in July 2013. The show continued and paid tribute with an episode dedicated to the late actor, which also acknowledged that the quarterback from the fictional William McKinley High School had died.
Watch on Deadline
“I think the fans definitely needed something, because they loved Cory so dearly like we did, and [loved] Finn so dearly,” Ushkowitz said. “But it’s a really hard thing to be grieving your friend and be a character grieving their friend at the same time.”
She continued, “It was like, too soon for that. [It] was not fun, [I] don’t want to remember that time. The show itself was never the same. He was the heart of the show, our friend, most importantly, and our leader. He really was the quarterback for us. He held everybody together. He hosted parties for the crew. He was the kindest. He knew everybody’s names. He just was such a good person, a kind person.”
Ushkowitz mentioned that at the time “even our creators, they were dealing with grief too” and “nobody had the tools” to deal with Monteith’s death.

The Keralam government has approved two new initiatives being launched by the Health department which aims at eliminating all preventable maternal and child deaths in the State.
Keralam, through its consistent mortality audit and course corrective measures, has maintained a good track record in minimising maternal and child deaths
“We have had excellent protocols in place to manage the most common causes of maternal and child deaths. We also have 'near-miss' maternal audits which systematically track what went wrong and what we did right to bring mothers back from the brink of death. Achieving the last mile reduction in maternal and child deaths means focussing on every preventable death possible. This involves investment in the continuum of care, right from pregnancy screening and care to making available the services of personnel trained in the management of obstetric emergencies, emergency transport facilities in the periphery hospitals and improved ante-partum and post-partum care,” a senior Health official said.
The action plans have been drawn up by the department in consultation with clinicians and professional bodies, including Kerala Federation of Obstetrics and Gynaecology and the State chapters of Indian Academy of Paediatrics and National Neonatal Forum.
Risk reduction
The Zero Preventable Maternal Deaths action plan begins with risk reduction before pregnancy and extends to antenatal care, safe delivery, critical care, emergency transport and surveillance.
It proposes preconception screening, risk-stratification tools and links with adolescent health services to optimise maternal health before pregnancy.
A Statewide online High-Risk Pregnancy Registry linked to Unique Health Identification (UHID) and Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) is proposed.
The State is planning to roll out a Keralam Pregnancy Risk Score (KPRS) for the structured follow-up of high-risk pregnancies, along with the implementation of Keralam Maternal Obstetric Early Warning Score (MOEWS), which will help clinicians in the timely recognition of clinical deterioration in obstetric cases.
“We have proposed that while Gynaecology OP clinics can be run in the periphery on select days, deliveries be restricted to a few well-equipped public hospitals in every district so that obstetric emergencies are not rushed from various periphery hospitals to referral hospitals. The services of all trained personnel may be pooled and redeployed in select delivery points in every district, which can be developed as centres with 24 x 7 provision of obstetric services,” an Obgyn specialist at a district hospital said.
Standardised protocols
The plan calls for round-the-clock availability of trained personnel, 24-hour blood bank readiness, intensive care pathways, high dependency units and standardised protocols for management of common obstetric emergencies like post-partum haemorrhage in every district
As many obstetric emergencies take a turn for the worse during transport — the 108 ambulance service does not have advanced life support facilities — the action plan has proposed that a Keralam Maternal-Neonatal Emergency Transport Network with GPS tracking be set up.
Experts have sought the setting up of contingency funds in public hospitals for the emergency transfer of women from vulnerable groups which the hospital Superintendents can directly manage.
Hospitals are required to report maternal deaths within two to four hours, with detailed reviews by experts in the next few days.
Within seven days
The child-death prevention plan mandates that all infant deaths are notified under the Kerala Clinical Establishments Act within seven days.
To improve survival immediately after birth, the plan mandates the presence of providers certified in neonatal resuscitation at every birth. Round-the-clock in-house paediatrician coverage is proposed at designated delivery points, alongside standardised perinatal care protocols across public and private healthcare facilities.
For small and sick newborns, the government proposes a tiered network of Special Newborn Care Units and Neonatal Intensive Care Units, supported by a real-time bed-occupancy dashboard and organised neonatal transport.
The plan also calls for strengthening life-threatening congenital anomaly care pathway and priority interventions for the tribal settlements in the State and migrant families.
The Keralam Child and Maternal Survival Task Force will review overall implementation and strategic milestones quarterly, while a technical steering committee and district child and maternal committees will also monitor the execution and review of the initiatives planned.

There was this man-against-machine match in chess in 1998. If you thought the machine might have won, you are wrong. The man, named Viswanathan Anand, beat Fritz.
The computer had white pieces and it opted for the Spanish Game. Anand, who hadn’t yet won any of his World titles yet, played the Berlin Defence. It is a solid option when you are playing with black pieces.
And it was Berlin Defence that D. Gukesh opted for the opening game of his World Chess Championship match against Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva on Tuesday.
The chess world had indeed been curious about the opening of the opening game in the widely anticipated match between two 20-year-olds. Sindarov began by pushing the pawn in front of him by two squares, to which Gukesh replied with a similar move. Just seven moves later, the queens were off the board, and a draw later on would become the likeliest result.
And it was a draw. But it wasn’t a tame, dull, goalless draw.
There were some anxious moves along the way, and there was also a battle on the clock, which Gukesh was losing for most of the time. There were several periods when it seemed he could get into serious time trouble that could cost him dear.
At one stage, he had to make his 22 moves in 24 minutes. Sindarov at that stage was very comfortably placed. And then later on, Gukesh had some six minutes for nine moves.
The Chennai Grandmaster was indeed struggling. He, however, kept his calm, even as the game continued on even terms more or less.
Later on, Sindarov was also forced to take more time to make his moves. He had been blitzing away earlier, and had enough time to move about inside the Fondation Martin Bodmer, the famous library in Cologny, the venue of the match.
The game, featuring a same-coloured-bishop ending, was eventually drawn by a repetition of moves, of which 38 were played in all. It was a game worthy of a World championship match.
Gukesh later said that he thought he was always under control. “It wasn’t in a place where I really needed to be worried,” he said.
Sindarov said he was trying to push at every moment because of the advantage on the clock. “But Gukesh defended well in the end,” he said.
