For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'
Sign up for NPR's Up First morning newsletter for the stories you need to start your day.
On Monday morning, a couple hours after Nvidia's board announced it had reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, President Trump shared an AI-generated image on social media.
It's based on that striking photo of the president from 2024, just after he survived an assasination attempt. Surrounded by Secret Service agents, his face bloodied, Trump hoists a defiant fist in the air.
In the doctored photo, instead of Trump, it's Huang. An Nvidia flag flies behind him. And in his hoisted fist, he holds a red bra.
"I was absolutely flabbergasted," says Bo Young Lee, who worked as chief diversity officer at Uber for five years starting in 2018.
To Lee, it seems Trump is suggesting that the Nvidia CEO is as important to the country as he is.
"But then also the red bra is an indication that it's open hunting season for women," she says. "It stirs up all sorts of stereotypes and misogynistic perspectives about women."
To others, the image drives home the idea that in Silicon Valley, as long as you're successful, anything goes.
The White House has not responded to NPR's questions about what Trump was trying to say with the image.
Spy intrigue overshadows workplace transgressions
Even as Huang's return to Nvidia has been cheered by investors, some employees and Trump, it has sparked shock and disbelief among others, including those who have long worked to improve workplace culture in Silicon Valley.
"It's actually unfathomable to me," says Lee, who now serves as an adviser to AI4ALL, a nonprofit dedicated to increasing diversity, inclusion, and responsible practices in artificial intelligence.
After The New York Times revealed that Huang had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S government believes is a Chinese intelligence asset, Lee watched as the broader conversation was dominated by concerns about national security, corporate governance and Nvidia's stock price.
That scandal overshadowed allegations of other problematic behavior in the workplace, specifically Huang's alleged affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, one of Huang's many direct reports.
"Everyone is minimizing that alleged relationship there because of who she is," says Lee.
The fact that Powell is herself a senior leader who makes a lot of money shouldn't matter, Lee says. She argues that people in subordinate roles, even powerful ones, can't properly consent, "simply for the fact that there is this power differential."
Nvidia's board did find that Huang's behavior was "inconsistent" with the company's code of conduct. By Monday morning, that didn't seem to matter.
"The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia," the board said in a statement.
Lee says that response sends a message to Nvidia employees and all of Silicon Valley that it's OK to break the rules as long as you come clean.
"'Just be transparent with us,'" she imagines the board saying.
Nvidia did not respond to NPR's questions about Lee's concerns.
A deepening of "tech bro" culture in Trump's second term
In Silicon Valley, there have been private conversations about Huang's alleged workplace transgressions and the power dynamics at play, but women don't appear eager to speak publicly.
NPR reached out to two dozen women who work in the tech space. Freada Kapor Klein was one of the few willing to talk. The social impact investor says conversations about workplace behavior are much quieter than they have been in other eras, such as in 2017 and 2018, when a number of venture capitalists resigned amid allegations they were sexually harassing female entrepreneurs.
In 2017, Kapor Klein and her husband, Mitch Kapor, used their positions as early investors in Uber to publicly call out the company over its toxic culture, one they said tolerated bullying and harassment. The co-founder and CEO Travis Kalanick ended up resigning. Kapor Klein hoped it'd be a teachable moment.
But now, she feels Silicon Valley has gone backwards.
"Tech bro culture is stronger now than I have seen it in decades," she says, adding that Trump's attacks on DEI have amplified that culture.
Among women and people of color in Silicon Valley, she says there's now real trepidation about the anti-DEI sentiment — the axing of programs, chief diversity officers and employee resource groups.
"All of the supports or mechanisms have been pretty much stripped away," she says.
"All that matters is money"
To be clear, Huang has not been accused of predatory behavior. Still, Kapor Klein says his swift comeback is troubling.
"It is a resounding message that all that matters is money," she says. "If you are thought of as a singular talent, you can violate corporate policy, you can possibly threaten national security, you can make up your own rules as you go, you can create toxic workplace culture — as long as you bring in the money."
By the end of last week, Nvidia's stock had fallen almost 49% from its peak in October, and about 27% from before Huang's resignation. On Monday, it rebounded significantly.
Lee says Silicon Valley has always had an unhealthy relationship with its "genius founders."
"We elevate these leaders to god-like levels, and that's been done to Mark Zuckerberg, and that's being done to Sam Altman, and that's definitely [been] done to Jensen Huang," says Lee. "You become untouchable at that point."
Kapor Klein says what's unfolded at Nvidia has made abundantly clear that AI companies need guardrails for their CEOs, not just for the tools they're creating.
"We see a board that ignored that," she says. "There are no guardrails on this CEO's behavior."
NPR's Scott Horsley contributed to this story.

This underrated Pixel feature is more versatile than you realize
If you're not using this feature, you're missing out on a lot of convenience.
If you own a Pixel phone, you probably look forward to the new features that pop up after an Android OS update and Pixel Drop. The latest Android 17 QPR2 and the November 2026 Pixel Drop, for example, upgraded Pixel Search and added cool customizable icon designs, Transit Mode for train commuters, Pixel VIPs real-time location sharing and a new Status bar settings menu for all Pixel 6a and newer phones, plus expanded Gemini Intelligence, Extreme Charging Mode and other features for the Pixel 10 and 11.
But there's one old, reliable and underrated feature that you may have missed, and it's actually quite versatile and convenient. It's called Quick Tap, and it transforms the back of your Pixel phone into a customizable shortcut when you tap it twice. Quick Tap allows you to accomplish common tasks with just one hand and without scrolling through any menus.
Finding and assigning actions to the Quick Tap feature on your Pixel phone
The Quick Tap feature is available on all Pixel 4a (5G) and newer phones. To access it and to customize the settings, open the Settings app on your Pixel phone, then tap System > Gestures > Quick Tap to start actions.
From there, you can then choose a built-in action for Quick Tap to perform when you double-tap the back of your phone. All of these actions are pretty convenient, but since Quick Tap only supports one action at a time, you should choose the one you're likely to use most.
You can assign Quick Tap to turn the flashlight on and off even when your phone is locked. Or set the feature to take a screenshot without having to hold the power and volume-down buttons at the same time. Quick Tap can also play or pause music, videos or podcasts using just about any of your favorite streaming apps with just a couple of taps. This is super convenient when you want to watch or listen to content while you're driving, cooking or working out, because you don't need to unlock the phone, navigate the apps and resume your media. Just double-tap the back of your Pixel.
Use Quick Tap to wake up Gemini without having to talk to the phone. Or assign Quick Tap to easily show notifications without having to pull the notification shade down from the top of the screen; Quick Tap pulls it down for you. You can also use the feature to open the multiple app overview screen and switch between recently used apps without navigating. Quick Tap can also launch any app installed on your Pixel phone — you just need to assign which app you use most.
One thing to consider: Quick Tap works perfectly on a naked Pixel phone. However, if you have a protective case on your phone, you might need to try a few things to get it working as it should. If your Pixel phone case is super thick, finger tapping may not be enough to get it going. Lighter-weight cases, though, should allow you to activate Quick Tap without much effort.
If you're having trouble, there is an option within the Quick Tap settings called Require stronger taps, designed to prevent accidental triggering of an app when you put the phone down or slide it into your pocket. Make sure that's turned off and then test it out. Messing around with where you tap your phone can also help. If you have a magnetic accessory on the back of the phone, keep tapping around until you find the sweet spot. For the foldable Pixel 9 Pro Fold and Pixel 11 Pro Fold phones, you can tap the rear glass panel whether the phone is unfolded or closed to activate Quick Tap.
How to get even more out of the Quick Tap feature
Quick Tap can be paired with other apps and automation tools to get even more out of the feature. The Tap, Tap app can be used to supplement Quick Tap by providing support for both double-taps and triple-taps, so you can assign more than one action and choose from a wider range of over 50 available actions to assign. You could also connect Quick Tap to a free pop-up menu or folder app so the double-tap triggers a menu of your most-used apps or tools.
Your Pixel phone is also loaded with built-in Gestures, which give you another way to access certain tools and features without having to unlock or swipe — or install another app like Tap, Tap. To find these, go to Settings > System > Gestures.
Let's say you want to use your Quick Tap action to toggle the flashlight when you double-tap the phone, but you also want fast access to your camera or Google Wallet. You can do this by customizing your Gestures to open either the camera or Google Wallet by double-pressing the power button. You can also press and hold the power button to summon Gemini. Then there's the Flip to Shhh feature that automatically enables Do Not Disturb when you place your Pixel phone facedown, as well as a shortcut that lets you tap or lift your phone to check the time, notifications and other info.
Between Quick Tap and Gestures, your Pixel phone is versatile enough to let you simply tap or press your way through a bunch of actions to maximize convenience and one-handed operation. That makes day-to-day phone use much more convenient. Assign it to your smart home device app for quick controllability, or have it open Google Wallet to quickly pay when you're at the store, for example. Anyone who uses a phone knows it's a whole lot easier to tap the phone than to unlock it or swipe through apps... especially if you only have one hand available.

US President Donald Trump's administration is reportedly preparing to increase tariffs on several countries, including China and India, arguing that their governments have harmed American companies by supporting domestic industrial production. Citing sources, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday (local time) that Jamieson Greer, the US Trade Representative (USTR), is likely to announce the tariffs as soon as this week. The move follows a months-long investigation into industrial subsidies provided by countries including China, the European Union, and 14 other nations. However, sources cautioned that the timeline could change. According to Greer, subsidies and other forms of government support provided to companies in certain countries have created excess industrial capacity in those economies. This allows their firms to flood global markets with cheaper goods, ultimately undermining US producers. While the final tariff rates remain unclear, Trump administration officials have repeatedly said they intend to impose duties similar to those introduced by the US President in 2025, before the Supreme Court struck down his first batch of tariffs in February 2026. The proposed tariff announcement also comes amid a separate controversy involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and allegations that the company's advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips were smuggled into China despite tighter US export restrictions. According to the WSJ, the timing of the tariff move could also be linked to an attempt by the Trump administration to divert attention from questions surrounding what the government knew about the alleged smuggling and its response to the matter. The USTR's announcement is also expected to bring higher tariffs for dozens of countries, including China, Japan, South Korea and the 27 member nations of the European Union. The new duties are likely to cover most products exported from these countries. However, certain industrial goods, including steel, aluminium and automobiles, are expected to be excluded as they are already subject to tariffs under a separate national security provision. Countries that reached trade agreements with the Trump administration, including Japan and the European Union, are expected to retain tariff rates in line with the terms they had agreed to before the Supreme Court's ruling, according to people familiar with the plans. Under this arrangement, the EU, Japan and South Korea could face tariffs of 15% or less, while countries such as Vietnam and India may be subject to higher rates depending on the terms of their respective trade deals with Trump. China, on the other hand, is likely to face higher tariffs than many other countries, as Trump administration officials have pointed to the extensive nature of Beijing's subsidies and their disruptive impact on the global economy. The administration may also introduce provisions allowing it to raise tariffs on countries if their industrial overcapacity increases or they fail to implement policy changes during future trade negotiations with the US, the report added. The proposed tariffs are expected to be imposed on top of duties announced under a separate measure in July. The measure targeted countries that failed to prevent the trade of goods manufactured using forced labour and set tariff rates ranging from 10% to 12.5% across 60 economies. However, the measure is currently facing a legal challenge in court. Earlier in July, the US announced fresh tariffs on several countries under Section 301. While India was initially placed in the 12.5% tariff bracket, it was moved to the 10% category following discussions on labour practices. The development followed the USTR's decision in March to launch investigations into 60 economies under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act of 1974. The probe aimed to determine whether their trade practices were linked to a failure to enforce restrictions on imports of goods manufactured using forced labour. The duties, ranging from 10% to 12.5%, cover several major US trading partners, including India, the UK, the European Union, Canada and Japan. According to the Office of the USTR, "Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting US commerce. Section 301 may be used to respond to unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory foreign government acts, policies, or practices that burden or restrict US commerce. A Section 301(b) investigation examines whether the acts, policies, or practices are unreasonable or discriminatory and burden or restrict US commerce." The Oscar race for visual effects is down to 20, and the road to the 99th Academy Awards runs through Ithaca, Motunui and a galaxy far, far away.
The Academy’s Visual Effects Branch notified the artisans behind the 20 films advancing to the next round ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. Through multiple sources, Variety has confirmed 19 of the finalists, including Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Three,” Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Phil Lord and Christopher Miller’s “Project Hail Mary,” Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day” and Marvel Studios’ “Avengers: Doomsday” from Anthony and Joe Russo.
The Academy does not release the top 20 externally and declines to comment or confirm which films advanced.
Disney leads the confirmed titles with four. Alongside “Avengers: Doomsday,” the studio lands Jon Favreau’s “Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu,” 20th Century Studios’ “Whalefall” and Thomas Kail’s live-action “Moana,” which brings Dwayne Johnson back as the demigod Maui.
Skydance (formerly Warner Bros Discovery) took three of the spots: “Dune: Part Three,” Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s Tom Cruise-led “Digger” and Craig Gillespie’s “Supergirl” from former DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran. But the studio also sees four contenders fall short.
Villeneuve’s stakes are historic. Both “Dune” and “Dune: Part Two” won the visual effects Oscar, and in March, “Avatar: Fire and Ash” made James Cameron’s franchise three-for-three in the category. “Dune: Part Three,” which opens Dec. 18, now puts Villeneuve two steps from the same trilogy sweep.
Universal Pictures booked both of its summer event films, “The Odyssey” and “Disclosure Day,” while Amazon MGM Studios goes two-for-two with “Project Hail Mary” and Kyle Balda’s “The Sheep Detectives.”
Nolan’s track record in the category is just as formidable. “Inception,” “Interstellar” and “Tenet” each won the visual effects Oscar. However, the branch famously left “Oppenheimer” off its top 20 for the 96th Academy Awards. Spielberg has been here before, too, with “Jurassic Park,” which won the category in 1994.
Two of the more intriguing finalists come from outside the Hollywood studio system. Takashi Yamazaki’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” follows “Godzilla Minus One,” which won the category at the 96th Oscars and delivered the franchise its first Academy Award. Laika’s stop-motion “Wildwood,” directed by Travis Knight, gives the studio a chance to return to a category it cracked with Knight’s “Kubo and the Two Strings,” one of only two animated films ever nominated for visual effects, along with “The Nightmare Before Christmas.”
Sony lands three big movies in the field. Leading the charge is Destin Daniel Cretton’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and the still-to-be-released “Jumanji: Open World” advancing alongside “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” the Indian mythological epic. “Ramayana” follows S.S. Rajamoulili’s “RRR,” which reached the top 20 for the 95th Oscars and signals the branch’s continued appetite for large-scale spectacle from outside Hollywood.
A24 also lands a spot with “Backrooms,” the feature directorial debut of 21-year-old Kane Parsons, whose YouTube series turned the internet’s liminal-space legend into a box office phenomenon, grossing more than $400 million worldwide.
Paramount received a split verdict. David Ayer’s survival thriller “Heart of the Beast,” starring Brad Pitt, advanced, but Variety confirmed that two of the studio’s other contenders, “Ebenezer” with Johnny Depp and the video game adaptation “Street Fighter,” did not make the top 20.
Netflix also breaks through with Peter Berg’s epic war drama “The Mosquito Bowl,” one year after the streamer placed “Frankenstein” and “The Electric State” on the shortlist.
That leaves one spot unconfirmed, with a few titles still awaiting confirmation. Variety will update this story as additional finalists are confirmed.
The preliminary voting period for the Oscars shortlist begins Monday, Dec. 7, at 9 a.m. PT and ends Friday, Dec. 11, at 5 p.m. PT. The shortlists in all categories will be announced Tuesday, Dec. 15. Afterward, the VFX bake-offs will take place during the Academy’s Jan. 8-10 voting events, when the 10 shortlisted films will be presented to branch members for final nomination consideration. Nominations voting runs Jan. 11-15, with the nominations announced Thursday, Jan. 21.
The 99th Academy Awards will be held Sunday, March 14, at the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood and will air live on ABC.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows RSS members armed with swords surrounding the Jama Masjid in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, injuring several Muslims and trapping others inside. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS members attacking a mosque in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, injuring several Muslims and trapping others inside.
Fact: The video is from Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh, and shows a group of Hindutva supporters brandishing swords and playing loud music outside Shahi Jama Masjid in April 2022. The Ghaziabad Police have also dismissed the claim as fake, clarifying that no such incident occurred within the Ghaziabad Commissionerate. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several social media posts from April 2022 featuring the same visuals (here, here, and here). According to these posts, the video is from Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh, and shows a group of Hindutva supporters brandishing swords and playing loud music in front of a mosque.
We also found an article published by Muslim Mirror on 12 April 2022, featuring an image identical to a frame from the viral video.
The same video was posted on X by Hindutva Watch on 12 April 2022. The accompanying caption identified the location as Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh.
The incident was also mentioned in a VICE News article published on 22 April 2022, which reported that Hindu groups carrying weapons, including guns and swords, marched through Muslim neighbourhoods during Ramadan, playing provocative and Islamophobic music and raising inflammatory slogans. The article alleged that Hindu extremist groups were linked to some of the processions associated with the violence.
To further verify whether the footage was recorded outside Shahi Jama Masjid, Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh, we checked Google Maps for Street View imagery and photographs of the location, but none were available. We then compared the surroundings visible in the video with an image of Shahi Jama Masjid in Sarangpur, published in a Dainik Bhaskar article. The mosque’s architectural features and other identifiable elements matched those visible in the video, confirming that the footage was recorded outside Shahi Jama Masjid in Sarangpur, Madhya Pradesh.
The Ghaziabad Police also responded to the viral claim through a post on their official X account dated 19 November 2026. They dismissed the claim as false and misleading, clarifying that no such incident had occurred within the Ghaziabad Commissionerate. The police further stated that legal action was being taken against those spreading the misinformation and urged the public not to circulate misleading claims.
To sum up, a video from Madhya Pradesh is falsely shared as showing RSS members attacking a mosque in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh.

The Rotary Club of Madras (RCM) and the Tamil Nadu government have entered into a partnership to provide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination to 3.5 lakh adolescent girls to prevent cervical cancer.
The partnership, valued at approximately ₹200 crore, is among the largest public-private initiatives for HPV vaccination in India. It was acknowledged in the presence of Darez Ahamed, Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department, Tamil Nadu government.
High-risk HPV infections account for more than 95% of cervical cancer cases. HPV vaccination during adolescence helps prevent infections caused by high-risk HPV types and reduces the risk of cervical cancer later in life.
Bobby Krishna, president of the Rotary Club of Madras, said the partnership was part of Rotary’s efforts to work with the government on large-scale vaccination programmes. The club also aims to vaccinate one million children as it approaches its centenary in 2028-29, building on its work under the Polio Plus programme.

'Pass, pass, slow, slow' - Man City's slick machine grinding to a halt
- Published
Manchester City's slick footballing machine is starting to grind to a halt.
The quick passing patterns and edge-of-the-seat action that was evident for so long under former manager Pep Guardiola was supposed to be taken forward by incumbent Enzo Maresca.
It started flawlessly under the Italian with the side winning their first eight games, but that smooth operation is beginning to turn into a turgid and pedestrian showing.
Similar to Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham, moans and groans filled a rather flat Etihad Stadium as the home faithful watched their side labour to a 2-2 Champions League draw against Napoli.
City's recent defensive issues also continued, now conceding in 10 successive games and letting in the first goal in seven of those matches.
Maresca said: "We are always looking for three points but when you are not able to win it is important you that don't lose. We take the point, five games [played],10 points and overall I think it is a good result in the end.
"Today, off the ball, once again we didn't concede a lot, the problem is that in this moment they are clinical when we concede a chance, almost every time it is finishing with a goal. We created many chances but in this moment it is like this and move on.
"The first 10 games we always scored first and then in this moment it is exactly in the opposite way, we just need to find a way to avoid that, but I don't think it affects the players in terms of their confidence. We fought until the end."
'Dull and predictable'
City were strong favourites for this game and should have had few issues in collecting all three points against a Napoli side that are languishing in eighth place in Serie A.
Their injury issues mean they were able to name only seven substitutes, two of those being goalkeepers, while they had suffered defeat in their past three meetings with City.
They threatened a shock result after twice going ahead through well-taken goals from Rasmus Hojlund and Noa Lang, but Rayan Cherki managed to salvage a late draw for the hosts.
Maresca's side had 62.7% possession and attempted 665 passes, which largely lacked incisiveness, and of that figure 303 were in the final third compared to Napoli's 77.
The latest disappointing result means City's perfect start is quickly unravelling, now having won only one of their past seven games in all competitions inside 90 minutes.
"It was really surprising to see Manchester City so dull in the first half and so predictable," former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on BBC Radio 5 Live.
"If you play a team that takes their time, you get yourself set. It is 100% easier to defend.
"You sit and watch City pass, pass, pass, slow, slow. You can get a cigar out."
Is Haaland lacking service?
Star striker Erling Haaland has been in prolific form again this season, scoring 20 goals for club and country, but the 26-year-old has drawn a blank in his past two games.
The Norwegian had chances but failed to score against Fulham on Saturday and though he was handed the captain's armband against Napoli, Haaland was on the periphery for much of the game.
The frontman managed only 14 touches of the ball against the Serie A side on Tuesday, the lowest figure of any player that started the match.
It raises the question whether he is receiving the service to try and find the back of the net.
"I feel I am getting more than enough chances to score," Haaland told TNT Sports. "We tried to push at the end for a goal but we couldn't. Not good enough and we let them in too easy.
"Football is easy and difficult; when you win it's easy and you know what to do, when you don't you start questioning everything. The perfect thing would be to not think but it's not so easy."
City are sixth in the Champions League table, before Wednesday's games, but in the Premier League they have failed to win their past four.
It does not get any easier this weekend, facing a daunting trip to leaders Arsenal on Sunday as they aim to find some form.
Haaland added: "It's the most difficult game of the season going to the champions away.
"We need a top performance from every single player."

Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.
The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)
Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.
Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, it also caused a rift within the family.
Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.
Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.
Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years
Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.
For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.
Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.
It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians
India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.
In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.
Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.
Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press
Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.
In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.
And it’s not just media …
The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.
Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.
The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.
In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.
She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’
Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.
Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.

Among the highlights of this year’s edition is artist Baaraan Ijlal’s collaboration with the celebrated lyricist Javed Akhtar, turning his evocative Urdu couplets into paintings. The two will be in conversation with curator Ranjit Hoskote on Friday.

Film | Bollywood’s ambitious rendering of Hindu epic Ramayana, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi, was released on 5 November. Touted as the most expensive Indian film ever made, it earned praise from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who described it as “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular”.
Your Diwali celebrations
Readers from India and around the world on the festival of lights and tell us how they celebrated.
 In India, Diwali comes to you. You can see it in the streets, hear it in the neighbourhood and feel it in the atmosphere. In the UK, it is different. Life carries on around you. But traditions do not have to disappear when you move countries – they can change shape. A small light in a quiet room can carry the same meaning as an entire street illuminated for Diwali. Aman, Plymouth, UK
 My favorite part of Diwali back home was getting up before sunrise on Narak Chaturdashi and having a ceremonial bath, followed by a breakfast of traditional Marathi Diwali snacks. I have been living abroad for over 10 years now and it’s always a bittersweet time of the year where I miss my family and the general vibe of Diwali in India. But I am trying to build new traditions as one half of an Indian-Austrian couple, which includes trading the traditional boxes of mithai for Manner Schnitten and marzipan. Charu, Germany
 There used to be more of a community spirit to Diwali. As kids, we would be tasked with going door to door, exchanging sweets and snacks with neighbours (sometimes to our great displeasure, because it made for awkward conversation with those we had annoyed with our antics). Nowadays, the celebrations are mostly private. Group celebrations are walled off within exclusive clubs, families light their own fireworks almost competitively, and people send each other sweets through a delivery service. Samyuktha, Chennai

According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.
Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft’s target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. “Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” Henderson wrote.
The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company’s post-incident report, dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.

The Hindu will conduct a free health webinar on Saturday, November 28, 2026, on the topic ‘Understanding Autoimmune Conditions’. The webinar will be held from 11.30 a.m. to 12.30 p.m.
Autoimmune conditions occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body’s own tissues and organs. These disorders can affect different parts of the body, including the joints, skin, nervous system and other organs, and may present with a wide range of symptoms.
The session will explore how autoimmune conditions develop, the role of the immune system, and the common signs and symptoms associated with these disorders. It will also discuss early warning signs, including persistent fatigue, joint pain, muscle weakness and neurological symptoms, and explain when these warrant medical attention.
The discussion will examine the challenges involved in diagnosing autoimmune conditions, the role of clinical evaluation and diagnostic tests, and the treatment options available. The panellists will also discuss long-term disease management, monitoring, and the importance of timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment.
Expert panellists include Aishwarya G., Consultant Rheumatologist and Clinical Immunologist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Chennai. She will discuss the immune mechanisms underlying autoimmune conditions, common rheumatological disorders, their symptoms, diagnostic approaches and current treatment options.
The panel will also feature Prabash Prabhakaran, Director and Senior Consultant – Neurology, SIMS Hospital, Vadapalani, Chennai. He will discuss autoimmune conditions affecting the nervous system, the neurological symptoms they can cause, approaches to diagnosis and treatment, and the importance of recognising neurological manifestations.
The session will be moderated by Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu.

England's state-run health service said Monday it has launched the world's largest AI-assisted breast cancer screening trial, which is set to involve nearly 700,000 women over the next three years.
The National Health Service (NHS) hailed the new trial as having the potential to transform breast cancer diagnosis, as it announced hundreds of women had been invited to take part at the outset.
The £10 million ($13 million) programme will assess if tools assisted by artificial intelligence can help improve early cancer detection in screening, which health officials hope will then free up specialist clinicians' time.
The AI-assisted reading tool will assist clinicians in reviewing images collected from routine mammograms, according to the NHS.
"This is the biggest AI breast cancer trial in the world," Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said in a statement, lauding the tech's "huge potential" while pledging "proper safeguards" to ensure safety and effectiveness.
"If successful, this technology could help women get a breast cancer diagnosis and start treatment much more quickly, giving them the best possible chance of recovery."
The trial is being led by the University of Warwick, the University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, working closely with NHS England.
Women attending routine breast screening at 30 planned sites nationwide will be given details about the trial and participate, unless they choose to opt out.
The NHS stressed screening appointments will proceed as normal, but the AI-assisted tool will be used alongside specialists checking the images to look for cancers that are too small to see or feel.
The trial will test whether AI-assisted tools could allow most images to be reviewed by only one specialist, rather than the current two.
Recruitment has started at Cambridge University Hospitals, in eastern England, with more of the 30 selected sites opening in the coming months.
Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, with around 55,000 diagnosed every year in the UK.
Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for screening every three years, amounting to around 2.1 million screenings annually. The NHS estimates this helps prevent around 1,300 deaths.
A study published in The Lancet medical journal in January said that AI can improve breast cancer detection through more effective screening while reducing radiologists' workloads.
It analysed nearly 106,000 mammograms performed in Sweden as part of its national breast cancer screening programme -- involving women with a median age of 53 -- from April 2021 to early December 2022.

Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?
- Published
Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?
If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.
A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.
Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?
Someone, somewhere, knows something.
The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.
Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.
"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.
"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."
His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.
They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.
"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.
"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."
Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.
The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.
Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.
What happened next, though, was not part of the script.
While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.
The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.
Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.
Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.
Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.
In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.
Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.
It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.
"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.
He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.
"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.
"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."
By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.
But there were plenty of theories.
Theory: it was not a real diamond
Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.
"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.
"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.
"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."
Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.
"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.
"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.
"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."
Theory: someone pocketed it
"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.
"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].
"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.
"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."
There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.
Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up.
"What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find.
"Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car.
"There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones.
"Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."
Theory: Klien crashed on purpose
Sidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.
And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose.
"For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.
Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to.
"Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell.
"He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond.
"No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."
While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond.
His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers.
"When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there.
"It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."
In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue.
"No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell.
"I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."
Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."
Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1.
"You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.
Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.

Pope Francis' diary reveals claims he saw the devil three times
- Published
Pope Francis claimed he saw the devil three times over the course of his life, as well as the "gates of hell", according to new extracts from his private diary.
In The Private Diary of Pope Francis, published on Tuesday, a 2021 entry lists the late pontiff as having three visions of the devil: once from a car, another "in the choir loft" during Mass, and a third during a meeting with Vatican officials.
"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote, recalling one of the visions.
In the diary, written from 1992 to 2024, he also expresses regret over his 2018 visit to Chile, when he was criticised for defending a bishop who was accused of covering up sexual abuse committed by a priest.
Francis, who led the Catholic Church for 12 years until his death in 2025, later apologised and summoned the country's bishops to Rome, where they all offered to resign.
"Devastated because of the situation in Chile," Francis wrote in a 2021 entry.
"It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."
Of his encounters, which Francis interpreted as meetings with the devil, he said he could not forget the devil's "menacing" eyes.
"He looked at me with flaming eyes... more intense than the previous one. They were like flashes of fire," he wrote of his second vision that he said happened inside a Carmelite chapel while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires.
He said the devil's presence intruded on his journeys, including during the visit to Chile amid the clerical sexual abuse scandal, and a meeting a few days after he had returned to Rome.
"I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant, possessing everything," he wrote, adding that "the Lord gave me the chance to free myself from these encounters".
The late pope also revealed that while getting ready to go to sleep in June 2018, he "saw the gates of hell".
"I watched a little, and it terrified me," he said, adding that he "took the rosary as a weapon".
"It's dangerous to get close to the gates of hell, because flames can spring out and burn," he wrote.
Cardinal Victor Fernandez, head of the Vatican's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and friend of Francis, edited the diaries, which are the first by a pope to be released to the public since the 1960s.
Pope Francis was elected pope in 2013 and died aged 88 in April 2025.

Nigerian monarch, 92, suspended after sexual assault claims
- Published
One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.
The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.
The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.
Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.
He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.
Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.
Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.
On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.
She posted a video, which has since been deleted, in which a man who appears to be the emir is holding her hands in his lap.
After some moments she was heard saying: "Stop, stop" as the hands reached for her chest.
According to a statement, Katsina Governor Dikko Umaru Radda directed the immediate constitution of a committee to investigate the allegations.
The statement said the state government was taking the allegations seriously and would rely on the committee's findings to determine the appropriate course of action.
It said the committee's findings and recommendations would be fully implemented, stressing that justice would be served.
However, it did not disclose the membership of the investigative committee, its terms of reference or the timeline for submitting its report.
The emir has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother Bashar dan Umaru, who reigned for 41 years.

Quick Answer
Ente Photos is a privacy-focused Google Photos alternative offering 10GB of free storage, end-to-end encryption, open-source code, selective album backups, cross-platform access, easy photo imports, collaborative sharing, and on-device AI features like face recognition and Magic Search.
When we think about a dedicated photo app, we instantly remember Google Photos or the default gallery on our phone. We do not have many trustworthy options. That’s when I came across Ente. Ente is a dedicated photo app available as a standalone app to install on Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, and Linux operating systems.
Is Ente the real challenger to the Google Photos app? Can we replace the gallery on our phones with Ente? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Features That Make Ente a Worthy Photo App
Ente has some exciting features that really make it stand out from the few others available. Here’s what makes it worthy.
Generous Free (Forever) Storage Plan
Ente offers a 10GB free storage plan for your photos and videos. Ente claims the plan is free forever. 10GB of free cloud storage dedicated to photos and video backup seems a good deal. That too without any ads.
Google offers 15GB of free storage space for each Google account. There is no dedicated storage space for the Google Photos app. As Google’s free storage is tied to all Google products as a whole, Ente’s 10GB looks big.
If you exhaust the generous free space on Ente, you can upgrade to a paid plan that offers storage starting from 50GB to 2TB for a monthly or annual subscription.
End-to-End Encrypted Backups
The photos and videos you back up on Ente are end-to-end encrypted by default. Ente claims they never use our data to train their models or spy on us.
The photos we back up via Google Photos are not end-to-end encrypted. Google may use our data to train their AI models, serve us customized ads, etc. You can prevent Google from using your data to show you personalized ads, but they can read your data. That’s where Ente succeeds.
The backup is end-to-end encrypted with keys before it leaves our device. The encryption keys are derived from our password using advanced key derivation functions. That means only the password you set can decrypt the data.
As the source code of Ente is publicly audited, the trust factor improves. When I tried to sign up on Ente, it provided me with a recovery key or the master key that I can use in case I lose my password.
The encryption process involves only us, the users, and they can never access the data. Even in the unfortunate event of a data breach, our data can remain safe as it is end-to-end encrypted.
Fully Open-Source Platform
Ente’s entire codebase for photos and its other apps is available for public audit on GitHub with more than 29k stars. The stars do not necessarily mean the project is good, but they give some form of trust.
The internet rewards the sensation. If someone had found a mismatch between Ente’s tall claims and the code, they surely would have flagged it and made an issue out of it.
Backup of User-Selected Albums
When you give permissions for Google Photos on our device, it backs up all the available albums, photos, and videos. We cannot select or ignore certain albums.
Ente, on the other hand, gives users the option to select which albums to back up. The albums that we choose not to back up are ignored by Ente as well. I loved this feature personally, as a lot of unnecessary data gets uploaded and wastes storage space. We can also customize the albums for backup anytime.
Easy Accessibility on All Platforms
Ente Photo has an app for every major operating system. We can install its app on Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. If we do not want to install the app, we can use it on the web through Ente.com.
Import Data From Google and Apple
Just download the Google Takeout that only has Google Photos data, import it into the Ente desktop app, and you are all set. It’s that simple to import data from Google Photos.
If you are an Apple user, just install the Ente app on your mobile device. Ente will read the data directly from your iCloud library and import it.
If you have iCloud shared albums, select the photos you want to import into the Ente app, and then save them to your device library for Ente to read them automatically.
Better Sharing and Collaboration Features
Ente Photo app provides us with three ways to share albums with others. You can share with a person on Ente, create a public link and share it with non-Ente users, or create a collaborative link to let non-Ente users add photos without an Ente account.
This does not put pressure on non-users to create an Ente account before collaborating with Ente albums, unlike the Google Photos app.
On-Device Machine Learning Features
There are a few machine learning-based features, like Magic Search, where you can search for photos with descriptions of how you remember them, Face Recognition, Memory Lane, Map and Location, and Jump to Date. These are all the latest advances in AI features.
To protect and maintain your privacy, all the machine learning happens on your device itself and is never sent to Ente’s servers. The machine learning feature is not enabled by default. You have to enable it manually and choose to disable it whenever you need to do so.
Is Ente Photos safe to use?
Yes, the Ente Photos app is safe to use to back up your photos and videos. It provides end-to-end encryption based on your password, and only your password can decrypt the data. Once you forget your password and also lose the recovery key they provided, you may never get to access the backup. The entire codebase of the Ente Photos app is available for public audit on GitHub.
How do I transfer photos from Google Photos to Ente?
You can transfer photos from Google Photos to the Ente Photos app in two ways. You can either download Google Photos data from Google Takeout, or download the entire library from the Google Photos app and drop it into the Ente Photos desktop app. It will read the data and import it to back it up safely.

A European Ariane 6 launcher propelled 36 satellites into orbit for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation Tuesday, continuing the network’s build-out after 40 satellites were lost earlier this month during a failure of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket.
The launch was an important rebound for Amazon, bringing the Amazon Leo fleet to 432 satellites as the company seeks to fill the void left by the grounding of ULA’s Vulcan rocket, Amazon’s primary launch provider. Now, an Amazon official tells Ars it is accelerating several Falcon 9 launches the company has purchased from SpaceX, which also owns the Starlink satellite network that Amazon seeks to dethrone.
The next Falcon 9 launch for Amazon Leo is now planned for December, Amazon said, moved forward from its previous launch date next year. Several more Falcon 9s are scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites in rapid succession after the December flight.
Winners and losers
Amazon cast a wide net when it started signing deals for launch services five years ago, securing rides on 108 flights with every available medium- or heavy-lift rocket in the West to place a fleet of 3,232 satellites into low-Earth orbit. As of Tuesday, Amazon and its launch partners have completed 17 of those flights, with one mission failure.
Amazon executives initially bought up capacity from US-based United Launch Alliance, Europe’s Arianespace, and Blue Origin. Nearly all of those launch contracts depended on rockets still in development: ULA’s Vulcan, Europe’s Ariane 6, and Blue Origin’s New Glenn.
Each launch vehicle faced development delays, as all new rockets do. New Glenn has been grounded since May after an explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in Florida. ULA’s Vulcan will be sidelined for months after misfiring during a mission with Amazon satellites on November 15.

Jensen Huang received a “hero’s welcome” from employees on Monday after Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated him as CEO, according to people who were present. An outspoken faction of Nvidia’s workforce had demanded his return and greeted him with chants, raucous applause, and hugs at the company’s headquarters.
But other employees were quietly stewing. Several current and former Nvidia staffers had viewed Huang’s abrupt exit earlier this month as a rare opportunity to change the “one team” corporate culture of unfettered unity and minimal bureaucracy that he had cultivated over the past three decades, according to interviews with the workers, as well as internal correspondence and social media posts reviewed by WIRED. Most spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared backlash from colleagues.
Some employees were alarmed by Huang’s alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and another with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. But their frustrations extended beyond the CEO’s personal conduct. Current and former workers describe a culture at Nvidia in which allegedly abusive behavior was tolerated and challenging leadership was perceived as discouraged.
“Everyone agrees that mistakes were made, the question is what we are ready to forgive,” one employee wrote on an internal platform before Huang’s return. “I don’t know how comfortable I’ll be working at a place where such affairs are not taken extremely seriously.”
Another added, “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
When Huang returned to Nvidia’s offices in California on Monday, he told employees who greeted him that he would do a better job with his second chance at CEO. (As of Monday afternoon, he had not yet sent a companywide note about his return, as he was still getting his laptop set back up.)

US President Donald Trump said he played a crucial role in convincing Nvidia's board to bring back Huang. A person close to Trump calls him an irreplaceable CEO and says they expect him to exercise better judgement going forward.
Nvidia’s board announced it will continue an independent investigation into whether Huang had been a target of foreign intelligence services and that it will double down on plans to step up corporate governance.
It’s difficult to gauge how widespread dissatisfaction with Huang’s leadership may be at Nvidia. The company’s emphasis on unity has historically made it difficult for people to openly question his leadership or choices, workers say. “There's only one team at NVIDIA,” the chipmaker’s official website declares.
A public petition campaign known as Stand with Jensen garnered signatures from more than 10,000 Nvidia purported employees, according to its website. Nvidia has roughly 49,000 employees and 18,000 contractors overall, according to a person familiar with its workforce.
But inside Nvidia, one employee told colleagues that “some portion” of the signatures appeared to be “illegitimate,” noting that the names included “Satan” and media personality Mia Khalifa, who does not work at the chipmaker. The employee wrote that they found 75 suspicious names in an hour of checking. WIRED was unable to independently verify the findings. The petition’s organizers did not respond to requests for comment.
Huang’s supporters have praised how he made the company feel like a “big super family.” They credited him for minimizing bureaucracy, making himself available to staff, and supporting employees during difficult periods, including the Covid pandemic. A former employee who attended numerous meetings with Huang and other senior executives says the CEO was particularly adept at preventing bureaucratic infighting. He could detect corporate “politics and nonsense before it was even born,” says the worker.
There are also powerful financial reasons for Nvidia employees to feel loyal to Huang. His bets on chips and software for artificial intelligence have transformed Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable companies and made many longtime employees wealthy in the process.
But for some employees, the revelations about Huang’s behavior have forced them to question that loyalty. Jason Sequeira, a longtime engineering leader at Nvidia, wrote on LinkedIn last week that he ultimately couldn’t decide whether he wanted Huang back as he weighed arguments from both sides. “Some believe his contributions to NVIDIA and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” Sequeira wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. … I don’t have a clear answer.”
Several current and former workers say that Huang’s management style could come off as overly harsh at times, including, for example, toward longtime colleagues he viewed as having grown complacent as Nvidia’s market value surged. Two former employees say that he regularly raised his voice at workers, sometimes in ways they found belittling.
Other employees were more concerned about whether Nvidia’s board would hold Huang accountable for allegedly misleading the directors about his affairs. “That’s something we can’t have,” one employee says.
Another source of frustration for Nvidia workers has been the growing influence of Huang’s two children and son-in-law, who all hold senior titles at the chipmaker. In March, his daughter, Madison Huang scolded a colleague on a call with about 100 other employees, according to a participant who didn’t believe the anger was warranted. “I’m disappointed you asked that, are you fucking stupid?” the employee recalls Madison saying in response to a question about workshops on OpenClaw technology scheduled for an upcoming Nvidia conference. “Your mom can build a claw.”
Madison and her brother, Spencer Huang, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Praveen Mhapsekar, a senior system software engineer who was let go last week after disputes with his managers and HR, says he and colleagues stopped feeling comfortable complaining about practices that concerned them because of the trouble they believe it brought on themselves.
“This organization requires greater discipline and structured processes,” he says. One of the world’s most valuable companies “cannot be managed like a private startup operating out of a garage, where personal influence takes precedence over established procedures.”
Huang’s return doesn’t eliminate the prospect of Nvidia evolving to quell frustrations. But with internal issues more public than ever before, maybe the days of one big family all cheering along together are mostly gone.

That altered image showed Huang standing in Trump's place at the site of the Butler, Pennsylvania, assassination attempt in July 2024. A flag bearing the Nvidia logo hangs on the right side. Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
- Published
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.
There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.
"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).
Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.
In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".
Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.
Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.
In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.
According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.
