Quick Answer
LastWave, Musify, Convx, Spotube, and SimpMusic are free open-source clients for YouTube Music and Spotify. They unlock premium perks without subscription fees or ad tracking, offering background playback, offline downloads, time-synced lyrics, lossless audio, and customized interfaces without locked controls.
Subscription prices are going through the roof. And when you stack multiple subscriptions together, it can put a big hole in your pocket. For listening to music, we usually depend on Spotify and YouTube Music. They are the default music streaming sources for millions across the globe. Though there are alternatives from which you can hear high-quality audio, they just can’t match the ease of popular apps. But you are bombarded with ads, and several features are locked behind a paywall unless you pay.
Thankfully, you don’t have to search the internet for free options. Developers around the world have built free apps that give you many of those perks. Below are five of the best, what each does well, and what to watch out for before installing.
Table of Contents
Why are open-source music apps worth a look?
To be clear, most of these apps are clients. This means that they don’t store any music themselves. They plug into a service like YouTube Music and show it in a cleaner, ad-free interface with extra features on top, which you’d usually get after paying for a premium subscription. For me, Spotify has been the go-to music streaming app, but slowly the app has become quite greedy.
After a few times, the next and previous song buttons get locked, and it asks you to pay to unlock them. I mean, what is wrong with companies today? Thankfully, I have now ditched Spotify and have picked one of the below open-source music options.
That has three practical effects:
- No ads and no subscription fees. Everything below is free.
- Most of these apps have no ad trackers or tracking SDKs.
- New features are constantly added, and some of them aren’t even available in paid apps.
The catch is that these apps rely on unofficial methods to fetch music, so they can break when YouTube or Spotify changes something. Treat them as great free alternatives, but not as rock-solid replacements. Let us take a look at the free alternatives.
Best free open-source music apps
LastWave
If you care about how your music sounds, LastWave is the one to install first. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. Most of us would care about the free music that we get with LastWave, but you will soon appreciate the quality of music that it offers. And since it is a YouTube Music client, you are getting access to almost every song that is available on YouTube.
The headline feature is lossless FLAC audio, up to 24-bit/192 kHz. When you press play, the song starts playing right away on the fastest available stream, and while you listen, the app fetches the lossless version in the background and switches over once it’s ready. On compatible phones and headphones, LastWave also plays the Dolby Atmos version of a song automatically. For those who own a USB DAC or a pair of IEMs, there’s a bit-perfect mode that sends raw, unprocessed audio straight to your device.
The app is packed with features that normally sit behind a subscription. The lyrics are synced word-by-word and pulled from sources like Apple Music, Musixmatch, and LRCLIB. There’s a 10-band equalizer with presets for thousands of headphone models, and smart playlists that build mixes from your listening history. Plus, you have the option to import playlists from Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube Music in seconds, and even sync your Spotify liked songs.
Musify
Not everyone wants a hundred settings and toggles. Some people just want to listen to their favorite music without having to deal with ads and a hundred pop-ups about purchasing the subscription between two songs. Musify is for people who just want to open an app, search for a song, and press play. It’s a lightweight Android app built around Material You, which means its colors automatically match your phone’s theme and wallpaper.
Using it is fairly easy. You search for songs, albums, artists, or playlists and start streaming over Wi-Fi or mobile data. If you want to save data or listen on a flight, you can download tracks and play them offline. It lets you create your own playlists, rename and reorder them, or import existing ones from online sources. The player shows lyrics so you can follow along. You can also control the quality of the audio.
There are no annoying banner ads, no audio ads, no sign-up, and no tracking inside the app, and the interface is translated into dozens of languages by the community. I found this to be a great choice for older phones, or for a parent or sibling who finds complicated apps annoying.
Convx
While most open source music apps work well, there are only a few that also feel nice to use. Convx comes in the second category. If you like iOS’s “Liquid Glass” design, then you would love Convx. It brings iPhone’s Liquid Glass design to Android, with frosted, see-through menus, floating controls, and album-inspired colors that change with whatever you are playing.
Under the pretty surface, Convx is a complete music player. You can browse and stream music, save songs for offline listening, build queues and playlists, set a sleep timer, change playback speed, and tweak the sound to your taste with an equalizer. What makes it stand out among the heavy hitters is its DJ-style playback. You also get automix, crossfade, and smooth transitions between one song and the next. Lyrics are synced word by word and come from several providers, plus it gets animated artwork.
Convx can play local files and even songs stored on a home server or NAS through SMB and WebDAV. You can choose the option to import your Spotify playlists, show what you’re playing on Discord, scrobble to Last.fm, recognize songs playing around you, and use Listen Together to sync playback with friends.
Spotube
Spotube is the veteran here, with over 46,000 stars on GitHub, and it works differently from the rest. Instead of being locked to one service like Spotify or YouTube, it runs on plugins. You choose your own music sources, metadata, and playlists through plugins made by the community, or if you’re good with it, you can write one yourself.
The biggest advantage is that it works everywhere. Spotube runs natively on Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. This means you can use the same app on your phone and your laptop. It’s small, fast, and light on data. You can import and sync playlists from popular music services or manage them locally. It gives time-synced lyrics from public lyric databases no matter which source you use. Offline downloads are supported, with proper metadata and ID.
Privacy is one of the biggest highlights of Spotube. It collects no telemetry and no user data. Installing it is also easy, because you can download it through winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, Homebrew, Flatpak, and F-Droid.
SimpMusic
SimpMusic is that one app that does everything. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android and desktop that borrows many of Spotify’s best ideas. You can play music from YouTube Music or regular YouTube without ads, and it gets you background playback. You can browse the home feed, charts, podcasts and moods, search everything on YouTube, cache songs for offline playback and use Android Auto.
SimpMusic Wrapped gives you a year-in-music recap just like Spotify’s. Then there is monthly recap playlists and listening charts that stay on your device. There are three Now Playing styles, including one that looks like Apple Music, and the lyrics are synced in 12 languages. You can even share lyrics as an image.
You can switch to 1080p video with subtitles, skip sponsor segments with SponsorBlock, see dislike counts with Return YouTube Dislike, and use a 10-band equalizer with AutoEq headphone profiles.
Which one should you pick?
If you care most about sound quality, I would suggest LastWave. If you want something simple, pick Musify. If design matters to you, try Convx. If you want plugins and an app that runs on every device you own, choose Spotube. If you want the most features in one place, install SimpMusic. The best part is that all five are free and can be installed side by side, so you can try a few and keep your favorite. You will get access to unlimited songs from the best sources in good quality. Let us know which one you chose, and comment below if you have a different app that you use for listening to music.

India invited Pakistan to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum held in New Delhi from 20 to 22 November 2026. Pakistan confirmed its participation, with Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik attending. The invitation was extended to SCO member countries as part of the forum, which focused on civilisational and cultural ties. The invitation sparked political criticism in India, with opposition leaders questioning the government’s stance on Pakistan amid tensions over terrorism (here, here, and here).
Amid this, a video purportedly showing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national president Nitin Nabin is circulating on social media (here, here, and here), claiming he said India invited Pakistan to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit under pressure from China.
In the video, Nabin allegedly says that China is pressuring India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit in exchange for an agreement to reclaim 200 sq km of Indian territory occupied by China. He also allegedly remarked that although the Tejas aircraft lack engines, their airframes have been built, adding that the US would supply the engines whenever it chooses to do so. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows BJP national president Nitin Nabin saying that China pressured India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. The original footage shows BJP national president Nitin Nabin speaking about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls at a rally in Chandigarh. The Hiya AI voice detection tool also indicated that the viral audio was likely a deepfake, suggesting that fabricated audio was added to make it appear as though he said that China pressured India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit in exchange for reclaiming 200 sq km of Indian territory. The BJP has also filed a police complaint over the manipulated video. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether BJP national president Nitin Nabin made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating the viral claim.
We noticed the viral video carries an ANI watermark. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 22 November 2026, featuring the extended version of the same footage of BJP national president Nitin Nabin, wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background. In the original video, Nitin Nabin is speaking about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls at a rally in Chandigarh, defending the removal of deceased voters’ names and duplicate entries.
We also found the full speech on the BJP’s official YouTube channel, where it was livestreamed on 22 November 2026. The original footage contains no remarks about China pressuring India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit.
We analysed the viral video using the Hiya AI voice detection tool, which indicated that the audio was likely a deepfake. This suggests that fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear as though BJP national president Nitin Nabin said that China pressured India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit.
The Delhi BJP filed a police complaint on 23 November 2026 against unknown persons over the manipulated video of Nitin Nabin, seeking an FIR and action against those responsible. The complaint was subsequently transferred to the Delhi Police’s Special Cell IFSO unit for investigation (here, here, and here).
To sum up, this video of BJP President Nitin Nabin allegedly saying that China pressured India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit is a deepfake.

It was just after lunchtime when the doctor’s phone started to vibrate and chime. On this summer Wednesday, a neurointerventionalist in Anchorage got the alert: Three hundred miles away, at a hospital deep in Alaska’s interior, a clot in a major artery was blocking the flow of blood to a patient’s brain. He needed it out — and he’d have to come to the state’s biggest city to get it done.
Time is never on a stroke patient’s side. Every minute without blood flow, 2 million brain cells die. And in Alaska — a state more than double the size of Texas, most of it inaccessible by road — it can take several hours to arrange a plane, airlift a patient to Ted Stevens airport in Anchorage, and deliver them by ambulance to one of the five neurointerventionalists in the entire state who can extract clots.
In his mid-60s, the patient on the doctor’s phone had arrived at a nearby emergency room after a morning fall, suddenly weak on his left side. Like most patients with stroke symptoms, he got a head CT, which helps diagnose a stroke, whether it’s caused by a clot or a brain bleed, and determine whether that clot can be broken up with drugs or needs to be extracted. Normally, once the scan is complete, it could take 45 precious minutes just to send those thousands of two-dimensional brain snapshots to Anchorage for review — 90 million brain cells before a doctor could accept his transfer.
But this summer day, the patient had a new type of technology on his team. Stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death in the United States, the majority caused by occlusions that block blood flow to the brain, and survival rates are significantly worse for rural patients. In recent years, states have built up stroke networks, including telestroke care and automated artificial intelligence analysis, to try to improve transfer times for patients without access to specialist neurological care. One of the latest additions was in Alaska — where, starting in 2023, a small network of hospitals had agreed to use the same AI software to triage stroke patients and get them to the right care, faster.
Nearly instantly, the tool, from RapidAI, analyzed his CT scan for signs of a large vessel occlusion, or LVO, a type of blockage that often needs to be mechanically sucked out or retrieved with a stent. Through an app used by other hospitals with the technology, the results went out to his local team of doctors and the faraway network of neurointerventionalists — one of whom was on call at Providence Alaska Medical Center in Anchorage.
The app alerted the doctor with the results just seconds after the scan was complete: suspected LVO. Less than a half hour after the patient arrived at his local ER, the team had called Providence for a transfer — two minutes before their on-call radiologist even delivered their official CT report.
Four hours and 23 minutes later, the clot was out. Without the AI assist, it would have taken at least an extra hour.
How tech brought hospitals closer
In 2026, it’s not rare for a hospital to use AI to triage stroke patients. Eight years ago, clinical trials showed that automated image analysis could extend the clot removal window for stroke patients as late as 24 hours after they were last well — before this, the window was just six hours. At the same time, the Food and Drug Administration approved the first AI to detect large vessel occlusions.
Those “were the wonder years,” said Stanford neurologist Greg Albers, co-founder of RapidAI. “Stroke centers scrambled to access the software.” Developers started to bundle different stroke algorithms in one package, driven by vendors like Viz.ai, Aidoc, and Brainomix, along with RapidAI.
As with most new medical technology, though, that adoption has been uneven. At the forefront of the deployment were large metropolitan hospitals, including those categorized as comprehensive stroke centers.
“Maybe it’s because they had more advanced workflows in place. Maybe it’s because they had the funding to acquire this AI software,” said Casey Pelzl, a researcher at the Harvey L. Neiman Health Policy Institution who studied some of the technology’s early adoption. “But what we know about stroke is that a lot of patients seek initial treatment at noncomprehensive stroke care centers, and these are the places that could potentially benefit from it the most.”
That’s the promise that a small group of stroke coordinators and neurointerventionalists in Alaska saw in 2023, when they established a volunteer nonprofit called the Alaska Stroke Coalition in a bid to improve stroke outcomes in a state that throws up obstacles at every turn.
“The distances that we have to cross are enormous. The weather that we have to face is awful. Resource availability is so low,” said Kelly Isaacs, Providence’s stroke program manager. Sometimes Alaskans arrive at their village clinics by snow machine or dogsled. The state doesn’t have consistent reporting of stroke outcomes. And in the summer months, when cruise ships wind up the coast, a seaside hub’s population can swell nearly tenfold, often enriched with older passengers. Jaded hospital workers sometimes call them the “stroke boats.”
Against those unfavorable odds, one thing that could improve patients’ chances of survival after a stroke is getting them to the right care as fast as possible. “‘Time is brain’ is still very much the case, and the more quickly you can start a treatment — whether it’s the drug to break up the clot or if it’s a big clot, to transport them where they can get the clot taken out — that’s going to make a big difference for people,” said UC Health neurologist and stroke researcher Joseph Broderick.
By 2023, a few hospitals in the state, mostly in Anchorage, had started using RapidAI’s software, but barely any regional hospitals in the state’s interior and on its far-flung coasts did. Even for those hospitals that had the tech, “the challenge was we existed in all these different systems, but we weren’t coordinated,” said David Stoffel, RapidAI’s chief business officer. Each hospital had its own software license and didn’t share information within the app, making it difficult to coordinate decision-making for patients who might have needed a transfer.
So the newly formed Alaska Stroke Coalition, whose founders included Isaacs, tried to build a solution. Lucy He, a neurointerventionalist in Alaska, found funding from a family foundation to buy RapidAI for six additional hospitals spread across the state, at a cost of about $450,000. The resulting network spread from Alaska’s very northernmost tip in Utqiagvik, all the way south to the state’s capital of Juneau, which can only be accessed by air or water. When the tech threw up an alert about possible LVO in a patient, the message wouldn’t just circulate within that hospital team — it would go out wide, to the neurointerventionalists in Anchorage who might be able to help.
In return for the coalition paying for the AI tool, the health systems agreed to report their performance over the next three years, to see if the technology could really make a difference.
Is ‘the Skynet of stroke’ saving lives?
Day to day, the stroke coordinators and doctors accepting patients from across the state saw the technology changing their decision-making. It wasn’t always about quickly transferring patients for treatment — sometimes it was about making the hard calls to stay put.
Kevin Myrick, one of the coalition’s founders and Providence’s stroke program coordinator, pointed to a patient transferred to Providence this summer: a man in his 80s with a large vessel occlusion and severe symptoms. Patients like him are usually paralyzed on one side and lose speech. When strokes are this bad, it is far from given that a patient will regain function after treatment: Dead brain tissue is dead, forever. And restoring blood flow to dead tissue can do more harm than good, reintroducing toxic metabolic byproducts into circulation and causing swelling and bleeding.
“We did not put this [technology] in to transfer every patient to Anchorage,” said Myrick. If a patient doesn’t have enough chance for recovery, it can be preferable to keep them closer to home — to save them expense, keep them near their support network, and avoid using limited EMS staff time and planes.
In these cases, it’s a head CT with a contrast agent showing detailed blood flow in the brain that can help doctors tell what intervention is worthwhile. In the Rapid app, that image looks like a series of brain slices colored in neon-bright, Lisa Frank shades of green and pink. Pink tissue is gone. Green is brain that has the potential to be salvaged if blood flow is restored in time. “In Alaska, where you’ve got those big distances, having that imaging is going to be really important about deciding who to send and why to send,” said Broderick, of UC Health.
For the patient in his 80s, the CT perfusion images that came through the app showed far more green tissue than pink, their volumes neatly tabulated in milliliters by the software. “This patient was definitely a go,” said Myrick. He traveled 750 miles — about the distance from New York City to Chicago — and within a few minutes of arrival was shuttled into Providence’s catheterization lab, its team ready and waiting.
A CT scan after the clot removal shows his brain in profile. Blood fills the main arteries and tangled branches that supply oxygen throughout the entire brain; in his first CT, nearly half of that field was blank, its roadways cut off by the clot. Still weak and with impaired speech after the mechanical thrombectomy, he has a long way to go, said Isaacs. But “when he got sent home, he’s got a much better chance of recovery than he would have otherwise.”
The technology isn’t perfect. Like most radiology algorithms, there are false positives — scans that the app will say show a large vessel occlusion that actually don’t. It takes a good image to work well, said Broderick: “Sometimes, when you look at the pictures, if the person moves or the study wasn’t done right, the data is not good.” That means a doctor still reviews every output, and that official read is what drives the call to transfer or not. And for the biggest returns, it requires a hospital to actually perform CT perfusion imaging, which hasn’t been uniformly adopted in hospitals that don’t remove clots themselves.
But despite the limitations, the hospitals that have received the technology through the coalition’s grant are enthusiastic about connecting more of Alaska with the same alert system. “In rural Alaska, at all these tribal health organization hospitals, I think that that really can change the narrative here,” said Dylan Latif, stroke coordinator at Alaska Native Medical Center, one of the program’s grantees, at a meeting of the coalition in early October.
“If we do this with a bunch of different hospitals, then we create, you know, the Skynet of stroke in Alaska,” said He, the neurointerventionalist, at the same meeting.
The stroke coalition hasn’t yet published research about how the technology has impacted stroke care for Alaskans. But early data point to a recent increase in the number of thrombectomies delivered in Alaska, which could be driven in part by the program. And once patients arrived in Anchorage, hospitals with cath labs saw about a 30% improvement in the time it takes to start threading a device in to retrieve a clot.
“Logistically, every cath lab in America during normal business hours is booked 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. all day, every day,” Isaacs explained. With coordinated alerts from referring hospitals, it can be easier to prepare for stroke patients’ arrival. “We’ve got our little flight tracker up, and we’re like, OK, they’re 30 minutes out,” she said.
As is so often the case with AI deployed in health care, it will be longer before Alaska can show whether the new technology is changing the outcomes that matter the most: rates of long-term disability and death from strokes. It’s especially challenging in Alaska, where detailed data has been scarce; more complete stroke intervention and outcome recording began at the same time the coalition expanded the use of AI.
“Can I give you statistically significant information that RapidAI has made a big difference in the state of Alaska?” said Isaacs. “I can’t, really.”
For now, some doctors who care for stroke patients in Alaska are optimistic. “Being able to take these people who are from way the heck out of the middle of nowhere, they got 45 minutes to the local scanner, and now they are deemed eligible for an intervention — it has saved countless numbers of patients,” said Ryan Wilson, a neurologist at Alaska Native Medical Center, to his colleagues during the October meeting. “They’re gaining their brain back.”
The advancing frontier for Alaska’s stroke care
As the members of the Alaska Stroke Coalition face down the end of their three-year grant period, that enthusiasm is translating into action: Each one of the six hospitals that got free access to RapidAI has said it wants to keep and pay for it. And there’s hope for even more significant changes to the landscape of stroke care in the state.
“Coincidentally, three things happened that help us further that mission,” said Isaacs.
The first happened this February, when the American Heart Association and the American Stroke Association released new stroke guidelines. The previous guidelines suggested narrow windows in which a patient could be treated with clot-busting drugs: They had 4 1/2 hours to get the medication. But in the updated guidelines, depending on how much salvageable tissue a patient appears to have in one of those pink-and-green CT perfusion images, they can still receive the drugs nine, even 24 hours after symptoms started.
That could dramatically increase the number of treatable stroke patients in Alaska — especially those who can be treated in place by clot-busting drugs. With RapidAI in more hospitals, Isaacs hopes that perfusion imaging will become more common, helping to make those calls about whether a patient falls in those extended windows. “Stroke used to be way more depressing to take care of, because our treatment options were very limited,” she said. “The windows were very short, and now with increased technology and increased time in our guidelines, it’s not quite as sad as it used to be, honestly.”
The second boost came in June, when Alaska enacted a law that will help establish statewide standards for strokes and heart attacks, like it already had in place for trauma. “We always sort of looked over at what trauma had, and we were like, ‘Isn’t that great? They’ve got designations, they get site visits, they’ve got data collection. We need these things,’” said Isaacs, who, along with several other coalition members, voiced support for the bill.
And in October, the final piece of the puzzle fell into place: The coalition got word that the work it’s been doing is primed to expand. “They got proof of concept that they can achieve this equity of care in Alaska for stroke,” said RapidAI’s Stoffel, and leveraged it in an application to the five-year, $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program.
In the first year of funding, the Alaska Stroke Coalition received $3.2 million of the state’s funding to start building a statewide AI imaging network.
With grant-funded hospitals and independent purchases combined, Alaska will soon have 21 acute care hospitals and two CT scan-enabled clinics with RapidAI’s stroke system in place. “This is phenomenal for Alaska,” said RapidAI’s Albers. “There are financial issues for some of these smaller hospitals, and I think they’re even more significant in Alaska than elsewhere.”
The group hopes to receive funding for at least two more years — first, to build support infrastructure that allows for rapid decisions to transfer or keep patients, and then track the financial impact of the technology on hospitals.
“As a girl who was born and raised in Alaska, this is the most Alaskan story that you can get,” Isaacs said to the room of her colleagues in the coalition’s October meeting. Earlier that day, she had gotten the email confirming the grant funding. “It’s like, ‘Oh, you don’t want to do it? Fine, we’ll go do it ourselves.’ And here we are.”

A 17-year-old girl in Keralam has developed a serious kidney ailment allegedly after using a fairness cream purchased online following its promotion by social media influencers, doctors treating her said on Saturday (November 21, 2026).
According to doctors at Aster MIMS Mother Hospital in Malappuram, the girl ordered the cream after watching promotional videos by Instagram influencers who claimed it could remove pimples, dark spots and pigmentation.
The girl told reporters that she contacted the sellers through a WhatsApp number provided on Instagram and ordered the product.
She initially found the cream effective and ordered several more bottles over a period of one year.
The girl said that she subsequently began experiencing health problems, including a sudden drop in blood pressure and fainting.
She also developed swelling in her legs, making it difficult for her to walk and climb stairs, following which she approached the hospital.
Nephrologist S. Gowri, who is treating the girl, told reporters that the detailed medical examinations detected dangerously high levels of mercury in her blood and body.
“Mercury can severely damage the filtering units of the kidneys,” she said, adding that the girl had developed membranous nephropathy, a serious kidney condition that could lead to further complications if left untreated.
Tests conducted on the cream allegedly revealed mercury levels of 12,500 parts per million (ppm), against the normal permissible level of less than one ppm, the doctor said.
She said the findings allegedly revealed that the mercury-containing product had caused the kidney ailment.
Dr. Gowri cautioned people against advertisements promising instant results or rapid improvement in skin tone through fairness creams.
Those experiencing skin problems should consult a dermatologist and seek proper treatment instead of relying on such products, she said.
The girl said she had informed the company about the health problems but received no positive response.
The company initially said its senior officials would be informed, but subsequently stopped responding to her messages, she alleged.
The girl’s family has decided to initiate legal proceedings against the company in the consumer court.
They have not disclosed the name of the cream as they are proceeding with legal action.

Baramulla, Nov 24: Police conducted inspection drives in the jurisdictions of Police Post Wussan and Police Station Uri to ensure compliance with prescribed regulations and security guidelines by scrap dealers, pesticide shops, SIM card vendors and fertilizer dealers.
At Wussan, police inspected scrap dealers and pesticide shops, checking their sales records and CCTV systems. Shopkeepers were directed to adhere strictly to the prescribed standard operating procedures (SOPs). Notices were also served to establishments without CCTV cameras, asking them to install functional surveillance systems at the earliest.
Meanwhile, Police Station Uri conducted a checking drive in the Main Market Uri, inspecting three SIM card vendors and two fertilizer shops. Their records, registers and relevant documents were scrutinised to verify proper documentation and compliance with established guidelines.
SIM card vendors were directed to ensure proper customer verification, maintain updated sales records and follow prescribed norms while issuing new SIM cards. Fertilizer dealers were instructed to maintain proper stock registers, sales records and purchaser details to ensure transparency and prevent unauthorised sale or misuse.
All establishments were also directed to install and maintain functional CCTV cameras to ensure effective surveillance of their premises. Police reiterated that such inspection and verification drives would continue across the district to ensure compliance with regulations, strengthen security arrangements and prevent the misuse of regulated goods and services.

Hospitals worldwide are ill-equipped to assess whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems deployed in their facilities actually improve patient outcomes, raising questions about the clinical and economic value of healthcare AI, Emmanuel Bacry, Scientific Director of France’s Health Data Hub, said at the Bengaluru Tech Summit.
“There are maybe six or seven hospitals in the whole world today that are able to evaluate medical devices deployed in their system,” Mr. Bacry said. Hospitals struggle to access and integrate patient information to track outcomes after discharge, including recovery rates and mortality, making it difficult to establish the actual impact of AI-based medical technologies.
“In hospitals, we don’t know how to compute that,” he said, referring to the return on investment of such technologies. “So imagine now, if they adopt AI.”
Unintended consequences
Mr. Bacry cited an alert system based on rules-based AI, or an expert system, designed to warn intensive care unit (ICU) staff about severe kidney failure. Despite functioning effectively, the system was associated with a doubling of deaths in two of the six US hospitals where it was deployed in 2022, he said. He did not identify the study.
While researchers had offered hypotheses, the precise cause remained unknown. Mr. Bacry suggested that the absence of a tested response protocol among hospital personnel could have contributed to the outcome.
“We just replaced the alert done by a human with the alert done by the medical device. And that changes the whole thing,” he said, underlining the importance of integrating AI into clinical workflows rather than treating it as a standalone technology.
He also cautioned against evaluating diagnostic AI tools solely through laboratory accuracy scores or comparisons with doctors. A system achieving 95% accuracy against a doctor’s 90% might not necessarily perform better in clinical settings. “When you deploy in real life, you can forget about these scores,” he said.
The black-box dilemma
Mr. Bacry flagged another concern: AI systems can identify patterns that even their developers cannot explain. Citing research, he said one model predicted ethnicity from chest X-rays with approximately 85% accuracy, while another inferred sex from eye images with 95% accuracy.
Such hidden correlations could influence medical decisions without clinicians understanding the underlying basis, potentially introducing unintended bias into diagnosis and treatment.
Western bias in healthcare datasets
In a separate interaction with The Hindu, Mr. Bacry warned that healthcare AI development was heavily skewed towards Western populations. By his estimate, nearly 70% of global healthcare AI training data came from male, white and Western populations.
“We are developing an Occidental AI and even narrow types of Occidental AI,” he said.
He advocated smaller, locally tailored AI models trained on representative population data, arguing that deploying large, general-purpose models without adaptation could have disastrous consequences, particularly in developing countries.
Mr. Bacry heads the Health Data Hub, established under French law in 2019 to facilitate secondary use of health data for research. He is also a research director at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) at Université Paris Dauphine–PSL.

Quick Answer
Nothing OS 5 brings a bunch of useful upgrades, from on-phone widget creation and new lockscreen clocks to split Quick Settings, Dual-View Video, easier iPhone sharing, the Glyph app, translucent themes, smarter QR scanning, and the new Geist font.
Nothing has updated all of its eligible devices to the latest version of its operating system, Nothing OS 5. It runs on top of Android 17, and in typical Nothing tradition, is clean and uncluttereds. And while it might seem broadly similar to its predecessor, there are a number of interesting new features – some important, some seemingly trivial – beneath that familiar surface. So if you have a Nothing phone and it has received the Nothing OS 5 update (there is a list of supported devices with rollout timelines here: https://in.nothing.tech/nothing-os), here are eleven things you must try out.
Table of Contents
Appy fizz: Now build snazzy widgets right on your phone, no coding experience required
One of the biggest innovations of the Nothing ecosystem was the introduction of Essential apps that let users, even with no coding knowledge, make widgets. In the past, you had to access Essential Apps on a computer to be able to make these widgets. Now you can do so right on your phone. And it is as easy as easy peasy apple squeezie. Mind you, you still need to sign up for Essential Apps and be part of a waiting list before you can get into design mode. No download is needed – the Essential Apps app comes to your Nothing phone when you update the phone to Nothing OS 5.g
Get a gooey or an info-loaded lockscreen clock!
On to the really serious stuff now. Perhaps the most noticeable visual change in NothingOS is the addition of two lockscreen clock widgets – Gooey and Micrographics. The Gooey clock has a bold and fluid look, with numbers looking a little melted. It is very eye-catching and, well, different. Those who want a truckload of information on their lockscreen and who opt for Micrographics get details like day, date, weather, temperature, upcoming appointments, and, of course, the time, all in rows that give it a very business ticker feel. This is how you clock into this feature:
- Long-press on the lock screen of your phone. This will show a Customize lock screen text bubble. Tap on it, and then tap on the fingerprint scanner to get into the Lock screen edit zone.
- Tap the clock widget space, which shows the time, and you will see Clock face options.
- Gooey is the second option, and right next to it is Micrographics. Choose the one you want, and also tweak its color as per your wish.
- Tap on Done, and hey, it’s, well…done.
Our own preference is the Micrographics widget, which is incredibly handy. We hope they add email and other notifications to it as well.
Split those notifications and quick settings
In the past – as on many phones – swiping down on a Nothing phone showed one new notifications, and swiping further down gave one access to Quick Settings (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Brightness, Torch, et al.). Well, you can split them into two separate zones if you wish. Once done, swiping from one side of the top will give you access to Quick Settings, while swiping from the other will show notifications. To do this segregation, just follow these steps:
- Open Settings and go to Notifications
- Go to the Notifications and Quick Settings Option
- You will see two options: Separate and Combined (classic).
- Select Separate, and now Notifications and Quick Settings will occupy different parts of the top panel.
Find out how long you have been away from your phone
One of the coolest new widgets on Nothing OS 5 is the Away Time widget, which lets you know how long you have kept away from your phone, and shows it in a simple, clean widget that can be placed on your home screen or your lock screen. It is a nice way to know about the “me time” you have given yourself away from your phone. Getting it is as easy as pressing on any place on the lock screen or Home Screen, and then selecting the Away Time widget option. We suggest going for the larger (4 x 2) one because it just looks so much better, especially with that zen-like blue background.
Keep what matters on the Home Screen – use Collector
Another widget (yes, Nothing seems to really like them widgets) that is very handy is Collector. You just open it and place images of what you want to keep seeing or consider important in it, and it automatically cuts out what it sees as important and keeps it handy on the home screen. It has a wonderful fridge sticker vibe, and keeps what matters close at hand. Just long-press on the home screen and select it from the widget collection!
Glyph Interface? There’s an app for that – finally!
The Glyph Interface has been one of the most eye-catching features of Nothing’s phones. This is basically a collection of LEDs on the back of the phones that light up in different patterns, showing notifications and battery levels, letting you know who is calling, controlling volume, setting timers, and doing more, all on the back of the phone. There was a catch, though. The Glyph UI had to be controlled from the settings of the phone, which seemed to be a rather roundabout way of doing things. This has now been fixed with the Glyph app, which gives one direct access to the Glyph Interface, letting one tweak it without having to get into the Settings. No downloads needed – the Glyph app appears on your Nothing phone the moment you update it to Nothing OS 5.
Lights, camera action…with both front and back cameras
Nothing OS 5 gives you the option to shoot videos using the rear as well as the front camera simultaneously. One can choose from having the footage one below the other, or having the selfie camera in an inset and the main camera in the larger part of the display. To access the option:
- Launch the Camera app
- Scroll across to More and choose Dual-View Video
It would have been nice to be able to take some stills with this feature, but as of now, it is limited to video.
There’s a glassy, classy “translucent” theme
Yep, your Nothing phone is now on the glass UI bandwagon. Mind you, this option is not turned on by default. You will need to follow these steps:
- Go to Settings, and then choose Customization
- Choose Theme & Style, and then choose Translucent. You can opt to have a dark theme in this if you wish.
- Honestly, it is not exactly eye-popping as of now. The translucence seems mainly to be around the widgets, and the app icons are not translucent. But it is a good starting point.
Scan that QR code, even if it wobbles
This is a pretty minor and yet handy change in Nothing OS 5. While camera icons have all been polished, a tiny yet useful tweak is in scanning QR codes, especially when using the scanner in crowded places or in slightly wobbly situations (think of paying in a moving vehicle). Now, when you use the camera to scan a QR code, the link it leads to remains on the screen, even if your hand moves and the QR code goes off or the code itself wobbles a little. So scanning codes is a whole lot easier, and you don’t have to bother about lining up the camera with the QR code all the time.
Send images to THAT friend with the iPhone easily (no app needed)
With Nothing OS 5, sending images to iPhones is pretty easy. Here’s how you do it:
- Ask your friend to switch on AirDrop on their iPhone and allow everyone to send images to it.
- Select the images you want to send on your Nothing phone.
- Select the Quick Share option, and then select the Use QR Code option.
- Scan the QR code with the iPhone’s camera. The images will be transferred.
Get the new font, Geist
Nothing’s marketing communications look very distinct because they use a font called Geist. Well, with NothingOS 5, you can now use Geist as the default font on their Nothing phones. This is how one does it:
- Head off to Settings again, and this time go to Display.
- Choose Font & Display Size.
- Once there, you can choose Geist as your default font.
- Once again, the difference is not going to jump out at you, but will become apparent as you use the phone.

Arteta says Arsenal need more luck to kill off games
- Published
It might be emerging more as a theme than as a major problem, but in recent weeks Arsenal cannot seem to finish off matches when they are on top.
In their past nine outings across all competitions, just once have the Gunners won a game by more than a single goal.
The latest frustration came in Tuesday's 1-1 draw with Borussia Dortmund, though perspective is needed. Arsenal might consider it as two points dropped having gone into half-time ahead, but they remain unbeaten in the current Champions League league phase and have not lost at this stage of the competition for more than two years.
But of late, despite dominating large parts of matches, Arsenal have had periods where they have dropped off and allowed opponents back into the game.
Against Slavia Prague away in the Champions League, after scoring twice in the first half, Arsenal's standards dropped. The same happened against Newcastle in the Premier League last weekend where they found themselves 2-1 behind in the second half having led at the break, before recovering to eventually draw 2-2.
They are producing periods of high-level football, but the struggles to consistently turn that into more goals can lead to nervy finishes.
In the draw with Bundesliga leaders Dortmund, Arsenal had 30 shots but just four of those attempts were on target.
Boss Mikel Arteta mentioned the failure to capitalise post match, though was keen to praise his side's "brilliant performance".
"The way we played, bearing in mind the opposition that we played today and what we've done out there, is just something to be very, very pleased [about] because there is very little more that you can demand from the team," Arteta said.
"But obviously, the feeling is that we should reward ourselves much more when you put that kind of performance in the amount of chances (and) situations.
"There is an element of luck; there is an element of us finishing the actions better. We need to insist because I think what the team has done and shown today, I think it's the right direction."
Missing chances or need more luck?
Arteta made six changes to the side that drew with Newcastle, with one of the biggest calls to rest striker Kai Havertz and bring in Viktor Gyokeres.
The striker has had a difficult season so far, with four of his seven starts coming in the Champions League against opposition where Arsenal have been favourites.
However, Gyokeres scored a powerful effort from outside the area to give Arsenal the lead against Dortmund.
Overall though, it ended up being a mixed night for the 28-year-old as he missed a header from inside the six-yard-box that would have surely won the game for the Gunners late on.
Arteta was asked if the chances his side are missing were down to mentality, misfortune or composure.
"Mentality, I don't know," he said.
"There is an element of luck here because how some of the goals they haven't gone inside, I don't know.
"The execution can be better, but everything that is in between that, I think it was really, really good."
Arteta was also full of praise for Gyokeres, with particular emphasis on the striker's link-up play; an element of his game at times criticised.
"What I love the most is how connected he was to the team," Arteta said.
"We used him many times in different ways. His link-up play, the way he held the ball, the way he threaded in behind and stretched the pitch.
"There was a lot to like in that performance and that's the Viktor that we needed."
City up next for the Gunners
Noni Madueke has been Arsenal's best attacker in recent weeks.
The winger, who was left out of the last England squad, is enjoying a run in the Arsenal starting XI with Bukayo Saka out injured and is taking his opportunity.
Madueke has registered a goal and two assists in his past three games and was again the best Arsenal forward against Dortmund.
The Gunners host Manchester City on Sunday and are currently six points clear at the top of the Premier League table.
Madueke, who was frustrated with the performance against Dortmund, said the clash with third-placed City is a great chance to get back to winning ways and shake off any frustration.
"I think these are the best games. I'm really looking forward to it. Two draws on the bounce now and I just desperately want to win on the weekend and I know my team-mates feel the same," Madueke told Amazon Prime.
"We are going to do everything we have to win the three points. We're champions, we're at home. We have a duty to perform well at the Emirates.
"There are things we need to improve but all in all we are going in the right direction."

DR Congo says military aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
- Published
The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.
The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.
On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a warplane that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.
Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.
The BBC has not independently verified the rebels' claim.
It is also unclear whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one rebels say they shot down.
Uganda's military on Monday denied any involvement.

A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company."
The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.
Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".
Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.
In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.
He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors.
South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".
"Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.
In 2022, DR Congo's army blamed M23 rebels, who are now part of the FRN, of shooting down a UN helicopter in which eight people died. The rebels denied it.
The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.
In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.
The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.
Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.
Over the weekend, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.
The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

The 60th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu looks at key developments in public including healthcare financing, reproductive health, antimicrobial resistance, tuberculosis, environmental exposures and diabetes care.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss the latest National Health Accounts estimates for 2023–24, which show a substantial increase in government health expenditure and a decline in the share of household out-of-pocket spending nationally. The episode also examines the contrasting trends in Keralam, where household healthcare expenditure has increased and the share of government spending has declined.
The episode looks at the drug regulator’s direction to pharmaceutical companies to comply with revised prices for 137 anti-cancer drugs and the potential implications for treatment costs. It also examines concerns over an illegal human egg collection racket in Telangana, including questions about informed consent, women’s safety and the regulation of assisted reproductive technology centres. Developments in Karnataka’s proposed mid-life women’s health programme and mandatory gynaecological check-ups for girls are also discussed.
Marking World AMR Awareness Week, the episode explores the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance and the need for appropriate antibiotic use, timely diagnosis, infection prevention and surveillance. It also discusses phage therapy, which uses bacteriophages to target bacterial infections, and its potential role in addressing infections that do not respond to conventional antibiotics.
The discussion also examines tuberculosis through the lens of social and economic vulnerability, highlighting the importance of nutrition, housing and social support alongside diagnosis and treatment. It looks at the latest figures on domestic funding for India’s TB response, which now accounts for 86% of total spending, even as external funding declines.
The discussion also examines the health risks of extreme heat for pregnant women and newborns. A survey of healthcare professionals across five countries found that 98% of Indian clinicians surveyed had treated pregnant women and newborns whose health they believed had been affected by extreme heat.
The episode also looks into how fear of diagnosis may discourage people from screening and discusses a Chennai initiative that uses dietary counselling by staff nurses to improve blood sugar control and support long-term diabetes management.

Bausch + Lomb said on Thursday its experimental eye-drop treatment failed to show a significant reduction in pain over the first 24 hours after laser eye surgery in a mid-stage study. However, the drug showed signs of benefit in secondary and exploratory analyses, including greater pain relief shortly after surgery and faster corneal healing.
The mid-stage trial tested two doses of BL1332 in 129 patients undergoing photorefractive keratectomy (PRK), a laser procedure used to correct vision. At six hours after surgery, complete pain relief was reported by 14% and 14.6% of patients receiving the two doses, compared with 3.7% of patients receiving a placebo.
Ocular surface pain is a common complication of eye surgery and certain eye diseases. The company said there are currently no approved treatments that directly target its underlying nerve pathways.
Bausch + Lomb said it plans to discuss the results with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration as it considers next steps for the drug, including a potential late-stage trial. Shares of the eye-care company fell 1.4% in extended trading.

An email intended for internal administrative communication ended up revealing some unwelcome news to employees of Australia's National Australia Bank (NAB). Several workers learnt that their jobs could be at risk through an automated notification before their managers had a chance to speak to them.
The bank has apologised after accidentally sending redundancy-related emails to employees before formally informing them about the outcome of their voluntary exit applications. The affected staff members were supposed to receive the decisions directly from their managers. However, an administrative or technical error resulted in the automated emails reaching them before those conversations could take place.
According to Reuters, NAB acknowledged the mistake and said it understood that receiving such news unexpectedly could cause distress.
"We are very sorry this happened, and that receiving an automated email this way would be upsetting and unsettling to many," the bank said in a statement shared with Reuters.
NAB said the notifications were not meant to be sent before employees were informed of the decisions through direct conversations. Following the incident, the bank said it would bring forward discussions with the affected workers.
The email blunder comes as the Australian lender prepares for a major workforce restructuring. Last month, NAB announced plans to cut 2,500 jobs over the next 12 months, affecting approximately 6% of its total workforce.
The bank said the restructuring is intended to simplify its operations and lower costs. As many as 1,500 roles, primarily across corporate functions, are expected to be affected by the end of this year.
NAB's planned workforce reduction comes amid a wider wave of layoffs across Australia. Several companies, including Qantas, Canva, WiseTech and Atlassian, have also announced job cuts this year.
For employees seeking voluntary redundancy, the process can already involve considerable uncertainty. Workers have to wait to find out whether their applications have been accepted, when their employment will end and what steps they need to take next.
Receiving an unexpected automated email about an employment decision before a formal conversation with management can make an already stressful situation even more difficult.
Businesses are increasingly turning to automated systems to handle routine employee communications, including recruitment updates, onboarding instructions, payroll notifications and internal announcements.
While these tools help organisations save time and manage communication more efficiently, the NAB incident highlights the potential risks of using automation to deliver sensitive employment-related decisions that can directly affect people's livelihoods.

Welshmen Donald & Salt demolish Australia as England level series
- Published
Second T20, Carrara
Australia 184-8 (20 overs): Chaudhary 45 (35); Curran 2-29
England 188-2 (13.1 overs): Donald 85 (32); Meredith 1-18
England won by eight wickets; series level 1-1
An astonishing opening partnership of 151 in 10 overs between England's Aneurin Donald and Phil Salt demolished Australia and levelled the T20 series on the Gold Coast.
Welshman Donald blitzed 85 from 32 balls, including nine sixes, while his compatriot Salt made 58 off 30 as England cruised to their target of 184 in just 13.1 overs.
Donald's 18-ball fifty was the joint third-fastest for England in the format as the pair raced to 79-0 in the powerplay, flogging Australia's wilting second-string bowling attack to all corners of the ground in a remarkable display of power hitting.
Salt, who was dropped by Joel Davies on 10, was mostly able to watch from the non-striker's end before accelerating to a 24-ball half-century of his own, which came during a brutal over from spinner Davies that went for 31.
Donald looked gutted to miss out on a century after he holed out to long-on off Riley Meredith's bowling, before Salt was brilliantly caught and bowled by Ben Dwarshuis an over later.
England's phenomenal top order - which still awaits the return of Jos Buttler from injury - finished the job with ease as Tom Banton finished unbeaten on 26 off eight balls including a monstrous six for the winning runs.
Australia's 184-8 looked competitive at the halfway mark on a surface that had assisted England's spinners and Sam Curran's slower balls - the hosts recovering from a stodgy middle over period after falling to 58-4 in the powerplay.
Davies added a handy cameo of 38 before Dwarshuis whacked Curran's last three balls for six to finish strongly but within just a few overs of the chase, Donald and Salt had silenced a lively Australian crowd in style.
The five-match series continues at the Gabba, Brisbane, on Friday.
Destructive Donald makes his mark
Donald made his T20 debut as a 29-year-old earlier this summer on the back of consistent county and Hundred performances, but struggled to really cement his place with 56 runs in four innings.
Still, a player known for an incredible strike-rate in particular, he was backed by Harry Brook and Brendon McCullum to play freely and showcased that strength against an Australia attack that had no answers.
Brook himself said he was "speechless" at the end of the game, high praise from one of the world's best, as Donald and Salt made what could have been a tricky chase look like a stroll in the park.
Only three international T20s had been held at the Gold Coast's Carrara Oval previously so England were in relatively unknown territory.
Not that it mattered to Donald, who swatted Davies for four from his first ball to start the demolition, and carried on in his usual leg-side dominant fashion.
His first couple of sixes off Jack Edwards sailed into the crowd despite looking like he had not timed them perfectly, giving Australia captain Mitch Marsh a bit of insight into Donald as his new Perth Scorchers team-mate when the Big Bash League starts later in the winter.
Though the pitch had looked difficult to face spin in Australia's innings, Donald and Salt both tucked into it with aplomb - before Salt's takedown of Davies, Donald clubbed Nikhil Chaudhary for 26 to bring up his fifty by the end of the fifth over.
Donald's showcase gives England a nice headache at the top of the order, with Buttler and Jacob Bethell still to come back into the fold - a frightening prospect for opposition bowlers.
- Donald aims for England T20 chance in Australia 
  - Published27 minutes ago
England's mixed bowling still a cause for concern
Despite the batting brilliance, there were mixed fortunes for England's bowlers with a contrast between their spinners and seamers.
Australia's powerplay was bizarre. Their run-rate was healthy, just shy of 10 runs an over, but they threw away four wickets which meant they had to be more cautious throughout the middle.
Marsh was caught and bowled by Henry Crocombe, Jake Fraser-McGurk was out slogging to Curran before debutant James Coles produced a fine run out to get rid of Sam Harper.
Coles then took the catch in the deep to get rid of Tim David, and that allowed the masterful Adil Rashid and Liam Dawson to get to work, bowling seven overs on the bounce as Australia's middle order came to a standstill.
Rashid tied Lachlan Shaw and Joel Davies in knots early on as they struggled to pick up his variations before he removed the former for a stodgy 10 from 17 balls.
Davies dug in before accelerating at the death, with assistance from the big-hitting Edwards as Jamie Overton's struggles continued.
The 18th over conceded 16 as he only bowled two overs for 28, before Crocombe's penultimate over flew for 16 and Dwarshuis got to work on Curran, who was also taken apart in the final over in Australia's win on Saturday.
Unfortunately for Curran, he had previously been sensational at mixing up his pace deceptively and had figures of 2-9 off his first three, but completely lost control of his yorkers in the final three balls which the powerful Dwarshuis sent flying.
England will be grateful for the return of Jofra Archer to their ranks as their difficulties at closing out an innings are becoming a concern.

Enterprise AI startup AidenAI has raised $32 Mn (₹297.1 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by growth investment firm A91 Partners, as it looks to expand its AI platform and engineering capabilities. The fresh capital will be used to invest in its platform and engineering talent as it looks to scale its global enterprise AI business. “With A91 as our partner, we are excited to invest in our people and platforms and help shape the next wave of enterprise technology services,” AidenAI founder and CEO Srinivas Kamadi said. How AidenAI Builds Its Enterprise AI Business Kamadi founded AidenAI in 2023 after spending nearly two decades with Infosys. Drawing on his experience of leading digital transformation at the company, Kamadi launched AidenAI to solve a recurring bottleneck faced by large enterprises: enterprise AI was stuck in the experimentation phase because outdated legacy systems made digital transformation too slow. The New Jersey-based startup, whose majority of workforce is based out of Hyderabad, helps large enterprises integrate AI into existing applications, data infrastructure and business workflows. Its proprietary AI Builder Platform is designed to help businesses move beyond AI experimentation and deploy AI applications within their existing tech infrastructure. This platform connects with an enterprise's existing systems and AI models, providing tools for AI agents. The startup also offers AiDAP, an AI-driven technology modernisation platform that helps enterprises modernise legacy software systems. This positions AidenAI in the enterprise AI implementation market, where businesses are increasingly looking for solutions to integrate AI into business-critical operations rather than deploy standalone tools. “While enterprise AI adoption is still in its early stages, AidenAI has spent the last 3 years helping over 30 large enterprises turn the promise of AI into live, measurable business outcomes," said A91 Partners' partner Kaushik Anand. AidenAI's Bet On Frontier AI Engineering Alongside its platform expansion, AidenAI plans to build a team of more than 1,000 frontier AI engineers through its AidenAI Builder Academy. The academy is designed to develop forward-deployed engineering talent that can work directly with enterprise clients to build and deploy production-ready AI applications using the company's platform and frontier AI models. The expansion comes as enterprises increasingly explore agentic AI applications to automate complex, multi-step workflows across functions such as finance, insurance, healthcare and human resources. AidenAI aims to tap this demand by combining AI agents, enterprise software modernisation and specialised engineering services. This comes as the broader Indian enterprise AI market, which was valued at $11 Bn in 2025, is projected to reach $71 Bn by 2030, according to Inc42’s Bharat AI Startups Report 2026. The Inc42 Take: Can AidenAI Scale Its Enterprise AI Platform? As more companies adopt GenAI in their daily operations, demand is growing for providers that can build and deploy AI solutions at an enterprise scale. AidenAI is positioning itself at this intersection via its AI Builder Platform and engineering-led deployment model. Its presence across six countries and a client base of over 30 enterprises provide an early indication of market traction. However, the startup’s ability to scale will depend on how effectively it can standardise its platform across enterprise customers with different technology infrastructure and business requirements.

It’s been a tremendous year for MacBooks. Between the launch of the MacBook Neo and the OLED MacBook Pro, there’s never been such a wide variety of Apple laptops to choose from.

MacBook Air for $310 Off
The M5 MacBook Air is the laptop most people should buy, and right now it’s $989, or $310 off its regular $1,299 price. This is the first time the MacBook Air has dropped below $1,000 since the June price hike. This is a fantastic deal for what you get: 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and all the other Mac hardware excellence we’ve come to expect.
And while it’s true we may see an M6 refresh in the MacBook Air sometime in the first quarter of 2027, I wouldn’t wait. From my testing of the M6 MacBook Pro, I don’t think it’ll be worth the extra $300 when the M6 MacBook Air eventually lands, especially since we're not expecting anything beyond a minor chip bump this time around. The M5 is still ahead of the competition in performance and can handle heavier workflows and applications than you might assume.
I’ll also note that the larger 15-inch model is on sale right now. It’s down 20 percent to $1,199, which is also a new low for this laptop. The 15-inch MacBook Air is identical to the smaller model in most ways, including display quality, ports, and performance. Aside from the dramatic difference in screen size, the 15-inch MacBook Air’s only other advantage is its speakers. They are loud, clear, and full of bass—and a big upgrade over the 13-inch MacBook Air.
MacBook Neo for $50 Off
The MacBook Neo is Apple’s first true entry-level laptop, and unfortunately, it’s only gotten more expensive since it was announced. The Neo was first announced starting at $599. That price rose to $699 in June and has largely held steady since. But finally, Amazon has started selling it for $50 off, bringing it down to $649.
Now, choosing between this and the MacBook Air can be tricky. Read my full comparison for all the details, but I would only buy the Neo for a student or perhaps someone with more limited computing needs. Put it this way: If you sit in front of a computer all day for work, it’s worth springing for the MacBook Air for the extra memory and performance alone. You’ll also appreciate the faster ports and storage, backlit keyboard, better speakers, and Touch ID.
MacBook Pro M6 for $50 Off
The 14-inch MacBook Pro is currently the only MacBook in the lineup to get the latest M6 chip. That doesn’t mean it’s the most powerful MacBook Pro, though, as the M5 Pro and M5 Max are still the options you want for true Pro-level performance. For now, the M6 MacBook Pro beats the M5 MacBook Air, but the M6 may arrive in the Air in a few months, so why pay more for the M6 MacBook Pro now? Well, it’s for someone who wants the premium experience of a brighter, HDR-ready screen. It also offers more storage, more ports, and broader external display support than the Air.
And while this deal isn’t a massive cut, it’s pretty impressive for a newly launched MacBook Pro. It’s only $30 more than the M5 MacBook Pro at this point.
