India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
- Published
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction.
The contrast between the two leaders was striking.
Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor.
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India.
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service.
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties.
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths.
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year.
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones.
The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan".
Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure.
While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy.
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India.
Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old.
His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.
According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs.
"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism."
Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions".
There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit.
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity.
The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita.
There was, however, disappointment on aviation.
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara.
Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects.
"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat.
India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional.
"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough."
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours.
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

Maharashtra GST authorities have initiated inspection, search and seizure proceedings against Turtlemint Insurance Broking Services (TIB), a wholly owned subsidiary of listed insurtech company Turtlemint Fintech Solutions. Turtlemint, in an exchange filing, said the proceedings began yesterday at the subsidiary’s registered office in Andheri East, Mumbai under Section 67 of the Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. The company did not disclose the specific alleged violations or a tax demand. It said the financial, operational, or other impact could not currently be quantified because the proceedings were ongoing. “TIB is extending full cooperation to the concerned authorities and is providing the requisite information, documents and clarifications as may be required in connection with the proceedings,” it said. Turtlemint added that regular business operations at both the parent company and its subsidiary remain unaffected. It said it would inform the stock exchanges of further developments, including the conclusion of the proceedings. Inside Turtlemint’s Distribution Business Founded in 2015 by Dhirendra Mahyavanshi and Anand Prabhudesai, Turtlemint operates an insurance distribution platform that enables financial advisors to sell motor, health, and life insurance. Its model combines an advisor network with digital tools for comparing and selling policies, training, and back-end support. The company earns revenue through commissions and fees from insurers and other financial services providers. Turtlemint had a digital partner network of over 6.59 Lakh at the end of FY26, following the addition of more than 1.15 Lakh partners during the year. It worked with 46 insurer partners and issued 7.83 Mn policies in FY26. The GST proceedings come less than five months after the company’s stock market debut in June. Its ₹882.7 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of ₹660.7 Cr and an offer for sale of 1.46 Cr shares. Its shares listed at ₹136.20 on the BSE, a 10.4% discount to the ₹152 issue price. The GST action adds to regulatory concerns surrounding Turtlemint, whose shares have faced selling pressure following IRDAI’s draft proposals to cap insurance commissions, potentially squeezing its distribution revenue. On the financial front, the company reported a 67% YoY reduction in its net loss to ₹25.8 Cr in Q2 FY27. Operating revenue increased 35.3% YoY to ₹342.2 Cr. Sequentially, revenue grew 16%, while net loss narrowed 32% from ₹37.8 Cr. Shares of the company ended today’s trading session 0.60% lower at ₹64.63 on the BSE.

Last week, the parent of Bombay Shaving Company, Visage Lines Personal Care, made an unexpected move by entering the recovery and wellness market with the launch of rE, a new brand offering massage guns, foam rollers, scalp massagers and other recovery products. The move is particularly interesting because the two categories are not just poles apart but also huge markets with enormous scope for vertical expansion. Let’s quickly steal a glance at some numbers. While the total personal care market in India is set to touch $40 Bn+ by 2034, another lucrative category is gaining ground. Once restricted to sports medicine and professional athletes, at-home recovery products (including percussion massagers, foam rollers, thermal therapy) have become everyday wellness essentials for people grappling with stress, poor sleep and posture, and muscle fatigue. In fact, some reports already peg the market for at-home recovery and massage devices alone at over $400 Mn. But Bombay Shaving Company isn't the only one that decided to slide into untested waters. Earlier this year, we witnessed men’s fashion brand Snitch foray into the travel gear market with their ‘luggage’ category. Cult.fit, a widely recognised gym chain, is positioning its sneakers for “non-gym, all-day moves”. In fact, Cult has already created a large portfolio of daily athleisure, relaxation and recovery gadgets, hydration products and more. These aren't new brands trying to find their product-market fit but the ones that have already made it to crossing ₹1,000 Cr in revenue or are running their annualised run rates quite close to that number. This makes us ponder: are D2C brands simply getting more ambitious, or is staying in their own lane becoming a little too limiting for their growth ambitions? How are these brands deciding which new categories to enter and what amount of resources to allocate? Let’s check out... Opening A New Turf: A Need Or Ambition? It's both. According to Inc42’s D2C 3.0 Report 2026, India’s D2C gross merchandise value (GMV) is projected to reach $310 Bn+ by 2031, growing at a CAGR of roughly 37% from $65 Bn in 2026. Yet, several prominent Indian D2C and consumer brands remain in the red — often despite strong top-line growth — as expenses, customer acquisition, or expansion costs continue to weigh on their bottom lines. The reason is simple: Once a brand reaches the limits of growth in its core market, it needs new avenues to expand. Launching a new brand allows it to tap into fresh categories, attract new customers and generate more revenue from its existing customer base. Ideally, the smart moves are adjacent rather than unrelated, so the playbook and learnings carry over. Besides, rising customer acquisition costs make it imperative for a brand to sell across categories. “It’s similar to how wealth management firms operate. Once a customer is acquired, the same firm can offer everything from FDs and broking services to F&O trading and pension plans. So, why spend more on acquiring new customers when you can sell more to the ones you already have?” said a sectoral expert. This, however, doesn't mean that a consumer who trusts a brand for one product will automatically buy everything else it launches. This is also where the choice of category becomes important. Brands need to identify their own strengths that can work to their advantage even in an entirely new market. Varun Gupta, the cofounder of rE and CMO of Bombay Shaving Company, cited three key factors behind entering a new market. “One is we are very consumer-obsessed. We talk to the consumers a lot. We understand how they use products, what their journeys are in life. Second, we know how to tell great stories. And third is our sourcing and product are extremely robust and efficient,” Gupta said. But flip the coin, and a rather exciting side of this story emerges. Until a few years ago, entering a new category meant building distribution networks, spending heavily on marketing and waiting months, sometimes years, to see whether consumers would even bite. Today, quick commerce can put a new product in front of consumers across multiple cities within weeks. Celebrity partnerships are also rewriting the marketing playbook. Instead of spending a fortune on endorsements, brands are onboarding celebrities as equity-holding cofounders. With this, they are turning their influence into a long-term customer acquisition engine. The Brand Architecture Dilemma Two brands in different categories don't necessarily mean two separate companies running two entirely different operations. “When a new brand is launched, functions such as HR, finance, supply chain, warehouses and even ecommerce relationships can remain common. So, it starts with having a different category marketing team. Everything else is shared,” said Gupta. And this is precisely what makes the multi-brand model tempting for companies that have an established core operations team. According to the founder of TDV Partners, Ujwal Sutaria, customer data, performance marketing expertise, distribution relationships and backend operations can carry over. However, product expertise and credibility in the new category still have to be earned. Therefore, brands must spend time identifying what deserves a separate name and what can continue running behind the scenes as one business. This is crucial because while sharing resources can make expansion more economical, maintaining multiple identities means multiple sets of expectations. And that’s where the excitement of building a brand portfolio begins to meet the realities of running one. Beware Of The Burn For brands already struggling to turn growing revenues into profits, one wrong bet could make the burn even worse. As highlighted by 3One4 Capital’s founding partner Pranav Pai, each category operates on its own set of variables: repeat cycle, ticket size, gross margin band, trust threshold, regulatory burdens, and service obligation. One vertical may run at low ticket sizes, high repeat and moderate margin, with replenishment measured in weeks. Another may be a single high-ticket purchase carrying warranty, after-sales commitments and a replacement cycle measured in years. So, even with an identical customer, the economics for both are not always comparable, and working capital, team composition and channel mix shift accordingly. Brand architecture is another constraint. A brand is a living entity with its own appeal and its own approachability, and it has to hold trust for millions of customers rather than reflect a single founder's preferences. “Expanding into a segment where it has little credibility could dilute the trust and reputation built in its core market, a cost that is difficult to quantify at the time of launch,” Pai said. While launching and testing new brands has become cheaper in India, getting customers to return and buy again remains just as challenging. This is where one needs to observe whether a brand can stand on its own financially, operate under dedicated leadership, offer something genuinely different and benefit from the parent company's existing infrastructure. The success of multi-brand companies also depends on how efficiently their supply chains, distribution and operations are being managed. The winners, therefore, won't necessarily be those launching the most brands, but those who hit the bull’s eye on what consumers want. THE STARTUP SPOTLIGHT | HOW AMNECT IS REINVENTING NUTRITION WITH GUMMIES Amnect Care is addressing age-related health concerns through its portfolio of specialised, sugar-free gummies targeting bone health, joint mobility, digestion, sleep quality and overall wellbeing, positioning them as convenient alternatives to traditional supplements. The National Medical Commission (NMC) has de-notified and withdrawn the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 (MSMER-2023) where medical colleges were liable to face penalty fines for violations of educational standards and infrastructure requirements at medical colleges.
Earlier reports in The Hindu stated NMC’s withdrawal of MSMER-2023 weakens accountability in medical education by removing provisions to fine individual faculty members and administrators up to ₹5 lakh for submitting false information. Although the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) can still penalise institutions up to ₹1 crore under separate regulations, institutional penalties may be less effective in deterring individual misconduct. Misleading faculty declarations, inflated patient records, or inadequate clinical training going undetected could ultimately put patients at risk.
The NMC justified the withdrawal by arguing that MSMER created overlapping assessment powers with MARB. However, scrapping the regulations entirely raises questions about the necessity of this move, particularly when non-compliance remains common and transparency in medical education is inadequate. Moreover, conflicting appeal deadlines under MARB regulations and the NMC Act could lead to legal disputes and delay enforcement. Ultimately, the NMC must clarify whether the existing regulatory mechanisms are being effectively enforced and whether their outcomes are publicly accessible without which the withdrawal of MSMER risks appearing to be a relaxation of regulatory oversight rather than a simplification of rules.
Medical experts have further warned that deterrence against practices such as ghost faculty and fabricated patient records would potentially expose students and institutions to greater malpractice and mismanagement. While some experts support the removal of regulatory duplication, they emphasise that effective oversight depends on rigorous verification, transparent reporting, consistent penalties and time-bound enforcement. The NMC must therefore demonstrate that MARB can enforce standards as effectively as the withdrawn framework; otherwise, regulatory rationalisation risks becoming a dilution of accountability.
The NMC has clarified that the MSMER introduced a parallel mechanism through which the undergraduate and postgraduate boards could assess institutions, thereby encroaching on the MARB’s mandate. While talking to The Hindu, NMC officials said the denotification is aimed at simplifying regulatory procedures and eliminating overlapping responsibilities, without compromising the quality of medical education.

Hindu outfits clash with cops after Karthigai Deepam not lit as per SC's directions
Hindu outfits and BJP leaders reportedly staged a protest and got into a scuffle with the police in Tamil Nadu's Thiruparankundram on Tuesday.
A scuffle broke out in Tamil Nadu's Thiruparankundram on Tuesday evening after the Karthigai Deepam was lit at the usual spot instead of at ‘Deepathoon’, the stone pillar, as was ordered by the Supreme Court last week.
Hindu outfits and BJP leaders staged a protest and got into a scuffle with the police, reported news agency PTI.
The ceremonial lamp was lit atop the Arulmigu Uchipillayar Temple in Thiruparankundram, despite the Supreme Court's mandate of lighting it at the disputed stone pillar, or ‘deepathoon’, atop the Thiruparankundram hill.
The Supreme Court had permitted the lamp lighting as a one-time arrangement, noting that doing so would not establish any customary right to perform the ritual at the site in subsequent years.
Although the Karthigai Deepam was lit on Tuesday evening, it was not at the location permitted by the Supreme Court. Hindu outfits took strong objection to this and resorted to a sudden protest at Thirupparankundram.
The protesters demanded that the authorities implement the apex court directive as a one-time measure, and some of them were detained after a scuffle with the police, reported PTI.
‘TVK govt a bunch of cowards’
Tamil Nadu BJP leader Vinoj P Selvam also lashed out over the lamp lighting spot.
Hitting out at CM Vijay-led government, Selvam said: “The TVK Govt is a bunch of cowards who do minority appeasement and they want to hurt the sentiments of the majority of this country and the state. The BJP and all the Hindu organisations stand in solidarity with the Hindus, with the devotees of Lord Muruga. People of Tamil Nadu will teach a lesson that Chief Minister Joseph will never forget in his life…," he said.
Earlier today, Tamil Nadu BJP president Nainar Nagendran was briefly detained on his way Thiruparankundram to visit the Thiruparankundram Murugan Temple. He alleged he was stopped from offering prayers despite the absence of a legally valid prohibitory order.
"In the absence of any legally valid prohibitory order, the police are preventing me from visiting the temple to offer prayers. Preventing us from leaving our homes in the name of arrest amounts to a violation of an individual's fundamental rights," he said, as quoted by ANI.

- The claim that Etsy's new terms of service allows the company to train artificial intelligence technologies using artwork posted on its platform appears true at face value, although it's unclear whether the company has any plans to actually do that.
- Etsy's new terms of use state that the company and its third-party partners have the right to use content posted on its platform "to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies."
- In response to backlash from vendors, Etsy said it does not and will not "use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity."
- The same statement gives examples of ways Etsy uses vendor content, such as creating advertisements using listings from artists, but it doesn't clarify whether Etsy plans to use AI or generative AI for those purposes. As such, we have left this claim unrated.
A rumor is spreading that global e-commerce marketplace Etsy updated its terms of service to allow the company to train artificial intelligence systems using artwork posted on the platform.
The allegations have caused an uproar in small business and independent artist communities, as many rely on Etsy to make sales. Artists with tens of thousands of followers have shared Instagram and X posts declaring that they had closed their Etsy shops over the company's new AI policies.
For example, one post with nearly 100,000 likes as of this writing claims that, in plain English, Etsy's terms of service allows it to "train generative AI on our artwork."
"They can package and resell that data to third parties," the post continued. "Stay on the platform, and your art is theirs to scrape. Sell. Train."
Etsy has, in fact, updated its terms of use with a new AI policy, which go into effect Dec. 16. The plain text of the updated terms of use states that any content posted on Etsy can be used "to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies."
In response to the uproar, however, Etsy's vice president of customer operations, James Ossman, said in a Nov. 16 blog post (archived) that the company does not use AI to copy artwork, nor does it claim ownership over sellers' creations (emphasis theirs):
"We do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity. Again, this is not changing. Our goal at Etsy has always been to connect you and your unique items with buyers."
However, it's unclear whether Etsy might use AI to create content in ways that artists may consider as equivalent to an AI model being trained off of their work. For example, Etsy's statement says it may use seller content to feature listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns. Etsy has not clarified whether that means the company might use generative AI to create an advertisement that uses an artist's listing photo. 
We asked Etsy for further clarification and await a response. As such, we have left this claim unrated.
The changes to Etsy's terms of use come after the e-commerce marketplace released clearer restrictions on AI use in October.
"We recognize we haven't always addressed the topic of AI as directly or as quickly as you may have wanted. It's changing fast, and like many of you, we're thinking seriously about what it means for Etsy, what's allowed on our marketplace, and how it impacts running a creative business," a blog post from Ossman said about those regulations.
Etsy's new terms of use, annotated
The updated language on AI is under Section 5, "Your Content," in Etsy's terms of use, which is available in full (archived) on the company's website.
Both the new terms of use and the older terms of use, which is in effect through Dec. 15, state that Etsy does not claim ownership over sellers' content, but that it has broad rights to use sellers' content for Etsy's own purposes (underlined emphasis ours): 
Content that you post using our Services is your content (so let's refer to it as "Your Content"). We don't make any claim to it, which includes anything you post using our Services (like shop names, profile pictures, listing photos, listing descriptions, reviews, comments, videos, usernames, etc.).
B. Permission to Use Your Content. By posting Your Content through our Services, you grant Etsy and third parties authorized by Etsy in its sole discretion a license to use Your content, including to operate, provide, improve, and promote the Services. We don't claim ownership of Your Content, but we have your permission to use it to help Etsy function and grow.
The "Your Content" section then goes on to explain what rights Etsy has over seller content posted on its platform. The older version of the document includes no mention of artificial intelligence. The newer version adds the sentence we underlined below:
C. Rights You Grant Etsy. (Here's the legalese version of the last section). By posting Your Content, you grant Etsy and, as authorized by Etsy in its sole discretion, third parties, a non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free, irrevocable, sub-licensable, perpetual license to use, display, edit, modify, reproduce, distribute, store, and prepare derivative works from Your Content. This allows us to provide the Services and to promote Etsy, your Etsy shop, other shops and listings, or the Services in general, in any formats and through any channels, including across any Etsy Services, our partners, or third-party website or advertising medium. […] This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy.
Etsy acknowledges in its terms of use that providing the platform with these rights "sounds like a lot" but argues that it's "necessary for us to keep Etsy going." The company's examples for reasons why it might need these rights include resizing or enhancing seller listings to optimize them for its mobile app, translating descriptions into other languages and featuring seller listings in marketing campaigns.
While the new language states that creators may have opt-out rights, a review of the company's privacy policy and supplemental U.S.-specific privacy policy found no evidence Etsy sellers can opt out of AI training entirely. It does note, however that those in the United States have the right to opt out of sales of personal data. Different states also have different data privacy laws that may be applicable.
It is also worth noting that whether or not it's legal to scrape copyrighted content is an issue that's still being hammered out in the courts, so Etsy's statement that it does not have ownership over seller content does not necessarily mean it doesn't have the right to scrape that content.
Etsy's response to backlash
Etsy's Nov. 16 post about its changes to the company's terms of use provides several examples for how the company may use content to train AI models, but it doesn't appear to be a comprehensive list (emphasis theirs):
How we use your content to train AI models: We made an update to our terms that says Etsy and our partners may use member content to develop, train, test, and improve AI and machine learning technologies. This change is meant to clarify the ways we use AI in our marketplace.
We do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity. Again, this is not changing. Our goal at Etsy has always been to connect you and your unique items with buyers.
We will continue to focus on using AI to support sellers and improve the Etsy experience, and we're committed to being transparent about how we use this technology. Here are a few examples of how we are using AI on Etsy today:
- We train models to identify potentially fraudulent accounts and related listings, helping us investigate potential issues and protect our members.
- We use AI to understand the inventory across our marketplace, so we can help buyers find your items through search and provide them with tailored recommendations.
- We build AI-powered seller tools to help you run your business more efficiently, and better understand and meet your buyers' expectations.
Etsy's post also states that its terms of use "prohibit scraping Etsy or unauthorized use of content from Etsy to train AI models."
"We use security tools designed to detect and limit unauthorized scraping, and we are continuously improving our abilities to protect your content and keep Etsy safe," the statement said.
Notably, the statement does not make it clear whether Etsy itself or authorized third parties might be able to scrape Etsy content to train AI models. In fact, Etsy's terms of use specify that users cannot scrape any Etsy page for AI training "without our express permission."

India’s health services has banned reuse of single-use medical devices. But who decides what’s safe?
Unsafe reuse can harm patients, and billing for a reused device as if it were new is indefensible. But there is a bigger question that needs answering: who decides whether a device can be safely reprocessed, and on what evidence?
India should make more of its expensive medical devices at home and fund independent Indian studies on their safety, performance and value for money.

I was at Asan Medical Center in Seoul, watching liver transplants at one of the best programmes in the world, just as my own transplant career was beginning. The surgeon fired an expensive surgical stapler, finished the job and threw the device away. I was astonished.

Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have heralded plans for new joint Quad military exercises designed to push back on China’s expansionist ambitions, with the US president promising the grouping with India and Japan will guarantee “peace through strength”.
Albanese met Trump, India’s Nahrendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi in Manila late on Tuesday in talks about enhanced cooperation on AI, critical minerals, infrastructure and maritime security.
“These nations represent some of the most important partnerships in the entire world,” the US president said.
“They’re among the most successful nations in the world, and in certain ways among the most powerful nations of the world. Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific.”
Trump said: “As we continue to protect peace through strength, we are also working together to advance super intelligence, SI, the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution.”
The Australian prime minister praised Trump and said a new Quad business forum to be held in 2027 would build economic growth across the region.
Leaders in the group – established as China seeks to build its military might and exert influence across the region – say they will cooperate to maintain peace and stability with Beijing.
“When we work together for our common view in the Indo-Pacific of peace, security, stability, and prosperity, then the world will be a safer and more secure place, and the Quad has a critical role in achieving that,” Albanese told the summit.
The plan for new military exercises involving maritime patrol aircraft is likely to prompt strong criticism from China.
Albanese said Australia would deploy its P8-A Poseidon and P3-C Orion maritime patrol aircraft as part of the operation in early 2027.
Asked what he would tell Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week about the plan, Albanese said military exercises were common.
“We want peace and security in the region. That’s the objective here. It’s not about any one country. It’s about our own sovereignty, but also about peace and security in the region,” he said
The Quad leaders want the group to present a multilateral coalition of resistance against Beijing, seeking to undermine its dominance, including in the South and East China seas.
Takaichi said the Quad would help shape the future of the region.
“We would like to realise a free and open Indo Pacific by strengthening resilience of countries in the region and promote their freedom to decide for themselves across a wide range of areas including maritime security, economic security, energy and critical and emerging technologies.”
Before the meeting, as the four leaders posed for a group photo, Trump praised Modi and Takaichi as “tough”, before gesturing to Albanese and saying: “We’re OK too.” Albanese laughed at the remark.
The first meeting of the Quad leaders since 2024 came as Albanese and Trump both prepare for setpiece engagement with China’s president later this week. Albanese will visit Xi in Shenzhen on Friday, a day after three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump said he wanted talks with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but conceded he was not the host of the China summit and it was up to Xi to issue an invitation. The US president said he could have a one-on-one meeting with Putin “if it’s available”.
Quad military exercises would build on progress from the recently completed Malabar joint exercise near Japan, where sailors completed anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare drills.
Trump also talked up the Aukus nuclear deal with Australia. “We make the greatest submarines anywhere in the world, and we’re working with Australia and others on that,” he said.
Trump said the US was poised to catch up to China on rare earth production within 10 months, backed up by speedy progress from Australia, Japan and India.
He was accompanied by cabinet members Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Howard Lutnick and Jamieson Greer, as well as his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.
Privately, officials believed the meeting alone showed the group was progressing. Australian officials welcomed the engagement of Trump in regional affairs as he enters the final two years of his presidency.
Trump took credit for reinvigorating the grouping, and said he placed a premium on relations with Albanese, Modi and Takaichi.
“When they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open, and the Oval Office is always open to you, and you know that,” he said.
Albanese said before the meeting he would push Trump on ending the war in Iran, a conflict which has produced an unprecedented global energy shock and badly distorted conditions in the Australian economy.
It was Albanese’s first meeting with Takaichi since a weeks-long saga about comments he made on a podcast about her gift of melons presented to him during a visit to Australia in July.
Earlier, Albanese took part in the East Asia Summit where he called for regional partners to work together to boost AI protections. Trump, who calls the technology “superintelligence”, said it represented “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution”.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the former OpenAI engineer who was fired and arrested in October on allegations that he bugged the company's office, is set to be released on a $1 million bond.
He'll be freed when his $500,000 share of that bond is posted, likely Wednesday — so he's set to be home in Millbrae, California, for Thanksgiving. He'll be fitted with an ankle monitor.
The decision, made by Magistrate Judge Alex Tse in a Tuesday hearing, marks a surprising reversal in the high-profile case. Tse had previously ordered that Alfozan remain in detention over concerns that he might flee to his home country of Saudi Arabia.
Alfozan then switched lawyers to defense attorney David Rizk, who pushed to get the engineer released from custody. Rizk excoriated the prosecution for surfacing discovery evidence too slowly and said they hadn't revealed anything indicating that Alfozan was a "spy" who'd committed economic espionage.
The former OpenAI employee is charged with using a device to intercept oral communications. He pleaded not guilty.
Rizk said after the hearing on Tuesday that he's "glad the court made the right decision," and told Business Insider that if all goes smoothly with Alfozan's release, he plans to delay the trial. The trial is scheduled for January.
Alfozan still has shares in OpenAI, fed says
During the Tuesday hearing, Assistant US Attorney Nick Parker, the case's lead prosecutor, said that Alfozan should remain detained.
He said the engineer remains a flight risk, stressing that Alfozan has fewer ties to the area since his wife and child have flown to Saudi Arabia and that he now has no job.
Parker also said that Alfozan has stock options from his time at OpenAI that have already vested, and so can't be "clawed back."
Judge Tse asked, "Even if he's convicted?"
Parker said that Alfozan could owe restitution if he's convicted, but his understanding is that when OpenAI goes public in its initial public offering — expected next year — the former employee will be able to cash out some shares.
Alfozan started at OpenAI in 2025. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Alfozan will turn in $500,000 and have his movements restricted
Judge Tse is getting Alfozan released on several conditions.
First, Alfozan gave Rizk a power of attorney so he could initiate the process of transferring $500,000 from a Robinhood account to a bank account and then to the court. He won't be released until that money is posted; Rizk said he's hoping to send it on Wednesday.
Alfozan will then need to report to pretrial officials to be fitted with an ankle monitor. He's barred from leaving his residence between 7 p.m. and 7 a.m., and is ordered to avoid airports, train depots, and other major transit centers. The government has already taken his travel documents. He isn't supposed to leave California's Northern District, which stretches along the coast from the Bay Area.
He also isn't allowed to access OpenAI records or information except through the case's discovery process.
If he reneges on any of these conditions, the government can come for the bond money. Alongside Alfozan's $500,000, three of his friends committed Tuesday to covering the remaining bond amount if need be.

A 15 second-long clip has gone viral on X, showing a man kicking and attacking a woman holding a mic, seemingly performing was on-stage. This prompted the woman and several other men from the audience to retaliate.
The clip was shared by X user Ben-Yehuda (@Tal7yvwr) on November 21 with the claim that a Muslim man attacked a woman for not wearing a Burqa in the United States. The post garnered 5.4 million views and reshared over 3,000 times. (Archive)
A Muslim man attacked a woman on stage in the US for not wearing a burqa. The same men then… See more https://t.co/Ir43xwGPR8
— 🇮🇱 Ben-Yehuda (@Tal7yvwr) November 20, 2026
The same clip was shared by X user Vivek Mishra (@Viveksagarbjp) with an identitical claim. This post received 1.1 million views and over 700 reshares. (Archive)
A Muslim man attacked a woman on stage in the US for not wearing a burqa. The same men then… See more https://t.co/CJdJyns0Mo
— Vivek Mishra (@Viveksagarbjp) November 21, 2026
Several other users also shared the viral clip with similar claims. Below is a gallery of some of these posts:
Fact Check
To determine the authenticity of the viral video and its associated claim, we ran reverse image searches on some of the keyframes. We came across a video posted on Youtube on November 14 by a channel called ‘The Channel’ which shows a set of Chilean stand-up comedian Luis Slimming. At the 0:07 mark, the same attacker who appears in the viral clip, gets up on-stage and attacks Slimming. The rest of the video shows an altercation between the attacker and Slimming, and seemingly other members of his team or audience.
We found similarities in the attacker’s face, movement, clothes and pattern of action in both the viral clip and the original video. Below is a gallery comparing keyframes from the two:
We found an article by The Free Press Journal — Chilean Stand-Up Comedian Luis Slimming Attacked During Live Show; Violent Scuffle Caught On Camera — reporting that stand-up comedian Luis Slimming was attacked by a man during his live comedy show on November 12, at Hotel Antay in Arica city of Chile. This confirmed that the viral video is a digitally altered version of the attack on Slimming, replacing him with a woman.
A closer look at the viral video revealed several inconsistencies in the woman’s response to the attack, indicating that it might be generated using AI. We ran the viral clip through AI-detection tool Hive Moderation, which revealed that it is 64% likely that the video is generated using AI.
To conclude, the viral video of a woman being attacked has been generated using AI by altering the video of stand-up comedian Luis Slimming, who was assaulted while performing on stage on November 12 in Chile. Thus, the claim that the woman was attacked by a Muslim man in the United State for not wearing a burqa is false and misleading.
Agniva Ray is an intern at Alt News.

The Telangana Standards Authority for Food and Essential Drugs (TG SAFE) has issued show-cause notices to 90 medical shops across Hyderabad for violations involving the sale of habit-forming drugs and antibiotics without following prescribed regulations.
The notices were issued following a special enforcement drive conducted by the drugs wing of TG SAFE, along with its enforcement wing and excise enforcement personnel, on Thursday (November 19). The department said it would initiate further action, including suspension or cancellation of drug licences, against the establishments found violating the rules.
The inspections were carried out at medical shops in areas including Koti, Abids, Basheerbagh, Nampally, Khairatabad, Panjagutta, Ameerpet, SR Nagar, Sanathnagar, Erragadda, Yousufguda, Madhura Nagar, Jubilee Hills and Banjara Hills.
Officials detected violations such as selling prescription medicines without valid prescriptions issued by registered medical practitioners, failure to maintain prescription and Schedule H1 drug registers, and dispensing medicines in the absence of registered pharmacists. Medical shops were also found selling drugs without issuing bills and failing to maintain or produce sales and purchase records.
The enforcement drive focused on the illegal sale and diversion of habit-forming drugs, including Tramadol, Alprazolam, Nitrazepam, Codeine-containing cough syrups, Tapentadol, Pregabalin and Zolpidem. Officials also checked the indiscriminate sale of antibiotics. Decoy operations and test purchases were conducted to verify whether such medicines were being sold without prescriptions.

On the heels of recent news reports on how keratin-based hair-straightening products containing glycolic acid derivatives led to severe kidney injury in women, researchers from Kerala have reported a series of cases wherein, the use of fairness creams has been linked to nephrotic syndrome.
(For top health news of the day, subscribe to our newsletter Health Matters)
In a study published in the latest issue of Kidney International (‘NELL-1 associated membranous nephropathy linked to skin fairness cream use — insights from an Indian case series’, ) doctors describe a series of 15 cases of Membranous Nephropathy, reported by Aster MIMS Hospital, Kottakkal, Malappuram district, that were traced to the regular use of fairness creams.
Heavy metal screening of the blood and urine samples of these patients revealed high levels of mercury, the toxic effects of which are well-known. An analysis of the fairness creams also showed that these contained high levels of mercury -- in some instances, 10,000 times above the permissible limit of 1 ppm.
Since 2021, Ranjith Narayanan, a nephrologist practising at two busy private hospitals in Kozhikode, had noticed a specific pattern in cases of membranous nephropathy diagnosed amongst his patients. They all had non-specific symptoms — fatigue, mild edema and frothy urine — but high levels of proteinuria, in the range of 6.5-22.2 g/day.

My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional, but might not meet your daily driving needs. It’s tucked away out of view, meant to live out the rest of its life in a drawer before finally being cleaned out and donated the next time someone opens the drawer and asks why you’re holding on to outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren’t hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.
The PhoneBox home screen displays useful stats and what’s currently playing in your browser.
Credit:
Nick Indge
The PhoneBox home screen displays useful stats and what’s currently playing in your browser.
Credit:
Nick Indge
I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible big-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I quickly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life like so many other forgotten devices in a drawer.
Launch applications on your PC from the connected Android device.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Launch applications on your PC from the connected Android device.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Installation is a doddle
Getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been any simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as simple as plugging the tablet into my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you’d like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.
Developer options and ADB are required for USB setup.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Developer options and ADB are required for USB setup.
Credit:
Nick Indge
I already had developer mode initialized on the tablet, but had to go back and allow ADB over USB in settings. The total installation time from copying the script from the project website to everything running on my PC and tablet was less than a minute. The app is MIT-licensed, works on Android 5.0 or later, and requires sideloading since it is not available on the Google Play Store.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Credit:
Nick Indge
The installation script also prints its own uninstall script before it finishes. So often these days, getting rid of an unwanted app feels more difficult than installing it, so I appreciate the straightforward approach the developer has implemented.
The script can install the APK directly to your device.
Credit:
Nick Indge
The script can install the APK directly to your device.
Credit:
Nick Indge
What your device becomes
The first time you fire PhoneBox up, you get live performance and diagnostic information from your PC, along with several pages of optional content that can be tweaked for your local setup to display information that’s pertinent to your uses.
Want to check on your system resources in-game?
Credit:
Nick Indge
Want to check on your system resources in-game?
Credit:
Nick Indge
Where PhoneBox really starts to shine is the widget catalog. A collection of free add-ons that can be added as pages to the tablet’s cycling page layouts. There are more general widgets like RSS feeds that display news highlights from your chosen sources, or simple displays like timers or world clocks.
No shortage of available add-ons.
Credit:
Nick Indge
No shortage of available add-ons.
Credit:
Nick Indge
I opted for a few different widgets that caught my eye. One let me view my library of installed Steam titles and launch them on my PC with a simple tap of the tablet screen. Another allows me to control smart home entities hosted by my Home Assistant server. I was controlling the lights in my office from my tablet within seconds of adding the widget. It’s brilliant.
Home Assistant connected device controls on PhoneBox
Credit:
Nick Indge
Home Assistant connected device controls on PhoneBox
Credit:
Nick Indge
Setting up additional widgets is as simple as adding them to the page layout from the PC’s web interface and hitting save. As soon as I updated things from the PC, the connected tablet immediately began reflecting the changes. I haven’t had the chance to test most of the 131 current options in the widget catalog, but the ones I did were simple to modify and worked on the first try.
I can launch installed Steam Library titles from the tablet controls.
Credit:
Nick Indge
I can launch installed Steam Library titles from the tablet controls.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Some frictions
While I didn’t have any major issues with PhoneBox, I did notice a couple of early annoyances along the way. Windows users should be aware that the PC companion app on that OS is currently unsigned, and they should expect a SmartScreen notification when attempting to install the software.
All control settings live in the web interface rather than the phone or tablet you’re connecting. When I first started messing with PhoneBox, I noticed it displayed my weather location as Tallinn. Nothing against the capital of Estonia, but that’s not weather information that does me much good here in the US Midwest. When I went into the widget settings to change the report location, there was nothing to be found. It turns out that you have to change those settings from the general user preferences section rather than within the widget itself. Not a deal-breaker by any means, but a slight hiccup for someone who was new to the software.
Connecting the Android tablet with my PC over USB was totally painless, but I never got the wireless route to work in my testing. Users are meant to generate a QR code from the PhoneBox web interface on their PC, and connect it to their device by scanning the code with their phone/tablet. Every time I tried to scan the code from my device’s camera app, the tablet refused. There’s no QR scanner built into the PhoneBox app, so if your camera app won’t cooperate, the documented path dead-ends. USB was my intended route anyway and works great, but if you’re planning a wireless-only setup, be prepared for possible friction. The documented flow depends on your device camera opening the pairing link, and mine wasn’t in the mood.
I may have to go back and try the wireless mode again.
I may have to go back and try the wireless mode again.
These minor gripes should be smoothed over before the release of 1.0. The project is early, but it seems to be moving quickly. I tested and installed PhoneBox version 0.9.29, which was one of several releases pushed to the project’s GitHub in as many days. One item of history worth knowing: On November 20, the project published a high-severity security advisory covering versions 0.9.23 and earlier. The vulnerability potentially allowed another app running on the connected Android device to execute commands or receive stored credentials from the host PC. The flaw no longer existed by the time I tested the package in version 0.9.29, but it’s a good reminder that you’re installing something with deep system access and should exercise appropriate caution.
Is it worth trying?
As long as you’re part of the group that has an old phone or tablet lying around somewhere, and these days I expect that most of us are, then it’s an emphatic yes. Repurposing old devices to find new lives is one of the things that keeps me a tech hobbyist. I love finding genuinely useful and practical applications for devices that may have been pushed aside by their manufacturers in favor of the latest and greatest in the lineup.
Monitor all your system processes live.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Monitor all your system processes live.
Credit:
Nick Indge
PhoneBox took a tablet that was destined to live in a junk drawer before being gathered up for a spring donation run, and gave it a new lease on life. I haven’t spent a single penny, and now I have a useful secondary display on my desk. The tablet is powered via a dedicated USB port on my PC, and only goes to sleep when my main monitor displays do. Go dig through those mystery drawers, because this one is worthwhile.
Nick Indge is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica covering hardware, embedded systems, and self-hosted infrastructure. A former security investigator turned tech writer, he writes to help readers escape subscription traps and regain ownership of their digital lives. He lives in Chicagoland with his family and a goofball husky.

A world-class winger - Louis Rees-Zammit 2.0
- Published
Australia wing Harry Potter had Louis Rees-Zammit exactly where he wanted him.
As Wales attacked in Cardiff on Saturday, Potter showed Rees-Zammit the outside – a four-metre channel between him and the touchline.
The touchline is a defender's best friend. An extra defender. The edge of the cliff. It would take something extraordinary to beat Potter without running out of ground.
A shake of the hips and a change of direction later, Potter was diving like a cricketer in the outfield, grasping at thin air. Rees-Zammit was on his way to setting up a wonderful try for Blair Murray.
Rees-Zammit has been turning heads for years. On the pitch with his pace, off it with his pristine teeth and pop star looks.
But it wasn't raw speed that had left Potter on the turf.
This was Rees-Zammit 2.0 - more than just speed.
- Who should Wales pick for autumn finale v Japan? 
  - Published1 day ago
- Did beaten Wales still show they have come a long way? 
  - Published2 days ago
- Wales coach Tandy frustrated by Australia defeat 
  - Published2 days ago
More wide receiver than running back
Alex Cuthbert knows a thing or two about running. A former national-level 400m runner and British and Irish Lions wing, he spent much of his rugby career working on his technique.
What fascinates him about Rees-Zammit now is not his speed but how he generates it.
"His leg drive and strength from his knee to his hip has got so much stronger," said Cuthbert, who scored 17 tries in 57 Tests for Wales.
The difference is most apparent not over 100 metres but over four or five, changing direction and accelerating before a defender can adjust his feet.
"If you do that shimmy and you stand any sort of player up, you can't recover. Literally can't recover," Cuthbert said.
Cuthbert attributes much of that development to Rees-Zammit's 18 months in American football with the Kansas City Chiefs and Jacksonville Jaguars.
"I thought last season he was a little bit heavy. He looked like a running back last year, whereas this year he is more of a wide receiver," Cuthbert said.
A running back, says Cuthbert, powers through traffic, a wide receiver thrives in open space. He now sees elements of both in Rees-Zammit.
'I'm a world-class winger'
Rees-Zammit's coach at Bristol Bears, Pat Lam, estimates he returned from America eight or nine kilograms heavier.
"What was very clear was his pace was still there, if not quicker, but he was a bigger man and he needed to adjust," said Lam.
Lam is arguably one of rugby's most system-driven coaches. Understanding your role is fundamental at Bristol, where only a select few are afforded the freedom to deviate from the script.
Having established himself as a wing before his American adventure, Rees-Zammit was keen to experiment on his return to rugby.
"He spoke to me about a desire to play full-back and give full-back a go," said Lam.
Lam sees the modern full-back as an auxiliary centre in attack, responsible for creating opportunities for others.
Rees-Zammit's greatest gift is exploiting them.
"But we had to go through that process for him to actually say to me, 'Pat, I'm a world-class winger and I'm a world-class finisher'. And I said, 'I agree'," Lam said.
According to Lam, Rees-Zammit now considers himself a wing who can cover full-back, rather than a full-back who can play on the wing.
The numbers behind the evolution
Another moment from Saturday offered a reminder of Rees-Zammit's extraordinary pace when Joseph-Aukuso Sua'ali'i intercepted a Welsh pass and set off downfield.
The Australian, a formidable athlete in his own right, had a head start of at least five metres.
One commentator confidently declared he would not be caught.
Rees-Zammit caught him.
The speed has always been there. The numbers reveal how much more there is to his game now.
Rees-Zammit scored five tries in 10 Premiership appearances for Bristol last season. This season he has matched that tally in five games, beating 28 defenders and making 12 clean breaks.
Against Japan earlier in November, he beat 13 defenders and made more line breaks in 80 minutes than in the entire Six Nations, when he started all five games at full-back.
But Rees-Zammit is not the only thing that has changed since March, Wales have changed too
Even the quickest wing in the world is of limited use if he receives the ball standing still with two defenders in front of him.
"But as a winger, you do rely on your boys inside you," said Cuthbert.
With Wales generating more momentum up front, Cuthbert highlights Blair Murray's ability to engage defenders before releasing Rees-Zammit.
Wales are also deploying both wings on the same side of the field. Rees-Zammit and Josh Adams combining for full-back Murray's try was a fine example.
Scrum-half Tomos Williams has perfected the art of the sharp, accurate pass that bypasses players and gets the ball into the wider channels early.
It helped create Rees-Zammit's try against New Zealand and, eight minutes into Saturday's game against the Wallabies, looked to have created another.
Having dived for the corner, Rees-Zammit's first instinct on getting to his feet was not to celebrate or appeal to the referee, but to fix his hair.
The try would not survive the television replays. The hair had survived the tackle.
Image matters to Rees-Zammit. He is Welsh rugby's most marketable player, its biggest draw. He puts bums on seats and gets people out of them.
There is a lovely soundtrack to Rees-Zammit receiving the ball in space at the Principality Stadium. A low hum of excitement followed by the rattle of thousands of seats folding up almost simultaneously.
The thrill is in the anticipation, and these days there is rather more to anticipate.

You don't have to look at your Apple Watch to get the time
You can keep track of the time without missing a beat, thanks to a discreet Apple Watch setting that comes in a few versions to suit your schedule.
One of the ironies of smartwatches is that for some people, telling the time is low on the list of priorities. You can always check your iPhone if you need to, and most of us spend hours every day in front of some form of clock, whether it's a PC or an old analog ticker hanging on the wall. It's actually features like fitness tracking and quick notification checks that elevate the best Apple Watches to must-haves.
One way or another, we need to know the time, and Apple Watches come with a variety of ways to communicate it. Something you may not have heard of, though, is the ability to get it via vibration. It's something Apple calls Taptic Time, a reference to the Taptic Engine that produces haptic feedback.
Here we're going to explain how to enable Taptic Time, how it works and, perhaps most importantly, why you'd want to bother. The short answer to the last item is that for some people, a visual check just isn't an option.
How to turn on and use Taptic Time on your Apple Watch
To enable Taptic Time, launch the Settings app on your Apple Watch. Next, select Clock, then Taptic Time. Toggle the feature on. At that point, you'll be presented with three options: Digits, Terse or Morse Code.
That last one should probably be avoided unless you're a 19th-century telegraph operator. Terse may not be much better, though. It uses long taps to indicate that five hours have passed since midnight, short taps for additional hours, then long taps again for quarter-hour increments. It's not hard to learn, but a 15-minute margin of error could mean the difference between catching your rideshare to the airport and having to rebook your flight.
The most precise and intuitive option is Digits. This uses long taps for tens and short taps for ones and applies that to both hours and minutes. For example, 10:09 would be one long tap, a pause, then nine short taps.
When VoiceOver is on, you can also turn on Taptic Time by double-tapping the watch face while the screen is inactive. Apple notes, though, that Taptic Time won't work in any fashion if your Apple Watch is set to always speak the time. To fix that, you can go to Settings > Clock, then turn on Control With Silent Mode under Speak Time.
Who should actually use Taptic Time on an Apple Watch?
The honest answer is that most people shouldn't. Even if it's just every 15 minutes, having your wrist vibrate repeatedly can be annoying, much less trying to interpret a coded pattern. That's particularly true on recent Apple Watches, which have motors strong enough that alerts can be startling, even when you're expecting them.
The main beneficiaries of Taptic Time are going to be the visually impaired. In that scenario, it might initially seem strange to buy one of the best smartwatches. But with the right accessibility options enabled, you don't need to see well to benefit from some of the Apple Watch's selling points, like fitness tracking, or controlling music and some of the best smart home accessories without having your iPhone nearby.
If your eyesight is fine, you might nevertheless want haptic feedback to keep you more mindful of the time, in which case Terse mode will be the least intrusive choice. It's also conceivable that your job or hobbies might put you in situations where checking your wrist is impractical. I like to ride electric unicycles, for example — while that keeps my hands free, sometimes I need to focus on carving the pavement.

SP releases first list of 5 candidates for UP Assembly polls amid seat-sharing talks
Samajwadi Party's first list of five candidates was announced on Tuesday, naming nominees for constituencies across Saharanpur, Shamli, Amroha and Lalitpur.
The Samajwadi Party on Tuesday night announced its first list of five candidates for the upcoming 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly election, naming nominees for constituencies in Saharanpur, Shamli, Amroha and Lalitpur. The first list comprises four Muslims and one non-Yadav OBC candidate.
Deep Dive
SPcandidates for UP assembly election
-Umar Ali Khan, Behat assembly constituency (01) - Saharanpur
-Ashu Malik, Saharanpur assembly constituency (04) - Saharanpur
-Nahid Hasan, Kairana assembly constituency (08) - Shamli
-Mahboob Ali, Amroha assembly constituency (41) - Amroha
-Jyoti Lodhi, Lalitpur assembly constituency (226) - Lalitpur
Nahid Hasan had won three successive elections on the seat - in the 2014 bypolls, 2017, then 2022 polls. Umar Ali is the sitting SP MLA from Behat, while Ashu Malik is the sitting SP MLA from Saharanpur assembly seat. Mahboob Ali is also the sitting SP MLA from Amroha and has won the seat five consecutive times till 2022.
Lalitpur is the only seat in the list that is not currently with the SP. BJP won the seat in 2017 and 2022.
Akhilesh signals seat-sharing discussions with Congress on track
Ahead of the announcement, SP president Akhilesh Yadav had signalled that seat-sharing discussions with the Congress were progressing smoothly, saying the two parties had made a beginning with '26 winnable seats' and would continue negotiations together.
ALSO READ: SP offers Congress 26 seats against its demand for 120, intensifying alliance talks
"The beginning has been made with the winnable 26 seats. Talks will move forward through understanding and cooperation," Yadav posted on X in Hindi later in the evening.
Congress-SP hold detailed seat sharing discussions
Congress and SP held detailed, seat-by-seat discussions on Tuesday, with the SP offering 26 seats to its INDIA bloc ally for the state elections to be held next year. The 26 seats are way lower than the Congress's demand for 120 seats, setting the stage for a tough negotiation between the two allies.
However, the SP leadership has indicated that the negotiations are still ongoing, suggesting that the Congress may get more than the 26 seats initially offered to it for the upcoming elections.
But Akhilesh, speaking to reporters on Tuesday, reiterated that 'winnability' will be deciding factor. He said, according to ANI, that it will be too early to comment on the outcome of the negotiations. He added the two parties need to "accommodate one another" to ensure electoral success.
ALSO READ: Ram Gopal Yadav calls seat-sharing talks with Cong ‘very positive’, says will finalise in 2 meetings
Congress had won two seats in the previous state elections, and the SP is willing to retain those constituencies for the party as part of the proposed seat-sharing arrangement. As reported by HT earlier, the SP's initial offer includes these two seats along with 24 others where the Congress had put up a relatively strong performance, including Jagdishpur, Kidwai Nagar and Kheragarh.
While the SP indicated that it had offered 26 seats to the Congress, the latter has denied receiving any such proposal, suggesting that the seat-sharing discussions are still underway.
AICC Uttar Pradesh in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam said the two parties held detailed discussions covering all 403 Assembly constituencies, but no specific seat demands were made as both sides were keen to contest the elections together.
“We had a detailed discussion on all 403 seats, and there were no demands made, as we want to fight unitedly,” Gautam said, according to PTI.

The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.
India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.
So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.
My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.
Ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.
‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’
One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.
Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.
The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.
The following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.
For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.
Walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.
The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she said. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.
‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’
The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.
Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.
But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” says Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.
Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.
Travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.
Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.
Discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.
What else we’re reading about
Politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry said that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.
Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.
Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
71
Firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board showed.
Vibe check
AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI company. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.
The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.
