Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
- Published
In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.
Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.
The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.
Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.
This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.
The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".
This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.
Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.
At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.
A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.
Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.
Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.
In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".
He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".
Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project".
"Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.
He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.
Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.
The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu, has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.
The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.
His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted.
"The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.
He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.
The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.
The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.
Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.
They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.

Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption.
He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.
Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.
His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.
Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.
The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.
He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive.
"Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."
But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted.
"The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.
He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.
The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.
Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings.
"Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.
He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.
Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".
Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.
On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job.
"Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted.
He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.
The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible.
It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.
Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly.
Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.
Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.
He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.
Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.
Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.
Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power.
"The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.
At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.
He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year, extending his rule into a fifth decade.
Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end.
He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership.
But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated.
At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported.
Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh, Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership.
There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president.
Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation.
Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion.
He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition.
"The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says.
The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify.
The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy.
The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition.
Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies.
Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba.
The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability.
For now, Museveni remains in power.
But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.

UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling
- Published
The UK has sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that the country had carried out genocide against the Rohingya minority – marking the first time a state has been found guilty of the crime.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma.
The UK is joined by several other countries, external in acknowledging the ICJ ruling, including Australia, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and Canada.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values and must be matched by clear action."
- How do you define genocide? 
  - Published4 April 2022
The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.
Miliband added that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing, who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" as he was head of the military at the time of the genocide in 2017.
He said: "Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again."
Miliband also called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement".
The foreign secretary confirmed that new legislation would be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.
Last week, he expelled Myanmar's defence attaché after the ICJ ruled the country had committed genocide during the brutal military campaign in 2017.
He told MPs on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention, external.
In its ruling last week, the court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal. Myanmar denied the claims against it.
Reports said that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.
Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.
Myanmar's leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi, was deposed by the military in 2021.
MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan army were still happening.

How king tides happen, and what that means amid flood warnings in B.C.
King tides can be around half a metre higher than average high tide levels, lasting for a few days
Officials on the West Coast of Canada and the U.S. are warning those living close to the ocean about potential flooding, thanks in part to what's called a king tide.
This perfect storm of alignment between Earth, the moon and the sun can create dramatic tides that can be about 0.3 to 0.6 metres higher than the average high tide mark.
The current king tide is expected to end on Thursday, but up until then, officials are warning people along the coast about the potential of flooding, as these higher-than-normal tides coincide with sea level rise caused by El Niño.
Oceanographer Gregory Crawford says this is a "worst-case scenario."
"Certainly low-lying places that don't have a lot of sea wall protection and such are going to potentially have some worse flooding than you would normally have," said Crawford, an adjunct professor at Ontario Tech University in Oshawa, Ont.
According to the Weather Network, current forecasts expect the highest tide on Wednesday morning, coinciding with the full moon.
A flood protection sign is seen at Boundary Bay in Delta, B.C., on Tuesday. The current king tide is expected to end on Thursday. (Hunter Soo/CBC)
How does a king tide happen?
There are a few different types of alignments that can produce higher-than-normal tides.
Tides are caused by the push and pull of the moon and sun on the ocean. As those celestial bodies shift, so do the tides.
There are spring tides, which happen every two weeks when the moon and sun align on the same side of Earth, resulting in tides that are about 20 per cent higher than normal.
There is also the perigean tide, which happens three or four times a year, when the moon is at its closest approach to Earth in its orbit.
When both of these alignments happen at once, you get the king of all tides, which typically happens in the late fall and early winter and can last for a few days.
"Essentially, the pull of the moon and the pull of the sun line up to kind of maximize the tidal range that you get. And that's what we call the king tide," said Crawford.
Tides predictable, storms are not
Crawford says these king tides are fairly predictable, as it's all astronomy, with the most dramatic conditions lasting for just a few days, so those close to the water know when to expect them.
And while the king tides themselves aren't overly dangerous, it's important to watch out for what else is going on around the ocean.
"When you get El Niño and king tides and weather, and/or tsunamis, when they all add up together, that can be a lot more serious," said Crawford.
A bus moves through floodwaters during high tides on Tuesday in Sausalito, Calif. (Heather Diehl/The Associated Press)
Crawford says king tides aren't typically on the mind of those who live inland, but if you spend time on the water, chances are you know about these more dramatic tides.
"If you're kind of up on a hill, you're probably not so worried about it," said Crawford.
Crawford says these king tides happen about two to four times a year.
According to the Weather Network, B.C. can expect more king tides next month, from Dec. 22-26.

Bisleri International has maintained that its packaged drinking water is safe for consumption, disputing the findings of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), which has sanctioned prosecution against the company after a water sample was declared unsafe following laboratory tests.
In a statement issued on Monday (November 23, 2026), the company said the matter related to a batch manufactured in September 2025 at its Goa facility, one of 143 plants in its network, and dated back about 14 months.
Bisleri said the FSSAI collected six samples from the facility on September 30, 2025, of which five met all applicable standards. The sixth sample recorded a bromate level of 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre.
Following an appeal by the company on November 22, 2025, the FSSAI referred the sample to a referral laboratory for retesting. Bisleri said the referral laboratory found the bromate level to be within the prescribed limit, but separately flagged the presence of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).
The findings came after the initial laboratory examination had found the sample non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits, and declared it unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The referral laboratory also declared the sample unsafe, citing the detection of PAHs. Based on the laboratory findings, the FSSAI subsequently sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri.
Questioning the differing test results, Bisleri said the difference between the two sets of findings raised questions that it believed warranted clarification. The company said it arranged for the same sample to be tested independently at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, where the bromate level was also found to be within the prescribed limit.
Bisleri said it submitted the independent test results to the FSSAI’s Western Regional Office along with a formal letter dated February 2, 2026.
“We received no further communication from FSSAI after that submission and understood the matter to be closed. To date, Bisleri has received no notice by email or in hard copy and has been unable to locate the reported notice on FSSAI’s website,” a company spokesperson said.
The company’s management is deciding on the next steps, the spokesperson said. The company said it maintained stringent quality controls, including more than 90 tests across its 10-step manufacturing process. It added that it would continue to cooperate with the FSSAI and address the matter through the appropriate regulatory process.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologised to employees on Tuesday for violating the company's code of conduct and admitted making “very serious personal mistakes” during his first all-hands meeting since returning to the top post. Huang acknowledged that his personal behaviour had hurt his family and wife. He also promised to hold himself to higher standards and undergo regular performance reviews based on feedback from employees.
“This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang said, according to a report by The Wired. “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife.”
Huang says he is undergoing therapy
Addressing employees, Huang said he had been attending therapy sessions every day for an hour and a half. He added that the sessions had been helping him.
“I made some very serious personal mistakes. I hurt my family, I hurt my wife,” he said.
Huang also stressed that Nvidia's code of conduct remained applicable to everyone in the company, including its top leadership. He said he had written much of the code himself and that it was designed to “create an environment that’s safe for people.”
He warned that violations would not be tolerated. However, he clarified that every violation would not automatically lead to an employee's dismissal.
“But that does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” he said. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” would determine the action taken.
Nvidia CEO promises regular performance reviews
Huang also addressed criticism of his intense management style and acknowledged that his behaviour had sometimes affected employees negatively.
While he maintained that his demanding approach helped push people to perform better, he admitted that he sometimes went too far.
“It disempowers them, and that’s not right,” Huang said.
He said he needed to find a way to maintain his commitment to Nvidia without hurting the people working for him.
“I need to hold myself to a higher standard at this time,” he said.
Huang also announced that he would undergo a 360-degree performance review. The process would involve seeking feedback from people working with him, potentially as often as once a month.
He said he would be the first and only person at Nvidia to undergo such a review and did not intend to introduce the practice across the company.
Huang rejects claims of preferential treatment
The CEO also pushed back against suggestions that he had been reinstated because of his standing in the technology industry.
“There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back,” Huang said.
He rejected the suggestion that his position gave him special treatment or placed him above Nvidia's code of conduct.
Huang also sought to reassure women employees, describing himself as “one of our greatest advocates for creating an environment for women”.
He highlighted the company's flexible work policies, saying they allowed employees to build their families while pursuing their careers.
“If I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it,” he said.
He further sought to reassure employees about the company's ability to function without him, saying his brief absence had demonstrated its operational strength.
“I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute,” Huang said.
Why Huang stepped down and returned as Nvidia CEO
Nvidia's board accepted Huang's resignation earlier this month following concerns about his personal conduct and lack of candour. The development came after media reports about alleged extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman accused of having links to Chinese intelligence services.
However, the same board reinstated him on Monday, just 11 days after accepting his resignation. The decision followed fresh assurances from Huang and information from the Trump administration that he was not under federal scrutiny.
His return has drawn mixed reactions within Nvidia. While some employees welcomed the decision, others reportedly remain concerned about his conduct and the board's move to reinstate him.
The controversy has also led to continued legal and regulatory scrutiny. Nvidia's board is investigating whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence. US lawmakers are also expecting him to testify before Congress next week.
Meanwhile, lawsuits and other investigations are ongoing into the company's disclosures about Huang's conduct and its compliance with US export controls on chips.

I return to my room as my mother-in-law leaves for her office in the building adjacent to our home. I am about to start my bath when I hear a series of explosions, as of firecrackers, but different. I freeze. Someone comes pounding frantically on my bathroom door. It is Ongmu, the children’s nanny, crying hysterically. I fling open the door, my heart thumping. She is gesticulating wildly, speechlessly, towards the garden.
I run along the path leading to Akbar Road. I see the white Ambassador car slowly moving towards the same path. I hesitate. I stop, heart in my mouth. Dread, panic, fear. I feel suffocated. I can’t breathe. I am about to collapse. No, no, I can’t. I have to walk to the car. I see her being carried into it. I understand; I scream.
I’m in the car now, crouching on the floor, facing her … Blood – blood on her sari, blood on her chest. Her large eyes are wide open; her face wears a surprised expression. She doesn’t move. I attempt to speak to her, to call out, “Mummy, Mummy”, but no word comes out. I try again; she doesn’t reply.
Her aides are in the front of the car, screaming. Heavy, slow traffic, the car barely moves, it has no siren. One red light, then another. Then the hospital. The gate isn’t opening. Chaos. We are stopped; someone looks through the window in a questioning attitude. They let us in.
We reach the emergency department, teeming with people. We are stopped again, not allowed in, we have to wait for our turn. Someone calls out to the driver, signals him to move forward. They identify us; she is placed on a trolley. We are led somewhere – an operation theatre? They ask me to follow. I’m taken to a room nearby. No, no, I want to stay by her, I insist. I want to know. I have to see. They don’t reply; they are immersed in their emergency procedures.
I feel confused, lost … I don’t recognise anyone there. I’m shivering under my dressing gown. I feel scared, my mind is racing. Where is Rajiv? I try to remember. I can’t, I can’t. The children, yes, they’re in school; they must be brought home. Oh God, no, no. Let them be safe, let Rajiv be safe … Whom do I tell, whom do I speak to? I sense someone in the room. I don’t know who it is. I try to speak, to put some words together; nothing comes out. “There’s blood all over her clothes,” someone says. Some clothes are brought in for me. I am helped into them in a nearby closet.
Hours go by, agonising hours. More people come in and crowd around. I signal a question to the doctor; he shakes his head. I understand, yes, I understand. I break into sobs, uncontrollably. Someone tries to calm me. I feel numb, cold.
At two in the afternoon of 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was declared dead. I was driven home to collect some clothes for her body to be changed into. On the way, a group of men tried to stop our car, banging on its windows. They were angry, shouting something I couldn’t understand.
At home, the children, Rahul and Priyanka, rushed to my arms in tears. When they had been abruptly picked up from school by black-uniformed commandos, they sensed a catastrophe. Once home, they saw some of the staff sobbing. They asked question after question. “Where’s Mama?” “Why have we been brought home?” “Where’s Papa?” “What’s happened?” “Where’s Dadi?” “You aren’t telling us the truth!” My friends Nina and Sterre had been with them, trying to calm them down, not knowing what to say to them. I wanted to sit with them and hug them, to break the news to them gently, but I was unable to – I had to go back; Rajiv was coming to the hospital.
Rajiv had been in West Bengal at a political rally when his cavalcade was stopped by a police patrol. He was told there was a message from Delhi to say he should rush back – a serious accident had taken place. He was driven to the helipad, from where he flew to Calcutta and then to Delhi. He’d heard on a BBC bulletin that Mrs Gandhi was wounded and in a grave condition. Nobody told him directly that his mother was no more, but he understood.
He landed at 3.30pm and was driven straight to the hospital. He walked in with other people, and I remember longing to be left alone with him for a moment at least. We held each other, and as he spoke to me, it sunk in that he was saying something I didn’t want to hear. “I have been asked … They want me to be sworn in as prime minister.”
I felt as if a knife had been plunged right into my heart. I felt a pounding in my chest, a rage welling up deep inside me. I was about to explode. I attempted to hold it in. “You have been asked to? How dare they ask? How dare they? Who are they? Why you, why does it have to be you? Why did you allow them to ask you? No, it cannot be; this time it’s not going to be!” Seized by utter pain and anguish, soaked in perspiration, I felt like throwing up. I wanted to scream, to ask for help. “Someone please help me put an end to this.”
I burst out crying, pleading, begging him with folded hands, “No, no, you can’t think of it. You have to stop them, you must refuse, you must say no – for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you; they will kill you, too!” I cried out. He replied, “They will kill me anyway.”
We brought my mother-in-law home. The dining room had been emptied out, and we laid her body down on the floor, her feet pointing south as Hindu custom decrees. The same evening at around 6.30pm, Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister of India. I was too broken to even register what was happening around me. His mother lay there, her body pierced with more than 30 bullet holes. I knew, I knew it then in my heart: Rajiv’s path would lead to the same end.

In a closely watched trial seen as one of this year’s most impactful immunology drug readouts, Kymera Therapeutics announced on Monday that its experimental therapy effectively and safely treated eczema patients’ itchy, inflamed skin.
In the Phase 2 trial, moderate-to-severe eczema patients randomly assigned to receive the biotech’s pill, KT-621, showed a statistically significant reduction in disease severity compared with those given a placebo. This was true across all three doses tested after 16 weeks of treatment, with a peak placebo-adjusted improvement of 45% among those given a moderate dose. Patients on this dose were also more likely to see an improvement of 75% or more in disease severity, with 62% of treated participants clearing that bar compared with 22% of the placebo group.
The BROADEN2 trial succeeded across all primary and secondary endpoints, including itch reduction and the fraction of patients who achieved clear or almost-clear skin. KT-621 was also generally safe and well tolerated. The only side effect that was more common among patients on the drug was conjunctivitis (i.e. pink eye), which appeared in 20%, 13%, and 11% of patients on a low, middle, and high dose, respectively. All of these cases were mild to moderate, and none caused participants to stop treatment.

Former Sequoia Capital India investor Sudhanshu Mishra has launched an agentic AI startup called Demi.AI in the US, seeking to build an AI assistant that can anticipate users' requirements and complete work before being explicitly instructed. Mishra announced the launch of Demi's invite-only beta earlier today on social media. He positioned it as an “AI assistant that lives on your Mac, learns how you work, and does the work before you ask”. Demi’s other cofounder is Mishra’s college roommate Logan Ford and currently employs about 10 people. Demi was set up in June 2025. Mishra was earlier associated with Sequoia Capital as an investor. He worked on early-stage investments, primarily leading the firm's crypto-focused efforts. He subsequently joined Paradigm, a crypto-focused investment firm, as an investment partner. In his launch announcement, Mishra said the idea behind Demi was to reduce the effort users currently need to put into making AI tools useful, including setting up workflows, providing context and figuring out which tasks to delegate. Unlike conventional AI assistants that largely respond to individual prompts, Demi aims to continuously build an understanding of users' work and identify tasks that need attention. How Does Demi Work? Demi builds context from users' meetings, connected applications and even their computer screens to understand ongoing projects, conversations and work patterns. Based on this context, it tracks commitments, deadlines and recurring tasks, and proactively surfaces reminders or prepares the next steps. For instance, if a user promises to share a document during a meeting, Demi can identify the commitment, locate relevant information and prepare a follow-up email. The platform can also handle repetitive administrative work, including drafting email responses, preparing meeting briefs, capturing meeting notes, updating customer relationship management (CRM) systems and tracking customer follow-ups. The agentic platform then executes these tasks either through its cloud-based computer or natively on a user's Mac through their browser. Moreover, users do not need to create custom workflows or write instructions for individual skills to get started. The platform still retains a human approval layer and messages, commitments and important changes to records are presented to users for approval before they are executed. According to its website, its individual paid plan starts at $25 per month, while team pricing is customised. Agentic AI has emerged as the biggest buzz word across the global tech ecosystem with most enterprises and individuals exploring ways to automate their workflows using AI. According to Grand View Research, the global enterprise agentic AI market is projected to reach $24.5 Bn by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 46.2%. Investor interest in agentic AI is also accelerating as a new crop of startups look to automate workflows across varied enterprise applications. For instance, Sol Foundry, founded by former CRED executives, raised $4 Mn from General Catalyst, Nexus Venture Partners and others in September this year to build a proactive AI assistant that acts on commitments made over email.

A suspected Ukrainian drone attack caused an explosion on a Russian warship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, Libyan officials have said.
The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy warship, and ignited a fire at the naval base, they said. Several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, the officials told the Associated Press.
The officials were affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya.
There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range barrages against Russia far beyond the frontlines.
Authorities in divided Libya’s east said in a statement that the vessel had stopped at Benghazi port to refuel and resupply on its way back to Russia, under maritime cooperation agreements between the two countries.
Two medical sources told Reuters no deaths had been reported, but there were injuries. The number and nationalities of those injured are not yet known.
In a separate attack, another sea drone hit a commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi on Sunday evening, Libyan military sources told Reuters.
The eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.
It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take legal and diplomatic measures against anyone found responsible. “The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
The specialist website Naval News also identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it was almost certainly destroyed.
HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”.
If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.
But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians in another continent and the working of the port.
A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.
Initial reports and footage suggest the Merkury was struck from above, potentially by a drone, launched no more than a few kilometres away from the target in port.
Russia is close to the Benghazi authorities that control eastern Libya. It uses the port, which has a growing importance since it lost bases in Syria, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean.
Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea continued to smoulder on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.
The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly injured.
On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

Jensen Huang is back, baby, and Wall Street is thrilled.
The chipmaker’s shares have surged more than 30 percent following the board’s announcement that it was reinstating Huang as president, CEO, and board member. The company’s valuation has soared by more than $1 trillion, which puts it on track to break Microsoft’s record for the greatest single-day gain in market value by hundreds of billions of dollars.
Huang departed the company he helped found on November 12 amid suspected asset-kissing and allegations of extramarital affairs with employees. Each report chipped away at the company’s value until nearly $2.2 trillion was erased over the past month.
Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said during the company’s earnings call that the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” WIRED also reported that Nvidia’s board had been alarmed by Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying.”
And yet, despite all this, the board announced on Monday that it had brought Huang back—with some help from the US government. Semafor reported that, hours before Huang was reinstated, President Donald Trump dialed into the publicly traded company’s board meeting to argue for the ousted CEO’s return.
Many questions remain unanswered. What happens at the conclusion of the board-led investigation into Huang’s behavior? Multiple government agencies and lawmakers are reportedly investigating Huang; given the Trump administration’s aggressive support of the executive, what sort of accountability can anyone reasonably expect?
The turmoil has also raised red flags about what happens when so much of the market revolves around one person at one company. Nvidia has massive sway over the wider artificial intelligence ecosystem, due to its deals with and investments in other companies. Last week, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 10 percent, in part due to Nvidia’s struggles—the index’s biggest decline since March 2020.
On Monday morning, CNBC asked Trump if Nvidia’s influence on the stock market influenced his decision to push for Huang’s return. “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term,” Trump responded.
Trump, who has worked closely with Huang during his second administration, established himself as a vocal supporter of the CEO amid the recent chaos. Trump told The New York Times that he believed the board responded positively to his argument for Huang’s return because of the stock market dip, with the president suggesting that investors didn’t have much confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress.
“I just thought he should be running the company, and I didn’t know it was going to have this kind of an impact,” Trump told The New York Times. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it, actually. The stock is up.”
According to Trump, however, his decision wasn’t guided solely by the market.
“The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about,” the president told CNBC. Sure!

Sooryavanshi, 15, breaks sixes record by scoring 204 off 53 balls
- Published
India's 15-year-old batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi hit the most sixes ever recorded in a senior men's innings in blazing 204 from 53 balls for India A against the United Arab Emirates.
While almost halving the record for the fastest double-century in List A cricket, Sooryavanshi hit 28 sixes and seven fours in the Asia Cup Rising Stars competition - easily breaking Chad Bowes' previous record of 103 balls from 2024.
The teenage opener also broke the record for the fastest century and 150, the latter of which he already held, before being caught at long-off with his side five runs from victory.
India A ultimately passed their target of 250, played against a UAE side that featured a number of internationals but was not their current first-choice side, in 14.2 overs in Doha.
Sooryavanshi now holds the following records in List A cricket, the categorisation given to senior one-day matches:
- Fastest fifty: 11 balls v Sri Lanka A, 21 June (previously Kaushalya Weeraratne, 12 balls, 1 November 2005)
- Fastest hundred: 28 balls, today (previously Jake Fraser-McGurk, 29 balls, 8 October 2023)
- Fastest 150: 40 balls, today (previously himself, 59 balls, 24 December 2025)
- Fastest 200: 52 balls, today (previously Chad Bowes, 103 balls, 22 October 2024)
The previous record for the most sixes in senior matches was 26, struck by Tanmay Agarwal in an innings of 366 for Hyderabad against Arunachal Pradesh in India's first-class Ranji Trophy competition in January 2024.
The record in List A cricket was 23 sixes, struck by D'Arcy Short for Queensland in his 257 against Tasmania on 28 September 2018.
Sooryavanshi has rapidly become a sensation in T20 cricket since making his debut in the Indian Premier League in 2025 at the age of 14.
He has hit two hundreds and six fifties in his first two seasons in the competition and has earned 10 caps for India in the shortest format since making his debut against England in July.
The left-hander, who was batting in only his 16th List A innings in Doha and made his second century in the format, is yet to play for India in 50-over cricket.
He put on partnerships of 68 with opening partner Abhishek Sharma, who scored 12, 40 with Prabhsimran Singh, who added just three, and 137 with Rinku Singh, who scored an unbeaten 27.
The India A side, which featured a number of internationals, restricted the UAE to 249-8 in 50 overs, external after their opposition had chosen to bat and swiftly reached 254-3 to win by seven wickets and guarantee their place in the semi-finals.
The Rising Stars competition features A sides from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Afghanistan alongside squads from the UAE, Nepal and Hong Kong.
India A, who now top Group B, beat Nepal and lost to Pakistan A in their previous two matches in the competition, with Sooryavanshi making scores of 26 and 11.
Pakistan A will retake the top spot if they beat Nepal on Tuesday, with semi-finals on Thursday and Friday to follow before Sunday's final.

For the first time in more than a year, the Food and Drug Administration has sent notices to companies for failing to report required clinical trial information.
The agency sends such notices when a trial sponsor fails to comply with a federal law that requires studies to be registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, a federal government database, within 21 days after the first human subject is enrolled. Summary results must also be posted to the database within 12 months after the trial’s primary completion date.
The FDA, however, has rarely sent noncompliance letters, despite years of criticism over lax enforcement. In recent years, calls for greater transparency have sparked a raft of studies showing a failure by drug companies, universities, and academic medical centers to comply with disclosure requirements. Following the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), the Special Summary Revision (SSR) is now underway in Uttar Pradesh, with the stated objective of preparing an error-free electoral roll. An analysis of Form 6 applications by Alt News, however, reveals a sharp and unprecedented surge in applications for inclusion in the electoral roll, with daily submissions rising from a few thousand in early November to over four lakh by November 22.
The SSR process began with the publication of the draft electoral rolls on November 17. About two weeks earlier, on October 30, Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath had said at a BJP state working committee meeting in Lucknow that the names of around 1.27 crore Hindu voters were missing from the electoral rolls. He urged party workers to launch a systematic campaign to ensure their inclusion.
Again, on November 22, The Indian Express reported that Uttar Pradesh BJP had instructed its workers to focus on Form 6 additions in the SSR is to ensure inclusion of names of individuals eligible to be voters but left out during the SIR for some reason.
Tracking Form 6 application data from the SSR process, Alt News found that between November 1 and 16, an average of around 10,000 applications were submitted daily across the state. The numbers began rising sharply from November 17, the day the draft rolls were published, and accelerated dramatically over the following five days. On November 22 alone, around 4.16 lakh applications were submitted.
What Alt News Found
An analysis of Form 6 application data from Uttar Pradesh shows that around 2,000 applications were filed across the state on November 1. The numbers began rising the following day, with around 10,000 applications submitted on November 2. A similar number were filed on November 3 and 4, followed by 9,000 on November 5.
The state recorded around 12,000 applications each on November 6 and 7, before the figure dropped to 4,000 on November 8. Around 9,000 applications were submitted on November 9.
On November 10, 11 and 12, the daily figures stood at 15,000, 16,000 and 15,000, respectively. Applications declined to around 11,000 each on November 13 and 14, and further to 9,000 on both November 15 and 16.
The pace of submissions changed significantly on November 17, when the SSR process began and the draft electoral roll was published. Around 31,000 Form-6 applications were filed across Uttar Pradesh that day. The numbers climbed further over the next two days, with 46,000 applications on November 18 and 68,000 on November 19. On November 20, the figure stood at around 60,851.
The surge became even more pronounced from November 21, when around 2.31 lakh Form-6 applications were submitted. The following day, November 22, the figure more than doubled to approximately 4.16 lakh.
Who Are Filing these Applications?
Alt News’s analysis found that some of the new applicants had been deleted from the electoral rolls during the SIR.
To identify such applicants, the Alt News team matched new Form 6 applicants against the 2.89 crore names deleted during the SIR under the categories of absent, shifted, dead or duplicate.
Of the approximately 10.4 lakh applications examined between October 29 and November 22, Alt News found around 45,000 applicants whose names had been deleted during the SIR and who were now applying for inclusion in the electoral roll of the same assembly constituency. These applicants accounted for around 4.3% of all the applications examined.
Put another way, the 45,000 applicants represent approximately 1.6 in every 1,000 people whose names were deleted during the SIR (45,000 out of 2.89 crore). Most of these applicants had previously been marked as absent or shifted before their names were deleted.
A Closer Look at Form 6 Applications
A closer examination of the Form 6 applications reveals several serious anomalies, like instances of multiple applications carrying identical applicant details.
In Siwalkhas assembly constituency in Meerut district, for instance, 44 applications were submitted from the same address: “Gotka, Gotka, Gotka, Gotka, 250344, Sardhana.” All 44 applications were filed on November 5 and 6.
Alt News also identified 6,969 repeat Form-6 applications submitted between November 20 and 22.
These repeat applications were found within the same assembly constituency and carried identical applicant names and father’s or husband’s names.
For instance, in Bindki constituency in Fatehpur district, an applicant named Himanshu submitted five Form 6 applications. Four were filed on November 21 and another on November 22. All five applications carry the same applicant name, his father’s name, Baburam, and the same address.
The application serial numbers also show that three of these applications were submitted consecutively.
In another instance, Alt News identified an applicant named Aadhya Seth who submitted six Form 6 applications over three days, between November 20 and 22. In all six applications, the applicant’s name, father’s name and address are identical.
To identify similar instances, we matched applicants by name and their father’s or husband’s name within each constituency for the period October 29 to November 22. The exercise identified 10,773 individuals whose names appeared more than once, accounting for 11,684 additional applications.
According to Alt News’s analysis, approximately one in every 90 Form 6 applications was a repeat submission. The analysis also identified 427 individuals who had submitted applications in two different assembly constituencies.
The data shows that most repeat applications were filed on the same day, often in immediate succession.
A closer analysis also reveals that repeat applications increased alongside the overall surge in Form 6 submissions. On November 17, 18 and 19, the number of repeat applications stood at 340, 458 and 699, respectively. Before this, the daily figure had rarely crossed 400, reaching around that mark only on November 10 and 15.
On November 22 alone, however, 4,325 repeat applications were submitted. This means approximately one in every 100 Form 6 applications filed that day was a repeat submission.
Making Sense of the Surge
The overall volume of applications saw a sharp increase ever since the SSR draft role had been published. Between October 29 and November 22, a total of 10,56,778 Form 6 applications were submitted across Uttar Pradesh. Of these, 1,65,289 were filed between November 1 and 16, while 4,37,235 were submitted in just five days, between November 17 and 21.
On November 22 alone, the number stood at 4,16,380. According to data compiled by the Alt News team, more Form-6 applications were submitted on November 22 than during the first 20 days of November combined.
According to the figures available from November 20 to November 22, Kheri district (33,836) saw the most number of Form 6 applications. Other districts such as Ghaziabad (25,438), Agra (24,715), Barabanki (21,652), Prayagraj (21,433), Azamgarh (20,642), Bareily (20,625), Lucknow (20,369), Unnao (16,376) and Bulandshahr (16,217) also saw significant number of applications.
Interestingly, Ghaziabad and Bulandshahr showed zero entry on November 20. So all the applications for these two districts are from November 21 and November 22.
Ghaziabad district recorded the highest number of Form 6 applications so far on November 22, with 39,828 submissions. Other districts with substantial numbers of applications include Agra (39,091), Lucknow (32,324), Kheri (27,904), Prayagraj (19,764) , Azamgarh (19,135) , Fatehpur (18,253), Bulandshahr (18,120), Barabanki (15,782), Bareily (15,096) and Gorakhpur (12,474).
A similar trend was observed in constituencies such as Loni, Ghaziabad, Lakhimpur, Etmadpur, Zaidpur, Bangermau, Dadri, Chakia and Barabanki.
Across the state, an assembly constituency typically recorded an average of around 17 Form 6 applications between November 1 and 16. However, the average rose sharply to 496 applications on November 21 and further to 966 on November 22.
Amid this surge, however, some pockets of western Uttar Pradesh recorded no substantial number of Form 6 applications. For instance, in Bijnor district, eight constituencies recorded no Form 6 applications, according to the compiled Form 9 lists on November 20 and 21. In Muzaffarnagar, six constituencies recorded a similar trend on November 20 and 21, while 22 constituencies did so on November 22.
Similar patterns were observed in pockets of Saharanpur, Moradabad, Meerut, Rampur, Bulandshahr and Shamli, among other districts.
The Back Story
On April 10, the final SIR roll for Uttar Pradesh was published. The total voters in the state plummeted from 15.44 crores to 13.39 crores in the process.
In December 2025, Yogi Adityanath warned that nearly 4 crore eligible voters could be missing during the SIR, claiming that 85-90% of them could be BJP supporters. Following the publication of the draft electoral roll on January 6, which reportedly recorded around 2.89 crore deletions, the BJP expressed concern, particularly over urban constituencies, and mobilised workers to help voters re-enroll.
In January 2026, a Newslaundry report said that the BJP was worried that large-scale deletions in urban constituencies could affect its electoral prospects. In 50 constituencies, more than one lakh voters had reportedly been deleted, 47 of which the BJP had won in 2022. The final roll, published on April 10, 2026, contained approximately 13.39 crore electors, down from around 15.44 crore before the SIR, with several BJP minister held constituencies reportedly recording substantial deletions.
On October 30, Adityanath claimed that 1.27 crore Hindu voters were missing, citing discrepancies involving panchayat electoral rolls, welfare beneficiaries and young voters. He mentioned 66 lakh names allegedly present on panchayat rolls but absent from Assembly rolls, 55 lakh welfare beneficiaries and approximately 4.5 lakh young voters.
On November 14, the BJP reportedly set targets of restoring 10,000–25,000 voters per assembly constituency, with party leaders estimating that 40–80 lakh voters could be re-enrolled. Following the publication of the SSR draft roll on November 17, the party planned to launch a booth-level voter addition campaign from November 20.

Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
- Published
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.
Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.
Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".
Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.
Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.
Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".
"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.
A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.
Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.
In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.
In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

Poch explains why Szoboszlai goal shouldn't have stood
Pochettino then insisted that Liverpool's opening goal should not have stood because Bradley Barcola was touching the Manchester United wall as Szoboszlai struck in.

The IFAB Laws of the Game state: "If, when a free-kick is taken, an attacking team player is less than 1 m (1 yd) from a 'wall' formed by three or more defending team players, an indirect free-kick is awarded."
Pochettino believes that the law applied to Szoboszlai's free-kick opener due to Barcola's involvement.

What did Webb say about Yoro decision?
In the latest edition of Match Officials Mic'd Up, Webb, chief refereeing officer at ProRef, described the on-field decision from referee Samuel Barrott as "decisive" and said the point of contention was around whether Isak would beat United goalkeeper Senne Lammens to the ball.
Audio from the officials reveals that the VAR, John Brooks, who backed Barrott's decision, determined Isak was "likely" to get on the end of the ball before Lammens. His assistant VAR, Paul Howard, agreed.

"There's a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens," said Webb. "Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would. That was the referee's call made on the field.
"The VAR checks that to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect and formed the opinion that it wasn't. If there was any doubt, then it was doubt.
"It wasn't going to be something that was clearly and obviously wrong and therefore allowed that decisive on-field decision to stand. And I think by and large most people would see that as a correct decision with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball.
"The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable, I guess. Certainly not clearly wrong."

New Delhi: The Centre is examining whether trade margin caps should be extended beyond cancer medicines to other high-cost and essential drugs, including antibiotics, diabetes and heart medicines, as well as biologics, while seeking to avoid disruptions to drug availability and hospital supplies, two government officials said.
The Department of Pharmaceuticals (DoP) and the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) are studying how such interventions could be structured, with officials indicating that any expansion would require product-level scrutiny rather than a uniform cap across entire therapeutic categories.
The exercise follows Supreme Court directions urging the government to look beyond cancer medicines and curb excessive markups across other therapeutic segments. In October, the Centre capped trade margins at 30% of the maximum retail price (MRP) on 137 non-scheduled cancer drugs. The move, effective 9 November, reduced retail prices by 70-93% for patients.
The review has implications for India’s $60-billion pharmaceutical industry, which is known as the pharmacy of the world for supplying low-cost generics and vaccines globally. It also comes amid growing scrutiny of healthcare costs, with state drug regulators flagging excessive markups not just on medicines but also on medical devices and hospital consumables. In September, Mint reported that Maharashtra FDA commissioner Tukaram Mundhe had flagged markups of up to 2,841% on products such as intravenous sets and syringes in private hospitals.
State drug regulators, including those in Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu, have also written to the pricing authority flagging high prices of medical devices, consumables and critical drugs.
“We are supportive of Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) for all medicines—including cardiology and diabetes drugs—provided it is a balanced approach that allows the industry to survive,‘’ said Anil Matai, director general of the Organisation of Pharmaceutical Producers of India (OPPI). “The focus should be on areas where there is a genuine issue, such as high-value antibiotics where margins are excessively high, sometimes reaching 90%, and where misuse is occurring.”
In an October 5 letter, Uttar Pradesh Food Safety and Drug Administration commissioner Roshan Jacob urged the NPPA to cap trade margins. Inspections across 214 hospital pharmacies in 22 medical colleges and 30 government and private hospitals had found pharmacies charging patients up to 67 times, or 6,623%, more than their procurement costs across 167 life-saving medicines and medical devices.
The challenge for regulators is that excessive margins are not necessarily spread uniformly across a therapeutic category. Antibiotics and anti-diabetes medicines, for instance, cover dozens of formulations, with unusually high markups often concentrated in a handful of products rather than across an entire class.
“In a category like antibiotics, we have oral tablets, injectables, and liquid formulations. Out of 30 antibiotics, perhaps only five may have an issue of high margins while the rest do not. We have to examine every category not just by therapy, but also by route of administration, while ensuring uninterrupted availability,” one of the officials said, requesting anonymity.
A key hurdle in assessing non-scheduled drugs is the absence of comprehensive market data. While the NPPA tracks retail pharmacy sales through third-party market researcher Pharmarack, some injectables and specialty drugs are supplied directly by manufacturers to hospitals, bypassing retail market audits.
“Because private hospitals and institutional stockists rarely disclose procurement records, retail datasets capture only a fraction of the actual market size in terms of sales value, leaving regulators with partial visibility,” the official added.
Enforcement challenges
For non-scheduled drugs, manufacturers are permitted to increase MRP by up to 10% annually over the preceding price. Regulators also face enforcement challenges within hospitals, particularly in the case of consumables such as syringes and intravenous sets.
“Even if trade margins on consumables are capped, hospitals, which fall outside the NPPA’s regulatory remit, can bill patients for higher quantities or raise bed, nursing, and consultation fees to protect revenues, diluting financial relief for patients,” the official said.
Queries emailed to the Department of Pharmaceuticals spokesperson and the NPPA chairman on Saturday, and to Max, Apollo, Fortis and Medanta hospitals, as well as the Tamil Nadu and Rajasthan drug authorities on Monday, remained unanswered till press time.
Mandatory disclosures for hospitals
The Uttar Pradesh government is seeking greater transparency in hospital pricing, even as it maintains that fixing prices and capping margins are outside its mandate.
“We will be checking compliance with the local directions we have issued, and we will also query any price-negotiated agreements between manufacturers and hospitals due to legitimate concerns over drug safety,‘’ Jacob told Mint over the phone. “Unlike food, where a person has a choice of what to eat, an ill person must take medicine and is therefore more vulnerable.‘’
“Everything we are doing is in the public interest because a patient, who is dependent on the institution, has a right to an informed choice that we must respect. At that point of need, there should be no exploitation. We are not capping margins or fixing prices, as that is not within our mandate; we are only asking for disclosure in the public interest,” Jacob added.
Still, some industry representatives defend standard trade margins.
“Hospital procurements differ from normal trade channels, as tenders for large quantities usually go for the lowest rates, and most mainstream companies that invest in quality, R&D, and branding follow standard industry margins of 10% to 20% rather than offering huge discounts. While the issue of hospital margins is currently sub judice before the Supreme Court, authorities must examine which specific companies or products are involved,” said Viranchi Shah, national spokesperson of the Indian Drug Manufacturers’ Association.
For now, health experts call for transparent oversight. “Capping excessive trade margins on life-saving medicines is a must to make healthcare more affordable and transparent," said Dr Aashish Chaudhry, managing director of Aakash Healthcare.
"However, hospitals cannot charge patients beyond the printed Maximum Retail Price (MRP) of any medicine. No hospital or pharmacy is permitted to bill a drug above MRP. Stronger monitoring, transparent procurement and billing practices, and effective regulatory oversight are essential to ensure that patients are not financially exploited,” Chaudhry said.
