Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving cola giants a tough fight in India
- Published
It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.
Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients.
They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially.
Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour.
The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin.
Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; £0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m.
Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts.
Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade.
There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu.
Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company.
"Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years."
Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades.
Parle Agro, external, one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012.
Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies.
The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033.
According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%.
"This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016.
"In global markets, established duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; an 8% swing in less than a year is a structural disruption."
Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand".
For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume.
With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal.
But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind.
Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that.
Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks.
This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth.
"The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC.
The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword.
While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin.
Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago.
Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category.
"Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements.
Coca Cola, which had acquired the cumin-flavoured Rimzim brand in the 1990s, is strengthening its play in this category and reportedly doubled production last year.
But the challenges haven't deterred the ambitions of the homegrown players.
"Indian flavours need to find a global spotlight," says Munjal, who is looking to tap the global market in the coming years.
"For generations, we've grown up drinking colas of the world, but I hope the next generations will drink the zeeras of India."

Change this Roku TV setting to watch movies how they were filmed
You don't have to leave your TV's refresh rate at 60fps.
If you were to travel back in time thirty years and show someone a smart TV from today, their head would likely explode. In addition to the seemingly limitless amount of content one can find and interact with on a modern television, your Roku TV also may have the ability to let you watch movies in a far more compelling way.
Buried deep in your Roku TV's settings is a way to alter the refresh rate, and there's a very specific reason that you might want to do that. Most Roku TVs default to a refresh rate of 60fps. While that's going to be perfectly fine for some situations, it doesn't make for the most theatrical viewing experience — for the most part, movies are filmed and projected at 24fps. It's the standard, and it has defined the way movies look and feel for decades. When you go to the movie theater, you're watching a 24fps output.
Roku allows you to alter your TV's refresh rate to match that, offering something a bit closer to the original intent of those films.
How to change your TV's refresh rate to 24fps to achieve a film look
There are a lot of ways to change the overall look and display of your Roku TV, but most of that discourse seems centered around colors and contrast. Those things are important, but if you really want to achieve a "movie look," then you'll want to change the refresh rate.
In your Roku TV, to match this unique look, you'll need to first go to the main menu. From here, select Settings, and then go into System. In this menu, you'll find something called Advanced System Settings, which will allow you to access Advanced Display Settings. You want to turn Auto-adjust display refresh rate on.
It's a one-click and done solution, as it will self-adjust itself to match the native refresh rate of any movie or TV show you put on. Because films have a native refresh rate of 24fps, your TV will now run them as such. The same goes for TV shows, which may be filmed at 30 or 60fps. It's a tiny adjustment, but it's one that will make your viewing experience even better.

Bengaluru-based robotics hardware startup Cosine Robots has raised ₹22.4 Cr (about $2.4 Mn) in a funding round led by Avaana Capital, with participation from WEH Ventures and angel investors. The startup will use the fresh capital to scale its new R&D and production facility in Bengaluru, expand its engineering team, and accelerate development of its integrated servo actuator portfolio. Founded by Kiran Mathew Koshy and Delip Thomas in 2024, Cosine Robots develops actuators and motion systems for robotic applications. Actuators convert energy into physical movement, helping control how precisely robotic joints move and how much turning force, or torque, they produce. “Our goal is to make high-quality robotics more accessible. This funding will help us strengthen our research and development and establish production capabilities for actuators designed and built by our team,” cofounder and CEO Koshy said. Building Robotic Motion Hardware Cosine Robots’ integrated servo actuators combine motors, gearboxes, sensors, electronics, and proprietary control software into a single system. The startup said developing these components together allows it to optimise precision, reliability, torque response, and cost. Its modular portfolio includes cycloidal and planetary actuators, which use different gearbox designs to address varying torque requirements. These are designed for applications ranging from industrial robotic arms and collaborative robots to quadrupeds and humanoids. The startup said its proprietary control architecture combines dual-position sensing with a 25 kHz control loop, executing 25,000 updates per second to regulate movement and torque. Cosine Robots aims to supply global robot manufacturers with an alternative to established actuator suppliers, competing on performance and cost. The funding comes at a time when investments in robotics and automation startups are picking up. Last week, Botsync raised $11 Mn in an IvyCap Ventures-led round to upgrade its factory automation software and mobile robots, and expand its engineering and project delivery teams in India. Earlier this year, industrial robotics startup Anscer Robotics raised ₹45 Cr in its Series A round to advance its product platform, scale US market operations, expand global partner network, and deepen international footprint.

- In early and mid-November, people shared videos allegedly showing what they called "jellyfish UFOs" flying over various cities, beginning with a repost of a genuine video recorded in Anchorage, Alaska, in June.
- The person who recorded the Anchorage video contended the object was not a kite or balloon. However, a woman with decades of experience in flying kites, including participating in a kite-flying group in the same area, told Snopes she believed that the clip "definitely" and "100%" showed an inflatable octopus kite.
- Research of the many videos users shared found no conclusive evidence of the objects involving extraterrestrials. Rather, some clips appeared to show popular jellyfish- or octopus-shaped kites (or balloons), while others displayed signs of generative artificial intelligence.
- This story involved three kinds of videos, including some clips appearing to quite clearly show kites or exhibit signs of AI, as well as others that looked blurry and lacked conclusive information about their purported originating date and location — making the content difficult to research. As such, Snopes has not rated this article.
In early and mid-November, people shared numerous videos online appearing to show jellyfish- or octopus-shaped objects hovering high in the sky. Users referred to the alleged phenomenon as "jellyfish UFOs," with some alleging the objects were the secret reason for the U.S. air travel ground stop and other service outages.
However, Snopes' investigation of the clips failed to uncover any definitive proof of aliens. Rather, of the many videos people shared, those with identifiable locations appeared to line up with parks or beaches, suggesting the clips simply captured people flying jellyfish- or octopus-shaped kites (or balloons). Some of the clips also appeared to have been created with artificial intelligence; for example, one video clearly displaying an AI-generated content label.
Snopes has not added a fact-check rating to this article, as our standards require comprehensive details and conclusive proof to establish a rating. This matter involves numerous videos, including some quite clearly showing kites, as well as others exhibiting signs of AI or lacking definitive information about their date and location.
We contacted a handful of users appearing to originally post some of the videos and have included the responses below.
Clips' spread started with Anchorage video
People have discussed supposed "jellyfish UFO" sightings for years. For example, a video from 2024 showed an object appearing to hover above a U.S. military base in Iraq.
Going back decades, The Associated Press, citing the Russian news agency TASS, reported (archived) about an event in Petrozavodsk, Russia, on Sept. 20, 1977, involving "a huge mass of light" that "hovered over the city in the form of a jellyfish sending down a multitude of fine beams." People now refer to that story as the Petrozavodsk phenomenon.
The wave of "jellyfish UFO" videos circulating in November appeared to begin with reposts of a video recorded in Anchorage, Alaska, in June, followed by some news media outlets reporting on the matter.
For example, a Nov. 3 Reddit post (archived) of the video displayed the title, "Video taken in Alaska of a strange jellyfish object. (Kite?)."
Video taken in Alaska of a strange jellyfish object. (Kite?)
by u/FrankMurphys in InterdimensionalNHI
The Reddit user linked to Facebook user Sara Jane Osborn's original post (archived) from June 15.
We identified Osborn's location in Google Street View after seeing the words "Alaska Geologic" on a building near the end of her video — matching the west side of the Alaska Geologic Materials Center. Osborn shared with us an image of the exact location where she recorded her video while her husband, Peter Osborn, sat in the driver's seat, confirming they faced directly east.
The object hovering in Osborn's video appeared clearer than the distant mountain haze, suggesting its closer proximity to the camera.
Using Google Earth, we moved directly toward where the object hovered, traveling over or very near at least three different parks or fields — nice spots for flying kites — first the large Russian Jack Park (about 1 mile east of the Osborns' location), then Creekside Park (about 2.4 miles east) and the Muldoon Elementary School athletic field (3.3 miles east).
Interviewing Sara Osborn
In an interview via Messenger, Sara Osborn said she and her husband were driving in Anchorage and stopped to take photos of a rainbow just after 10 p.m. (Sunset in Alaska occurs around 11:30 p.m. in June.)
She sent to us multiple photos, the video and metadata proof to help confirm she didn't use AI or other editing tools to create or manipulate her content. One photo, shown below, features the object hovering at 10:13 p.m.
(Sara Jane Osborn via Facebook, Snopes illustration)
Sara Osborn said she and her husband checked some nearby parks and kept searching but didn't locate the object again. She said she didn't believe it was a kite or balloon: "It was after 10PM… People were at home, getting ready for bed to go to work the next day." She added, "Only God & the government know what it is."
In 2010, Joint Base Elmendorf–Richardson, a military base located farther north and not in the same area of the hovering object's location, reported about launching weather balloons on an Alaskan island. Those weather balloons appeared white and round, and not in the shape of a jellyfish.
A spokesperson for the military base told us via email, "We are aware of a video circulating on social media regarding a reported aerial sighting near Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson from June 15, 2026, but have no additional information to provide at this time."
Local kite group member says 'definitely' octopus kite
To learn more about the Anchorage video, we reached out by phone to Debbie Wik, who represents the Alaskiters kite flying group and lives just southwest in Kenai.
Wik, who said she's been flying kites since about 1990 and has attended kite festivals for years, told us she believed the object in Osborn's video was "definitely" and "100%" an inflatable octopus kite, "probably at least a 50-meter inflatable black and white octopus." She also said she has no knowledge of anyone in her group flying that night.
She pointed us to recent photos and videos of her flying kites over Kenai in the daytime and LED-lit kites at night. Regarding the night flying Wik said, "I thought we were gonna cause an accident because everybody was pulling over and it was really cool."
The group created an interactive map in Google Maps identifying both Russian Jack Park and Creekside Park, as well as an area just south of Creekside Park, as prime flying locations.
Other 'jellyfish UFO' videos
Several social media accounts posted collections of various "jellyfish UFO" sightings. One of those collections began with an object resembling the two distinctly striped arms of an octopus foil kite that Amazon (archived) sells with 328 feet of string.
Another collection began with a video that the Pangram AI-detection website determined contained at least some inauthentic elements. That clip possibly originated from a Facebook post. We contacted that account to ask if the user created the clip. (Snopes does not entirely rely on AI detection tools to make conclusive determinations.)
The second clip in the collection, also a slideshow, featured two women looking at two jellyfish- or octopus-shaped kites, imaking fun of people who might believe the objects are aliens. The @swanvr Threads account recently claimed ownership of that clip, saying it dated back to 2024 and that "they're kites." The remaining four clips all appeared to show kites, as well.
A third collection displayed six still images of purported "jellyfish UFO" sightings, beginning with one from Osborn's Anchorage video. As one example, a search for the text caption's words, specifically "In the skies over Nashville," located a Facebook video appearing to show the man recording the clip of a "mysterious squid," including saying, "Nah, I think it's a kite."
Another example video (archived) out of Buffalo, New York, appeared to show the view out of a hospital window toward Ralph Wilson Park, also suggesting a kite.
One of the AI-generated videos
Another video showing a dark, octopus-shaped object flying in the sky displayed the words, "Clearest video to date thanks to my Canon EF-S 55-250mm Nov. 13th Arlington, Texas."
TikTok user @silversagag told us in a private message that he used AI to generate that video using images from two sources. The clip displayed an AI-generated content label, as well.
According to an AI prompt screenshot that the user shared with us, those two sources included Facebook user Deon Morris' post (archived), in which Morris claimed he found one of the supposed "alien babies" in his backyard, as well as a December Reddit post (archived) found on an Augusta, Georgia, subreddit mentioning Columbia County and "Evans Park."
In other words, the AI-generated video appeared to originate from some authentic content — meaning photos and videos genuinely recorded in reality — though the purported Augusta-area video still showed an object resembling a kite.
(Deon Morris via Facebook)
One close-up video (archived) that Morris recorded showed fibers, with commenters believing it was an old, dirty dog toy — potentially a rope dog toy that had unraveled or a no-sew octopus dog toy. We sent a private message to Morris to ask about his post and will update this story if we receive further information.
For further reading about similar untrue, fantastical matters, we recently investigated whether a video showed a pterodactyl flying in Mexico.

Seeing a rise in caesarean deliveries in India -- from 8.5% in 2005 to 21.5% in 2021 -- which is well above WHO-recommended levels, researchers are calling for policy measures, including more regulation in private healthcare, in an analysis published in The Lancet Regional Health Southeast Asia journal.
Study highlights
Delivering a baby via a caesarean section (C-section) involves making a surgical cut in the mother's abdomen and uterus.
The researchers, including those from the Institute of Public Health Bengaluru and Christian Medical College in Vellore, Tamil Nadu, said that while a medically indicated C-section is vital to preventing maternal and newborn mortality, rates of caesarean deliveries exceeding 10 per cent in the population are not linked with reduced mortality -- as noted by the World Health Organization.
An unjustified caesarean delivery is related to longer hospital stays and higher healthcare costs, with babies born through the procedure known to be at an increased risk of asthma, obesity, type 1 diabetes and allergies, among other health problems. The team reviewed 75 previously published studies -- mostly from India, followed by Bangladesh and Pakistan -- and examined factors in the countries' health systems contributing to caesarean procedures in the population.
Financial concerns
The authors said that an avoidable caesarean delivery can be financially stressful for families across South Asia, where a substantial fraction of deliveries occur in the private sector.
For example, out-of-pocket expenditures for a C-section in India will cost around Rs 43,000 in private hospitals, and around Rs 8,500 in public ones, suggesting that avoidable caesarean deliveries unnecessarily burden the healthcare system and families, they said.
Limited regulation and insurance coverage were among other factors associated with increased C-section rates. Decision-making at the healthcare provider's level was influenced by financial incentives, medico-legal concerns and scheduling convenience, the researchers said.
Driving factors
Mother's education, socioeconomic status and age, and family preferences were found to be individual and community-level factors driving an upward trend in caesarean deliveries.
Caesarean deliveries in Bangladesh are estimated to have increased from 18 per cent in 2011 to 45 per cent in 2022, while those in Pakistan rose to 20 per cent in 2018 from about three per cent in 1990. Data from national surveys were analysed for arriving at the figures.
The authors said that caesarean deliveries are being resorted to at nearly double the rates since 2000, with one in every five births involving the surgical procedure.
Coordinated policies needed
C-section rates in Asia rose from 4.4 per cent in 1990 to 19.5 per cent in 2014, with south Asia reflecting similar upward trends seen across the continent, they said.
"The review highlights the need for coordinated policy responses across levels, including payment reforms, regulatory oversight, and improved antenatal counselling, to ensure (C-section) use aligns with clinical need rather than socio-economic or institutional pressures," the authors wrote.

Sonia Gandhi, in her recently published memoir, recalls being advised surgery for suspected breast cancer in 2010. Since she is a prominent public figure, she wonders, in her book, whether she was entitled to even a modicum of privacy with regard to her health. Her account assumes renewed significance following a recent petition before the Madras High Court that inquired about the health of Kolathur MLA V.S. Babu (now deceased). These episodes expose a fundamental legal tension between the privacy politicians may want about their health, and the accountability they owe their constituents in a democracy. Does the public’s right to information justify waiving or limiting an office-holder’s medical confidentiality? How should a democracy reconcile these competing interests?
Medical information is among the most sensitive forms of personal information. A diagnosis may reveal not merely someone’s present condition but also their reproductive history, genetic predispositions, psychiatric illness or future health risks. Disclosure can invite discrimination, political exploitation and public speculation. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court recognised privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21. Holding public office does not automatically extinguish this protection. A politician receiving treatment need not publish laboratory reports. Nor does a disability establish an inability to govern. State intrusion needs lawful justification, not curiosity.
The Constitution does not prescribe a general medical-fitness requirement for occupying high public office. Article 58 sets eligibility conditions for the President but requires no medical-fitness certificate. Article 65(2) allows the Vice-President to perform presidential functions when the President cannot do so through absence, illness or another cause. The Constitution recognises presidential illness but does not specify a detailed procedure or medical authority to determine contested incapacity. This distinction between eligibility to assume office and capacity to continue functioning deserves closer scrutiny.
For legislators, Articles 102 and 191 prescribe disqualification when a person is of ‘unsound mind’ and stands so declared by a competent court (not by a medical board). Section 16(1)(b) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, similarly provides for disqualification from electoral registration (by court not medical board). For Supreme Court judges, Article 124(4) permits removal on proof of incapacity, while the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, provides a procedure that may involve a Medical Board. Article 317(3)(c), governing Public Service Commission members, permits removal for unfitness arising from ‘infirmity of mind or body’.

Wondering if you can buy houses in GTA 6? If so, how many safehouses are in Grand Theft Auto 6? There are a total of five safehouses in GTA 6. Each plays a pivotal role in the game and unlocks as you progress through the story’s missions. So, here are all the safehouse locations in GTA 6.
All GTA 6 Safehouse Locations
You cannot buy safehouses in GTA 6; rather, the five safehouses unlock as you progress through the game’s main story. Here is an overview of all the GTA 6 safehouse locations:
| Safehouse | Location | Chapter | 
|---|---|---|
| Jason’s House | Key Lento | Chapter 1 | 
| Starlet Motel | Port Gellhorn | Chapter 2 | 
| Bayside Apartments, 201 | North Vice City | Chapter 3 | 
| Y Hotel, Room 701 | Washington Beach | Chapter 4 | 
| Pegassi Residences | South Vice City | Chapter 5 | 
Jason’s Key Lento House
This is the first safehouse that we are introduced to. The house basically belongs to Brian Heder, but he lets Jason live in it rent-free if he maintains it.
With Lucia joining Jason, you, as a player, have to fix the house, and doing that creates a connection with it. Sadly, the house blows up at the end of Chapter 1 in GTA 6, and that’s when everything goes south for Jason and Lucia.
Do go through GTA 6 Chapter 1 missables to gain access to certain items, missions, and even a few collectibles, essential for 100% completion, that you won’t be able to get later on.
Starlet Motel
Starlet Motel is the second safehouse that Jason and Lucia have to take refuge in while running away from Mendez and his men. However, this temporary stay came with its fair share of issues.
Lucia has to find money to pay the rent, deal with annoying and creepy neighbours, and take care of Jason at the same time. Still, this safehouse holds a special place because of how important it was for Jason and Lucia to rebuild themselves.
Do go through GTA 6 Chapter 2 missables before you move on from this safehouse and restart your life in Port Gellhorn.
Bayside Apartments, 201
After Jason and Lucia finally depart from Port Gellhorn after yet another police chase, they make their way to Vice City. However, they come here with much less money than they would’ve hoped for.
Thankfully, Jason’s friend and one of the important GTA 6 characters, Dre’Quan Priest, fixes them up with an apartment.
This is the Bayside Apartment, owned by Boobie Ike. The place is much smaller than Jason’s house, but it still feels like a home that the Starlet Motel failed to feel like.
Y Hotel, Room 701
Finally, Jason and Lucia start to climb their way up the wealth chain, with Chapter 4 giving them a luxurious room in the Y Hotel.
After completing the Cartel Heist, Raul makes her money woman, Valentina, check Jason and Lucia into the luxurious hotel, which becomes their base of operations in Chapter 4.
However, the honeymoon period doesn’t last long, as betrayals and another chase force Jason and Lucia to leave once again and settle elsewhere.
Pegassi Residences
The final safehouse for Jason and Lucia is Pegassi Residences, which unlocks in Chapter 5 after finishing the Operation Savage Glory mission. This is the best safehouse, with a storage garage that has space for three vehicles. This is one of the nicest garage locations in GTA 6.
However, as Chapter 5 is the shortest in the game, neither Jason nor Lucia can enjoy it much, eventually reaching the GTA 6 endings.
So, these are all the safehouse locations in GTA 6. Have any questions about the safehouses? Let us know in the comments section below.

NorthEast United hit back close to the half-hour mark as Moyano displayed exquisite ball control, trapping dead a deft lobbed pass from Nikhil Barla. Escaping the Delhi backline, the Spaniard cut back inside to fire a low shot past Nora Fernandes at the near post.

‘The Jhulan effect’ — that’s what a near-obsessive search for the next Jhulan Goswami in the Indian women’s cricket ecosystem is called in jest. Who wouldn’t want another speedy maverick cut from the same cloth as the Bengal superstar? Tall, quick, incredibly disciplined, handy with the bat and, perhaps most importantly, commendably fit until the very end.
Jhulan, who walked into the sunset as the leading wicket-taker in ODIs with 255 scalps, belongs to a bridging era in Indian women’s cricket when pace bowling wasn’t the trendy option. Spinners headlined proceedings, while pacers were the fillers.
“In the beginning of my career, Amita Sharma [the incumbent selection committee chair] and Rumeli Dhar were there alongside me. Then came Snehal Pradhan and Shikha Pandey, followed by Mansi Joshi, Meghna Singh and Pooja Vastrakar, who made space in the team. India was always considered a spin-bowling side. That myth changed when our generation — Ami, Rumi and me — came in. Our pace attack started being talked about,” Jhulan tells Sportstar.
Cut to 2026, and India is a flourishing cradle for seamers.
While raw, explosive pace is not yet as abundant as India would like, bowlers with control, variations and gusto have emerged from various parts of the country. The existence of the Women’s Premier League (WPL) has only fanned the flames of a desperate need that was identified close to a decade ago: developing a pace pool that can pose problems for opponents, especially on international wickets.
However, India seems stuck in an unimaginative loop of emerging talent getting caught in the quicksands of injury and losing valuable time at the topmost tier of the game.
Pooja, Amanjot Kaur and Kashvee Gautam have missed World Cups due to persistent niggles and lengthy recoveries, while others, like Renuka Singh Thakur, have had patchy game time due to workload issues and stress fractures. A depleted pace attack, among other factors, left India red-faced after another group-stage exit at the T20 World Cup.
When Jhulan was settling into the sport, players had no access to speed-gun metrics. Indians are masters of jugaad (hacks), and this issue had one too.
“We often procured them when we toured abroad. Before that was possible, I used to tell our coach, Sudha (Shah) ma’am, to note our speeds and keep from broadcasting them. I also spoke a lot to the opponent batter and would ask how the ball felt. The ball needed to hit the sticker of the bat. I wanted to beat the batter, come what may. In the nets, I also always asked the keeper, and tried to train with one facing me. Today, things are much different,” she notes.
Now, empirical tools are widely used. CricViz consistently places Jhulan in the 125-128 kmph range, despite competing in an age where modern-day staples such as nutrition monitoring, biomechanical experts and strength-and-conditioning staff were hard to come by. One outlier reading even puts her at 132.1 kmph during the 2016 Women’s T20 World Cup.
Among Indian pacers since the 2000s, Amita Sharma has a recorded fastest speed of 128.90 kmph, while Shikha Pandey’s top speed is 124.35 kmph. Kranti Gaud and Arundhati Reddy, with 119.62 and 118.51 kmph respectively, are the closest to the 120 kmph mark. But the former — young and still developing her game — has struggled with consistency in control. Arundhati, meanwhile, relies more on disciplined rhythm and variations to stay economical, take wickets, or both.
But is the search for a speedster who can match or, better still, surpass this benchmark possible in a system that forces its talents to bowl slower?
Winning or developing?
Some of India’s best spinners today — from Deepti Sharma and N. Sree Charani to even Poonam Yadav — started out as medium-pacers. However, factors such as a relatively small build or the tendency to concede runs because of their pace steered these players towards spin.
“After close to 10 years of senior cricket, I found a coach who told me to become a leg-spinner,” Ananya Upendran, former cricketer and lead scout for Delhi Capitals, told this publication back in 2024.
Four years prior, and periodically since, Ananya would remind anyone listening and reading on her socials about all things big and small the system continues to get wrong with pace bowling in the women’s game. In 2020, one such post aired her frustration about teams in the Women’s T20 Challenge – a three-team exhibition tournament for women attached to the IPL before the Women’s Premier League was breathed into reality – not giving pacers enough match opportunities.
“There is this constant pressure on pacers in India to hit the high standards of Goswami the minute they don international colours. This is unrealistic. We need to give them room to develop, and tournaments like this (and India A) are the perfect platforms,” she said.
“We don’t use pacers enough in domestic cricket,” declares Neetu David, former chief selector of the women’s national team (2020-2025). Incidentally, 12 seam-bowling options were handed debuts across both white-ball formats during her committee’s tenure.
“Even today, we tell State associations to give pacers at least 10 overs, even if they bowl in spells of two, three or four overs. If they don’t play in the States, it gets tough to bring them up to the national level. But States want to win championships, and that’s understandable too. Coaches worry about results ruining their record. They find their spinners are more proficient wicket-takers and turn to them. Rajeshwari Gayakwad used to open the bowling for Team India,” Neetu recalls.
Pace brings an unpredictability that both Ananya and Neetu feels domestic decision-makers largely wish to avoid. The ball could beat not just the batter but the fielders too, running away to the boundary.
“I can tell you from my own state, Uttar Pradesh, where we had very good pacers, but the earlier coaches used to say, ‘You are too erratic and bowling too fast. Please slow down and just swing it.’ So the kid would start thinking: If my catches get dropped, there’s no point; the coach will drop me from the team,” Neetu explains.
Shikha corroborates this experience.
“We play in smaller grounds, with 55-yard boundaries and fast outfields. There were so many instances when I would bowl, just miss the stumps or get an inside edge. I might have a slip and a third in place, but the edge would hit a hand and run away for four. That four would be remembered. I had mentors like Purnima Rau who encouraged me to bowl fast, but that was in a domestic system where only one medium-pacer would be fielded.”
“I just hope our girls get really strong and start hitting spinners too,” she quips.
Neetu’s tenure also saw the BCCI organise several pace-bowling camps, which brought age-group talent under the Board’s ambit for monitoring and high-performance training. But a foundational change in the selection process itself was also needed.
“When V.V.S. Laxman took charge at the National Cricket Academy, which later became the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence, we discussed clear criteria for every player. For spinners, that was 12-15 wickets, and a similar bar was set for pacers too. But we had to tell him that pacers don’t get enough match time or overs. So the criterion was relaxed to a lower wicket bracket. We brought in specialist coaches to work with these girls. We even had Australian bowling consultant Troy Cooley at the NCA and later with the women’s team too,” she says.
Ananya remembered that Cooley stint being a breath of fresh air for the player pockets he worked with, but believes it wasn’t largely different from what high-performance pools anyway get exposed to.
“He encouraged experimentation and learning more variations, too. So a lot of bouncers, yorkers, and such. They also had a speed contest, but these have never been an issue at the national setup tier. The issue is that the attitudes don’t trickle down. You can’t come back to the domestic level and implement your learnings. If you’re told no bouncers or pacey deliveries when you get hit or concede runs, and lines like, ‘Who allowed you to try that?’, you’re almost taking a step back. What’s the point of learning a skill you can’t use?” she asked.
Doubling up as all-rounders
“The runs bowlers get for you are the ones that give you games,” Shikha Pandey recalls former head coach W.V. Raman telling the team. She remembers a tense international match in which she and spinner Radha Yadav stitched together a crucial 17-ball, 22-run stand to snatch a three-run victory.
For years, India’s inability to make its tail wag has been a bête noire. As a result, domestic coaches no longer view batting as a luxury for fast bowlers; it is an absolute prerequisite for survival.
Sukhwinder Singh Bawa, coach to medium-pacer Nandni Sharma, explicitly trained her to finish tight games under pressure. In the nets, he created situational simulations — 15 runs needed off 10 balls — forcing Nandni, who bowls a clever 110 kmph seam-up delivery and a dipping slower ball in the low 80s, to master lower-order hitting.
“My trademark has always been developing all-rounders, from Yuvraj Singh to Reema Malhotra,” Bawa explains. “The idea was to ensure selectors saw that she could bat, maybe even promote her higher up the order.”
Nagesh Gupta, coach to international seamers Amanjot Kaur and Kashvee Gautam, is equally blunt about the national setup’s demands. “The team suffers because the batting thins out after number six. Just bowling is a tough pathway now. Everyone is bowling — so who in the pool can bat well? Producing all-round performances in pressure games is a necessity.”
This push reflects a global game increasingly dominated by pace-bowling all-rounders — from South Africa’s Marizanne Kapp and Annerie Dercksen and England’s Nat Sciver-Brunt and Issy Wong to Australia’s formidable assembly line featuring Ellyse Perry, Annabel Sutherland and Nicola Carey, among a host of others.
It’s a tough balance. Nagesh’s academy trains 55 girls in the 8-10 age bracket, of whom 25 are pure batters and 16 are pace bowlers.
But in India, this dual requirement has not settled in seamlessly and has come at a steep physical price. Nagesh notes that as young seamers rise through the ranks, the demands of bowling express overs and contributing with the bat can trigger severe workload issues.
Gaps at the grassroots
“The spike in injury rates is natural and will continue for a few years. The women’s game has exploded, and bowlers are now expected to do something different from what they trained for,” Welsh high-performance fast-bowling coach Steffan Jones says.
“There are biological differences, and so pace programmes for men and women, or boys and girls, need to accommodate them. India largely has a one-size-fits-all approach,” he explains.
“Early specialisation is a problem in India. A youngster who likes cricket takes it up, and that’s it. The robustness and athleticism needed for it are never developed. On the other hand, in England, for instance, a young bowler would probably do a lot of gym work and training, but not enough bowling. No country has really nailed the balance,” says the newly announced Mumbai Indians bowling consultant.
After the 2017 ODI World Cup, Shikha Pandey approached Jones hoping to unlock higher speeds. His recent work with Indian men’s team all-rounder Nitish Kumar Reddy, whose marked improvement in pace was there for all to see, underlines that this can be done. But the parallels end there.
“Nearly 20 per cent of ball speed comes from your run-up. Too many female bowlers have short run-ups. So if you’re removing the momentum you get from a proper run-up, the force goes somewhere else. That’s potentially the crease, with angular momentum and rotation, which takes a lot out of the body because this depends on strength and muscle.
“Women can run as well as men, just a bit slower. If we’re discouraging them from running and attacking the crease, we’re making the game harder for female fast bowlers,” he says, citing run-up tweaks as one of the elements he worked on with Shikha.
An Australian study on non-elite female pacers shows that, unlike men — who generate velocity by bending forward at the waist — female seamers show no statistical relationship between forward trunk flexion and release speed. Instead, 89 per cent of speed variation in female pacers is driven by delayed arm circumduction and torso rotation.
“Female bowlers should be encouraged to have a more midway or front-on bowling action. We can’t teach them to be side-on, with the back foot parallel to the crease. I call them hip-and-knee-dominant bowlers. Men run with their pelvis open. But the female body can’t get its foot around because it needs a lot of internal hip rotation and strength, which the female body often can’t do. I encourage my trainees to be more like jumpers and sprinters, not side-on bowlers.”
But the route to that is not about overdoing any one element. “Practice doesn’t make perfect; practice makes permanent,” he underlines, advising against overbowling young cricketers and emphasising the need to “bulletproof the body” instead.
Matt Mason, former England women’s pace-bowling coach, found the lack of foundational bowling work a challenge. “The first difference between men and women is how they’re brought into the game. They haven’t bowled as many overs as young men. Usually, the age-group programmes available to boys aren’t available to girls. Males bowl more and so have built a little more resilience. Add the biomarkers that are different for both genders to this. What we’ve found is that when we put our athletes in safe positions, we put them in better positions to perform well,” says Mason, who is now with London Spirit in The Hundred.
He cites Freya Kemp as an example of a pacer who took up 50-over cricket and made her international 50-over debut in the span of a few months. That would never happen in the men’s game.
“Women and girls recruit a lot of their physical strength to bowl fast, whereas men don’t. Men use the technical model far more efficiently. The girls rely on strength and rotation. So that means they have to be very strong because they’re going to use those muscle groups. But then, obviously, we know there’s a gap in that area as well. The frustration for me is that, at the very beginning of their cricketing journey, potentially in the 12-14 age group, some of these habits have already formed. That’s where our coaches need to be,” he adds.
Repeatable actions also do not guarantee adaptability in high-pressure situations. This is Jones’ biggest gripe with how training systems work.
“A net session or an intensive training block is still not up to match-day intensity. It isn’t preparing bowlers. The stress of competition, crowds and the context of a match cannot be replicated in the nets. But the game still runs on this notion that we need to bowl more and train more. If you get a bowler to go at the stumps for an hour, I promise you the deliveries they bowl in the second 30 minutes will not be hard enough. Fast bowling is a mental activity too. It’s about going flat out for a few seconds and then having full recovery,” Jones argues.
Jhulan’s own experiences corroborate this.
“As a new-ball opener, we barely got new balls to train with in the open nets. So, learning to control was done on the go in matches and was quite challenging. I’d have people casually tell me, ‘You’re going too fast and erratic. Bring down the pace, swing the ball more.’ With all due respect, I quite happily ignored them,” she gushes.
The many deaths of pace
In a batter’s universe, a bowler’s currency is the dot ball. Accuracy over speed, then, becomes the formula to dry up runs.
“You’re given these cones and asked to bowl 30 balls in that box. When you’re young and quick, you’re not accurate. And if you want to finish that session, you have to do as told. Pace dies in that compromise,” Ananya adds.
Visakhapatnam-based pacer Shabnam Shakil, who emerged as a credible raw-pace option at the U-19 level, is a case in point.
“We just bowl young quicks into the dust. Look at Shabnam. She’s been playing cricket non-stop since 2022. She was clocking 113 kmph at one stage. Her body is developing. She was invariably in every state and NCA-level camp. It’s good to see faith in them this way and a desire to keep them in the system. But we need to remember these are developing women and we shouldn’t push them ahead until they are ready. The 5 kmph drop in pace she had at one point, with a heavily strained action, was inevitable,” Ananya had pointed out.
Shikha believes age tiers exist for a reason. Promoting youngsters should also come with pragmatism.
“Shabnam was playing U-16, U-19, U-23 and senior cricket at the domestic level. You have an U-23 side because you don’t want players dropping off after U-19, but you don’t want U-19s playing seniors all the time either. Their development needs to follow that physical gradation too, sometimes,” she points out.
It doesn’t help that fast bowling has been quantitatively identified as the single most injury-prone role in women’s cricket, according to an Australian review of shoulder injuries from 2015 to 2023.
Furthermore, a study conducted at the University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, found injury prevalence reaching up to 53.8 per cent among pacers. Among the potential problem areas, lower-back pain affects up to 53.9 per cent of elite female pacers, while shoulder pain impacts up to 46.5 per cent.
““Honestly, players are afraid to speak up to some extent, because they don’t want to lose opportunities they’ve fought so hard to get. They have to be told repeatedly to be open.””Nagesh Gupta, Kashvee and Amanjot’s coach
Take Pooja’s case. Long viewed as India’s premier pace-bowling all-rounder, she has spent years navigating a relentless cycle of injury and return — most recently enduring an 18-month layoff following surgery to repair a torn supraspinatus tendon in her bowling shoulder, a textbook casualty in a sport where rotator cuff-related pain accounts for 59 per cent of all time-loss shoulder injuries among seamers. She’s also had previous surgeries on both knees.
During her recovery, Royal Challengers Bengaluru signed her for the WPL strictly as a batter. Working under England seam legend Anya Shrubsole, she gained a vital psychological lifeline.
“My pace was all over the place, but RCB told me my batting was enough,” she recalls. “That confidence came at a time when I felt inadequate for this game.”
“ Injuries toh hoga (injuries are inevitable). Look at the spurt in matches and series now. We played two or three series tops, and then there was the odd year with ICC events or tournaments like the Asia Cup. Now that number has tripled, and so has the intensity,” Jhulan argues.
There’s an incongruence in the way injuries are handled in this environment, according to the veteran pacer.
“The issue is that players get injured, work on recovery and slot right back into the national side. Game time there becomes wonky, and you give it your all in the odd chance you’re given. That actually isn’t good for your recovery. This is where the domestic system should be used. Go back, play games and work your way out of the injury. We have the infrastructure to monitor and tweak things there, in synergy with the national side.”
For Pooja, the hardest part of rehabilitation is overcoming the mental fear of re-injury during load progression. “No athlete at the highest level is ever 100% fit,” she explains. “When coming back, your body isn’t used to the load, so everything is sore and the fear of re-injury takes over. Eventually, a moment has to come when you rise above the pain and stop responding negatively to it,” she explained.
Learning from the best
India has plenty to learn from its two main international adversaries.
Australia, easily the mecca of pace in women’s cricket purely because of the quantity of credible pacers it regularly produces, has more granular initiatives such as Project130. A partnership between Cricket New South Wales and the University of Technology Sydney (UTS), its stated objective is to plug the research gap that pushes cricket to condition female bowlers according to frameworks designed for men. The venture aims to help female fast bowlers reach the 130 kmph-and-above spectrum and stay there, while keeping injuries to a minimum.
England’s Women’s Pace Bowling Programme, launched in 2024, has also been working closely with tier-one counties to groom and induct pace-bowling talent into the mainstream. An important additional focus of the initiative is identifying taller athletes transitioning from sports such as netball and basketball, and tapping into their natural potential for bounce and, maybe even, raw pace.
It helps that their domestic teams are closely intertwined with franchise systems and, by extension, the national side’s interests. The Women’s Big Bash has State-based teams, making the pathways uncomplicated, as does England with its county setup.
India’s WPL, in this regard, stands out. With just five teams carrying the ambitions of a nation of 1.4 billion, calls to add another team (or two) got a renewed push after the recently concluded auction for the 2027 edition.
“In the initial stages, not many franchises looked at grooming as a priority or at building players over four to five seasons within the setup. It’s a new tournament, and teams are still finding their feet. We’ve started seeing that change slowly now. The next couple of years, and perhaps the addition of teams, will make a difference to how much ownership teams take of their players’ growth arcs,” Ananya explained.
The road ahead
Mason hopes the system will eventually render someone like him redundant, where bowlers won’t need him anymore — something a coaching-intensive setup like India’s can adopt. He cites Lauren Bell’s example while illustrating how a bowler who never really set her own fields is now a free-thinking phenom. Likewise, he cautions against changing bowling techniques for the sake of it, suggesting intervention only when necessary. Both are areas where Indian systems still have considerable catching up to do at the domestic level.
Neetu and Jhulan, apart from sharing an almost military-level precision in their bowling, also believe players should learn to deploy their skills on flatter tracks without the usual creases on the forehead.
“The modern game values runs, which is why these wickets are a lot more popular now. I’m not praising myself, but back in my time, people used to say that David could turn the ball even on a cement wicket. I feel even today, despite it being a batting wicket, as a bowler, you can still do well there,” Neetu says.
“International cricket is played on flat tracks, right? The younger kids coming through need to hone their skills on flat tracks, so let that be an added challenge. Spinners can maximise turners, and seamers can make use of moisture early in the morning to effect some damage. We see bowlers often clueless on flat strips. We want to avoid that,” Jhulan adds.
She also vehemently denies that height is a prerequisite for a pacer, despite an Australian study titled ‘In-match analysis of elite female cricket pace bowlers’ identifying height as the single best physical predictor of release speed. It explains that 53 per cent of speed variation in female fast bowlers is due to longer lever arms. Taller bowlers also have higher run-up velocities.
“Look at Shabnim Ismail [the South African pacer who bowled the fastest recorded delivery in women’s cricket, at 132.1 kmph during WPL 2024, according to official broadcaster JioHotstar]. She’s not tall, but she bowls so fast. She is a genuine seam bowler. She runs so smoothly. I often feel there are springs under her feet,” she adds.
A new appreciation for speed also brings with it a rush of people claiming they can help players go up a few gears.
“First, assess whether the action is injury-inducing. Once the action becomes safely repeatable, drills for fast bowling, such as brace-leg or arm-delay routines, can be done. Posture can be fixed as well, and we can safely see a 4-5 kmph increase. That’s the maximum you should aim for. Many academies claim to make a 15 kmph increase possible. Do not fall for that. Fast bowling is a natural thing, and you must listen to your body,” Nagesh warns.
Most importantly, Jhulan believes, it is perhaps high time India separated its pace pool by format to ensure smoother team outcomes and, more importantly, player welfare.
“We need 10-15 players in a seam-bowling pool whom India can use rotationally. Place players in ODI, T20I and Test duties, respecting their strengths and limitations. Batting roles are so well-defined. Do that with bowlers too. And the push India had a few years ago to make the top and middle order bowl as well was novel. It gives the captain options and contingency plans,” she explains.
Pace bowling in the women’s game has long needed greater intent. The next step may not be finding another Jhulan, but building a pool deep enough that India never again depends on one. Only then will the chase for 130 kmph become realistic.

The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this “smoke taint” adversely affected not only local wine production, but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant.
That’s why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists.
As previously reported, the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018, OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper—identified the growing popularity of “dry hopping” (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon.
All beer contains hops, a key flavoring agent that also imparts useful antimicrobial properties. (Beer spoils quickly without them.) Brewers mash and steep grain in hot water, which converts all that starch into sugars. This is traditionally the stage where hops are added to the liquid extract (wort) and boiled to give the beer that hint of bitterness. During the boiling process, a portion of the resins (alpha acids) in hops isomerize into iso-alpha acids. That chemical rearrangement of the molecules is what produces bitterness. Yeast is then added to trigger fermentation, turning the sugars into alcohol.

Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
- Published
As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She is thinking about getting around more easily.
The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.
For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.
"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.
But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.
It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.
Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.
The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.
The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.
But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?
The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.
Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.
"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza
"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."
DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.
A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.
The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.
The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.
The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.
At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.
When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.
The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.
Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.
LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.
For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.
"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.
Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.
But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.
"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."
Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.
"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.
The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.
Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.
"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.
But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.
The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.
"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."
For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.
State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.
LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.
"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.
"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.
Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing.
"Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.
But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?
Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas.
The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.
The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups.
"The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst
"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."
At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.
"We want the partnership to support local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.
Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.
There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.
While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere.
"When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.
Areias shares that concern.
"We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.
Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life.
For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.
But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.
Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.

By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history.
No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years.
As it turns out, Belonging does not read as incendiary. It errs, rather, towards discretion and legacy-building. It is also, at its best, a heartbreaking story of love and loss.
Gandhi’s voice is measured and generally frill-free. Flourishes do accompany the meet-cute at a Greek restaurant in Cambridge in the mid-1960s that sets off the story. “That January Sunday, which was to change my life,” she writes, “the sky [was] a beautiful azure dotted with puffy white clouds as in a Tiepolo fresco.” The introduction to fellow student Rajiv Gandhi was “a bolt of lightning”.
And, as in a film, there is parental resistance. Sonia’s father, a businessman who worked in construction in a small Italian town, is a second world war veteran, nicknamed Maino the Lion. A 1998 New Yorker profile by Patrick French, briefly a collaborator on Belonging, had him down as “an unrepentant fascist” until his death. Well, was he? We don’t get to find out. Wherever expedient, Gandhi maintains her strategic silence.
Stefano Maino, at any rate, is “padre padrone” – literally, “father master”. When he hears about his middle daughter’s love interest, he brings “his fist down on his writing table” with a shout of “Basta!” And yet, he buys her a ticket to India the moment she turns 21.
On the boy’s side is the person who would come to be described as the world’s most powerful woman, Indira Gandhi, the daughter of India’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Barely has Sonia landed in Delhi than Indira decides the pair must wed (the news reaches the Mainos via radio; Signor Maino stays away). Indira then manages Sonia’s first pregnancy, directs the name-giving ceremony – you get the picture. Gandhi refers to her, factually, as “my mother-in-law”, but, subverting the stereotype, she becomes a devoted daughter. Walking us through her induction into elite Indian family life, she draws an affectionate portrait of this formidable 20th-century figure.
But family and party allegiance are a distorting lens through which to view history. Charged events, such as Indira’s crushing of a huge railway strike, acquire a benign gloss. The 21 tumultuous months of the 1975 Emergency – which saw members of the opposition arrested, civil liberties curtailed, the press censored, while a despotic nepo-baby (Sanjay, Indira’s younger son) ran amok – are rendered with a brisk calm. Tenderness is reserved for the repercussions on the family in its subsequent period out of power.
Sanjay’s death at 33, just after Indira’s return to power in 1980, leaves the matriarch broken. “In her eyes [Rajiv] was the only one who could come to her rescue.” Gandhi does not interrogate the hereditary approach to democratic politics, but she does recount, affectingly, the fight to protect herself and Rajiv – a commercial pilot with no greater ambitions – and their two children from the inferno.
In the book’s strongest scene, she waits disoriented in a crowded hospital in 1984, “shivering under my dressing gown”, having ferried her mother-in-law’s bullet-ridden body there. Indira was slain by her Sikh bodyguards in revenge for ordering the army into the Golden Temple, Sikhism’s holiest site. As Rajiv embraces her with the words “they want me to be sworn in as prime minister”, Gandhi feels “a rage welling up deep inside me”. “They will kill you too!” she says. “They will kill me anyway,” he replies. The “they” is unspecified, and gives these pages an air of foretold tragedy.
Rajiv’s eventful term plays out under this death cloud. It starts with a pogrom against Sikhs, spearheaded by Congress leaders. Gandhi goes some length to eulogise her husband’s tenure: in reality, it was a troubled and contradictory record. Rajiv was 40, severely underqualified, and grieving. Miscalculations abounded, among them clumsy religious manoeuvring that played into the Hindu-nationalist BJP’s hands, and a military entanglement in Sri Lanka designed to end the civil war with Tamil separatists.
And that death cloud never blows way. The children are withdrawn from school; Gandhi, perpetually anxious, finds her hands trembling in public; Rajiv is once shot at. When he loses the election his successor vindictively withdraws his special security cover. Their son Rahul (the current leader of the opposition) predicts the worst. At a rally in Tamil Nadu in 1991, a Tamil Tiger operative makes to place a garland around Rajiv, then 46, with explosives strapped around her body.
The graphic photograph of the aftermath of that scene is seared into Indian memory. Thanks to the vigilance of her children, Gandhi has never seen it. “I had become the child to be protected, they the parents,” she writes, in a wrenching section. Years later, when she collapses in Japan, a nurse is startled to find her grown children lying on either side of her on the small hospital bed.
Gandhi’s first reaction on hearing the news about Rajiv? “I wanted to die.” Gradually though, she picks up the smithereens of her life. As the remaining Gandhi elder, she picks up the pieces of the splintering Congress party, too.There are few parallels to a life as singular as this. A century ago, Congress had its first foreign-born female president, the British theosophist Annie Besant; farther afield, Janet Jagan, the American-born Jewish wife of Cheddi Jagan herself became president of Guyana – but both women were political activists to begin with. Gandhi, in her words, “had no right – except for the fact that I carried the family name”.
The exhortations to Gandhi to take over the party reveal plenty about Congress culture, and they are eventually successful: the spectator becomes the player. We watch her bone up on her Hindi, lead campaigns, stitch up alliances (including with a party sympathetic to the Tamil Tigers), and combat the BJP, which brands her, among other things, a “Monica Lewinsky” who would establish a “Rome Raj”. In 2004, she leads an alliance of parties to victory.
To her children’s horror, Gandhi is badgered into nearly accepting the post of prime minister. Instead she handpicks a candidate, Manmohan Singh, while keeping charge of the party (eventually leading it for a staggering 22 years) and chairing the ruling coalition as well as an advisory council that keeps a hand on policy levers.
“It had been my choice to become Indian,” she reflects after the long night of the soul that leads her to decline the premiership – a source of fascinated speculation over the years. “I made it out of love for a man, but that love came to encompass his family and his country. And it was this love for India that had demanded the most from me.”
Belonging comes into its own when unpacking those demands, and showing the transition from grief to its successor emotion, resilience.

Owning a home does not always mean that monthly expenses are low. A couple living in Noida has revealed that they spend around ₹1.25 lakh every month, even though they own their house and do not have to pay rent. The couple shared a video on Instagram explaining their monthly expenses. Their spending includes groceries, household help, gym memberships, grooming, food and travel. The expense breakdown has started a discussion on social media, with many people questioning how a couple can spend so much every month without paying rent. According to the couple, groceries are their biggest monthly expense at ₹30,000. They also spend around ₹20,000 on grooming. Their gym memberships and Pilates classes cost another ₹15,000 every month. Supplements such as protein powder and multivitamins add ₹15,000 to their expenses. The couple said they spend around ₹30,000 on groceries every month and another ₹20,000 on grooming. Their gym and Pilates sessions cost ₹15,000, while supplements add another ₹15,000 to their monthly expenses. They also pay ₹10,000 for household help and spend another ₹10,000 on eating out. Home maintenance costs them ₹8,000, while electricity bills come to around ₹5,000. Internet, mobile and OTT subscriptions together cost ₹6,000. Their monthly commute expenses are between ₹5,000 and ₹6,000. Together, these expenses add up to around ₹1.25 lakh every month. The couple also spends ₹10,000 on household help, which includes cooking and cleaning. Their electricity bill is around ₹5,000, while home maintenance costs them another ₹8,000. They spend ₹6,000 on internet, mobile bills and OTT subscriptions. Travelling to work costs them between ₹5,000 and ₹6,000 every month. The couple also explained how much more they would have to spend if they did not own their home. According to them, renting a similar 3BHK flat in their area would cost around ₹45,000 to ₹50,000 every month. This could take their total monthly expenses from ₹1.25 lakh to nearly ₹1.75 lakh. Their video has received mixed reactions online. Some people questioned the ₹30,000 grocery budget, while others were surprised by the ₹20,000 spent on grooming. Some users also pointed out that spending ₹15,000 on gym memberships and another ₹15,000 on supplements was a personal choice rather than a necessary monthly expense. Others said that the couple's spending showed how expensive certain lifestyles can become in a city like Noida. The couple's video has also started a wider discussion about monthly expenses in Indian cities. Even without rent or home loan payments, costs such as food, fitness, personal care and household help can take up a large part of a family's income.
