Bengaluru-based spacetech startup GalaxEye has awarded Bellatrix Aerospace a multi-year contract to supply propulsion systems for its next 30 Drishti Gen-II satellites, part of an OptoSAR constellation it aims to deploy by 2030. Under the phased delivery schedule, Bellatrix will design, build, test, and deliver its Arka Hall-effect electric propulsion systems for the satellites. The companies did not disclose the contract value. GalaxEye cofounder Pranit Mehta told Inc42 that deliveries will begin with systems for the first two satellites before scaling to the planned 30-satellite constellation. Bellatrix will be the programme’s primary propulsion supplier, he added. Announced today at the fifth India International Space Conclave organised by the Indian Space Association (ISpA), the agreement is India’s largest order between private space companies by satellite count, the startups claimed. The propulsion systems will help move satellites from their initial drop-off orbits into assigned positions, maintain spacing across the constellation, avoid space debris, and deorbit at the end of their operational lives. Mehta said GalaxEye is also in active discussions with other Indian companies for its satellite programme, covering power systems, control systems, communications, and other subsystems. “The Indian private ecosystem is here and now, and it is time that we partner with each other and not just rely on the government. The government has already done its job, and it is time for us to step up and help each other out,” he said. Other Indian space companies also announced domestic partnerships at the conclave. Earth observation startup Pixxel signed MoUs with Centum Electronics and CS TECH Ai (Ceinsys Tech) to explore collaboration across satellite hardware, geospatial applications, and orbital sustainability. With Centum, Pixxel will explore developing advanced electronics for satellite payloads and related subsystems. Its agreement with CS TECH Ai covers potential applications combining satellite data with geospatial analysis and engineering, including infrastructure monitoring. The partnerships come as Pixxel looks to expand its satellite manufacturing and Earth intelligence capabilities after raising $100 Mn in a Series C funding round earlier this year. Building Beyond Mission Drishti Founded in 2021 by Mehta, Suyash Singh, Denil Chawda, Kishan Thakkar, and Rakshit Bhatt, GalaxEye combines optical imaging and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) on a single satellite. Its OptoSAR technology supports Earth observation through clouds and at night for defence, agriculture, disaster management, maritime monitoring, and infrastructure. The startup launched its first satellite under Mission Drishti aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in May. However, in July, it said it lost communication with the spacecraft following an anomaly it linked to a geomagnetic solar storm. GalaxEye said the mission validated deployment, attitude control, onboard computing, and in-house mission operations. It subsequently outlined plans to launch two more OptoSAR satellites within 24 months while strengthening its engineering capabilities. In September, GalaxEye secured a US patent for its OptoSAR technology, which synchronises optical and radar sensors. Later that month, the Technology Development Board committed ₹63.84 Cr through optionally convertible debentures under the government’s Research, Development and Innovation Fund for multisensor satellite technology targeting imaging resolution finer than 0.5 metres. The startup also acquired spacecraft engineering company StarOps in August to deepen its in-house capabilities. Meanwhile, Bellatrix develops electric and green propulsion systems for satellites. Its Arka electric thrusters offer greater propellant efficiency than conventional chemical systems. The startup tested its propulsion technology aboard ISRO’s PSLV-C58 POEM-3 mission in January 2024. Bellatrix raised $20 Mn (₹189.7 Cr) in a pre-Series B round led by Cactus Partners in March 2026 and is expanding manufacturing to serve satellite operators in India and overseas.

Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.
Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.
President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation, according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton.
The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got.
Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit.
“If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.”
Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday. When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock.
“Some tech companies have become so big—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses,” says Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics.
Fishman sees a parallel in Wall Street’s slow reckoning with sanctions. “It took years of aggressive enforcement to get banks to take US sanctions compliance seriously,” he says. “We haven’t seen anything comparable in the tech sector, which helps explain why US export controls remain so weak and leaky.” Reinstating Huang on the administration's assurances before Nvidia’s own investigation has concluded “does not inspire confidence that meaningful enforcement is coming,” he says.
Emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant US trade representative who now directs the Energy, Economics, and Security program at the Center for a New American Security, says the administration’s record gives little reason to take those assurances at face value. “We cannot rely on the administration’s judgment, as it has repeatedly failed to enforce export controls over the past year,” she says.
On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, and the administration has recently moved to tighten rules on China’s AI industry. But Kilcrease says it acted only under pressure. “Given the poor track record on export controls and their broader accommodationist stance toward China, it’s fair to ask whether they are willing to really enforce the new controls,” she says.
The board’s assurances appear to have come mostly from the Justice Department. Attorney general Todd Blanche allegedly told Trump and vice president JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was neither a target nor a subject of any department investigation, and that the department had no evidence he had broken the law or posed a national security risk, the Journal reports. Vance then reportedly sought assurances for the board that the administration did not consider Huang a threat and that he would not face criminal charges. Trump told the Times he also consulted Clayton before pushing for Huang’s return. (“I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted,” he said.)
Nvidia did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Whether Huang broke any laws is a separate question from whether Beijing gained anything through him. “Did [the assurances] reflect a counterintelligence damage assessment by the intelligence community or the FBI, or were they political in nature?” says Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations who previously directed the Foreign Malign Influence Center at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. “Lawmakers should press on that.”
Senior officials may have seen intelligence that isn’t public, so the assurances shouldn’t just be dismissed, says Sunny Cheung, a China studies fellow at the Jamestown Foundation. “However, we still don’t know who provided those assurances, what evidence they reviewed, or how they reached their conclusion, particularly when Nvidia’s own independent investigation remains unfinished,” he says.
Lawmakers appear to have seen little of that evidence. At a briefing this month by CIA director John Ratcliffe and Clayton that was scheduled to cover Iran, lawmakers pressed for answers about Huang, and the responses left some of them puzzled, according to the Times. A follow-up briefing for senior national security staff was postponed.
Cheung says the Ministry of State Security may not have needed Nvidia’s secrets to profit from the relationship. “From a counterintelligence perspective, I think people are too focused on whether Jensen handed over trade secrets,” he says. “China’s Ministry of State Security wouldn’t necessarily need Nvidia’s next-generation chip blueprints to benefit from access to him.” Insight into Huang’s direct conversations with the president, senior officials, and other top tech executives, along with his views on China and Taiwan and his role in Washington’s export-control debate, “could already be extremely valuable to Beijing,” he says.
Brandt sees the same mix of risks. “Information about Nvidia’s proprietary chip designs could help China advance its own chip design efforts,” she says. “Insight into Nvidia’s conversations with the White House and Congress could help Beijing anticipate where US export control policy is headed.” Investigators should also ask whether Alice Huang compromised Huang’s devices, what security clearance he held, and whether he still holds it, she says.
Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to roll back restrictions on Nvidia’s chip sales to China and negotiated a deal giving the US government a 25 percent cut of sales of certain chips approved for export there, the Times has reported. In April, minister of state security Chen Yixin made overcoming the “blockades” that limit China’s access to key technologies like AI a sixth core mission for his ministry, known as the MSS. Alice Huang’s network of chip-buying companies “lines up precisely” with that mission, Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Trump’s first term, told the paper.
“A further question is whether Alice Huang was tasked by Chinese intelligence to influence Jensen Huang's views or approach to US export restrictions on China, and, if so, to what extent she succeeded,” Peterson says. The Journal also reported that the intelligence is inconclusive on whether she was actively tasked to collect information on Huang, and Cheung says “whether any such information was obtained or influence exercised remains unproven.”
Megaspeed’s purchases are better documented. A Malaysian subsidiary bought at least $4.8 billion worth of equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records the Times reviewed. Its subsidiaries have also served Chinese clients, including Alibaba. US intelligence indicates Alice Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from spring 2025 until this fall, and that her business partner, Kang Wei, also worked with the agency, the paper reported Sunday. Her network has been linked to efforts to supply Nvidia chips to China’s state-owned military contractors. Enough has been reported to suggest that Huang, “wittingly or not, may have played a role in helping Megaspeed as it sought access to advanced Nvidia chips,” Kilcrease says.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nicholas Eftimiades, a former CIA and Defense Intelligence Agency officer who teaches homeland security at Penn State Harrisburg, says Huang himself poses no security risk. Now that the relationship is public, he says, Huang has little chance of unwittingly passing along more information about US government policy or Nvidia’s board deliberations. Peterson agrees that scrutiny from Nvidia’s board, its compliance staff, federal agencies, and Congress likely limits any further exposure. But “we are still in the dark as to whether any sensitive information may already have been compromised,” she says, “or whether any resulting harm can be identified or mitigated.”
Huang’s defenders have repeatedly noted that he never received a defensive briefing, a warning the government sometimes gives Americans whom foreign intelligence services target. Nvidia’s board says its investigation will continue with Huang’s cooperation, and the company is searching for a chief compliance officer. A committee of independent directors is examining whether Huang shared corporate or national security information with Alice Huang. The board has also formed a new committee of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.
Peterson says the company’s leadership matters. “Nvidia is an exceptionally important company, and there are legitimate arguments about the implications of losing its leadership at a critical moment in the global AI race,” she says. “But those considerations should not determine the conclusions of national security investigations.”
Trump told CNBC Monday that keeping the United States ahead of China made reinstating Huang imperative. “If we didn't do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China?’” he said.
For Brandt, the bigger cost may come with Washington’s next warning. “This erodes the credibility of US government warnings about China’s technological ambitions and how far it will go to achieve them,” she says. “How will those warnings land going forward, both with our own companies and with foreign governments? We risk making a hard problem harder: emboldening Beijing while weakening our own defenses.”
That cost extends to the allies Washington depends on to police its controls, adds Sarah Bauerle Danzman, an associate professor of international studies at Indiana University’s Hamilton Lugar School. The Commerce Department has few enforcement agents abroad to monitor transshipment, she says, so the system relies on partner countries to run checks and share information about problematic buyers. Singapore says it repeatedly raised concerns with US authorities in this case.
“These types of incidents make such cooperation more difficult to sustain,” Bauerle Danzman says.
Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to closed-door, transcribed interviews with three House committees on December 1 and 2. “The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now [borne] by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens,” Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, said on X.
“I think Congress has gotten fed up,” says Kilcrease, who cites bipartisan concern about Megaspeed and what she calls the administration’s broader accommodation of China. “We can expect hearings and investigations from multiple committees, and Congress is highly motivated to pass legislation to tighten export controls, increase its oversight of administration decisions, and bolster enforcement.”
“Jensen may be back, and he should not be presumed guilty of wrongdoing,” Cheung says. “But his reinstatement should not be mistaken for a clean bill of health. Nvidia and the administration still have important questions to answer.”

Meity revises ‘Made in India’ rules for govt IT hardware purchases
India’s new government procurement rules reward local R&D, design and chip manufacturing, not just assembly, to boost domestic value addition.
The ministry of electronics and information technology (Meity) has changed how laptops, desktops, servers and other IT hardware are judged as ‘Made in India’ for government purchases. Companies will now get more weightage for research, design and chip-level work done in the country, not just assembly.
Under government procurement rules, buyers give preference to suppliers whose products meet set local content thresholds. Those suppliers are classified as Class-I or Class-II local suppliers. The new notification decides how that local content is counted.
The rules cover central government purchases. They also cover purchases by states and local bodies under schemes fully or partly funded by the Centre.
The notification, dated November 20 and setting a six-month deadline for the new rules to come into effects, sets out a new method for calculating local content in six products: desktop and all-in-one PCs, laptops, thin clients (low-cost terminals that rely on a central server for computing), servers, computer monitors and interactive flat panel displays (IFPDs), which are smart boards used in classrooms and offices. IFPDs have been brought under the framework for the first time.
The notification gives each manufacturing stage a fixed share of a product’s total bill of materials (BoM). That share counts as local content if the stage is carried out in India.
Some steps are compulsory. Motherboard assembly and final assembly and testing must be done in India, as must monitor assembly for desktops and display glass assembly for IFPDs. Otherwise the product cannot bid for government contracts at all, whatever supplier class the company would otherwise qualify for.
For a laptop, motherboard assembly counts for 15%, making the bare printed circuit board in India adds 10%, the chassis 10%, the battery pack and power adaptor 5% each, and final assembly and testing 5%.
A Meity official, who asked not to be named, said the new framework is aligned with the production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme for IT hardware. Companies under the scheme should be able to meet the local content thresholds as well, the official said.
The IT hardware PLI scheme offers incentives to companies making laptops, PCs, servers and tablets in India. The new procurement rules could give such manufacturers an added advantage in government tenders if they localise deeper stages such as circuit board making, R&D and design.
For the first time, the framework gives weightage to work beyond the factory floor. In-house R&D done in India can account for 8% of the BoM. It must be carried out through the company’s own facilities or through units registered with the department of scientific and industrial research (DSIR), and must be linked to the specific product model. Indian design or intellectual property can add another 10%.
The notification says localisation, minor modifications, or simply registering or licensing in India a design developed abroad “shall not qualify as domestically conducted designing”. Claims for R&D and design must be certified by a chartered accountant or statutory auditor.
The rules also reward semiconductor-level work. Memory (RAM) and solid-state storage assembled on circuit boards in India count for 4% each. That rises to 10% if the chips are also assembled, tested and packaged (ATMP) in India. Display assembly earns extra weightage if it includes chip-on-glass and chip-on-flex processing.
For servers, a board carrying the CPU and GPU together counts for 25%. Where they are on separate boards, the CPU board counts for 15% and the GPU board for 10%.
In a press release on November 20, the government said it had changed its methodology for calculating domestic value addition (DVA) “with a view to promoting domestic manufacturing, strengthening indigenous capabilities and generating employment.”
“MeitY has taken an important step by recognising actual manufacturing and value addition taking place in India through activities such as PCBA, display assembly, ATMP, R&D and product design. This provides a more meaningful measure of domestic capabilities than relying solely on overall product value, which can fluctuate with component prices. Alongside initiatives such as PLI and ECMS, this framework can encourage manufacturers to localise more processes, deepen component manufacturing and build stronger technological capabilities in India,” Pankaj Mohindroo, chairman, India Cellular & Electronic Association (ICEA) said.

The US Food and Drug Administration said on Thursday it had established a new internal safety body within its biologics center, formalizing independent oversight of approved products such as vaccines, gene therapies and blood products once they reach the market.
The CBER Safety Council will report directly to the director of the FDA’s Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, structurally separating post-market safety reviews from the offices responsible for approving those products, the agency said.
Here are some details:
The council supersedes CBER’s existing Safety Working Group, bringing together senior scientific and regulatory officials to review safety signals, conduct benefit-risk assessments and recommend regulatory actions as warranted.
The new structure formalizes an independent post-market review process at a time when regulators face mounting pressure to closely monitor newer biologic products, including gene and cell therapies, after approval, when they are used across far broader patient populations.
Its mandate will cover emerging safety concerns, potential labeling changes, risk-management measures and safety-related post-market studies, as well as advising on potential market withdrawals.
The FDA said the council is intended to improve accountability and transparency as biologic products grow increasingly complex, particularly in cell and gene therapy, a sector that has seen rapid regulatory expansion in recent years.
The council will coordinate with external bodies including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the National Institutes of Health, drawing on surveillance systems such as the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) and the FDA Sentinel program.
The council takes effect on November 19; the agency said additional details on its structure and membership will be released later.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

Good morning. We’ve got a “Beaver Moon” today. And, of course, there’s Thanksgiving later this week. Here’s a poem for both and neither.
An FDA milestone for limb girdle muscular dystrophy
Yesterday the FDA approved the first drug to treat limb girdle muscular dystrophy, a broad collection of progressive muscle conditions that has long received scant attention from physicians and drug developers. The drug, developed by BridgeBio, is specifically approved for patients with a subtype of the disease that the company estimates affects 2,000 to 3,000 patients in the U.S. and 4,000 to 5,000 in Europe.
“I’m pretty excited about it,” Nicholas Johnson, an LGMD specialist at Virginia Commonwealth University, told STAT’s Jason Mast. “It does appear that they had actually surprisingly robust effects on clinical outcome measures… and it also looks like it’s incredibly safe, so that’s a win-win.” Read more on the approval.
Why Barbara Kingsolver stopped signing books
The Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist Barbara Kingsolver was learning to play hand drums when her fingers started curling in on themselves. She was diagnosed with a genetic condition called Dupuytren contracture, in which the tissue of a person’s palm thickens and tightens, pulling on the fingers.
While the condition is genetic, doctors believe that the gene needs to be turned on in some way — either through age or perhaps a trauma. The drums may have been Kingsolver’s trigger, according to her hand surgeon at the University of Virginia, Bobby Chhabra.
The condition quickly began to impact her work. As a sort of celebrity author, Kingsolver’s book signings are no small feat. “The way I have to do it is sign 60,000 books — that’s an actual figure,” Kingsolver said at a media briefing with UVA on Monday. “It involves hours every day of clenching a pen. And every time I did that, I’d have to go in for another surgery.”
Kingsolver has stopped signing books en masse, but she bristles when people recommend speech-to-text technology for her writing. “This is the way I write, and I need hands,” she said. “As long as I’ve got them, and as long as I can keep them, I’m going to keep writing books.”
4.9 million
In June 2026, that’s how many menopause hormone therapy medications were dispensed to cisgender women in the U.S. between the ages of 40 and 74. It’s a major increase — 141% — from the roughly 2.1 million meds dispensed monthly between July 2023 and February 2024. That’s according to an analysis of national data published last week in JAMA.
The study found that dispensing rose before and after the FDA’s removal of the black box warning in November 2025. Menopause and its precursor, perimenopause, received a flood of attention in those years, reflected in a still-booming business.
AI offers hope in the Last Frontier
Stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death in the U.S., the majority caused by occlusions that block blood flow to the brain. Survival rates are significantly worse for rural patients, and in Alaska, the challenges sound almost insurmountable.
There are five neurointerventionalists in the entire state who can extract clots. Sometimes Alaskans arrive at their village clinics by snow machine or dogsled. Every minute is precious in the aftermath of a stroke, but it can take several hours to arrange a plane, airlift a patient to the airport in Anchorage, and deliver them by ambulance to one of those specialists.
“The distances that we have to cross are enormous. The weather that we have to face is awful. Resource availability is so low,” said Kelly Isaacs, the stroke program manager at Providence Alaska Medical Center in Anchorage.
That’s why, in 2023, a small network of hospitals agreed to use the same AI software to triage stroke patients and get them to the right care faster. STAT’s Katie Palmer reported on how it’s going and what the future of stroke care looks like in Alaska.
The pros and cons of routine PSA screening
A systematic review published yesterday in Annals of Internal Medicine provides important insight into the cost-benefit profile of routine PSA screening. According to the findings from nearly 800,000 men in 13 randomized trials with follow-up for about two decades, routine screening every two to four years between the ages of 55 and 69 led to fewer cases of metastatic disease and prostate cancer deaths. However, increased screening was also linked with an increased risk of false positives (about 150 per 1,000) as well as overdiagnosis (about 20 cases per 1,000).
The review is especially timely. Earlier this month, the American Cancer Society updated its prostate cancer screening guidelines, recommending that men at average risk be tested every two years for prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels in the blood. Routine PSA screening had gone out of favor since 2010 specifically because of the problems identified in the review, though new evidence linking it to reduced disease-specific mortality led to reconsidering the approach. — Annalisa Merelli
‘I worry how easily we can grow used to being alone’
Second-year medical student Brian Zhang is what he calls a “class-goer,” meaning he, and most of his classmates, show up physically to class each day. But in a new First Opinion essay, he notes that preclinical lecture attendance among medical schools has been declining nationally since the pandemic.
“Hard workers are remarkable at hiding stress. Intelligent people are good at forgetting to be kind to themselves,” Zhang writes. “Class gives us a place, an excuse, not only to struggle through challenging coursework in real time together, but be part of one another’s lives.” Read more.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast isolated heavy rainfall over Kerala, Mahe, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, and Karaikal through November 27 under the influence of easterly waves.
Meanwhile, the weather agency has warned of dense fog conditions across several northern states—including Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Chandigarh, and Delhi—over the next few days.
South India: Rainfall and thunderstorm alert
Under the influence of prevailing weather systems, including troughs in easterlies and upper air cyclonic circulations, the Met Dept said that South Peninsular India is set to witness continued wet weather:
- Tamil Nadu, Puducherry & Karaikal: Isolated heavy rainfall is likely through November 27, with isolated to scattered rainfall continuing till November 30. Isolated thunderstorms, lightning, and gusty winds reaching 40–50 kmph (gusting to 60 kmph) are expected through November 28.
- Kerala & Mahe: Fairly widespread to widespread rainfall is forecast through November 28, followed by isolated to scattered showers on November 29–30. Isolated heavy rainfall, along with thunderstorms, lightning, and gusty winds (30–40 kmph gusting to 50 kmph), is likely through November 27.
- Lakshadweep: Fairly widespread to widespread rainfall is likely from November 25 to 29, with isolated to scattered rainfall on November 30. Isolated thunderstorms, lightning, and gusty winds (30–40 kmph gusting to 50 kmph) are expected through November 27.
- Coastal Andhra Pradesh & Yanam: Isolated to scattered rainfall is likely through November 30. Isolated thunderstorms, lightning, gusty winds (30–40 kmph gusting to 50 kmph), and strong surface winds are forecast through November 28.
- Rayalaseema: Isolated to scattered rainfall is expected through November 30, accompanied by isolated thunderstorms, lightning, gusty winds (30–40 kmph gusting to 50 kmph), and strong surface winds through November 28.
- Karnataka: Isolated to scattered rainfall is likely over Coastal Karnataka and South Interior Karnataka through November 28. South Interior Karnataka may also see isolated thunderstorms and lightning through November 26.
- Telangana: Isolated to scattered rainfall is likely on November 25.
North India on dense fog alert
The IMD has warned that dense fog conditions are very likely during night and morning hours across parts of northern India:
- Punjab: Through November 27
- Himachal Pradesh: Through November 26
- Haryana, Chandigarh & Delhi: November 26 to 27
The IMD weather agency warned that dense fog could affect airports, highways, and railway routes, resulting in longer journey times, difficult driving conditions, and the possibility of power lines tripping. 
Commuters have been advised to drive cautiously, use fog lights, and check schedules with airlines, railways, and state transport. 
Highlighting health risks—including wheezing, coughing, eye irritation, and respiratory issues for people with asthma or bronchitis—the Met office advised residents to avoid stepping out unless necessary and to cover their faces.
Delhi-NCR weather forecast 
IMD has forecast mainly clear skies with mist or shallow fog in the morning hours over the next three days for Delhi.

India’s Vaibhav Sooryavanshi scored the fastest double century in List-A cricket during India’s Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026 match against UAE on Tuesday.
Sooryavanshi reached the milestone off just 52 balls, overtaking the previously held record of 103 balls by Chad Bowes for Canterbury against Otago in 2024.
The 15-year-old youngster eventually scored 204 off 53 balls before getting out. He hit 28 sixes during his knock and seven fours.
He had earlier smashed the world record of fastest List A century, reaching the milestone off just 28 balls.
Fastest double centuries in List A cricket:
1) Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (India A) - 52 balls
2) Chad Bowes (Canterbury) - 103 balls
3) N. Jagadeesan (Tamil Nadu) - 114 balls
4) Travis Head (South Australia) - 114 balls
5) Harry Brook (England) - 114 balls

A friend of mine sent this to me. I'd rather be safe than sorry. 
The people relaying the message on Facebook appeared to live in Alabama, Virginia, Georgia or Michigan. None specified an exact location for the supposed attacks.
One version of the introduction to the message said it came from a "valid source," adding "Magga is upset," presumable referring to U.S. President Donald Trump's movement, Make America Great Again, which lost significant ground to Democrats in the 2026 elections (archived):
As in many instances of copypasta and urban legends, those who shared the message claimed to have received it from close relations — a tried-and-true way of giving a claim the appearance of credibility. Our reporting, however, indicates that there is no truth in it.
In reality, versions of this message have been circulating since at least 2024 (archived), before the day of the presidential election. A version we checked then, which said the warning came from the sheriff's office in Gwinnett County, Georgia, read, in part:
Fwd:
Hey ladies, I just received this from a friend who works in the Gwinnett County Sheriff's office!!!
Be on Alert… Last night, a deputy told a family that local White Supremacists/ KKK members originating out of Lexington, NC, are planning to attack from now until the Inauguration.
They are plotting against Blacks, especially black women because in their eyes, we are easy targets! Please be vigilant! Try not to do anything alone, especially after dark! This is not a hoax or a rumor! The deputy showed paperwork that the police department has. In their words…They're taking their country back!"
It's really scary, and please take what I'm telling you SERIOUSLY! We have to continue to live, but just be careful and watch your surroundings!
This is happening everywhere. Stay safe!"
Take care of yourself.
Watch and make people aware of anything abnormal!!!
Snopes reported on this message at the time.
As part of our research then, Snopes contacted the Gwinnett County's Sheriff's Office, which told us it was aware of such a message circulating. The office directed us to its social media posts addressing it. The post on its Facebook page indicated that while it had not received any information about this specific threat, it would remain attentive to any concerning activity designed to derail the voting process. It also suggested that the reason some people are spreading this rumor might be to discourage voters — especially Black women — from going to polling stations to cast their ballots (archived):
(Facebook/Gwinnett County Sheriff's Office)
The Gwinnett County Sheriff's Office has been made aware of a circulating text thread suggesting potential attacks on African American women "from now through the inauguration." We have not received any information indicating threats to any group(s) on or after election day.
Hateful discourse such as this aims to instill fear in the community and disrupt us from exercising our constitutional rights. The Gwinnett County Sheriff's Office remains dedicated to protecting all citizens and we will continue to monitor and respond accordingly to all suspicious and threatening behavior.
We will continue collaborating with local, state, and federal authorities to stay current on any potential threats surrounding the general election. Please immediately report any information regarding threats or suspicious behavior to your local law enforcement agency or call the Tip Line at 770.619.6655.
The lack of specificity of the 2026 version of this message made it more likely to spread across the country. However nothing indicated a heightened level of threat. We searched Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo for reports of such a threat. No such story appeared in any reputable news outlet as of this writing, indicating there was no basis to believe the posts' claims.
For further reading, Snopes has covered several instances of copypastas, including one that made false and misleading claims about registered voter numbers and fraud in Wisconsin and Texas in November 2026.

84 days, four titles, one historic feat - Alcaraz's remarkable return
- Published
The men's tennis season ended as it began, with a beaming Carlos Alcaraz holding aloft one of the sport's biggest trophies.
In January, he won the Australian Open to complete the career Grand Slam. Ten months later, he stood as the victor in Turin, having ended his wait for a first ATP Finals title.
Watching Alcaraz over recent weeks, it would be easy to forget that for a four-month period this year, the 23-year-old barely picked up a racquet.
He missed the majority of the clay and all of the grass-court season with a wrist injury, but he has made a remarkable return, culminating in a dismantling of world number one Alexander Zverev on Sunday.
It is 84 days since Alcaraz made his comeback at the US Open, where his lack of match fitness understandably showed. He came through the early rounds but lost a five-set quarter-final epic against Ben Shelton.
Since then, the Spaniard has won 21 of his 22 matches - including each of the past 14 - and captured titles at four of the five tournaments he has contested.
He continues to make history, too, becoming the youngest man to win all four Slams and the season-ending Finals.
This was the third straight tournament he has won, following victories at the Vienna Open and Paris Masters earlier in November, and he has now won his past nine matches against fellow top-10 players.
The former world number one, currently ranked third behind Zverev and Jannik Sinner, continues to make up for lost time as he seeks to quickly reassert himself at the top of the sport.
"I think everybody feels he's the number one," Alcaraz said, stressing each player in the game has to treat themselves that way.
"Me, Sascha [Zverev], Jannik [Sinner], [Ben] Shelton. Having that confidence in yourself is really important.
"But right now the number one is Sascha. He really deserves it."
- Alcaraz outplays Zverev for first ATP Finals triumph 
  - Published11 hours ago
Crowd-pleasing variety, devastating power and astonishing athleticism did not take long to return to Alcaraz's game.
Even with a heavily strapped left leg after injuring his hamstring on Wednesday, he could not be stopped by the world's top players in Turin.
That included Zverev, who this year rose to the top of the rankings for the first time after claiming his first two major titles and recording a tour-leading 69 match wins.
Alcaraz, already a seven-time Slam winner, feels his own growth in the mental side of the sport has taken him to a different level in recent months.
He has specifically pointed to the new sense of perspective he gained from his time away from tennis in inspiring his scintillating year-end form.
"The injury made me realise what's really important," Alcaraz said.
"It's not winning. It's just about playing tennis. I realised that it is a gift every time that I can step on the court and compete healthy.
"When you realise that, everything comes easier.
"I don't feel stressed most of the time. I think right now I'm more mature, or I feel that, on a tennis court, I'm facing the problems and difficult moments in a different way."
Alcaraz threw himself to the ground after ending his wait to win the season-ending tournament before racing into the stands to celebrate with his team and family.
It marked the 30th title of his career, drawing him level with rival Sinner and behind only men's record 24-time major winner Novak Djokovic (102) among active ATP players.
More could soon be around the corner - should he manage to stay injury-free.
Victory in Paris has left him two titles away from emulating Sinner and Djokovic by completing the career 'Golden Masters' - winning all nine Masters 1,000 events, the level of tournament below the Slams.
Should he achieve that next season in Canada and Shanghai, it would leave him only an Olympic singles gold away from completing the sport.
His main obstacle to achieving such dominance still appears to be Sinner, given Alcaraz's positive head-to-head against Zverev.
Italian Sinner has been absent with a knee issue since Wimbledon but is aiming to return, external at the Australian Open, where Alcaraz will defend his title in January.
"In today's final, I needed to put the three Cs - cabeza, corazon, cojones - that my grandpa always tells me I have to give every time I step on the court," Alcaraz said.
"The three Cs in English is head, heart and balls. Today, that was what it was about.
"Lifting this trophy is something I have been chasing for a really long time. It means the world to me."

The U.S. government is investigating Iranian ties to as many as 50 hacked commercial vessels
The U.S. government has intelligence suggesting that up to 50 commercial shipping vessels were recently compromised by cyberattacks, activity federal officials are investigating as potentially linked to Iran.
That's according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record, a former military cyber operator and an industry executive briefed on the attacks. The series of breaches was first reported by the The Wall Street Journal.
The attacks against the maritime sector, if officials' suspicions are correct, may be the latest example of Iranian cyberattacks against global critical infrastructure during the ongoing war with the United States.
NPR has reported that cybersecurity experts and U.S. officials believe Iranian hackers were responsible for a series of digital attacks against U.S. water treatment systems across the country in August as well as a pattern of attacks targeting refrigeration cooling systems that led to spoiled food at grocery stores on U.S. military bases and all across Europe as recently as early November.
The Coast Guard and the FBI first partnered in August to send a "highly specialized team" to board two different foreign commercial vessels "in the Gulf of America" heading to U.S. ports, according to a statement provided by the FBI and the Coast Guard. "The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," according to the statement.
The FBI and Coast Guard press offices also told NPR that there are no current "reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts."
However, there are dozens more ships in international waters that the U.S. government believes have been compromised by hackers and many others who might be vulnerable to similar attacks.
According to the U.S. official familiar with the investigation, bad actors took advantage of known vulnerabilities in Fortinet FortiGate devices, which are frequently used in the maritime industry. The Coast Guard and FBI released a cyber bulletin in September warning the industry that bad actors were breaking into these devices, which help manage firewalls and virtual private networks. "Threat actors routinely scan for specific, unpatched vulnerabilities to gain a foothold," the bulletin read.
According to the U.S. official, in some cases, employees aboard the ships suspected something nefarious was going on when they noticed email disruptions or couldn't log in to their accounts, or, in at least one case, an extended communications blackout. The U.S. official declined to comment on how the U.S. government knows about the extent of breaches across the sector.
However, according to the U.S. official, hackers were able to break in using the Fortinet vulnerability and then pivot from the ships' IT systems over to their network of devices controlling physical processes on the ships, what's called operational technology.
The U.S. official said the bad actors "could have impacted the systems on board that control propulsion, steering, navigation, and cargo management," though they did not share any examples of that kind of activity occurring. In at least one case, one of the ships affected was an LNG tanker designed to transport liquified natural gas. It's important to keep systems at a certain temperature to prevent dangerous accidents if a ship's cargo includes explosive materials –from chemicals to fuel.
While commercial vessels are accustomed to physical security reviews entering the United States following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, digital threats are becoming all the more important to track as adversaries can break in and cause damage from afar. "It's a totally new paradigm that these tankers are networked in this way," the U.S. official said.
Even so, national security officials have feared something like this might happen for years. A former Navy official who requested anonymity to discuss internal operations tells NPR that "we had been tracking the possibility to exploit and take control of [operational technology] systems on Navy ships and Merchant [Marine] ships for a long time, and now this is coming to fruition."
While the U.S. government is wary of advertising Iranian hacking efforts during the war, officials also want to spread awareness of the vulnerability of internet connected devices, particularly those that are linked to the technology that controls critical processes. "These are not sophisticated attacks," the official said. "This is a known vulnerability that could be mitigated with some pretty basic cyber hygiene."
"Modern ships are highly integrated systems. A cyberattack presents significant risks, including the potential for a collision, grounding, oil spill, or even an explosion. The Coast Guard regularly publishes bulletins on cyber vulnerabilities and actions vessel owners and operators can take to secure their networks," according to a statement from the Coast Guard.
Ahead of the winter and a busy holiday season for commercial shipping, officials are bracing themselves to investigate any ship entering U.S. ports that could be compromised.
"People never think about what a modern blessing electricity is until it goes out. People take the marine transportation system for granted until there's a problem and their stuff doesn't get there by Christmas," the U.S. official said. "I wish more Americans knew how complex this system is."

South Korea on Friday reported its first case of cholera in 10 years, with health authorities urging people to take precautionary measures, use only safe water and wash their food properly.
The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency said health workers confirmed cholera from test samples of a person who had visited a hospital emergency room in the southeastern port city of Changwon earlier this month, showing symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea.
The agency said the unidentified person, who recovered and was discharged on Tuesday, had not travelled overseas in the past two months. It said health workers were trying to trace the source of infection and the people the person had been in contact with.
It was the country's first case of cholera since 2016, when authorities identified three cases suspected to be caused by contaminated seafood. At least 162 people got sick in a larger outbreak in 2001.
The agency issued guidance urging people to stick to safe water and cooked food and to wash and peel fruits and vegetables. It also urged medical facilities to promptly test and report suspected cases.

Streaming platform Lionsgate Play has cast an AI performer, Yug R.Ai, as the lead of “Eklavya,” a mythological series that is the platform’s first AI-led original.
Rohit Jain, founder and CEO of Lionsgate Play, presented a first look at the show and introduced Yug R.Ai as the company’s first AI actor. The series is in production now. It will premiere in 2027 exclusively on Tiger TV, the Punjabi- and Hindi-language service that sits inside the Lionsgate Play app.
Indian National Film Award winner Vibhu Puri (“Hawaizaada,” “Gustaakh Ishq”) is directing. His credits also include the series “Heeramandi” and “Taj: Divided by Blood,” along with hundreds of large-scale commercials.
“Eklavya” retells the legend of a boy rejected by his guru who teaches himself to become a master archer. The show will be offered in several Indian and international languages and is the first entry in a broader slate of AI-led originals.
The series is also the first project in a long-term alliance that Lionsgate Play has struck with Google Cloud, pairing the streamer’s storytelling with Google’s AI technology.
“Every leap in technology has opened new doors for storytellers, and AI is opening more of them, faster, than anything before it. But technology alone doesn’t create magic on screen. Great stories and the people behind them do. That’s why every title on our AI slate is driven by a strong creative team, from the writers and artists to the director,” Jain said. “‘Eklavya’ is our boldest statement of intent, an eight-episode first season built to grow into a multi-season franchise, and Yug R.Ai is just the beginning.”
Jain has spent more than 30 years in the industry. He took Videocon d2h from launch to a Nasdaq listing via a SPAC and later built Lionsgate’s Asia business as its founding executive. He then bought the regional streaming arm through a management buyout, the first of its kind in India’s media industry, and Lionsgate Play has been under founder-led ownership since 2025. The service runs in eight Asian markets, claims more than 40 million viewers in India and keeps access to the studio’s film and TV catalog through a multi-year licensing deal.
Puri said that Eklavya, never given a teacher, made the bow his own, and that the series felt much the same way to him.
“I’ve spent my career making ambitious ideas fit inside budgets and schedules. With ‘Eklavya,’ for the first time, the canvas is as big as the imagination,” he said.
Lionsgate Play set up Tiger TV to bring Indian stories to a global audience. In India, the service costs INR349 ($4) a quarter or INR799 ($8) a year. It is set to expand to the U.K., the U.S., Canada, Australia and New Zealand, aimed at Punjabi and South Asian audiences in those markets.

In November, a video (archived) circulated that social media users claimed authentically shows a group of Muslims calling themselves "Soldiers of Allah" and demanding Shariah be put in place in Manchester, England.
According to the Council on Foreign Relations, a U.S. foreign policy think tank, Shariah is "the divine counsel that Muslims follow to live moral lives and grow close to God." Interpretations of Shariah, the principles of which stem from the Quran and hadith, the latter of which are sayings attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, form the basis of Islamic law.
The video in question shows people gathered on Wilmslow Road in Rusholme, south of Manchester, a stretch of road that is also known as the "Curry Mile" for its large number of restaurants specializing in South Asian and Middle Eastern food. The footage shows large groups of people, who appeared to be majority male, chanting and beating their chests.
One Instagram user who shared the video wrote:
A large group of military-age men took to the streets in a Manchester suburb calling themselves soldiers of Allah and demanding sharia law be put in place because they now form the majority in the neighborhood. The march was open and organized, not a quiet gathering. When a neighborhood shifts demographically and then the new majority starts openly calling for a different legal system, the question is how far that demand is expected to go. Local officials and residents are left deciding whether this is just free expression or the start of parallel rules. Do you think this is being handled the right way in the UK?
The footage also circulated on Facebook (archived). Snopes readers searched our site for information about the clips.
The video appears authentic, meaning it shows an event that actually happened and wasn't created used artificial intelligence. However, people who shared in it November miscaptioned the footage.
It doesn't show Muslims calling themselves "Soldiers of Allah" or calling for Shariah in the U.K. Rather, the videos show Shiite Muslims marking Ashura, the culmination of 10 days of mourning to mark the martyrdom of Husayn ibn Ali, the grandson of the prophet Muhammad, on June 21.
According to the Encyclopedia Britannica, Shiite Muslims mark this day with assemblies such as the one seen in the video that feature, "sermons, poetry, chest-beating, and passion plays reenacting Husayn's martyrdom."
The Ashura assembly on the "Curry Mile" is an annual event in Manchester that local news media has covered for more than 10 years. The Manchester Evening news called the event a "ritual self-flagellation procession" in 2015 but did not report that the people participating called themselves "Soldiers of Allah" or demanded Shariah be imposed in the U.K.
The source of the video that circulated in November was unclear, though at least two of the clips featured (at 0:06 and 0:16) camefrom a separate video (at 1:20 and 1:59, archived) posted on Instagram by 
Murtaza Ali Shah, a journalist for a Pakistani news outlet.
Shah confirmed to Snopes via Instagram he recorded the footage and it showed the Ashura event in Manchester in June.
In addition to misrepresenting what the video showed, the social media post above also made a false claim about the alleged "Soldiers of Allah" calling for Shariah in the U.K.
The poster wrote (emphasis ours): "A large group of military-age men took to the streets in a Manchester suburb calling themselves soldiers of Allah and demanding sharia law be put in place because they now form the majority in the neighborhood."
Manchester, where the June Ashura assembly took place, is not majority Muslim. According to the latest U.K. Ccensus data from 2021, 22.3% of people — less than one in four — within the Manchester City Council governance area identified as Muslims. Rusholme, where the "Curry Mile" is located, is part of Manchester City Council. According to census data, 38.5% of people in the Rusholme East census area, which borders the "Curry Mile," identified as Muslim.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether a video showed U.K. shoppers standing in gender-segregated lines and another video of Shiite Muslims marking Ashura in Dearborn, Michigan.

New Delhi: India has initiated inter-ministerial deliberations on a possible review of its liberalized wheat export policy, just three months after allowing unrestricted overseas shipments of the grain, as it assesses domestic production for the current crop year through June 2027, said two people aware of the matter.
The discussions follow a sharp slowdown in wheat sowing and concerns over soil moisture after the southwest monsoon ended with a 13% rainfall deficit this year. Wheat acreage stood at 5.007million hectares (mn ha.) as of 13 November, down 15.3% from 5.910 mn ha. a year earlier, according to the latest available data from the agriculture ministry.
The government is assessing domestic wheat availability, food security requirements and the availability of water for irrigation before taking a view on the existing export policy, said the first of the two persons cited earlier, both speaking on condition of anonymity.
“The discussions are at an initial stage and are precautionary in nature, given the decline in wheat acreage and its potential impact on production. However, this does not mean that the government is moving towards restricting exports,” said the second person.
“Since sowing is still underway, a decision will be taken at an appropriate time after considering all relevant factors and keeping farmers' interests in mind,” said the second person.
Queries sent to the spokespersons of the ministry of consumer affairs, food and public distribution, as well as the secretary, department of food and public distribution, on Monday remained unanswered till press time.
Periodic bans
India has banned wheat exports periodically in recent decades to ensure adequate domestic supplies and keep a lid on prices. India banned wheat exports in 2007 to curb a price rise and lifted the ban only in September 2011 after successive years of good harvests. It again prohibited wheat shipments in May 2022 and eased restriction on overseas despatches in February 2026 before lifting the ban altogether in August 2026. The country, however, has allowed government-to-government deals in limited quantities to accede to diplomatic requests even while keeping a generalised ban on wheat exports.
The latest sowing figures have raised questions about the outlook for the next wheat harvest, particularly as water availability and soil moisture conditions remain important determinants of crop development.
Industry experts said that Indian wheat is currently relatively expensive in the international market, limiting the immediate commercial incentive for exports.
"At the moment, export of wheat is not a lucrative proposition as international wheat prices are currently very low, partly due to the depreciation of the dollar and appreciation of the rupee. Also, supplies from the Black Sea region, particularly Russia and Ukraine, are keeping global prices subdued. In India, wheat prices are largely governed by the minimum support price (MSP), which is relatively high and keeps prices elevated. Unlike domestic prices, international prices are driven primarily by market forces of demand and supply," said Navneet Chitlangia, former president of the Roller Flour Millers' Federation of India.
"At present, we are not receiving enquiries from international wheat buyers, possibly because Indian wheat is not competitively priced in the global market. The price parity gap between domestic and international markets appears to be discouraging buyers, as global wheat prices remain lower, making Indian supplies relatively expensive for overseas importers," said Varun Verma, proprietor of Delhi-based Nidhiraj Exports.
Substantial stocks
The government currently has substantial wheat stocks in its central pool, providing a cushion against near-term supply concerns.
According to the Food Corporation of India (FCI), which procures and stores foodgrains from farmers, wheat stocks in the central pool stood at 447.60 lakh tonnes as of 1 November, compared with the prescribed minimum quantity of 20.520 million tonnes (mt) for 1 October. The stocks were also significantly higher than the 30.727mt held on 1 November 2025.
The central pool stocks comprise grain held by the FCI and state government agencies.
However, the stock position will need to be assessed alongside procurement requirements for the next marketing season and the government's foodgrain distribution commitments.
Under the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY), eligible beneficiaries covered under the National Food Security Act (NFSA) receive 5kg of free foodgrains per person per month under Priority Households (PHH) and 35kg per household per month for Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) families. This free foodgrain distribution arrangement has been extended until December 2028.
For FY27, the government has allocated 21.855mt of wheat for distribution and sale, around 2.7mt higher than it did in FY26. Of the total, 21.447mt has been earmarked for distribution under the National Food Security Act and the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana, up from 17.133mt in the previous fiscal.
This assumes significance as the government seeks to balance rising distribution requirements with adequate buffer stocks amid the risk of lower wheat production. It has set an initial procurement target of 30.3mt for the 2026-27 marketing season, marginally lower than 31.0mt targeted for the previous season (2025-26).

In 1832, a Belgian astronomer and mathematician named Adolphe Quetelet wanted to understand if height and weight measurements could be used to understand human populations.
He collected and analysed these measurements to determine what parameters would constitute what he called the “average man”. While doing so, Quetelet realised the weight of a person increases approximately in proportion to the square of the height. He expressed this relationship as the ratio of weight to the square of height.
This measure, the Quetelet Index, was one of the earliest metrics for relative body weight. Researchers also used other approaches, including simple weight to height ratios or weight to height-cubed ratios.
In 1972, the U.S. physiologist Ancel Keys and his colleagues set out to compare these different measures and examine how well they represented the amount of fat in the body. They concluded that of the lot, the Quetelet Index was the best, and they renamed it the body mass index (BMI).
Since then, BMI has become one of the most widely used measures of relative body weight. Even though it cannot distinguish between the source of body weight — a high value could reflect greater muscle or bone mass rather than excess body fat — it soon became the principal measure used to classify obesity.

Xi's anti-corruption campaign ensnares rising star in Chinese Communist Party
- Published
Chinese authorities are investigating Shanghai's party chief, a rising star in the Communist Party, as part of Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption drive.
Chen Jining, 62, is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws", according to a statement published on Tuesday by the party's anti-corruption body.
Chen is now the fourth member of the elite Politburo to be investigated, in the widest purge yet of the party's top executive body since the end of the Cultural Revolution.
As the party prepares to appoint fresh leaders at next year's National People's Congress, uncertainty looms over what its new command will look like - except that Xi will remain at the helm.
Before Chen, three other members of the current Politburo - appointed in 2022 - were investigated and subsequently expelled: ex-generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.
While Chen has not been removed from the Politburo, it's rare for officials to return after such investigations.
"Who on this Politburo feels safe, especially as the personnel machinations for next year's Party Congress intensify?" China analyst Bill Bishop wrote in his Sinocism newsletter.
Chen's investigation came as a surprise, according to Bishop, given rumours were swirling that another senior official, not Chen, would fall next in the anti-corruption campaign.
The role of Shanghai party chief, which Chen assumed in 2022, is known to be a prestigious springboard to the country's top office.
Chen's long list of predecessors include former president Jiang Zemin, his premier Zhu Rongji, incumbent premier Li Qiang and Xi Jinping himself.
As Shanghai party chief, Chen hosted foreign leaders visiting the city, including former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer in January and former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken in 2024.
Chen was also a prominent champion for the development of the city's artificial intelligence industry - a sector that the party has stipulated as an area of strategic focus.
Chen graduated with a degree in environmental engineering at Tsinghua University, where he returned to teach in 1998 and became its president in 2012. He also spent a few years in the UK, and received a PhD from Imperial College London.
Since Xi's anti-corruption drive in 2012, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", according to the party.
Specific charges are often not made public, and broad allegations about disciplinary and legal violations have become routine in the crackdown.
Analysts note that corruption also extends to ideological impurity - or simply put, disloyalty.
Party discipline took centre stage at the fifth plenum last month, which had the most empty seats ever seen after a record 33 members were expelled from the party's central committee.
Chen's ongoing probe suggests that the crackdown is not slowing down.
Shanghai's communist party standing committee said in a statement that its members "unanimously expressed their firm support" for the decision of the party.
The investigation of Chen, the committee said, shows that "the fight against corruption will not stop".

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

President Donald Trump may want a piece of the Nvidia pie.
After saying he intervened to support the reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang, Trump said he has also considered seeking out an equity stake in the chipmaker for the US government.
"I thought about it," Trump told the New York Post on Tuesday. "I said, 'You know, maybe I should do it,' but I didn't bring it up at this point. It's probably not too late."
Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, less than two weeks after resigning from the company he founded when reports emerged of extramarital affairs with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy and an executive who reported to him.
Huang's return came days after Nvidia's board said they had no plans to bring him back. Trump, who has repeatedly praised Huang, played up his role in the CEO's return and said he spoke directly to the board.
The president's suggestion of the government taking an equity stake in Nvidia would align with similar moves made under the current administration. In August 2025, the US government reached a deal to invest $8.9 billion in Intel in exchange for a nearly 10% stake, a move aimed at supporting the semiconductor industry.
Prior to Intel, the administration said it took a "golden share" in US Steel in exchange for approving its acquisition by Nippon Steel, a Japanese company. The government has also invested in critical minerals firms MP Materials, Lithium Americas, and Trilogy Metals, as well as established a strategic partnership with the nuclear energy company Westinghouse.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

The same clip was shared by X user @yadavanoop08, with the claim that certain “RSS goons caused a ruckus” at a restaurant in West Bengal after they were asked to pay their bill. (Archive)

होटल द्वारा बिल मांगने पर RSS के गुंडों ने ये आरोप लगाकर दुकान में तोड़फोड़ करने लगे कि खाने में चिकन दिया गया है।

Several other users also shared the video with identical claims on X.
Fact Check
In order to determine the veracity of these claims, first, we ran a reverse image search on some of the keyframes of the viral clip. This led us to images of a restaurant called Durbin Bangla located in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Below is a comparison of a frame from the viral video and an image of the restaurant we found online.
The viral video also contains footage of the incident shot from outside the restaurant. We examined keyframes from this clip and compared them with photographs of the outside facade of the restaurant available online. See below:
These comparisons prove conclusively that the restaurant shown in the viral clip is not in West Bengal, but in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Further, the viral clip shows a police officer in a green uniform in the midst of the chaos. This matches the uniform worn by Bangladesh police.
A keyword search then led us to several news reports (The Daily Star, The Financial Express and Dhaka Tribune) on a mob attack and vandalism at Durbin Bangla restaurant in Dhaka’s Mohakhali on November 13, 2026.
The Daily Star reported that a disagreement over a vacant seat at the restaurant eventually escalated into a heated conflict, followed by a clash with the restaurant employees and vandalism at the restaurant.
To sum up, the viral video is from Bangladesh. It shows an incident at Durbin Bangla restaurant in Dhaka. The claim that a group of RSS members is seen vandalising a restaurant in Bengal over non-payment of bill and being served chicken is false.

Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence.
Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support for Hasina’s planned return in December, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on Thursday.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent protests demanding her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card to facilitate her return. Her supporters are protesting against the government’s rejection of that request.
To deter violence, 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard fanned out across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, considered to have many Hasina supporters, a spokesperson said.
Police said former interim leader Yunus’ ancestral home in Chattogram, about 300km (186 miles) south-east of Dhaka, was set on fire late on Wednesday.
It is likely that flammable substances were thrown into an unused ground-floor room, police told Reuters, adding that Yunus’ paternal family members, who live on the upper floors, are safe.
Reuters could not immediately reach the Yunus Centre thinktank that speaks on his behalf to seek comment. Yunus and his government, which led Bangladesh after Hasina’s ouster, have faced hostility from her supporters.
During the last 10 days of protests, police have reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles being set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public, media have said.
Late on Tuesday, an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest near Hasina’s home district of Gopalganj, police said.
On the same night, a crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of cultural affairs minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and shops belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district of Pirojpur after two buses were set on fire, authorities said.
Tuesday marks a year since Hasina was sentenced to death by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising against her in 2024. She has lived in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka.
On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, who faces charges over several killings during the 2024 protests, from his house in Dhaka, police told Reuters.
At least 37 branches and offices of Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, have been targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires since 10 November, with 14 more attacked since midnight on Tuesday, the bank said.
On Tuesday, the home minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved in violence would be identified and prosecuted.
Awami League leaders, most of them in hiding, could not be reached for comment.

The Department of Medical Education is preparing to start two new government medical colleges in Ramanagara of Bengaluru South District and Puttur of Dakshina Kannada District for the academic year of 2027-28, and a proposal will be submitted to the National Medical Commission (NMC) soon.
“The construction work for the medical college on the Rajiv Gandhi University of Health Sciences (RGUHS) new campus in Ramanagara is progressing rapidly. The tender for the medical college in Puttur has been finalised, and the construction will commence shortly. We will apply to the NMC to start these colleges from 2027-28 with a capacity of at least 50 seats,” Medical Education Minister Sharan Prakash Patil said.
“There is also a proposal to start medical colleges in Vijayapura and Kolar districts. The cabinet will decide on that soon,” he added.
The government has decided to start a medical college in every district of the State. There are 25 now. If colleges are established in Ramanagara, Puttur, Vijayapura, and Kolar districts, only Tumakuru, Bengaluru Rural, and Udupi districts will have to have a government medical college of their own.
Currently, there are 76 medical colleges in the State, comprising 25 government and 51 private institutions, with a total of 15,745 seats available for the 2026-27 academic year. If the Ramanagara and Puttur colleges are approved for the next academic year, with 50 seats each, this will go up to 78 colleges with 15,845 seats.
Will NMC approve this year?
The NMC has rejected the State’s applications for starting medical colleges in Kanakapura and Ramanagara four times from 2023-24 to 2026-27, for want of infrastructure, including teaching and non-teaching staff. Will the commission approve the proposals this year at least is the moot question.
In this context, the State government decided to construct a medical college and hospital in Kanakapura at an estimated cost of about ₹550 crore, and the construction work is in progress. However, the work of the medical college planned to be built on the proposed Rajiv Gandhi University of Health Sciences (RGUHS) campus in Ramanagara is only 70% complete. Therefore, the government has decided to start the medical college using the district hospital.
“The construction of medical college on the RGUHS new campus in Ramanagara will be completed soon. Consequently, steps have been taken to shift the university to the new campus within the next three to four months. Meanwhile, the construction of a medical college and hospital in Kanakapura is progressing rapidly, and once the work is complete, a proposal will be submitted to the MNC for the commencement of the college,” Mr. Patil said.
