Stating that it shouldn't postpone pending elections "unreasonably", the Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) said it is inclined to stay a Calcutta High Court order deferring the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) polls till the issue of ward delimitation is decided.
A Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to seek instructions on the issue by November 30.
The KMC has undertaken a revision of municipal ward boundaries ahead of the next civic polls. As part of the plan, the number of wards in the civic body may rise to 209 from the current 144.
The High Court had restrained the West Bengal State Election Commission from issuing a notification for the KMC election till a single bench disposes of a plea on ward delimitation.
"We are inclined to stay the impugned order for the reason that the factual and legal issues which have been highlighted, the division bench will pass a fresh order, an appropriate order.
"The writ petition before the single judge will be directed to be transferred to the division bench. And till the division bench forms a view the polls can be held off," the Bench observed.
During the hearing, Justice Bagchi said,""We shouldn't postpone pending elections unreasonably."
The division bench of the High Court had directed the State Election Commission (SEC) to not issue a notification for elections to the KMC till the disposal of a petition pending before a single bench.
Challenging the delimitation exercise, the petitioner, a former CPI-M councillor, sought a declaration stating that the entire exercise of determination of the number of KMC wards is void and the quashing of the September 11 gazette notification on expansion of wards is bad in law.
Dipu Das alleged that the delimitation exercise has been undertaken based on electoral rolls instead of the actual population, thereby excluding a substantial number of residents from consideration.
The petitioner claimed that the civic body had no elected council, and the corporation's former chairperson Smita Pandey had been appointed its administrator after the House's dissolution on June 8. He also sought an interim order of stay of operation of the delimitation notification and to restrain the SEC from issuing any notification calling an election to the KMC.
The single bench on October 29 refused an interim stay.
Aggrieved by the refusal, Mr. Das moved the division bench.
The State government, the order had said, could empower its chosen administrator to make a tailor-made recommendation and then be bound by it, effectively allowing the government to recommend amendments to itself and undermining the provision's independence.
"Such puppetry cannot be compatible with the scheme of the KMC Act. The key feature of Section 601 of the KMC Act is the institutional autonomy vested in the Corporation in making a binding recommendation to the state government, which confers authority on the Corporation, an autonomous institution, to decide the delimitation of its own wards, in other words, its electoral constituencies," the order said.
It stated that the manner in which the corporation was dissolved mid-term, and an administrator was appointed, followed by "the hasty chronology of events thereafter" lent substance to the appellant's arguments "that there might have been a method in the madness".
The observations made in the division bench order came with a rider that they were "tentative in nature insofar as the final disposal of the writ petition is concerned."

These dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
- Published
The livestream begins.
A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.
Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.
It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."
"Purebreds," says the woman filming.
Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting
In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.
In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.
Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.
Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.
One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.
170 carcasses found
When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.
Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.
On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.
Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting – taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.
"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."
In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.
"The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.
"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.
By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."
LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.
Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.
Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.
There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?
As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.
"So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."
'God knows what was inside those urns'
The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.
A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.
As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.
"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."
These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.
Or not, as the case may be.
Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.
Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.
When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.
"Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."
Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.
According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT – but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.
One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.
But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.
There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law – estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them – and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.
Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.
The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".
Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.
"I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his."
Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns."
In response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.
The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.
Animal-cruelty law 'doesn't apply'
On 2 November, Percival Vilar Cendaña of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace.
"Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations."
Neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real – and Cendaña was giving voice to a common sentiment.
"Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.
At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.
But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.
Cabrera says the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".
The scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like Cendaña are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.
Meanwhile, Cabrera says Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.
One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak".
"I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she said.
Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says.
"They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them."
As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he says.
The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN.
"Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez said.
"To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families."
Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.
On Monday, the National Police Commission announced an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.
Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more.
"We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," says Calling. "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever."
Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated."
She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days."

When discussing cervical cancer, what often gets left out is that it is one of the most preventable of cancers. Despite this, cervical cancer continues to be a cause of thousands of deaths among women every year, not only in India, but in many parts of the world. In many such cases, the condition is detected far too late, leaving limited room for intervention. The issue therefore, is not a gap in science, but a gap in awareness
The main culprit in cervical cancer is a virus that is very common, human papillomavirus, or HPV for short. HPV primarily spreads through close skin-to-skin contact, most often during sexual intercourse. The virus is so widespread that virtually everyone, both men and women, at some point in their lifetime, will be infected without even realising it. More often than not, the immune system gets rid of the virus without causing any damage.

From its origins as a racing game called Race ‘n’ Chase to billion-dollar sales records, GTA has a fascinating history. Here are 11 surprising facts about the franchise, including Hollywood connections, hidden ghosts, clever anti-piracy tricks, celebrity lawsuits, and its Scottish roots.
After more than a decade of waiting, Rockstar Games has finally launched perhaps the most anticipated game in the recent history of gaming. Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6). It has been barely a few days since the game hit the stands and the Web, and it already has the world (gaming and non-gaming too) in its grip, and is setting sales records.
Its release means saying goodbye to the legendary “we got (this/something) before GTA 6” meme, but GTA 6 is already carving a place for itself in the franchise’s history, a history marked by crime, cars, and chaos and a lot of other things that even diehard fans might not be aware of.
From celebrity lawsuits to ghosts and many controversies, the world of GTA is filled with insane stories. So even as you set yourself up for another session of GTA 6 or wait for your copy of the game to download, or just turn your nose up at “crazy gamers who will line up for anything”, here are eleven amazing facts you might not know (but should know) about the legendary Grand Theft Auto franchise.
Table of Contents
It was originally supposed to be a racing game (and called Race’n’Chase)
It may look completely different today, but GTA was originally supposed to be a fast-paced, addictive racing game called “Race ‘n’ Chase.” Development of the game got underway in the mid-nineties, but the developers did not quite get things right. Early models had car-crashing issues and coding glitches that made police cars ram into player cars aggressively, instead of just chasing them. This, of course, took away its traditional racing game feel. But during testing, players enjoyed this glitch and chaos, so the developers decided to move away from a “Race n Chase” sort of setup and decided to create an open world action-oriented game. They called it Grand Theft Auto (GTA). The rest, as they love to say, is history.
Play the OG GTA online and free of cost
Want to experience the original Grand Theft Auto that was released in 1997? Well, you can actually play it for free online in a browser at https://www.playdosgames.com/online/grand-theft-auto/. Just make sure you have a keyboard handy, as it struggles with touch controls.
Thank you, Tony Montana! GTA: Vice City was inspired by Scarface!
Even the greatest video games have to draw inspiration from somewhere, and in the case of GTA: Vice City, inspiration came from Brian De Palma’s 1983 crime classic, Scarface. The developers used the movie as a blueprint to showcase how Miami looked back in the 80s. The protagonist in the game also follows a very similar arc to the protagonist in the film, the iconic Tony Montana, and even has a location similar to that of Tony Montana’s (Scarface’s protagonist) infamous mansion in it.
GTA has a lot of Hollywood in it…but is not too fond of stars
GTA has not just drawn inspiration from Hollywood, but has also featured many famous actors from it. The game has cast a number of actors, comedians, and musicians to either play themselves or voice a character. A key reason for hiring musicians and comedians to play themselves in the game or be a part of an extensive radio or DJ set is to make the city in the game feel even more real and lived in. Famous actors like Ray Liotta, Samuel L. Jackson, Burt Reynolds, and many more have been a part of the franchise. This tradition lives on with GTA 6, as this time around actors Dylan Rourke and Manni Perez have voiced the two leads of the game.
That said, problems with a number of high-profile stars (most notably Burt Reynolds) led Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser to say in an interview with Vulture “We don’t bring in name actors anymore because of their egos and, most important of all, because we believe we get a better sense of immersion using talented actors whose voices you don’t recognize.”
The Ghost Town of GTA 3 that is ‘out of bounds’
Imagine having a small part of the game that you cannot explore? Well, that is exactly what the Ghost Town in GTA 3 is. It has nothing to do with gameplay, lacks the general collision mechanism of the game, and yet it exists. The ‘out of bounds’ area was actually designed as part of GTA 3’s opening cinematics and was put away from the main map, and kept in the game only for the intro scene. However, players found their way to the location using glitches and modifications, although they could not interact with it like the rest of the game. Before Vice City, there was Ghost City in the GTAverse.
Punishing pirates, the GTA way
By the time GTA 4 was released in 2008, the GTA franchise had become insanely famous. And with great celebrity and terrific sales comes…great piracy. As pirated and unauthorized units of the game became a problem, Rockstar Games used some very creative countermeasures to punish/ annoy those who bought pirated copies of the game. Unauthorized copies ended up with constant drunk effects on the camera, sudden and auto acceleration, broken mission scripts, damaged cars, and more, which were put in place to make the pirated game actually feel pirated. You do not pirate a gangster game easily!
Macabre and moving Easter eggs
The GTA franchise is laden with Easter eggs, but two of the most amazing ones are found in GTA 5. What makes them special is the attention to both detail and sentiment. These are not your run-of-the-mill “press this key and your car changes into Superman” or “use this key combo to start driving on Mars” kinds of easter eggs, but much more somber and sensitive ones.
In GTA 5 between 23:00 and 00:00, you can actually find a translucent figure at the peak of Mount Gordo. There is a flat rock where the ghost of “Jolene Cranley-Evans,” who was said to have been killed by her husband, Jock Cranley, appears around midnight. Jock had pushed her off the mountain peak, which is also why, when the player goes near the ghost, it disappears and “Jock” written in blood appears on the flat rock!
The other Easter egg is not as eerie but definitely heartbreaking. A small dog can be seen sitting quietly next to the grave of his owner in the Pacific Bluffs cemetery between 10:00 am and 11:00 am. This is the game paying tribute to a real grieving dog, Greyfriars Bobby, a 19th-century dog who guarded his owner’s grave for 14 years.
Watch the moon in GTA 5!
It was not just the easter eggs that were amazing in GTA 5. Rockstar Games upped their detail game (pun intended) by several notches, paying attention to the tiniest of details. The best example of this is the moon in the game. Yes, the moon. The moon in GTA 5 does not remain the same through the gameplay and actually goes through proper lunar phases– something many players might not even notice during regular gameplay. So you get full, crescent, waxing gibbous, and other phases of the moon while playing the game. Now, that’s one moonshot that worked.
GTA and controversies go hand in hand, and even the Guinness Book agrees
Ever since its release in 1997, the GTA franchise has been surrounded by controversies. And these have only gotten bigger with each new version. Celebrities like Lindsay Lohan, Karen Gravano, Michael Washington have filed lawsuits against Rockstar Games’ parent company Take-Two Interactive, for modeling its characters on them.
The game has also attracted a lot of criticism for its alleged glorification of violence and sexual themes – GTA: San Andreas was hit by the Hot Coffee controversy in 2004, when developers left explicit, sexual interactive code in the game instead of deleting it. They had disabled the code, but players used mods to access it, which allowed them to make the main character (CJ) have sexual encounters with characters after inviting them for coffee. The franchise had over 4,000 news stories published in July 2008, all related to violence, crime and misogyny perpetration. It is hardly surprising that it has been recognized as the most controversial video game franchise in history by Guinness World Records. Of course, millions still love it. But that is another story…
Generating the kind of revenues that make Hollywood envious
GTA games generate the kind of revenue that Hollywood blockbusters can only dream of. GTA 5 hit one billion USD in retail sales within three days, making it the fastest entertainment property overall to hit that milestone at that time. And GTA 6 seems to have followed in its footsteps. While no official figures have been released, it is estimated that nearly 25 million copies of the game were sold on the first day, and its earnings come to around 3.8 billion USD. Just for context, Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey has made USD 1.8 billion at the box office at the time of writing.
It is made in Scotland!
It might be released by a US company (Rockstar Games) and might feature US cities in its gameplay, but Grand Theft Auto is actually made in Edinburgh, Scotland, by Rockstar North, which was previously known as DMA Design, a company that was incorporated in Dublin. So yes, believe it or not, the game that many consider to be classically all-American was actually made by the Brits. And that too, by the ones that wear kilts. Bravehearts, truly.

The US Army is moving ahead with plans to detonate the nation’s stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, at approximately 9:00AM CST on Wednesday. The Verge reached out to experts on what to expect, and will keep this post updated.
Why the US Army is about to blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa
The US Army is scrambling to contain any potential lead pollution that could spread if an old stockpile of explosives blows up.
What material is the Army planning to detonate?
There are 68 drums holding about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, an unstable chemical compound created to detonate munitions like grenades. The US started using lead azide as a primary explosive almost a century ago before “moving away” from it about 15 years ago because of how difficult the material is to store and transport, Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), said in a Tuesday press briefing. At that point, the US transferred its remaining stockpile of lead azide to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Lead azide will explode at 350 degrees Celsius (662F). But it is also sensitive to flame, friction, or sudden shock, including fluctuations in temperature.
Some of the material on site in Iowa is more than 60 years old. The material can crystallize as it degrades over time, becoming unstable enough to explode even at ambient temperatures. The Army noted some deterioration of the material in 2009 — but not any “dangerous crystallization” at the time, according to Cekada.
“It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”
The chemical was stored in liquid form, embedded in sawdust and burlap bags inside the drums. Water and ethanol were also added to the containers to keep the lead azide from freezing in the winter. But during a March inspection, Cekada said ATF noticed “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels.” That made the material too unstable for them to open the barrels to add more water and ethanol, Cekada said. Removing a lid might cause the barrels to detonate.
Why is the Army detonating it now?
Officials have been trying to figure out what to do with the crystallized lead azide since that alarming March inspection. The Army initially hired a contractor to safely dissolve the chemicals but canceled the contract earlier this year, according to reporting by The New York Times. Using a chemical neutralization agent “proved to be an unsafe method,” Army Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the 71st Explosive Ordinance Disposal Group, said at the Tuesday briefing, because crystallization on the outside of the barrels made it too risky to open the lids.
“Everyone that we’ve spoken to through their experience has determined that this is the only safe path forward,“ Cekada said at the briefing. If they leave the chemicals as is, he said, they’re still at risk of exploding. “It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”
What are the risks?
Compared to an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion, a controlled detonation is supposed to limit the amount of lead dust unleashed on surrounding communities and the environment. Still, the dust plume could reach as far as 100 miles away from the site. The Army has released maps showing where lead dust is expected to travel based on its modeling.
The last time the Army disposed of lead azide this way at a comparable scale was in 1977, according to Teller. At the time, they detonated 7,000 pounds of the material in Colorado in open air “with zero mitigation.” Even then, 75 percent of the lead particulate stayed on site, Teller said at the briefing. The Army now believes it can “significantly reduce” the spread of that last 25 percent of lead using walls made up of four 16,000-gallon water tanks to capture lead particulate and hopefully prevent it from escaping into the atmosphere.
The 80-year-old earth-covered magazines holding the lead azide are cracked and deteriorating, Teller noted, and they are likely to break open after the detonation. To prepare, they’ve covered it with tarp and a special containment screen for lead. They also plan to flood it with 2 feet of foam to capture particulate pollution. Adam Telle, Acting Secretary of the Army, also said the Army has set out “state of the art gel blocks in huge quantities all around to ensure that we absorb as much of this blast as we possibly can.”
There is no “safe” level of exposure to lead
Last week, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club sought a court order to stop the explosion from taking place, pending an Environmental and Health Impact Statement and an investigation into alternatives to detonating the material. President Donald Trump chimed in on social media, calling for a pause until a federal appeals court gave the Army the green light after previously granting a temporary stay. The court on Monday denied the emergency motion to stop the explosion, clearing the way for the Army to move forward.
What precautions can people nearby take?
The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (Iowa HHS) recommends that anyone in potentially affected areas stay indoors and keep windows shut for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation. Iowa HHS also suggests switching off HVAC systems that might bring outdoor air inside or set them to modes that recirculate air, and using an air purifier with a HEPA filter.
FEMA is helping relocate Middletown residents and others within a voluntary 5-mile evacuation zone. People who are pregnant, children, and individuals with chronic diseases should evacuate the affected areas, Sean Kaufman, principal deputy assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, said at the briefing. “Outside of that area, if you’re close to that proximity and you’re uncomfortable, I think you need to do what you need to do to take care of your family,” Kaufman said.
There is no “safe” level of exposure to lead, a neurotoxin that poses health risks when inhaled or ingested. Kids are at increased risk because their brains are still developing and are also more likely to touch contaminated surfaces and then stick their fingers in their mouths. But most adverse health effects — which can include fatigue and gastrointestinal upset alongside impacts on brain development — are connected to chronic lead exposure rather than as a result of a one-off event.
“It is likely this exposure will not result in any observable acute clinical signs,” Will Sander, associate professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, says in an email to The Verge. “Overall, the risk is minimal, and there should be no long-term concerns.”
What happens after the explosion?
“The Army has done this before a long time ago and took lead measurements afterward that were low but hazardous (in my opinion),” Chris Kohler, an adjunct instructor at Indiana University who is an expert on hazardous waste, environmental remediation, and chemical hygiene, says in an email to The Verge. “The detonation will spread lead in the atmosphere. Not a desirable outcome.” Kohler and other experts say it’ll be important to continue monitoring the explosion site and surrounding areas to see if there needs to be any more remediation.

Even as Christian communities continue to face attacks allegedly from Hindutva groups across various parts of West Bengal, Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) state president Samik Bhattacharya on November 15 issued a warning to Christian missionary school, saying it they were found promoting “anti-India activities”, they would not be allowed to function.
“If any Christian missionary school, due to religious reasons, promotes anti-India activities, we will not let that school run,” he said while addressing a gathering at Birsa Munda’s birth anniversary celebrations in New Alipore, Kolkata.
“Guardians should become alert that an official at a school placed a Pakistani flag on the table of his chamber… in a school here in Kolkata. Please correct yourselves… We will let this happen in West Bengal no matter how powerful they are. All Christian missionaries can take to the streets; we are not opposed to any religion, but sitting in our state, in our country, we will not let you insult saffron [colour]… We will not allow it.”
Prior to issuing the warning, Bhattacharya claimed that a woman BJP worker was prevented from entering a “prestigious school in Kolkata” for wearing a saffron saree. “A prestigious school in Kolkata…I am not naming the school right now because a few days later I will sit outside its gates. One of our sisters, our BJP worker who was seen wearing saffron attire…was told [by the school] that ‘wearing these saris, you cannot come to school, you cannot pronounce the name of lotus flower while teaching the students.’ This is happening in the land of Kolkata where several eminent personalities have walked,” he said.
He further went on to insinuate that Christians were continuing to uphold British mentality in India. “It’s been 75 years since the British left the country, but the mentality has not left. You have come here; you are holding your establishments; you are Catholics, you are Protestants; you can propagate your religion. But remember, this government is not Babur’s government. This government is not trying to uphold British legacies. West Bengal has an independent government,” he said.
A report published by The Telegraph stated that the BJP president alleged that a reputed college in Kolkata was carrying out religious conversions in Asansol forcibly through “allurements”. “There is an obhijato (elite) college in Kolkata whose principal is carrying out religious conversion in Asansol. This cannot be allowed to continue. This is not the government of the Trinamool Congress, this is not the Left Front government…We are against political intervention in any educational institution. We want schools to create their own curriculum,” the report quoted him.
Bhattacharya, however, did not name any Christian missionary schools or colleges or provide any evidence behind the severe allegations he levelled against the community.
Upon being asked about Bhattacharya’s allegations against Christian missionaries, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on November 17, Tuesday, told the media, “…I get information on this and verify the facts. If the information is true and a written complaint is filed, if an individual did it, action will be taken against the individual; and if it was done institutionally, we will withdraw the NOC given to the institute.”
Murshidabad, West Bengal: On a Christian missionary school in Kolkata bars a teacher from wearing a saffron sari, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari says, “…I will verify the facts. If the information is true and a written complaint is filed—if an individual did it, action will be taken against the individual; and if it was done institutionally…”
— IANS (@ians_india) November 17, 2026
Christian Bodies Condemn Remarks, Issue Statements
The Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP) in a statement on November 18 reacted to Bhattacharya’s statement saying “sweeping accusations without evidence” maligned a peace-loving community and endangered social harmony, and demanded “specific facts, accountability, and immediate legal action”.
BCP posed eight questions to Bhattacharya and the state administration, questioning the lack of legal action against alleged perpetrators of illegal conversion, if any, and the silence over recurring vigilante attacks on Christians. It asked why attacks and vandalism of prayer meetings by ‘militant groups’ had not been condemned, whether such groups were allegedly being used to intimidate Christians, and sought the status of FIRs filed in connection with alleged threats and attacks against the community in the state.
ALSO READ: Christian families in Bengal attacked, allege ‘rape and death’ threats by ‘Bajrang Dal’ members
The BCP also demanded documentary evidence of alleged conversions in Christian-run educational institutions, pointing out that millions studied in these schools, and urged ruling party leaders educated in missionary institutions to share their experiences.
The association further questioned the administration’s silence on around 50 alleged attacks on Christian prayer gatherings over the past four to five months, contrasting it with their vocal responses to issues like an official allegedly displaying a Pakistani flag or wearing a saffron saree, without conclusive evidence.
Concerns Ahead of Christmas
Following Bhattacharya’s remarks, Paritosh Canning, moderator of the Church of North India and bishop of the Calcutta diocese, on Sunday sought chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s intervention against the rising number of attacks against the Christian community in West Bengal. Issuing a statement under the banner of Bengal Christian Council, he urged Adhikari to take appropriate measures to ensure the safety and security of Christians, churches and places of worship, to uphold the constitutionally guaranteed right of practising one’s faith.
“Our concerns are not without reason. Reports of attacks, intimidation and disruption of Christian religious activities have emerged from several districts of Bengal…These reported incidents include attacks on priests, pastors and worshippers, vandalism of churches and crosses, disruption of prayer meetings, intimidation of Christian families and interference with religious activities,” the statement read.
“These developments have caused considerable anxiety and apprehension among members of the Christian community. West Bengal has traditionally been a land of communal harmony…With Christmas approaching, the apprehensions of the Christian community have become particularly serious…the prevailing atmosphere of insecurity has raised genuine concerns about whether Christians will be able to observe their religious services and celebrate Christmas without fear or disruption,” the statement added.
Condemning Bhattacharya’s remarks, representatives of BCP and the West Bengal Association of Christian Schools held a joint press conference on November 16, Monday. Representatives of the associations dismissed the allegations of forceful religious conversion as baseless. They demanded that Bhattacharya name the two institutes and provide evidence to back his claims against Christian missionaries.
ALSO READ: Another attack on a Christian family in Bengal: Woman alleges mob assault, desecration of Bible
“A viral video has recently come to our attention. While we cannot verify its authenticity at this moment, the remarks recorded in it feature four grave allegations: claims of widespread religious conversions, an accusation that a…principal is involved in conversion activities; an allegation regarding a person wearing a saffron sari coming to a school; and a sweeping insinuation that even though the British have left, Christian missionary school administrators continue to carry a ‘British mentality,” read a statement by the representatives.
“At a time when vigilantes and hooligans are taking the law into their own hands across various districts — vandalising and launching brutal attacks on peaceful prayer meetings under the false pretext of forced conversions and desperately trying to build a fabricated narrative — the Christian community is both shocked and deeply angered to hear such an incredible, hate-mongering and aggressive speech from a usually balanced and sagacious leader like Samik Babu,” it added.
Speaking to Alt News, Moloy D’Costa, secretary of the West Bengal Association of Christian Schools and vicar-general of the Roman Catholic archdiocese of Calcutta, said, “The comments made by Mr Bhattacharya are vague. Every school has its own dress code, and there is no universal colour code. The authorities should either provide evidence or identify specific institutions and take appropriate action against them, rather than making general statements that vilify an entire community and a network of institutions.”
D’Costa also pointed out, “Several leaders in the party attended Christian missionary institutions; have they converted to Christianity? Converting to Christianity is a lengthy process. Simply visiting a church or sprinkling water is not part of that process. Accusations of forced conversion are being made from all sides, yet not a single case has been reported where anyone has been proven guilty of such actions.”
National Christian Council (NCC) state general secretary Arpan Rana strongly condemned Bhattacharya’s remarks on Christian missionary institutions, stating that “sweeping allegations without evidence” risk fostering suspicion and hostility towards the Christian community.
Rana told Alt News that Christian institutions were primarily invested in “education, humanitarian service, moral development and nation-building, not forced religious conversion,” adding that students from diverse religious backgrounds have studied in these institutions without abandoning their faiths. “Thousands of students from Hindu, Muslim, Christian and other communities have received education from these institutions while preserving their respective religious identities,” he said.
He also termed the portrayal of Indian Christianity as a legacy of British colonialism ‘historically misleading’, noting that Christianity existed in India long before colonial rule. “We expect scholarly arguments backed by evidence, not broad political claims. If any institution is found to engage in unlawful conversion, we support impartial investigations, but the entire Christian community should not be collectively accused,” he added.
Akin to other Christian associations in the state, Rana, on behalf of the NCC, urged the state government to protect Christian institutions, churches and communities, and ensure they can celebrate Christmas peacefully.
As precautionary measures, the BCP also advised churches to inform local authorities about upcoming programmes, establish a community alert system, ring church bells thrice if suspicious groups enter church premises, immediately notify police, and install CCTV cameras at vulnerable points. It also urged members to seek legal aid from BCP, maintain discipline and peaceful conduct, refrain from retaliation, and involve neighbours of all faiths and civil society members in Christmas celebrations to foster communal harmony.
Alt News has been documenting instances of hate crimes against the Christian community in West Bengal since early this year. Instances of violence, attacks, vandalism, and intimidation have often been carried out by Right-wing groups including Bajrang Dal, Vishva Hindu Parishad, and others, against individuals practising Christianity, house churches, and small Christian communities. However, in most of the cases we have reported, police action has been sparse, with fresh instances of harassment emerging regularly.

As India achieved a milestone by administering over one crore HPV vaccines, Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday (November 23, 2026) said every dose is a step towards protecting girls from cervical cancer and ensuring a healthier future for them.
India has administered more than one crore doses of the HPV vaccine to 14-year-old girls under its national vaccination campaign in less than nine months, covering nearly 87% of the identified annual target, the Health Ministry said on Saturday (November 21, 2026).
“A significant milestone in our journey towards preventive healthcare. Every dose is a step towards protecting girls from cervical cancer and ensuring a healthier future for them,” Mr. Modi said in a post on X.
The Prime Minister said he commends all the stakeholders whose efforts have ensured this remarkable feat.
The nationwide HPV vaccination campaign provides free, voluntary and single-dose vaccination to 14-year-old girls at designated government health facilities with parental consent.

One group of scientists has successfully trained a single species of wasp to successfully recognize human faces in an artificial laboratory setting. Other researchers have conducted experiments showing that a different species of wasp has the ability to recognize the faces of other wasps.
Expert say there are around 150,000 known species of wasp. Therefore, it is improper to apply the findings of the experiments to all wasps without further research. We found no evidence that wasps will remember a human face following chance encounters.
Among the animal kingdom, wasps have a pretty bad reputation. To the general public, they are often thought of as the bee's angrier, more aggressive cousin, with a more painful sting to boot.
Adding to people's fear of wasps is a rumor that has spread for years, which warns that they can remember people's faces. One concerned reader even got in touch to ask, "Can wasps remember faces?"
The claim seemingly alludes to the common perception that wasps are aggressive in nature. Some posts even imply they seek revenge against their enemies, including humans.
To figure out whether the rumor is all buzz, no sting, Snopes spoke to experts who have researched wasps and their facial recognition capabilities.
We found no evidence suggesting wasps remember human faces following chance encounters, but researchers told us about one experiment that trained a single species of wasp to successfully recognize human faces in an artificial laboratory setting. Given how many different species of wasp there are, it would be wrong to apply this finding to all wasps without further research. As a result, this claim is mostly false but with an element of truth.
First, some context
There are thousands of different species of wasp, according to Elizabeth Tibbetts, a professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Michigan. Princeton University Press puts that figure at roughly 150,000 known species.
Despite their public perception, Tibbetts said most species don't sting at all, though yellowjackets and hornets are exceptions. A wasp's social environment also changes dramatically from species to species. While some live in large nests and have a bee-like hierarchical social structure complete with a queen (this being a feature of eusociality), many species live completely solitary lives.
As a result, it would be improper to universally apply any characteristic to all wasps (some species even feature wingless females). The research pool, which is small to begin with, on wasps identifying and remembering faces — human or otherwise — only focuses on a few species. The studies have found relatively solid evidence of those species' facial recognition abilities, but it would be incorrect to apply any findings to all the thousands of wasp species without more research. 
Can wasps remember human faces?
Adrian Dyer — an associate professor of physiology at Australia's Monash University, who studies the cognitive capabilities of various animals, including bees and wasps — has trained both the western honey bee (Apis mellifera) and the common wasp (Vespula vulgaris) to recognize images of human faces, utilizing a test that is also used to check facial recognition capabilities in humans.
In his 2017 experiment with common wasps, Dyer's team presented two platforms to the wasps, each featuring a different human face. One platform rewarded the wasps with a droplet of sugar, while the other punished them with a droplet of quinine hemisulfate, which tastes bitter to the insects. The wasps repeatedly trained with the rewards for several days. Then, the team removed the rewards and ran the tests again. The wasps chose the face they had learned would reward them with sugar quite consistently, even when the reward was absent, and even when they were presented with new alternative faces. The only time they tripped up was when the faces were turned upside down.
Speaking via phone call, Dyer said his experiment was more of a testament to the creatures' learning abilities than anything else, though. His studies were performed in a lab setting, and recognizing human faces was not a natural ability — the bees and wasps needed to be specifically trained, instead of having an innate system for facial recognition, like humans do. (Scientists have found some facial recognition abilities in babies as young as a few hours old, he said).
So, if you've ever swatted a wasp away, the research does not suggest that it can simply look at you, remember your face and track you down a few days later. "The wasps are acting in the way they evolved to act," Dyer said. "They are not trying to seek revenge."
Some wasps can recognize faces of nest-mates
Tibbetts' research mainly focuses on Polistes fuscatus, the northern paper wasp. It is a common species in the eastern United States that forms nests near humans and wooded areas. They do sting when threatened, but Tibbetts said the wasps are more docile than one might think. "I didn't get stung until after I completed my PhD," she said via phone call.
At the beginning of her research career in the late 1990s and early 2000s, Tibbetts said she noticed something interesting about the paper wasps she was studying — they all had different facial and abdominal markings, sometimes behaved in selfish ways and had individual personalities. Their social dynamics, she added, are incredibly complex and interesting.
Tibbetts wondered whether those social dynamics meant the wasps were also aware of the physical differences between individual members of their species. So, she gave some of the wasps makeovers, using paint to alter each one's facial appearance. Then, she returned the wasps to their nests and recorded their behavior.
At first, nest-mates acted more aggressively toward the wasps with painted faces, by lunging and biting at them. Perhaps they thought the wasps with painted faces were impostors? No, according to Tibbetts. Studies show numerous species of wasp use chemical signals to identify their nest-mates and will quickly chase out or attack an impostor, but none of the wasps with painted faces were chased out in Tibbetts' experiment. All were accepted back into the nest.
But within two hours of being reintroduced, the aggressive behavior towards the wasps with painted faces died down. The wasps had adjusted to their nest-mate's new look. Tibbetts concluded that the wasps were using the facial markings to recognize each other, and the aggressive behavior she saw represented the wasps attempting to determine where the face-painted wasp fit in the social hierarchy.
In the years since Tibbetts first published her findings in 2002, she has continued to study the impressive cognitive and social abilities of the paper wasp. "Their capacity has really shocked me," she said. 
In one follow-up study, Tibbetts found northern paper wasps will "socially eavesdrop" on others, changing how they interact with a nest-mate after they have seen that nest-mate fight. In another, she found the wasps were better at identifying whole faces than partial faces, suggesting they could be learning faces by taking in all the information at once — the same way humans do. In a third study, Tibbetts described raising hybrid hives of three different, related paper wasp species. No matter their surroundings, P. fuscatus continued to perform well on facial recognition tasks, but remarkably, P. metricus, one of the other species, seemed to learn some basic facial recognition abilities when raised alongside P. fuscatus.
It is clear these small insect brains are a lot more complex than they might initially appear. Dyer said the findings are so important because they show it does not take a large, mammalian brain to perform complex tasks. "Think of a bee as a million neurons floating in space," he said. In comparison, human brains have somewhere between 50 and 100 billion neurons.

It was only a matter of time before Russia’s war in Ukraine reached deep into Asia. With signing bonuses as high as $35,000 and promises of a $3,000 monthly income, it should be no surprise that men from Indonesia and the Philippines are taking on jobs advertised as logistics, security, construction and administration, only to be pushed onto the front lines when they arrive.
Moscow has a manpower problem, and as governments from India to Nepal along with some African nations step in to prevent their citizens being lured into its forever war, Russia is turning to Southeast Asia’s vulnerable migrant-labor market to help fill the gap.
Shady recruitment agents are using social media, opaque contracts and the promise of high wages to attract people desperate for a job, the same ingredients that make migrant workers vulnerable to trafficking networks and scam compounds. Some believe they’re going to work in hotels, construction or other civilian sectors in Russia before discovering that the documents they signed are military contracts.
Governments should view this as an early warning signal for their migrant-labor economies. Indonesia is just the latest frontline — and police are treating recent cases as human trafficking when they believe recruits were deceived or coerced, as opposed to voluntarily enlisting.
Jakarta should be ideally placed to help citizens caught in this trap. Since he came to power in 2024, President Prabowo Subianto has gone out of his way to build a close relationship with President Vladimir Putin, and has described Indonesia as Russia’s gateway to Southeast Asia. During his time in office, Indonesia has joined the BRICS group of developing nations, while the two upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership last year. A personal president-to-president plea would go a long way.
The government has asked Russia to include Indonesia on the list of countries exempted from official recruitment into the military. It’s an important first step; however it’s not clear if Moscow has responded. Police were still intercepting travelers as recently as Nov. 18 and investigating whether they were being trafficked — recruitment is ongoing and will be until Russia says so.
Beyond making Indonesia a no-go zone for these agents, the government has another pressing problem: how to bring home those already trapped in the conflict. The Jakarta police say that the contracts run until the recruit’s death or the end of the war. At the very least, Prabowo’s administration could suspend legal job placements to Russia, which go to sectors including manufacturing, construction and hospitality, until the employers can be verified as legitimate.
Moscow controls the entire process: It sets the pay and the list of countries whose citizens it no longer takes — and brokers go wherever they can, Radityo Dharmaputra, a lecturer in International Relations at Universitas Airlangga in Surabaya, told me. Radityo is tracking a range of cases, including a prisoner of war held in Ukraine, two reported deaths, and police investigations into 58 victims. Most were lured by the offer of civilian work, he noted.
The Philippines is particularly vulnerable, given the size of its migrant labor force. At an Association of Southeast Asian Nations forum on migrant labor last month, Manila reported that it had helped to take down as many as 250,000 online posts linked to fraudulent overseas job offers through cooperation with Meta Platforms Inc. and TikTok.
Ukrainian military figures indicate that 128 Filipinos were recruited in the first nine months of the year, a sharp increase from the small numbers previously identified. The Philippines, like Indonesia, doesn’t appear on Russia’s list of excluded countries.
Last week’s meeting of Asean leaders missed an important opportunity to intervene. The gathering adopted a declaration on fair and ethical recruitment of migrant workers that explicitly addresses illegal hiring, labor exploitation, cross-border employment scams and human trafficking — precisely the mechanisms Indonesian police say are being used in some Russia cases. Yet it did not publicly single out Moscow or the plight of citizens lured to fight in the Ukraine conflict.
Governments and the tech companies used by these networks need to take urgent protective measures, including issuing clear public warnings and guidance on the risks of fraudulent job offers linked to working in Russia. It’s heartening to see that some nations have recognized that many of those who’ve signed up aren’t willing mercenaries. Treating them as trafficked victims creates an opening to negotiate with Russia for their safe return, or with Ukraine if they’ve already been captured on the battlefield.
This also lines up with findings from the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine released last month. It reported compelling evidence that Russian authorities, collaborating with overseas agents, had trafficked people from 29 countries using deception or coercion to recruit them into the armed forces.
Russia has successfully weaponized economic desperation. Southeast Asian nations need to act before this new channel of underground labor exploitation becomes permanent.
More From Bloomberg Opinion:
Russian authorities maintain an unofficial a list of countries whose citizens are barred from being recruited to fight in Ukraine. It reportedly includes nations seen as friendly to Moscow, such as China, India, Brazil, South Africa, Turkey, Cuba, Afghanistan, Venezuela, and Iran.

What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump
- Published
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.
Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.
The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.
Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.
But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.
Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.
Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.
The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.
The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.
And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.
He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.
If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.
What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.
Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.
What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.
Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.
Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

Canada's defense minister says his country answers to no one in Washington
Canada’s defense minister says that his country answers to no one in Washington, asserting Canadian sovereignty after the Pentagon accused Ottawa of failing to meet its military commitments
TORONTO -- Canada’s defense minister said on Tuesday that his country answers to no one in Washington, asserting Canadian sovereignty a day after the Pentagon accused Ottawa of failing to do enough to defend North America.
The Pentagon said Canada lacked a credible plan to meet NATO’s spending targets, accusing Ottawa of relying for decades on American taxpayers to foot its defense bill. Relations between the two neighbors have been strained by U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st state.
“Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States,” Defense Minister David McGuinty told reporters.
He insisted Canada remains on track to spend 5% of gross domestic product on defense and related security investments by 2035, while emphasizing that NATO allies had agreed to review the spending pledge in 2029.
“We also said by 2029 we would be examining that 5% commitment,” McGuinty said.
McGuinty said Canada’s plans would bring spending to 4% of GDP by 2030, a “significant, significant step” from 1.25% of GDP 14 months ago.
NATO’s 2025 agreement calls for at least 3.5% of GDP for core defense and up to 1.5% for related security investments by 2035. The scheduled 2029 review will examine the pace and balance of spending against security threats and military needs.
The Pentagon’s unusually blunt fact sheet on Monday accused Ottawa of postponing its largest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election.
“Canada’s defense shortfalls speak for themselves,” it said. “Canada must get serious and focused.”
The Pentagon said U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military. The U.S. criticism followed a classified directive from Hegseth that Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said largely restricts officials’ participation in Canadian think tank events and social engagements.
The Trump administration barred Pentagon officials from attending the Halifax International Security Forum under restrictions imposed in 2025 on think tank participation. Now in its 18th year, the gathering draws about 300 military officials, U.S. lawmakers, diplomats and scholars annually. Previous administrations of both parties sent senior Pentagon officials, including defense secretaries.
Democratic U.S. Sen. Andy Kim, who attended the Halifax forum this past weekend, criticized the restrictions in a social media post.
“Hegseth did not allow a single American servicemember in uniform to show up,” he wrote.
Rounds said Saturday that the directive was not expected to affect joint military operations or intelligence sharing.
Canada reached NATO’s previous 2% target. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, including 2.6% for core defense. Canada’s parliamentary budget watchdog has questioned how the government will reach 5%.
McGuinty said cooperation with Washington through the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, and work with NATO remained unchanged.
“We’re making the investments we announced. We’re executing on those plans,” he said.
The Pentagon also criticized Ottawa’s review of its planned purchase of 88 American-made F-35 fighters, warning that a mixed fleet could worsen personnel shortages and create uncertainty for NORAD.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the review as Trump threatened Canadian sovereignty and imposed tariffs. Canada has examined Swedish-made Gripen fighters, which could bring manufacturing jobs.

On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army. It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.
The email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.
Massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.
“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he says.
Massner wasn’t alone in being caught off guard. The sudden announcement that the Army would be exploding 9,500 pounds of lead azide with seemingly little to no notice caught nearly all of Iowa by surprise. Governor Kim Reynolds’ office said last week that they’d learned about the explosion the same way Massner did: via the press release sent out by the Army on November 15.
Now, despite a court order blocking the detonation, the Army announced late Sunday night that it plans to blow up the lead azide on Wednesday, a day before the Thanksgiving holiday. (On Monday, President Donald Trump posted that he was ordering the Army not to detonate anything without court approval.) Many Iowans are left with more questions than answers. Iowa’s unofficial state subreddit is filled with posts from people trying to plan holiday travel and safety around the event, which has switched dates twice in the past week. One local official in the path of a potential fallout told WIRED on Friday that she was leaving the area and staying at a hotel with her immunocompromised child.
Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the University of Iowa who has studied exposure to lead in his laboratory, says his lab has been “deluged with concerns,” with everyone from pediatricians to parents to people who run cleaning facilities and are worried about their staff exposure reaching out. Like most Iowans, Thorne also heard about the explosion from the Army’s press release.
“My first reaction was, They’re going to do what?” he says.
The 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Middletown site have been there for more than 20 years. In March, according to a document released by the Army on November 18, the material was officially labeled hazardous waste, and officials began looking into how to dispose of it. In a court filing published Saturday, the Army says that there is an “immediate risk” of the material exploding by itself after temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit. It is now invoking emergency powers to detonate the barrels by November 24.
“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the filing states.
The Army did not immediately respond to a list of questions sent by WIRED.
The Army does seem to have looked into other options besides blowing up the azide. The New York Times reported Friday that the Army awarded a contract in late March to a private company to handle cleaning up the chemicals onsite. However, that contract was pulled two months later; the company told the Times that the Army did not give a reason for changing its mind on the cleanup. A contracting officer in the Army told the company that the Army’s decision to pursue detonation “was not based on deficiencies” with the company’s science.
In a letter sent to Governor Reynolds on Friday, the EPA Region 7 administrator said that the agency only learned that the material had degraded to a dangerous state in March. The letter also listed a number of strategies the EPA had considered besides detonation, including chemical cleanup, which also risked causing an explosion.
The Army has blown up expired munitions before, although not at the scale of what it plans to do in Iowa. Thorne says that any exposure to lead from the explosion is expected to be “quite a bit lower” than lead exposures in communities exposed to legacy pollution sources. But “there is no safe level for lead, especially for young children,” he says.
The Army did have some public meetings and communications in late October with officials in Middletown, where the explosion will take place and where it has recommended temporary evacuation measures for some neighborhoods. But it’s not clear why its initial direct outreach around public health didn’t extend to towns in potential fallout ranges for a blast, including Mediapolis, beyond asking for permission to test soil samples. (The Army did include recommended public health measures in its November 15 press release.)
Thorne, a former chair of the EPA’s Science Advisory Board, says that a successful public health outreach program has lots of opportunity for public engagement for all affected areas.
“You have public meetings. You answer questions. You have extensive Q&A and FAQs, and you have people speaking to why this is the only choice, what are the burdens, and some kind of a cost-benefit comparison between the options, and then you roll it out through the media, through social media, through many ways,” he says. “Best practice is not what they’ve done—I think this is closer to worst practice, from a public health perspective.”
For his part, Massner, Mediapolis’s mayor, said on Friday that he planned to take “standard precautions” and follow the Army’s public health recommendations. (The Army has not released fallout modeling for a Wednesday explosion, but if winds carry the material south, it would be possible for Mediapolis to no longer be in the affected zone.) But Massner says he understands why people in his town were freaked out.
“What people saw was the map they drew, which showed a [red] cloud going over everybody’s head. I don’t think that was the intent of the map,” he laughs. “When you see a map covered in red, you’re supposed to run for shelter immediately—your life is in danger.”
Update: 11/23/2026, 2:01 PM EDT: WIRED has updated the piece to clarify that President Donald Trump said he will defer to an appeals court on whether the material will be detonated.

A train passenger’s overnight journey took a frustrating turn when he boarded his AC 2-tier coach with a confirmed ticket for berth number 54—only to discover that the coach had just 52 berths.
The passenger, Ishan Bajpai, took to social media platform X to share his ordeal while travelling on Train 15132 (BCY-NPR Express) from Varanasi City.
His post, accompanied by a screenshot of his confirmed ticket and a video from inside the coach, quickly drew attention online and prompted a response from Indian Railways.
According to the ticket screenshot shared by Bajpai, his booking showed a confirmed status for berth 54 (Side Upper) in coach A1 (CNF/A1/54/SU).
However, upon boarding late at night around 10:45 PM, he found that the berth numbering in the coach ended at 52.
Tagging Railway Seva and the Ministry of Railways in his post, Bajpai wrote: “Travelling on Train 15132 tonight. My ticket confirms A1/54, but the coach has only 52 berths. Being left without your confirmed seat at 10:45 PM, on an overnight journey, is extremely frustrating. Complaint raised on 139. How can this happen?”
In the video clip, he can be seen walking through the coach and recording the berth numbers to show that seat 54 did not exist. He also noted that he had lodged a formal complaint via the railway helpline 139.
Following the viral post, Railway Seva—the official grievance-handling handle of Indian Railways—acknowledged the complaint and expressed regret over the inconvenience.
“We regret the experience you had,” Railway Seva responded, stating that the matter had been escalated to the concerned official for necessary action.
The handle also advised Bajpai to wait for the Travelling Ticket Examiner (TTE), noting that the onboard official would have the correctly mapped seating chart and his actual berth number.
The mix-up sparked a wave of reactions on X, with several social media users questioning how the reservation system could allot a non-existent berth.
“These incidents create fear among the public. The railway must resolve this,” one user commented.
Another user advised waiting for the TTE to resolve the mapping issue, while others shared similar experiences of unexpected coach and berth changes during their journeys.
“Railways seems to have overdelivered. More than 100% berth numbers. Stupid software!” a user said.
Another added, “These incidents create fear among the public. Railways must resolve this.”

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has levied a total of ₹2 crore penalty on Star Health and Allied Insurance Co. for violations of certain regulations.
In its order, arising from an inspection by the regulator from January 31-February 11, 2022, IRDAI said a penalty of ₹1 crore is being imposed as the claims processed by the insurer were, in a manner, inconsistent with its own policy terms and conditions and a violation of IRDAI Circulars on Covid Claim settlements and Regulation 27 (v) of IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016.
The insurer is advised to ensure all policies are serviced as per the terms and conditions of the policy documents and no arbitrary deductions/denial are made to the claim without proper justification, IRDAI said.
IRDAI levied one more penalty of ₹1 crore, on the insurer, for various violations, including resorting to arbitrary deductions and not communicating its decision to repudiate the claims to the policyholders and by not mentioning the specific terms and conditions under which repudiations were made. The insurer has violated Regulation 27(v) and 33(d)(ii) and (iv) of IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016; Regulation 21(3)(c)(i)(c) of IRDAI (TPA – Health Services) Regulation, 2016, it said in the order.
The penalty of ₹2 crore pertained four of the eight charges. For other charges, IRDAI issued a caution and advisory; warning and direction; warning and advisory; while not pressing a charge.
