Norwich City 1-1 Queens Park Rangers: Anthony Musaba earns a point for the Canaries
Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Norwich City and Queens Park Rangers at Carrow Road on Tuesday night; Canaries draw their first game of the season as Anthony Musaba cancels out Harvey Vale’s opener.
Tuesday 24 November 2026 22:09, UK
Norwich's impressive run of victories came to an end as QPR held them to a 1-1 draw at Carrow Road.
The Canaries had won their previous five Championship fixtures but had to come from behind to pick up a point this time around after Harvey Vale had fired the visitors in front just before the break.
Philippe Clement's side were quickly back on level terms in the second half through a well-taken Anthony Musaba effort, but were well contained after that as Rangers registered a well-deserved point.
After a slow start, the match burst into life with a flurry of activity around the mid-point of the first half.
Norwich thought they had taken the lead on 19 minutes when Harry Darling got a touch on an in-swinging Jacob Wright free-kick but the effort was ruled out for offside.
Andre Brooks then saw a low shot from the edge of the area come back off the upright, while at the other end Dan Grimshaw did well to palm away a goal-bound effort from Vale.
Rangers were giving the hosts plenty to think about and took the lead four minutes before the break when Vale made another opportunity count.
The Republic of Ireland international had plenty to do after latching on to Kealey Adamson's pass but despite having Ruairi McConville and Darling in close attendance, he worked himself some space in the area before firing a powerful shot past Grimshaw.
Norwich were back on level terms within three minutes of the restart after a poor clearance by goalkeeper Pierce Charles was punished. It went straight to Musaba, who played a quick one-two with Mathias Kvistgaarden before confidently finding the roof of the net.
Vale fired inches wide as Rangers sought a quick response while substitute Oscar Schwartau was foiled by a good save from Charles as the game entered its final 10 minutes.
Norwich continued to press for a winner but could find no way through as they drew a game for the first time this season.

Two potential vaccines against the deadly Ebola strain gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo are set to enter trials in the outbreak's epicentre next week, the World Health Organisation announced earlier this week.
There are currently no vaccines or treatments for the less common Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the explosive outbreak declared in May, triggering an international public health emergency.
A total of 5,568 deaths out of 11,376 cases have been confirmed in the vast central African country's worst-ever Ebola outbreak, according to the WHO.
"We expect two candidate vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo virus to begin testing as early as next week," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told a press conference at the UN health agency's headquarters in Geneva.
The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC is a single framework that can test the safety, efficacy and ability to trigger an immune response of multiple vaccines. The trial uses ring vaccination: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
Ervebo, a vaccine already approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, kicked off the Tumaini trial on October 23, at the full-scale Phase 3 level, to determine if it also offers any protection against Bundibugyo.
Different vaccine types
The trial will now also incorporate the two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which have both gone through earlier-stage, smaller-scale Phase 1 clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab developed by the University of Oxford; the other, mRNA-1469, was developed by the US-based Moderna group using the mRNA technology made famous during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Meg Doherty, head of the WHO's science for health department, said Phase 2 clinical trials with the candidate vaccines are scheduled to begin on November 26 or 27 in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's northeastern Ituri province at the epicentre of the outbreak.
If the safety and immune response data from the Phase 2 trial pass the next stage of review, the candidate jabs can move forward to a full-scale Phase 3 trial.
Children paying 'terrible price'
Doherty said that more than 140 people were enrolled in the Tumaini trial, with thousands of contacts ultimately expected to sign up. The trial will also eventually expand beyond the current single site in Bunia.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
Tedros said 400 to 500 new cases were still being reported every week, with two-thirds of confirmed deaths still taking place outside Ebola treatment centres.
"Children are paying a terrible price. They account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and one third of deaths," he added.

Just look at the gold necklace in your house. It probably didn’t begin as an “investment.” Maybe your mother saved for years to buy it. Maybe it was put away for a daughter’s wedding. Maybe it came down through a family that trusts what it can see and touch.
So when prices drop, the worry isn’t just about the market. It’s personal. Should we buy more? Hold on to what we have? Wait and see?
I get the attachment. But decisions made on feeling alone can get expensive. Gold deserves a place in your savings, but its price can fall, its returns aren’t guaranteed, and a full locker doesn’t mean you are secure. Give gold the same care you would give any other investment.
So why is it falling?
Market reports through November 20, 2026, point to a stronger US dollar, higher US Treasury yields and expectations of tighter American monetary policy. Some investors have also cashed in profits or sold to raise money. These are market explanations, rather than government-certified findings.
The logic is simple. Gold pays no interest. When bonds and cash start paying more, they look better. And since gold is priced in dollars, a strong dollar makes it costlier for buyers in other currencies.
Here’s the part that surprises people. Gold has a reputation as a safe haven, but in tough times investors sometimes sell even “safe” assets just to raise cash. So gold can fall while fear rises. Safe haven never meant immune to the market.
Your necklace’s price story begins far from Srinagar’s jewellery shops. London is a major wholesale bullion centre. New York’s COMEX leads in futures and options. Shanghai has big physical and derivatives markets. India’s bullion trade and the Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX) tie local prices to the world. Dubai, Singapore, Hong Kong and Japan serve their own regions.
These markets affect one another, but they don’t sell the same thing at the same price.
Bullion, futures and finished jewellery all cost different amounts and serve different purposes. And nobody, whether government, exchange or jeweller, announces one worldwide price.
Now walk into a jewellery shop in Srinagar. The price you are quoted starts with international rates and the dollar-rupee exchange rate. Then come supplier costs, premiums or discounts, and import costs.
The India Bullion and Jewellers Association (IBJA) publishes domestic price references, and MCX futures give another benchmark. But IBJA is an industry body, rather than a government department, and a futures price isn’t the price of your necklace.
The rupee matters too.
When it weakens, a global fall in gold may show up as only a small dip here. When it strengthens, the effect flips.
So ask for quotes on the same purity and weight at the same time, and check making charges, taxes and buyback terms before you pay.
Government policy shapes your bill as well.
On July 23, 2024, the Union Budget cut customs duty on gold and silver from 15 percent to 6 percent. That was a one-time policy change, instead of a promise about what you will pay later. There’s also a special 3 percent GST rate for gold and certain precious-metal categories.
Checking purity is easier than it used to be. The six-digit Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) system began on July 1, 2021. Since April 1, 2023, old-style hallmarked jewellery without a six-digit HUID can’t be sold.
What you bought earlier stays valid, and you can check HUID details on the BIS Care app.
Just remember that a hallmark proves purity and traceability. It doesn’t promise a profitable resale or stop deductions when you sell.
Gold has mattered to India in bigger ways than most lockers show.
In the 1991 crisis, the Reserve Bank of India pledged 46.91 tonnes of gold with the Bank of Japan and the Bank of England to raise $405 million. The money was repaid between September and November that year.
At the end of March 2025, the RBI held 879.59 tonnes, 511.99 of them in India. Those are official figures for that date, rather than current holdings.
It’s a great example of gold as a reserve and a source of quick cash. But a central bank has very different duties and resources than a family does. If you are saving for your child’s education, you can’t just copy what the RBI does.
You may have seen the “₹10,000 became crores” headline too. Here’s the math behind it.
A Government of India publication lists gold at ₹88.62 per 10 grams in 1947. Assume an ending price of ₹1,25,590 per 10 grams.
On paper, ₹10,000 back then would have bought about 1.128 kg, worth roughly ₹1.42 crore.
That works out to about 9.62 percent growth a year over roughly 79 years.
Fun sum, but it hides a lot.
The starting price has no exact date. The math ignores premiums, making charges, storage, taxes and inflation. And annual averages, daily peaks and retail quotes shouldn’t be tossed together.
If you want a fairer comparison, the RBI publishes historical average-price tables.
So what should you actually do when prices fall? Start with your financial plan, rather than the price chart.
Say your portfolio is worth ₹10 lakh and you want 10 percent in gold. That’s ₹1 lakh. If you already hold ₹60,000 in gold, you need ₹40,000 more. Buy it in four instalments of ₹10,000. That way you spread your risk and don’t have to guess the bottom.
Once you reach your target, stop. Another price drop isn’t a reason to buy again. Gold can help diversify a portfolio because it often moves differently from equities and bonds. But it can also stay weak for a long time, and it pays no interest or dividends.
World Gold Council research from March 2026 found that holding 7.5 to 15 percent in gold improved historical risk-adjusted performance in a hypothetical Indian portfolio from December 2006 to December 2025.
Remember, that’s industry research built on historical assumptions, rather than a government recommendation or a promise about the future.
A 20 percent cap can work as your own limit against putting too much in one place, but it isn’t a government rule or a target.
And please count the jewellery you already own. That wedding necklace or inherited set may be worth a lot, even if you would never dream of selling it.
Most of all, don’t let fear spend your money. Nobody should borrow, dip into emergency savings or rush a purchase because they are afraid of missing a bargain.
Jewellery, emergency funds and investments each do a different job. Blur the lines, and you could be caught short when education, healthcare or retirement bills show up.
A well-filled locker is a real comfort, especially after years of saving. But security also means having cash when life surprises you.
Gold can be part of that, as long as you know what you own, what it cost and how much of your savings you have tied up in it.

Pentagon prepared to 'up the ante' in defence dispute with Canada
U.S. official warns of further measures in defence spending conflict
The war of words between the Pentagon and the Canadian government escalated on Tuesday as a senior U.S. defence official warned of further unspecified measures if Canada doesn't focus its military investments on protecting the continent.
The remarks were made in a background briefing given to Canadian journalists and approved for release by the U.S. Department of War.
The senior official described how they have been taking a very deliberate, graduated approach to get the attention of the Canadian government, starting with the suspension of the Permanent Joint Board on Defense (PJBD) last spring.
"That sent a message but has not solved the problem," said the Department of War official.
"We're postured to up the ante when we need to. If Canada cannot credibly turn its defence spending pledges into investments important for North American defence, we'll have no choice but to start looking at more significant mitigation measures."
The official did not spell out what those measures might look like, but suggested there's a sense of urgency.
"Prudence demands the department explore how we protect the United States in a situation where we cannot rely on Canada to prioritize military optimization and meet its obligations in a meaningful time frame," the official said.
"Canada has dismissed a lot of our concerns, including in NORAD, for many years. So, we want to communicate in a credible but also intelligent way that the current situation is not acceptable."
Mounting pressure
The pressure began building over the weekend with a leaked report in The Washington Post that said the U.S. military now had restrictions for interacting with Canadians. On Monday, the Pentagon publicly released a fact sheet that said Canada is not a credible defence partner and pointed to subpar Canadian military readiness statistics.
"Canadian political leadership continues to pursue unfocused global commitments, resulting in personnel and platform overextension, deferred modernizations for key equipment and low readiness rates," said the fact sheet.
"Ottawa's prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for NORAD and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer."
The fact sheet accused Canada of not being able to meet its NORAD and NATO commitments.
In the background remarks, the senior U.S. official went further, saying when it comes to delivering to allies "the gap between rhetoric and reality in Ottawa is the widest in all of NATO."
The official pointed to Germany as a model ally that quickly turned around its defence spending and is on track to deliver.
The official also said there are a group of European countries that are on track to meet NATO's five per cent of gross domestic product defence spending target by the end of the decade — five years ahead of the timeline agreed to by allies last year.
"Canada has an extraordinarily long way to go," the senior official said. "We are encouraged by the modest progress thus far, but we need to see much more credibility in terms of spending commitments."
Going into cabinet on Tuesday, Defence Minister David McGuinty was peppered with questions about the Pentagon's fact sheet.
"Canada's a sovereign nation. I'll be very direct: We don't report to the United States," said McGuinty.
He pointed to the recent federal budget, which laid out a defence spending path to four per cent of GDP by 2030.
In its fact sheet on Monday, the Pentagon said Canada needs to be more specific about how it's going to meet the five per cent target.
The federal budget was vague on spending beyond 2030 and both McGuinty and Prime Minister Mark Carney said much will depend on NATO's planned review of the goal in 2029.
Kerry Buck, Canada's former NATO ambassador, said there's obviously more at play in the Pentagon's complaints than defence spending.
She acknowledged the U.S. concerns about Canada's military readiness and its effect on NORAD, but said decades of underinvestment will not be rectified overnight.
The fact that Carney is pulling Canada closer to Europe and has made buying military equipment from suppliers other than the United States a priority seems to be the subtext of some of the arguments she's seeing.
"Maybe the U.S. complaints aren't really about what we're doing at NATO," said Buck. "Maybe the U.S. complaints are about what our focus is and the fact that we're diversifying away from an overreliance on the U.S. military, including buying American."
Steve Saideman, a defence expert at Carleton University, also acknowledged military readiness is a problem in Canada, but he sees U.S. domestic politics at play.
"This is about [U.S. Secretary of War] Pete Hegseth," said Saideman. "He's trying to do something he thinks of as being manly … bullying allies as opposed to actually getting his own house in order."
In Washington, Hegseth is facing intense congressional scrutiny and recently survived a bipartisan effort to impeach him.
That pressure is only expected to increase as Democrats take both the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate in the new year.

With his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure. For weeks, the seasoned election denier had promoted the baseless conspiracy theory that the midterms were rigged. He said he had sent the White House a 75-page report laying out in excruciating detail a conspiracy theory about how former Venezuelan officials had infiltrated the US electoral system to rig the outcome in favor of the Democrats. (There is no evidence to support this theory.) He had even, he claimed, spoken on the phone to President Donald Trump.
But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.
In the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot. While he shared some election conspiracy theories in the days after the election, he’s taken very little action since.
Oltmann is among a group of influential election deniers who believe, without evidence, that the midterms were rigged and who claim to be in direct contact with Trump, but are frustrated by the president’s lack of fervor or seeming interest in overturning the results. These figures are making increasingly desperate demands of the president, including declaring martial law and ordering military tribunals.
“We can walk into every voting [location] and say: ‘Take this equipment, throw it out in the street,’” says Oltmann. “We can do that … that's not violent … We're just doing our jobs as Americans.”
These calls for action echo very similar demands made in the weeks leading up to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, and some of the same figures are involved—though allies in the administration that once boosted their lies appear to have gone silent.
“This is a carbon copy of 2020,” said Patrick Byrne, the founder of Overstock.com who claims to have spent $100 million on promoting election integrity over the last six years, on a podcast on Saturday. He also claimed that, two weeks before the attack on the Capitol, he was in a room with Trump advocating for the same measures he is asking Trump to take now.
The big difference this time around, however, is that, so far, Trump has not been leading the charge. In the weeks after his election loss to former president Joe Biden in 2020, Trump was quick to seize on claims that the election had been rigged. In the lead-up to this year’s midterms, Trump and his administration did everything they could to promote baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizens and mail-in voting; they also weaponized the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice to target those they believed were responsible.
Days after the election this month, as the midterm results rolled in, Trump shared screenshots of X posts from election deniers on his Truth Social account, boosting baseless conspiracy theories about the midterms.
On November 9, he appeared to be ready to embrace those conspiracy theories, writing on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter! President DJT.”
Election deniers on X and Telegram celebrated, believing that Trump was about to fully endorse their community once again. But in the weeks since, Trump has refrained from posting much of anything about stolen or rigged elections, save for a few limited references.
“I am going to give evidence to the president today … I have a wealth of evidence,” Peter Ticktin, a lawyer and former schoolfriend of Trump, told WIRED in an interview on November 11. Ticktin refused to share the evidence with WIRED and said the documents came from “various sources, some who prefer to be anonymous.”
Ticktin also said he would speak directly to Trump about the issues and would be advocating for the president to “nullify all of the results of the last election and declare martial law.” Ticktin told WIRED on Monday that he had not yet spoken with the president and was hoping to soon. Ticktin appears resigned: “If we take him for what he's saying at this point in time, he's not planning to do anything beyond cooperate with the globalists.”
While many on the right have followed Trump’s lead in ignoring claims about rigged midterms, a significant number of Republicans believe that the midterm votes were not “free and fair,” according to a new poll from UC San Diego.
Major election deniers are split over what to do now. Byrne, for example, disagrees with Oltmann’s suggestion to seize voting machines—but he has another plan: reinstate Michael Flynn, a prolific election denier, to his former role as Trump’s national security adviser.
“Instead of going straight to insurrection, [Trump] uses current authorities to go inspect hard drives in 12 cities, and you bring Michael Flynn in as national security adviser, and then turn it over to Michael. Michael can get this all done by December 1,” Byrne said over the weekend. “If you do find foreign activity … then say, OK, I'm nullifying this election, I'm declaring a new election in 120 days.”
But there is no indication from the administration that anything like this will happen, and Flynn himself has called the election “a master class by the GOP in how to fail.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Conspiracy theorists claimed the video served as evidence that "lizard people" walk among us. Wright reportedly told the New York Post that he's "obviously" a human.
A video circulating online appears to show a man rolling his eyes in a so-called "reptilian" fashion while standing behind New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a news conference.
The clip, which was posted on X, Facebook and other platforms, reignited a decades-old conspiracy theory claiming shape-shifting reptilians secretly hold positions of power, which Snopes has previously reported on.
Snopes readers wrote in to ask if the video was real or generated using artificial intelligence.
This is a real clip of Democratic New York City Assemblyman Jordan Wright, who reportedly told the New York Post that he is "obviously" human.
Wright's eye roll is visible in multiple credible livestreams of the news conference in question, which Mamdani held on Nov. 20 to announce a plan to shutter Rikers Island, the city's largest jail, by 2032.
For example, Wright's eye roll is visible at the timestamp 1:51 in a YouTube livestream posted by the official New York City mayor's office account, whereas USA Today's livestream shows the eye roll at 1:54.
There's no evidence that the livestreams in question were enhanced using AI, nor would there be any reason to do so.
According to the New York Post, Wright said he has "no idea what was going on in that video."
"Obviously I'm a human being, and my humanity can be seen through my legislation like the $4 million for the WE ACT environmental justice center in Harlem," he reportedly told the Post. "I can't speak to any reptiles or aliens."
We reached out to Wright, who assumed office in the New York State Assembly in January 2025, to verify that he spoke to the Post and await a response.
Background on reptilian conspiracy theories 
As we previously reported, the "reptilian" conspiracy theory was popularized in the modern era by David Icke, a British man who is barred from holding events in countries like the Netherlands and Germany over antisemitic conspiracy theories.
According to the UK anti-fascist advocacy group HOPE not hate, "the 'reptilian theory' is just one element of the hugely convoluted narrative Icke has developed over his long career" that promotes longstanding antisemitic tropes.
In the United States, officials have previously examined whether the conspiracy theory was a possible motive for the Nashville Christmas Day 2020 bomber.
There is, of course, no evidence that a secret race of reptilians controls the world.

Srinagar, Nov 24: Jammu and Kashmir Police conducted “Know Your Beat Officer” and “Know Your Beat” programmes in Bandipora and Baramulla districts, taking its public outreach to neighbourhoods and strengthening engagement with residents at the grassroots level.
The initiative follows directions from Inspector General of Police, Kashmir Zone, Sujit Kumar, who has emphasised the need to revitalise beat policing, maintain updated beat records and ensure regular people-to-people contact across the Valley.
In Bandipora, the programmes were held at Dawar in Gurez and Ganastan in Nowgam. The session at Dawar was attended by the SDPO Gurez and beat officers of Police Station Gurez, while beat officers of Police Post Nowgam Sumbal participated in the programme at Ganastan.
During the interactions, residents were briefed about the duties and responsibilities of beat officers, the importance of police-public cooperation and the mechanisms available for grievance redressal.
Beat officers shared their contact numbers with locals, enabling them to report criminal activities, drug-related concerns and other anti-social behaviour directly. Residents were encouraged to maintain regular communication with their respective officers to facilitate timely intervention and help preserve peace and order.
Police said the outreach was aimed at building mutual trust, improving coordination at the local level and making policing more responsive to the concerns of residents.
In Baramulla, District Police organised a series of “Know Your Beat” awareness programmes across different beats of Police Station Baramulla.
Residents were sensitised about the role of beat policing in maintaining law and order, preventing crime, identifying emerging local issues and strengthening confidence between the police and the community.
Police also shared the Closed User Group (CUG) contact numbers of Police Station Baramulla and informed participants about the Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) helpline 112 for reporting emergencies.
Officials said the face-to-face interactions provide beat officers an opportunity to understand local grievances, obtain timely information and improve coordination with residents.
Similar programmes will be conducted in the remaining beats in phases, police said.
District Police reiterated its commitment to accessible, people-friendly and responsive policing, emphasising that public participation remains vital for effective law enforcement and community safety.
The district-level initiatives come amid a sustained push by IGP Kashmir Sujit Kumar to strengthen beat-level policing and make it more proactive, accountable and citizen-oriented.
In recent conferences with Range DIGs, SSPs, SHOs and field officers, the IGP has stressed the need for police personnel to step out of police stations, maintain regular contact with people and address grievances without delay.
He has also called for updated beat books and technology-enabled digital records to improve monitoring and accountability.
The IGP has underscored the SMART Policing framework—Strict and Sensitive, Modern and Mobile, Alert and Accountable, Reliable and Responsive, and Techno-savvy and Trained—while directing police stations and posts to function as accessible centres for public service, crime prevention and grievance redressal.

Arlie Sisson is one of the most interesting executives I've met who's actually putting AI to work in the real world.
Sisson is chief digital officer of restaurant chain Chipotle. I met her recently at a dinner hosted by Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy, whose company supplies some of the technology Chipotle uses.
Sisson was the center of attention that evening. While plenty of executives are still talking about what AI might eventually accomplish, she shared fascinating examples of what it's already doing.
And they involved guacamole. What's not to like?
I followed up with Sisson for a longer interview to understand how Chipotle is using AI, what it's getting in return, and what this means for the thousands of people who run its restaurants.
The answer is encouraging, because it shows this technology is helping workers be more human, not less. AI is taking over some of the tedious work of running a restaurant, giving managers more time to do what humans are particularly good at.
Chipotle has three main projects underway. One is already producing results. Another is expanding rapidly. A third could change how restaurant managers organize their days.
Hiring employees quicker
Let's start with the clearest evidence.
Hiring employees is a big job when you operate thousands of restaurants. Managers have to review applications, communicate with candidates, arrange interviews, collect paperwork, and get new employees ready to start.
Chipotle has an AI assistant called "Ava Cado" that handles much of this work.
Ava communicates with applicants in multiple languages, answers questions, gathers information, schedules interviews, and helps move candidates through the hiring process.
The results are striking.
Before Ava, the average time between someone applying for a job and starting work was 12 days. Now it's four.
That's eight days eliminated from the hiring process.
The number of applicants coming through has nearly doubled, while the proportion who complete their applications has jumped from about 50% to almost 88%.
These are meaningful improvements for a company that constantly needs to recruit employees across more than 4,200 restaurants.
And this frees managers from spending so much time chasing paperwork and coordinating interviews.
"At our scale, that's meaningful," Sisson told me.
How much guacamole?
The second project is my favorite.
Every morning, Chipotle managers face a deceptively difficult question: How much food should we prepare?
Too little chicken or guacamole, and customers may be disappointed. Too much, and food gets wasted.
Traditionally, managers arrive around 7 am, consult historical sales figures, and work through their plans by hand, often using clipboards and calculators.
But last year's sales figures don't necessarily tell you what's going to happen today.
A restaurant near a college campus might get a sudden rush when classes finish at 10:50 am. Another location might be busiest at 12:30 pm.
Weather, local events, and promotions can also change demand.
Even the size of avocados varies throughout the year, depending on where they're grown.
"Wait a minute, wait a minute," I interrupted Sisson when she mentioned this during our interview.
Yes, apparently avocado sizes are another thing restaurant managers have to worry about.
Chipotle's answer is an AI system called Cook to Needs.
It analyzes demand and recommends how much fresh food each restaurant should prepare throughout the day.
Consider Chipotle's promotion offering free chips and guacamole to new rewards members. That changes how many avocados restaurants need. But because it's a new promotion, last year's sales figures won't capture the extra demand.
AI can help account for that change, along with local conditions and other factors, so restaurants are better prepared.
The system is being tested at 500 locations, with plans to expand nationally.
Sisson said the old manual processes could consume hours each day. Chipotle hasn't provided a precise figure for how much time Cook to Needs saves, but the company is already seeing encouraging results.
Restaurants that use the system most consistently report higher customer satisfaction and fewer complaints than those that use it less frequently, according to Chipotle.
The company is also tracking food waste, preparation time, and the efficiency with which employees are deployed.
There's an important financial opportunity here: Less wasted food saves money, while having enough fresh ingredients on hand can help prevent lost sales.
An AI assistant for restaurant bosses
The third project brings these ideas together.
Chipotle is developing an AI assistant specifically for general managers.
Imagine arriving at work and asking what you need to know about the day ahead.
The assistant could flag a large catering order, warn about an unusual staffing situation, or explain how a local sporting event might affect customer traffic.
It could also help managers find answers to routine questions about restaurant procedures without having to dig through documents.
The system is in an early testing phase.
Chipotle plans to make these tools available on mobile tablets, so managers can use them while moving around their restaurants rather than sitting in an office.
The idea is to give managers the information they need without making them spend hours finding and analyzing it.
The human payoff
There's a bigger point here that goes beyond burritos and guacamole.
Companies are spending enormous sums on AI, and investors increasingly want to know whether the technology is actually delivering a financial return.
Chipotle's experience suggests that some of the most useful applications are relatively mundane. Hiring people faster. Preparing the right amount of food. Helping managers make better decisions.
Those improvements can translate into lower costs, higher sales, and more productive employees.
But there's another benefit that's harder to measure.
A manager who spends less time staring at spreadsheets can spend more time training employees, solving problems, and helping customers.
Sisson, who previously worked at hotel companies including Marriott and Hyatt, sees this as a return to the basics of hospitality.
She doesn't approach AI primarily as a way to eliminate jobs. Instead, she wants to change what employees spend their time doing.
"I don't think anyone goes into a general manager job because they're like, 'I love spreadsheets and check boxes,'" she told me.
I couldn't agree more. I don't like spreadsheets either.
Sisson describes restaurant managers as coaches and quarterbacks. Their real value comes from leading people, especially during the frantic lunch and dinner rushes.
And that's perhaps the most interesting lesson from Chipotle's AI experiments.
The technology is doing more of the boring work so people can concentrate on the human stuff.
Or, as Sisson put it: "If a tool doesn't make that crew member's day easier, it doesn't matter how cool it is, how much AI is in it."

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has proposed a set of safeguards against electronic payment frauds, including an account-wide ‘Stop Switch’ and a ‘Trusted Person Mechanism’ (TPM) for high-value transactions. The central bank has invited feedback on the draft directions by December 14, 2026, with the proposed rules set to come into effect from July 1, 2027. Under the Draft Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026, banks will have to provide a ‘Stop Switch’ that allows customers to immediately disable all outgoing debits, new payment mandates and new UPI app registrations. The switch will not block incoming credits or existing standing instructions. Customers will be able to activate, modify or deactivate it through bank branches, ATMs, mobile apps, internet banking and interactive voice response (IVR) services. Banks will also have to ensure that re-enabling digital payment channels or deactivating the Stop Switch requires at least the same level of authentication as its activation. The RBI has also proposed a voluntary Trusted Person Mechanism (TPM) for high-value transfers. Under this facility, account holders can nominate an adult as an additional authentication layer for transactions above a specified threshold. The nominated person will have to approve such transactions within a one-hour window. However, the trusted person will not have any legal authority over the account or access to its details. Banks will be responsible for verifying the identity and eligibility of nominated individuals. Any activation or modification of the TPM will also be subject to a 24-hour cooling-off period. The RBI had first floated a similar proposal in June this year, suggesting an additional authentication layer for digital transactions above ₹10,000 made by citizens aged 70 and above. Beyond these measures, banks will have to offer customers granular controls over their digital payment channels. These will include options to enable or disable individual channels, set time windows for their deactivation and establish transaction limits per transfer, per beneficiary or through aggregate daily caps. The draft also proposes that all digital payment channels remain disabled by default during customer onboarding and be activated only with explicit consent. Further, newly issued physical and virtual cards will be restricted by default to domestic contact-based ATM and point-of-sale (POS) transactions. Newly enabled digital payment channels will also be subject to a transfer limit determined by the bank for the first 24 hours. Earlier this year, the central bank issued directions requiring banks to compensate eligible victims of digital payment frauds. The latest proposals take a more preventive approach, giving customers greater control over payment channels and adding authentication safeguards to help stop fraudulent transactions before they are completed.

Jammu, Nov 24: The Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Tuesday asserted that the message of Baba Jitto, whose sacrifice continued to inspire society to stand against injustice and uphold respect for labour, transcended caste, class and community and represented a shared national heritage.
He was addressing the gathering after paying homage to Baba Jitto and Bua Kaudi at the annual Jhiri Mela.
The Lieutenant Governor said the annual fair was a living symbol of faith, cultural heritage and collective consciousness. He said the annual visit to Jhiri was a sacred pilgrimage and the deep spiritual bond associated with the place reflected centuries of devotion and reverence towards Baba Jitto.
Highlighting the legacy of Baba Jitto, the Lieutenant Governor said that his life represented an enduring message of truth, courage and justice. He noted that Baba Jitto’s struggle was not merely about a crop, but about protecting the dignity, rights and self-respect of every hardworking farmer.
The Lieutenant Governor emphasised that the true tribute to Baba Jitto and Bua Kaudi would be the creation of a society where no farmer was left alone in the struggle for rights and dignity. He called for a “whole of society approach” to ensure inclusive development and social justice.
“We must build a society where every person receives respect, where social harmony endures and where the benefits of development reach the last person in society. To contribute to a developed India, we must build a developed Jammu and Kashmir and three values must always remain at its foundation- truth, hard work, and mutual respect,” he said.
“For this, farmers must continue their hard work. Teachers must educate the new generation in accordance with a changing world. Youth must come forward for innovation. Government officials must serve the public with complete dedication and every family must instil good values in young children. From ordinary citizens to government officials, everyone must remain honest in their actions, discharge their responsibilities with sincerity, and work together in difficult circumstances,” LG Sinha said.
The Lieutenant Governor underlined the contributions of farmers in sustaining the nation and enriching its traditions. He highlighted the transformative impact of the Holistic Agriculture Development Programme (HADP) in UT, noting progress in agriculture, horticulture and dairy sectors through modern infrastructure, diversification and market-oriented reforms. He urged farmers, particularly small and marginal cultivators, to adopt modern technology and align production with emerging market demands.
LG Sinha also encouraged greater adoption of millet cultivation. He said the millet crops were a climate-resilient and income-enhancing option in the face of irregular rainfall, rising temperatures and declining groundwater levels.
Calling upon youth to transform agriculture through technology, entrepreneurship and scientific practices, the Lieutenant Governor urged them to view farming and allied sectors as dynamic engines of growth.
“Jammu Kashmir's agricultural landscape offers immense opportunities for innovation and employment, and youth must play a leading role in making farming more productive, profitable and future-ready,” LG Sinha said.
He also commended the growing participation of women in the rural economy. The Lieutenant Governor said that women farmers, self-help groups and rural entrepreneurs were playing a pivotal role in driving economic self-reliance across Jammu Kashmir.
He called for expanded opportunities in education, skill development and entrepreneurship for women in rural areas.
“Many self-help groups are now working alongside women farmers to give a new direction to the rural economy. The women in villages are setting new examples of economic self-reliance through local products, handicrafts, food processing and small enterprises. In the agriculture and allied sectors, our daughters are setting new benchmarks of innovation and entrepreneurship,” the Lieutenant Governor said.
Highlighting the rich legacy of Dogra culture, he urged the youth to take pride in their language, folk traditions and regional history. He encouraged the use of digital technologies to preserve and promote cultural heritage globally.
“Sit with your elders. Learn old songs from them, listen to folk tales and learn the history of your region. Preserve such heritage through digital means, so that future generations can also become familiar with it. I believe that technology today places in our hands a power through which we can take our culture to every corner of the country and the world. We must use this technology to introduce the world to the identity of Dogra culture,” the Lieutenant Governor said.

At least 13 people have died, and more than 300 have been hospitalised since November 18 after they consumed spurious liquor in Manipur's Chandel district, police said on Saturday (November 21, 2026).
The patients are mostly from Chakpikarong and surrounding areas and have been hospitalised across multiple healthcare facilities in Imphal, including JNIMS, RIMS, Shija and Babina Hospital.
"Thirteen people have been reported dead till 9 p.m. on Friday, while 346 patients have been admitted to hospitals due to suspected methanol poisoning, as they consumed spurious liquor," an official told PTI.
Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited Shija Hospital and Babina Hospital on Friday afternoon (November 20, 2026) to assess the situation and meet patients undergoing treatment.
In a social media post, Mr. Singh said, "Visited Shija Hospital at Lamphelpat, and Babina Hospital at Sajiwa, today [on Friday] to enquire about the health condition of the persons undergoing treatment after consuming spurious liquor from Chakpikarong area in Chandel District."
The Chandel district administration has intensified emergency response measures, and a team has been constituted for coordinated monitoring of the situation, an official notification said.
Four rapid response teams, equipped with adequate medicines and oxygen supplies, have been deployed in the district, the official said.
"Over 140 patients were admitted to Shija Hospital and over 41 patients at Babina Hospital. The death toll has touched 11 during the last 48 hours. The patients are undergoing medical evaluation and treatment under the close supervision of the doctors," he said.
"A medical team, led by a Specialist in General Medicine, along with essential medicines, has left for Chandel District to strengthen on-ground treatment and response", he said adding, "The government will conduct an enquiry and the culprits will be punished."
Joint managing director of Shija Hospitals, Chetan .K, told reporters that the patients admitted to the hospital reported symptoms of dizziness, stomach pain and other complications.
"Some patients are also undergoing hemodialysis", he added.
A JNIMS doctor said, "Many of the hospitalised include individuals who had consumed local liquor and had come to the hospital due to fear."
Shija Hospitals also informed that "over 312 patients [have been] attended [to] till now at Shija Hospitals due to methanol poisoning."
Preliminary reports suggest that the suspected contaminated alcohol was purchased from Sugnu in Kakching district.
Chandel constituency MLA S.S. Olish said arrangements are being made to bring more patients up to Imphal and has requested the chief minister to look into the situation.
She said, "I have spoken personally to CM Yumnam Khemchand, and requested him to look into the situation affecting Chandel. He agreed willingly and has visited the patients at Shija Hospitals and will visit Babina later."
"Moreover, party workers, especially in Chakpikarong, are working constantly, arranging vehicles to bring patients up to Imphal", she added.
Bishnupur, Senapati, Kakching and Thoubal district administrations have issued separate public advisories, requesting people "to refrain from consuming locally brewed liquor or alcoholic beverages of doubtful or unverified origin."

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

A crude bomb was allegedly hurled by ABVP activists at a bookstall set up by the Students’ Federation of India (SFI) in College Street, Kolkata’s principal hub of bookshops and publishing houses, late on November 18.
Titled Sangrami Boipotro (Literature of Struggle), the stall was set up by the Calcutta University unit of the SFI to commemorate the November Revolution. ABVP activists allegedly attempted to vandalise the stall, accusing the Left student outfit of selling ‘anti-national’ books, resulting in day-long tension in the ‘boi para’.
The confrontation began around 11 am on Wednesday and continued late into the evening. Tensions escalated when ABVP activists allegedly hurled a firecracker, locally known as a ‘chocolate bomb’, into the SFI stall as activists, including women, were packing up the books before closing for the day. Video footage shows the firecracker exploding in a small burst of flames and smoke filling up the area.
The incident took place in the presence of a large contingent of Kolkata Police personnel. SFI activists alleged that the police attempted to shield the ABVP activists. The Right-wing student organisation, on the other hand, claimed SFI activists had assaulted its members and vandalised its bookstall.
Reacting to the allegations and counter allegations of violence, BJP state president Samik Bhattacharya said, “These are matters related to student politics. They are young. Political movements were never entirely peaceful here. These things happen.” He also said ABVP was not related to the BJP.
The SFI’s Version of Events
According to SFI activists and videos circulated on social media, the confrontation began around 11 am. The bookstall was scheduled to open at that time, with senior Left leader Biman Bose slated to inaugurate it.
However, as SFI activists were setting up the stall, a group of ABVP activists gathered outside the main gate of Calcutta University, which opens onto College Street, and attempted to prevent them.
To contain the situation, a contingent of Kolkata Police personnel formed a human barricade between the two groups. Videos show ABVP activists repeatedly raising slogans and displaying aggression. However, the police did not remove them from the spot.
Around 1 pm, tensions appeared to ease somewhat, with ABVP workers setting up a makeshift bookstall a few metres away from the SFI stall. The two stalls were positioned on either side of the university’s main gate, with the ABVP stall to its left and the SFI stall to its right. Police personnel placed metal barricades in front of the SFI stall to prevent a direct confrontation between the groups.
Around 2 pm, Left leaders Biman Bose and Sujan Chakraborty visited the stall.
However, as Bose was leaving, ABVP workers were heard raising slogans such as “Biman Bose Go Back” and “Slap Biman Bose across the face with shoes”.
The ABVP protest blocked a section of College Street. Its activists allegedly charged towards the SFI stall several times in the presence of police personnel. They also threw water and eggs at the stall, staining a National Flag at the venue and several books, the Left outfit alleged.
Around 7 pm, the situation escalated with the ABVP gathering allegedly hurling bricks, wooden sticks and water bottles towards the SFI enclosure, while police personnel continued to maintain a barricade between the two groups.
Videos also show plastic chairs being hurled form either side.
Around this time, SFI activists were packing up the stall for the day when a ‘chocolate bomb’ was seen flying towards it from the direction of the ABVP gathering.
The firecracker exploded inside the SFI enclosure, producing a flash and filling the area with smoke. The explosion further escalated tensions, with SFI activists seen rushing towards the ABVP gathering. Police personnel struggled to pull them back and prevent a direct confrontation.
Following the incident, the SFI decided to lodge an FIR at the nearby Jorasanko police station. Activists also organised a protest march from College Street to the police station.
According to SFI activists, police initially resisted registering a written complaint but eventually agreed following their sustained pressure.
SFI activists further alleged that after they had left for the police station, ABVP workers vandalised the stall site, damaging tables, benches and chairs.
The SFI is scheduled to reopen the bookstall at the same location on Thursday. It will remain open until November 20.
Trouble Erupted on November 17 as well
According to SFI sources, the organisation has been setting up the bookstall at the same location for the past four years. This year, too, its members informed the Joint Commissioner of Kolkata Police about the stall and its schedule through an email. They also paid the requisite fee to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) for setting up the stall. However, on Monday, the police informed them that they would not be allowed to erect any permanent structure at the site.
On Tuesday morning, a contingent of Kolkata Police personnel arrived in front of Calcutta University and attempted to prevent SFI activists from setting up the bookstall.
Around 12:30 pm, SFI activists blockaded College Street and began selling books while sitting on the road.
This led to a scuffle with the police, following which 41 SFI activists, including the organisation’s West Bengal state secretary, Debanjan Dey, were detained and taken to Lalbazar, the headquarters of Kolkata Police.
In response, the SFI organised a mobilisation outside Lalbazar, demanding the release of those detained. Around 6 pm, all 41 activists were released.
According to SFI activists, the joint commissioner of police held lengthy discussions with them, following which it was agreed that they could set up the stall without erecting any permanent structure. They were also asked to ensure that the stall did not obstruct traffic on College Street.
The SFI activists attempted to set up the stall on Wednesday in accordance with these conditions. However, their efforts were disrupted by ABVP activists, who objected to the organisation’s programme.
The ABVP’s Response
ABVP further alleged that SFI activists had destroyed books on Swami Vivekananda, claiming that its own bookstall had been set up to encourage reading among students. It accused the SFI of sabotaging an initiative intended to promote education.
The Facebook page of ABVP Paschimbanga also shared a clipping from Bengali news channel TV9 Bangla, which purportedly showed Arunava Dutta, an ABVP national executive council member, being assaulted by SFI activists.
In a separate post, ABVP shared a video showing a stone being hurled from near the Left book stall.
In a separate Facebook post, ABVP Paschimbanga condemned what it described as attacks on its activists at Calcutta University, Calcutta Medical College and Presidency University. “The throwing of bombs inside university campuses and the targeted attacks on ABVP activists by SFI and Left organisations are deeply alarming and condemnable,” the organisation said.
In the video, ABVP national secretary Shravan B Raj said, “The SFI and Left extremist groups are unleashing violence on ABVP karyakartas.”
Vandalism at Calcutta Medical College
In another incident on the same day, intern doctors at Calcutta Medical College, located adjacent to Calcutta University and barely a 100-metre from the site of the book-stall clash, alleged that ABVP-backed miscreants entered the college campus and assaulted them.
The incident came amid a protest by students and junior doctors against show-cause notices issued to eight interns who had spoken out against alleged mismanagement at government hospitals following the stampede at a Durga Puja pandal which claimed 19 lives.
According to a Facebook post by the West Bengal Junior Doctors’ Front, the college principal and other senior officials had initially agreed to withdraw the notices after acknowledging a shortage of medicines. However, following a phone call from a “higher authority”, the principal reportedly refused to issue a written order confirming their withdrawal. This prompted students to stage a sit-in protest.
The post alleged that around 70–80 outsiders subsequently entered the campus, vandalised property and assaulted interns and medical students, leaving several injured. It further alleged that the principal left the campus under heavy police protection while the attackers continued their rampage in the presence of police personnel.

Kalshi made the “difficult decision” to pause operations in Utah after losing a court fight to block the state’s ongoing enforcement actions under Utah gambling laws, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick said Monday.
It seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved.
Kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either.
“This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi,” McGavick said. “We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated.”
Utah drops criminal charges
Utah’s attorney general, Derek Brown, had filed both civil and criminal charges against Kalshi, as he defended the state’s 130-year ban on gambling.
In a press release discussing the initial lawsuit, he accused Kalshi of running “an online casino” that violates the state’s constitution. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution,” Brown said. “For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Late Monday, a major Utah-area news outlet, KSL.com, reported that Brown was prepared to jail Kalshi’s co-founders, who had been summoned to be booked on 14 charges on December 5. He defended those plans, saying, “There is a question I have seen from people asking, ‘Well, do we modify this booking process if someone is a very wealthy and well-known tech billionaire?’ and the answer is ‘No, the process is the process; we don’t modify it based on who you are.’”

Cyclone Akvan: 7 Andhra fishermen go missing in Bay of Bengal; Indian Navy launch search
Initial information suggests that the missing boat was last reported to be at sea, approximately 200km from Paradip in Odisha
Indian Navy, Coast Guard and other maritime agencies are undertaking extensive search operations to trace seven fishermen from Andhra Pradesh’s Kakinada who ventured into the Bay of Bengal on November 4 and went missing, officials said on Tuesday.
According to additional director of fisheries Dr P Shankar Rao, the missing fishermen were identified as D Simhadri (boat owner), Kodanda Rao, Gampala Prakash, Tirri Narayana, Korada Chinna, Merugu Narayana and Kandala Ramu.
He said two fishing boats from Subbampeta village in Uppada mandal had ventured into the sea on November 4. “They reached Visakhapatnam by November 11 and informed their family members that they were going deeper into the sea for fishing,” Shankar Rao told HT.
While one of the boats returned safely, the other went missing along with its seven-member crew.
On November 14, Simhadri called his wife and informed her that they had been caught in turbulent waters due to cyclonic conditions. “That was the last call from the fishermen,” he said.
Also Read:West Bengal announces ₹212cr relief for 5.73 lakh farmers hit by cyclone-triggered rain
Cyclone Akvan originated as a low-pressure area on November 12, intensified into a cyclonic storm on November 16 and made landfall near Ganjam in Odisha on November 20.
“Till then, the family members of the missing fishermen were hoping that their boat, too, would return. When it did not, they informed us, and we immediately alerted the Indian Navy and Coast Guard authorities to take up search and rescue operations,” Shankar Rao said.
Initial information suggests that the missing boat was last reported to be at sea, approximately 200km from Paradip in Odisha.
In a separate statement, state agriculture minister Kinjarapu Atchannaidu said the state government had initiated special measures to locate the missing fishermen and was coordinating with maritime agencies to establish the whereabouts of their boat.
“Search operations have been intensified in coordination with the Coast Guard units at Kakinada and Paradip, besides the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) in Chennai. The state government is maintaining constant contact with officials of the Indian Navy and Coast Guard to monitor the search efforts and explore all possible avenues to trace the fishermen,” Atchannaidu said.
He said there was a possibility that the missing boat might have been swept towards the maritime waters of another country due to the impact of the cyclone.
“In view of this possibility, the authorities have also alerted Bangladesh and Myanmar and shared information about the missing fishing boat with the two countries to facilitate its identification and rescue, if it has drifted into their respective maritime zones,” he said.
The minister said the families of the missing fishermen had informed the authorities that the boat was carrying around 1,500 litres of diesel and sufficient food supplies to last nearly 30 days. “These provisions have raised hopes that the fishermen may have been able to sustain themselves despite being stranded at sea,” he said.
He assured the families of the missing fishermen that the government was taking the matter seriously and making every possible effort, in coordination with central maritime agencies and neighbouring countries, to trace the boat and bring the fishermen back safely.
In August this year, too, seven fishermen from Dr B R Ambedkar Konaseema district went missing for three weeks in the Bay of Bengal before being rescued near the West Bengal coast and brought ashore.
The fishermen, who had set out from the Odalarevu Fish Landing Centre on August 3, became stranded at sea after a series of mechanical failures crippled their boat. After travelling about 50 nautical miles, the engine failed completely. With no fishing boat in sight and no immediate possibility of outside assistance, the seven men were left stranded in the open sea.
The fishermen drifted helplessly for days as strong winds pushed the vessel hundreds of kilometres towards the West Bengal coast. Finally, on August 26, a fishing boat from Kolkata spotted the stranded vessel and came to their rescue.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed an amendment to the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, to include ‘antimicrobials’ in the definition of ‘New Drug’ under Rule 2(1)(w)(v).
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global public health concern and the proposed amendment has been initiated in view of concerns regarding the grant of manufacturing licences for antimicrobial products without adequate regulatory scrutiny, including the requirement for studies such as bioavailability and bioequivalence and stability studies.
The proposed amendment seeks to bring antimicrobials within the regulatory framework applicable to new drugs under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019. Accordingly, manufacturers would be required to obtain permission from the Central Licensing Authority before applying for a manufacturing licence from the concerned State Licensing Authority. This is expected to strengthen central regulatory oversight and help ensure the quality, safety and efficacy of antimicrobial products.
Meanwhile, the Ministry has also proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, to introduce a separate application form (Form 19-BC) and licence form (Form 20-BC) for the sale of bulk drugs (active or inactive bulk substances), distinct from the existing licensing provisions for formulations.
At present, a common licence covers the wholesale sale of both formulations and bulk drugs. The proposed amendment seeks to establish a dedicated licensing framework for bulk drugs, enabling more focused regulatory oversight of their wholesale sale and greater accountability in the pharmaceutical supply chain.
The proposal was agreed upon by the Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) in its 67th meeting held on November 17, 2025, and by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) in its 93rd meeting held on February 16, 2026.
Under the proposed framework, the licence will capture the categories of bulk drugs handled by wholesalers, including drugs covered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985. The sale of bulk drugs will be carried out under the personal supervision of a competent person, thereby strengthening accountability in their distribution and handling.
“Upon implementation, the proposed amendment will: give better control over the sale of bulk drugs by way of wholesale, strengthen enforcement control in relation to antimicrobial resistance and the movement of NDPS drugs and require wholesalers of bulk drugs to obtain a separate license for sale.” Stakeholders and members of the public are invited to submit their objections and suggestions.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Meta restricted 5.44 million items from view in India on local-law grounds between January and June 2026, a significant increase from 41,357 in July to December 2025 and 28,030 in January to June 2025, according to its Content Restrictions Based on Local Law report. These restrictions were based on legal requests and proactive enforcement of local laws, and do not include content removed under Meta’s Community Standards, which is reported separately.
Identical copies
The India figure was approximately 131.5 times higher than the previous half’s count. Meta states it began large-scale content restrictions using automated detection of “100% identical copies” under the amended IT Rules in select countries. This increase results from changes in restriction methods and underlying demands. It does not represent the number of legal requests.
Facebook and Instagram
Meta’s India product data shows:
- Facebook: 2.82M restrictions, up from 27,353 in July- December 2025; 2.80M were posts.
- Instagram: 2.62M restrictions, up from 14,004 in July-December 2025; 2.60M were media items.
Facebook and Instagram counts combine Meta’s product categories, as Meta does not publish platform totals. Meta also reports restricting “over 20,000” items on Threads, which is not included in its country or product totals.
India and the world
Meta’s eight Facebook and Instagram product categories recorded a global count of 27.11M in January–June 2026, a 2.7% decrease from 27.86M in July–December 2025. India represented 20.1% of the total. Indonesia reported 20.59M, a 24.4% decline from 27.25M in the previous period.
India had the second-highest number of content restrictions worldwide, following Indonesia. South Korea ranked third with about 410,000 restrictions. India and Indonesia together represented approximately 96% of Meta’s global content restrictions.
What Meta does not say
Meta’s India account does not specify a legal basis for most of the January-June 2026 restrictions, other than citing proactive measures under local law. For July-December 2025, it reported restricting ‘over 9,000’ items at the direction of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, and over 22,000 items following court orders relayed by local law enforcement. These figures represent minimum counts, not precise totals.
India is among seven regions where Meta does not disclose to users which authority requested a restriction.
