I have watched garbage trucks pass through the saffron fields of Patalbagh and Galandar, near National Highway 44, for almost three years.
October and November are the worst months.
This is when the saffron flowers bloom, but the garbage trucks keep coming. I have written about it, filmed it and shared videos online. Still, nothing has changed.
The dump sits in a small valley between two raised saffron fields. It is Kahcharai land, which means village grazing ground for sheep and cattle.
About five years ago, the Pulwama district administration gave around 67 kanals, or 8.3 acres, to Municipal Committee Pampore to build a waste management plant. That plant was supposed to sort and treat the waste.
What the land got instead was four years of untreated, mixed garbage, tipped straight onto the ground.
Nobody asked the village.
The deputy commissioner made the allotment without speaking to the Halqa Majlis or the Ward Committee, and state land belongs to those bodies, not to the Revenue Department.
Neither body has worked for three years, and the elected government doesn’t seem keen on holding panchayat and urban local body elections.
So the people with the best claim to that grazing ground weren’t there when it was handed away.
Officials like to tell commoners that ignorance of the law is no excuse. Fine, then the same goes for the municipality and the deputy commissioner.
Dumping mixed waste breaks the Solid Waste Management Rules of 2016 and their 2026 update. It breaks the Saffron Act of 2007 too, and this land was never meant for a dump at all.
Who should have caught it?
The Agriculture Department calls itself the guardian of saffron farming in Kashmir. On July 10, 2026, its extension officer in Pampore wrote to the Sub Divisional Agriculture Officer in Tral, asking him to take it up. He could have acted himself.
Meanwhile, rats and rodents have eaten saffron corms on about 2,000 kanals. Growers watched their crop go while a letter moved one desk higher.
The Pollution Control Committee was no faster. Its divisional officer in Pulwama did nothing for four years. I told the Regional Director at least a dozen times. A notice went to the municipality only after I complained to the chairman, Vasu Yadav, and the site stayed open even then.
The Supreme Court has given these committees the power to impose environmental compensation on their own. Four years have gone by and they haven’t charged Pampore’s municipality a single rupee.
I ended up doing a job that officials are paid for.
So I went to the National Green Tribunal, with around 40 saffron growers as co-petitioners. Our case was listed first on 17 November 2026. My lawyer, Saurabh Sharma, showed the bench geotagged photographs and the pollution committee’s own report. He had a three-minute video ready, but the judges had seen enough. Chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava and Expert Member Dr Afroz Alam set up a Joint Committee at that first hearing.
The committee has people from SKUAST-K, the Regional Director of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and a nominee of the pollution committee.
Within eight weeks they must visit Patalbagh, assess the damage to the 2,000 kanals and the land around them, and check whether the dump has the clearances the law demands.
The Deputy Commissioner of Pulwama, the officer who allotted the land, will coordinate the visit.
I am glad the tribunal moved quickly, but the speed bothers me.
Photographs, one report and two judges were enough for a single hearing. Comparatively, four years of local offices gave us a letter passed between desks.
If the evidence was always this clear, the failure sat in the offices closest to the fields.
I could reach a tribunal. Most people who farm that soil can’t, and nobody has told me where they are supposed to go.
SKUAST-K now has a seat on the committee, and it can use that seat well. Its draft Mountain Development Policy says little about protecting saffron land or the karewas where much of the saffron grows.
Illegal digging of soil and sand has stripped those karewas for years, and now garbage stations are going up on them too.
I took a similar case to the tribunal over a dump Municipal Committee Pulwama set up on karewa land in Newa. I have written about a Karewa Protection Authority, and Bijbehera MLA Dr Bashir Veeri has tabled a private member’s bill on the same idea.
The university could suggest how to restore and landscape these fields. I plan to put that to its Vice Chancellor soon.
At the end of the day, a tribunal can order an inspection, but it can’t make a municipality ask a village before it fills the village’s grazing ground with garbage.
Only an elected body can do that, and the grazing ground is still waiting for one.

Easy daily use. Lots of LEDs and medical-grade lasers. Simple to wear. FDA-cleared tech. Results started to appear within a month.
TIRED
Must be used consistently. Portable battery is an extra $99.
The Aging Process is hard. It’s jarring, for example, when the luscious, flowing locks of your youth start to disappear before your very eyes. But there's nothing to do about this natural hair loss—or is there? While still the subject of ongoing research, red-light therapy has been used to treat inflammation, pain relief, and wrinkles, and—as it turns out—it may also help with hair regrowth. It’s also a much more accessible option than flying to Istanbul for a full-on hair transplant.
I learned about iRestore’s Elite Laser Growth Hair System after it came across my TikTok FYP. My algorithm likely served it to me because of my own hair woes (scalp irritation and eczema). Upon learning more about the system, I hoped it could help me with cell regeneration and kill off the bacteria causing flares on my scalp.
However, an even better test subject stood before me: my sweet husband, who is dealing with a rapidly receding hairline. So I roped him into testing this laser helmet—for science, of course. And to better understand said science, I spoke with Zakia Rahman, MD, FAAD, a clinical professor of dermatology at Stanford University School of Medicine.
The Scientific Crown
Photograph: Julia Forbes
Red-light therapy didn’t start as a treatment for antiaging and recovery. It actually came about as an accidental solution for hair loss in the 1960s, when Hungarian scientist Endre Mester was researching whether exposure to red light could treat cancer in hairless mice. Imagine his surprise when the mice started growing hair.
Red-light therapy has come a long way since then. According to Rahman, red-light wavelengths are thought to activate the mitochondria in skin cells, which may encourage an uptick in the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to promote new growth. Red-light therapy may also improve blood flow to hair follicles.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
Importantly, iRestore's devices are FDA-cleared—a safety designation from the US Food and Drug Administration indicating that a product is “substantially equivalent” to another legally marketed device. There are three hair-growth devices in iRestore's lineup: the entry-level Essential ($425), the mid-tier Professional ($799), and the Elite ($1,699). Each contains iRestore’s proprietary Lumitech technology, which combines LED lights and medical-grade lasers. These laser diodes, called Vixo lasers, operate in the range of 655 to 680 nanometers (nm). (Preliminary studies with mice have shown that using red light in the 600- to 660-nm range, and infrared wavelengths in the 800- to 850-nm range, can promote cell regeneration, pain relief, and more.)
The idea is that this dynamic duo of lights and lasers can penetrate deeper into the skin than ordinary red light with lasers, while the LEDs ensure light is distributed across the scalp for maximum efficacy. Together, they reach a maximum of 2,500 milliwatts (mW) in the Elite, compared to the Professional's 1,410 mW and Essential's 600 mW.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
The Elite is iRestore’s top-of-the-line offering and has the most LEDs of the three laser hair-growth systems, with 500 diodes in total—that's 300 lasers and 200 LEDs. The Essential has 51 lasers and 69 LEDs for a total of 120 diodes, while the iRestore Professional has 82 lasers and 200 LEDs for a total of 282 diodes. The Elite was also designed to cover more of the scalp than the other two models and requires 12 minutes of daily use, while the Professional and Essential require 25 minutes every other day.
If price is not a factor, the Elite is the no-brainer choice due to its higher-concentrated light therapy, shorter use time, and potentially faster results.
Growth Spurt
Photograph: Julia Forbes
The helmet arrived in hefty red packaging containing the helmet, a portable battery pack (annoyingly, this is a $99 add-on purchase), a charging cord, and a red-and-black zippered travel case. It feels very fragile, and I wouldn't throw it around—then again, you probably wouldn't plan to shove such an expensive device in the back of your bathroom vanity.
During the daily 12-minute sessions with the Elite helmet, you'll feel as if you're sitting under bright, hot sunlight. The remote displays a countdown of how many minutes you have left, and it beeps once the cycle is complete. Because I was testing the helmet to treat my dry scalp and eczema, I grew increasingly concerned with every passing minute of feeling warmer and warmer. (Sweating is a big no-no for eczema, so I wasn’t thrilled to experience this side effect.) With time, my husband was able to get used to the heat-lamp effect, as it’s not painful, just initially uncomfortable.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
Within the first two weeks of continuously using the helmet, I was thrilled to see baby hairs begin to pop up around my husband's hairline. The growth continued through two months of regular use. The top of his crown had more volume and overall hair density, while new growth appeared in the more drastically affected areas near his forehead. While the additional hair didn’t completely cover his scalp, the change was stark enough for old college friends and family members to remark on how good his hair looked.
The effects aren't permanent, though. Unfortunately, my husband stopped his iRestore routine after a few months due to travel. While the iRestore Elite comes with a case that makes it super portable, my husband was nervous about misplacing it while we were on the go. (Also, the thing takes up a decent amount of space.) Unfortunately, stopping the treatments reversed the progress in a matter of weeks. Just like that, he was back to square one.
Rahman likens this phenomenon to the importance of a commitment to a healthy daily diet and regular exercise; one instance of either won't make a difference in your health. Rather, consistency is required to drive results. When I told her that my husband's hair growth had fallen off, she strongly encouraged us to pick it back up.
A Hairy Situation
In addition to using the red-light therapy helmet as recommended, iRestore suggests adding thickening haircare products (shampoo, conditioner, supplements, and serum) to your regimen to get the best results. The star ingredient in the serum and shampoo is plant-based Redensyl, which is meant to fortify hair follicles during their regrowth. Additional elements—like the shampoo's castor oil and biotin, and the conditioner's vegan keratin and argan oil—act as natural strengtheners.
The supplements contain natural dihydrotestosterone (DHT) blockers derived from saw palmetto. These blockers work to prevent the enzyme (5-alpha reductase) from transforming testosterone into DHT. In essence, this hormone is a driver of pattern hair loss and can lead to general inactivity in hair growth.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
The supplements, strengthening serum, shampoo, and conditioner come included with the purchase of the iRestore Elite. The extras didn't seem to boost my results but may have supported my husband's regular use of the helmet. (Full disclosure: He was also using his usual Rogaine throughout this entire process.)
Ultimately, these included products are a nice bonus, but you don't need to go out of your way to buy them from iRestore or to replenish your stash. Plenty of anti-hair-loss treatments are available, including oral and topical medications and hair-transplant procedures. All have their merits in slowing hair thinning and promoting fuller hair. Even so, “combination therapy will work better than a stand-alone," says Rahman, in response to my question about whether red-light therapy could work as an isolated treatment or if it's best to include it as part of a multicomponent regimen. Essentially, the potential benefits of red-light therapy only stand to increase when you supplement it with minoxidil and other highly researched hair-loss measures.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
As for my eczema, the iRestore Elite did quell my scalp flare-ups, but I don't think I'd throw down so much money for just that. For hair regrowth, that's a totally different story. My husband was already using Rogaine before the iRestore Elite showed up. But combined with the helmet and iRestore's hair-growth products and supplements, he experienced greater results. For those pursuing thicker hair at home, the iRestore Elite is surprisingly effective.

Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.
The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.
Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”
Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.
“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.
The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.
Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.
“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”
Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.
The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”
Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.
The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.
A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

Owono did not deserve 12-match ban - Pique
- Published
FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique says goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not deserve the 12-match suspension he received following his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel late on in the second-tier match between Andorra and Tenerife on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30, and a disciplinary committee from the Spanish football federation confirmed Owono's ban last week.
In a video posted on social media, Pique said players past and present, plus coaches and other goalkeepers, felt the incident was "an accident".
The former Spain and Barcelona defender added: "I truly believe that imposing the maximum sanction on Jesus for this action puts him in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened."
- Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision 
  - Published3 November
- Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban 
  - Published3 days ago
The 12-match suspension was the maximum punishment Owono, 25, could have received, as the disciplinary committee could only consider the offence on the pitch and not "the tragic outcome of the incident".
Following the decision, Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera said he accepted the regulations do not specifically account for what happened, but acknowledged the ban "might feel light".
Pique also highlighted a recent on-field incident in Spain, when Albacete winger Jose Corpas accidentally kicked Sabadell midfielder Quadri Liameed in the head during a Spanish second division match.
Nigerian Liameed was knocked unconscious but was later discharged from hospital following medical checks, while Spaniard Corpas was shown a straight red card and handed a three-match ban.
"Fortunately Quadri is fine, the consequences in this case were not fatal, and the committee decided to sanction Corpas with three matches," Pique said.
"With all this, my reflection is: what is being sanctioned, the action or the consequences?"
Owono has withdrawn from Equatorial Guinea's squad for Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Zimbabwe this month, and Pique said it was unlikely he would return to action as soon as his suspension is served.
He added: "Jesus is going to need far more than 12 matches before he is available and able to compete.
"No sanction is going to bring [De Miguel] back to us."

Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the companies said Tuesday, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs.
The purchase, which includes another drug in Phase 3 trials, reflects the pressure Sanofi has been under as it faces looming revenue losses from its massive blockbuster Dupixent, an inflammation-targeting drug approved in nine indications. The company, where Belén Garijo took over as CEO earlier this year, had been vocal that it was looking for takeover targets with late-stage or even commercial assets that fit with its existing focus in immunology and rare diseases.
Sanofi is paying $175 per share for New Jersey-based Insmed, through a combination of debt financing and cash. Insmed’s share price was roughly $120 before Bloomberg reported last week that the deal was in the works, which sent the stock up.

The news of Jensen Huang’s resurrection at Nvidia felt like a practical joke or an Onion headline. Here was a cofounder and CEO of a trillion-dollar company who did just about all the bad things a CEO could do — including maybe involvement in espionage — who’d gotten his comeuppance. The board did its job. The investigations commenced, and Huang resigned in a rare moment of accountability in Silicon Valley culture.
Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia takes founder worship to a dangerous level
What the heck is Nvidia thinking?
But that’s not how the story ended. Huang quickly returned to the helm of Nvidia thanks to his personal friend, the president of the United States, Donald Trump, who had pressured the board to reinstate the disgraced founder. (“I made the deal,” Trump told a television audience.) When the newly vindicated CEO walked back into Nvidia headquarters on Monday, ecstatic employees cheered his name — “Jensen! Jensen!”
Considering the larger context, this is absurd. Huang is still under investigation at Nvidia, the company that he’s once again running, over his relationship with a tech executive, Alice Huang, who’d been talking to China’s top spy agency during the affair. And she’s under investigation over her alleged role in smuggling illegal Nvidia chips into China.
“It’s the worst degradation in corporate governance in American history and the greatest business-government scandal in US history,” Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at Yale School of Management, told me a couple of hours after the news broke. “I mean, this is crazy.”
Key takeaways
- Silicon Valley’s founder worship started with a bad founder. In the 1950s, eight employees could no longer work for their mercurial visionary founder, so they became visionary founders themselves.
- Huang’s comeback shows how tech company boards still can’t control their founders. President Trump pushed Nvidia’s board to reinstate him while the company was still investigating him.
- Nvidia supplies the chips behind the AI boom and finances the companies buying them. When so much rides on one company, failing to hold its founder accountable can put the entire economy at risk.
This is not just a matter of poor corporate governance; it is a profound collision of two visions for the future: First, there’s the founder-worshipping tradition of Silicon Valley, where visionaries not only can but should get away with anything in the name of profit and progress. Then there are the people and institutions, like the media and the government, who hold power to account and make sure this big beautiful American experiment doesn’t unravel completely.
It’s not unusual for these two groups to clash. But the stakes today are higher than they’ve been in a long time. Nvidia is not only the primary supplier of chips and software to the AI boom, it’s also the industry’s chief financier, funding startups that will buy those chips and infrastructure that makes everything work. If Nvidia faltered, the whole house of cards could come down, bringing the American economy down with it. Many of the founder-worshipping class considered Huang irreplaceable, which would mean the future of the nation depended on his employment status.
Jensen Huang’s restoration to his seat of power shows that Silicon Valley’s vision for the future may be winning out: The wealthiest individuals in our society operate with no baseline accountability. And even when they make colossal mistakes, their friend, the president, can restore their power.
It wasn’t supposed to be like this, but in a sense, we’ve been heading this direction for a long time.
Founder worship is as old as electricity
The cult of the founder lives on X these days. That’s where you could find tech leaders and venture capital types calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia and then cheering the news when it happened. Their specific arguments or grievances about Huang being pushed out seem both ridiculous and familiar (investor and podcaster Jason Calacanis seems to think that journalism is the villain here). But beneath the rhetoric is a philosophy about the importance of an all-knowing and all-powerful tech founder that’s as old as computers and electricity itself.
The tradition of worshipping the infallible founder dates back to Thomas Edison, and it’s always been central to the American tech industry, which values visionary thinking and nimble leadership above all else. You can trace the roots of this culture back to the 1950s, when a startup called Fairchild Semiconductor laid the foundation of Silicon Valley as we know it today. Fairchild made some of the first microchips, which would have made it legendary in its own right. But there was a cultural component to how the company was founded, how it was run, and what its alums went on to do that has shaped tech culture ever since.
Fairchild was actually a spinoff of another chip company, Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory, founded by the co-inventor of the transistor, William Shockley. You could argue that Shockley was the original visionary founder-CEO in Silicon Valley, down to his problematic management style, which drove employees to start their own firm in 1957. Known as the “Traitorous Eight,” a group of them — including Robert Noyce, founder of Intel, and Gordon Moore, the Moore in Moore’s Law — left Shockley to start the new company. Fairchild Semiconductor got its funding and name from Fairchild Camera and Instrument, an East Coast company that thrived on military contracts for its spy satellite equipment. They eschewed the idea of letting a founder-visionary dictate its business in favor of a flat organizational structure.
The pursuit of wealth is actually where you’ll find some of Nvidia’s ancestral roots. After leaving Fairchild Semiconductor, Eugene Kleiner and Don Valentine became the pioneers of modern venture capital, starting Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia Capital, respectively in 1972. Valentine went on to fund early Silicon Valley success stories — Atari, Apple, Cisco, and Oracle, to name a few — and revered the so-called brilliant entrepreneur. According to the venture capitalist Fred Wilson, Valentine once said, “Sometimes we make money with brilliant people who are easy to get along with, most often we make money with brilliant people who are hard to get along with, but we rarely make money with normal people who are easy to get along with.”
It was during Valentine’s era that we saw the cult of the founder start to form around people like Steve Jobs or Larry Ellison. Then, Sequoia Partners became the first major investor in a little chip company called Nvidia. He was actually in the room when Jensen Huang gave the original pitch in 1993. Huang apparently bombed the pitch, but Valentine invested in the venture based on the Nvidia cofounder’s reputation. The way Huang tells it, when Valentine shook his hand, he looked him square in the eye and said, “If you lose my money, I will kill you.”
At market close Monday, the day Huang was reinstated, Nvidia was worth nearly $4 trillion.
“The misfits, the rebels, the troublemakers.”
The founders still worshipped in Silicon Valley have always been hailed as outsiders and disruptors. Look no further than the commercial Steve Jobs narrated not long after his triumphant return to Apple about “the misfits, the rebels, the troublemakers.” It ends: “The ones who are crazy enough to think that they can change the world, are the ones who do.”
There’s something very American about this idea of taking risks and changing the world — it’s also a great way to get rich. Noyce and Moore went on to become some of the wealthiest businessmen in the country. Huang’s net worth surged by $36 billion the day he returned as Nvidia’s CEO.
Tech founders’ success has also always come with baggage. Icons like Jobs and Ellison changed the world — but also had reputations as bad bosses. Jobs was known for publicly humiliating his employees, for being spiteful and controlling. He took credit for his employees’ work, and his biographer, Walter Isaacson, has called him “the world’s worst manager.” Apparently, everyone who worked for Ellison hated him. Both men started out as outsiders, but then they became billionaires running some of the biggest companies in the world. Their abusive management styles then became something of a hallmark, proof of their durable genius.
Corporate boards exist to rein in this kind of behavior. But in reality, they often do no such thing when it comes to dealing with visionary founders. The board of OpenAI fired Sam Altman as CEO three years ago over an alleged lack of transparency — or simply lying to them, if you want a shorthand. But following a loud campaign by his supporters in Silicon Valley, not unlike the campaign to reinstate Huang, Altman was back to work less than a week later, and the company replaced its entire board.
Then there’s Elon Musk, who had to resign as Tesla’s chair to settle fraud charges in 2018, although he kept his role as CEO. Although he’s faced calls to step down as chair, Mark Zuckerberg has been CEO of Meta since he started the company in his Harvard dorm room, despite losing $77 billion on his failed metaverse bet. WeWork’s Adam Neumann, Theranos’s Elizabeth Holmes, and Uber’s Travis Kalanick were all founder-CEOs who lost their jobs due to bad behavior — intense risk taking, defrauding investors, and just lots of scandals, respectively. Those three stand apart because their boards did not invite them to come back.
Huang, for what it’s worth, had been a pretty boring founder-CEO up until recently. Well before the free money era, Nvidia got its start making graphics processing units (GPUs) which were primarily used in video game systems. Huang eventually steered the company in more ambitious directions, leveraging the company’s technology to become central to the burgeoning AI industry.
It wasn’t until the release of ChatGPT in 2022 kicked off the AI boom that Huang became a household name. In the years that followed, as demand for Nvidia chips skyrocketed and zeroes started multiplying on the ends of its revenue numbers, we got to know him as a showman, a storyteller, and a lover of black leather jackets. He had become a tech titan and, according to one magazine cover, “The Sorcerer of Silicon.”
Over the years, Huang had also developed a reputation as an abusive manager who humiliated employees in front of their peers. He reportedly told one that he’d rip off their arms and beat them over the head with them. He hired his family members as subordinate executives. Huang became the epitome of the visionary founder, personality flaws and all.
What really sets Huang apart from his visionary founder predecessors is the scale of what Nvidia’s become — and what he’s come to represent. Huang has made himself indispensable at Nvidia in a number of ways, guarding his role as the company’s primary dealmaker, and ensuring through his 60 direct reports that succession would be complicated. And because Nvidia plays such a central role in the AI boom, as the main supplier of advanced chips needed to train and run the most powerful models, Huang made himself the main character of the entire AI industry, much like Trump made himself the singular figure in Republican politics.
Margaret O’Mara, an American history professor at the University of Washington, called Huang’s reinstatement “remarkable even by Silicon Valley’s founder-centric standards.” There have been plenty of examples of tech founders who lost their companies but held onto the support of their cult-like following. Some people even think Elizabeth Holmes still deserves another chance. But the scale of what Huang is responsible for and the scale of what he’s accused of doing have reached new heights.
“America has never experienced such extreme concentration of wealth and market value in such a small number of leaders and companies, and I don’t think this move will do much to slow Americans’ growing unease with the AI boom and its biggest boosters,” O’Mara said.
The US economy finds itself at a choke point that’s not dissimilar to where Nvidia found itself when Huang resigned, surrounded by scandals. The company had been organized around a single visionary who had led them to unprecedented success but, upon his fall, could represent an existential threat.
It actually seemed like it could be good news for Nvidia to rethink its leadership structure in the wake of Huang’s scandals; perhaps even the AI industry would find more stability when it didn’t depend so much on one company’s brilliant entrepreneur to call the shots. Plus, companies do better when they take their leaders’ misbehavior seriously.
The most dangerous part about this moment is not only that we’re back where we started. It’s also that we can see where we could have corrected our course — the exact moment where we could have held a visionary founder accountable for his reckless behavior — but didn’t.

Private sector project announcements surged 58.5% year-on-year to ₹26.6 trillion in the first half of FY27 (H1 FY27), signalling a sharp expansion in India's investment pipeline, with manufacturing, electricity and technology-related infrastructure emerging as key drivers, according to industry body Confederation of Indian Industry (CII). According to the second edition of CII's Private Investment Barometer, project announcements in H1 FY27 were 4.4 times the average recorded in the same period between FY17 and FY25. The private sector's share of total project announcements also rose to 86.2% during April-September 2026 from 74.2% a year earlier. The increase comes amid sustained policy reforms, infrastructure development and improvements in the regulatory framework, which have strengthened the foundation for private investment, the industry body said on Tuesday. It urged companies to step up capital expenditure, innovation and project execution to support the government's Viksit Bharat agenda. The improvement is also reflected in actual capital formation. Gross capital formation by around 1,800 listed private companies touched ₹12.4 trillion in FY26, equivalent to 3.6% of nominal gross domestic product (GDP), compared with an average of 2.2% during FY17-FY21. On a comparable-company basis, investment increased 8.7% in FY26. Further, 54% of companies increased their fixed investment rates, while approximately three out of four added net productive capacity. Private-sector project completions during April-September 2026 stood at ₹1.8 trillion, the highest for the corresponding period since FY17. "The government deserves considerable credit for creating a strong enabling environment for private investment through sustained policy reforms, infrastructure development and improvements in the regulatory framework," CII president R. Mukundan said, adding that Indian industry had been responding to these opportunities. The investment pipeline also reflects a shift towards manufacturing, infrastructure and emerging technology-related sectors. Manufacturing project announcements stood at ₹8.1 trillion in H1 FY27, 3.2 times their historical average, while electricity-sector announcements reached ₹7.7 trillion, 5.1 times their historical average. Information technology project announcements, largely comprising data centres and artificial intelligence-related infrastructure, reached approximately ₹9.5 trillion during the period, against ₹70,000 crore in the corresponding period last year. Mukundan said private enterprises were investing in manufacturing, infrastructure, energy and digital technologies, supported by stronger balance sheets and greater confidence in India's economic prospects. CII also highlighted the government's efforts to modernize financial markets and strengthen the regulatory framework. It said the consultative approach adopted by regulators, including the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi), had contributed to deeper and more resilient capital markets. The industry body said investor protection, market integrity, regulatory predictability and proportionate compliance requirements would remain important to mobilising long-term domestic and international capital. Looking ahead, CII said achieving the Viksit Bharat vision would require closer collaboration between industry and the government, with a focus on accelerating investment and project execution, creating quality employment, improving productivity and strengthening domestic manufacturing and supply chains. It identified research and innovation, skill development, export expansion and deeper integration into global value chains as key priorities. The transition to clean energy, adoption of emerging technologies, development of globally competitive Indian enterprises and greater participation of micro, small and medium enterprises would also be important to sustaining growth. While acknowledging progress in improving the ease of doing business, Mukundan said the next phase of reforms should focus on the speed of doing business, particularly faster decisions, approvals and project execution. "The government has demonstrated its commitment through sustained reforms and substantial investments in building India's economic foundations. It is now incumbent upon industry to match this commitment with greater investment, innovation, risk-taking and long-term capacity building," he said. CII said better access to long-term finance and faster project implementation would be critical to translating investment intentions into productive capacity and employment. It added that it and its members were committed to working with the government to improve investment, employment, competitiveness, sustainability and inclusive growth. India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is making his first defense of the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek star Javokhir Sindarov over the next three weeks in the affluent Geneva suburb of Cologny. Both players are 20 years old, making it the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title. But is that all you need to know? What about the format, how much they’re getting paid and why the world’s No 1-ranked player is watching from the sidelines? Read on for all the answers … When and where is the World Chess Championship? The best-of-14-games contest is set to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, the picturesque enclave overlooking Lake Geneva. The opening ceremony is scheduled for 22 November, with games played once daily from 24 November except for designated rest days on 27 November and 1, 5 and 9 December. It’s the first time a world title match has been held in Switzerland since 2004, when Vladimir Kramnik retained his title by drawing 7-7 with Peter Leko in Brissago, two years before the sport’s rival championships were reunified. Who is Gukesh Dommaraju? Gukesh Dommaraju, commonly known as Gukesh D, was only 18 when he became the 18th and youngest ever undisputed world chess champion by defeating China’s Ding Liren in 2024. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai native rose to international prominence when he became the second-youngest grandmaster in history at the time, aged 12 years and seven months. Five years later he stunned the chess establishment by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament at 17 to secure a world title shot. He went on to win and shatter the age record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in their 1985 rematch in Moscow. His victory made him a national hero in India, where he was mobbed by supporters on his return and feted by prime minister Narendra Modi. But the 20-year-old has struggled badly for form since then, plummeting to No 26 in the world from a career-high ranking of No 3 after an extended string of underwhelming performances. Gukesh Dommaraju receives a hero’s welcome at Chennai airport after becoming the youngest undisputed world chess champion in December 2024. “Clearly so far I’ve not been able to handle it in the best possible way,” Gukesh admitted in a recent interview. “There have been major setbacks ... Obviously there is something with a lot of expectations, a lot of pressure that I’m dealing with and I’ve not found the right way to maybe handle it.” From Bobby Fischer to Magnus Carlsen: 22 of the most famous world chess championship games Read more Who is Javokhir Sindarov? Javokhir Sindarov is an Uzbek prodigy, roughly six months older than Gukesh. Known for his cool-headed precision and ability to mine advantages from seemingly quiet positions, the Tashkent-born grandmaster earned his crack at the world championship with an imperious performance at this year’s Candidates in Cyprus, finishing unbeaten with six wins and eight draws to turn back a stacked field that included longtime stars Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Anish Giri. The first player from Uzbekistan to challenge for the title, Sindarov has climbed into the world’s top five after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup last November in Goa. He enters the biggest match of his life on a tailwind of confidence, having won a four-player rapid tournament in St Louis three weeks ago over Nakamura, Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, capped by a brilliancy against the world No 2 that showcased his tactical brio. His ascent has added fuel to a remarkable chess boom in Uzbekistan, where he belongs to a golden generation of grandmasters, along with Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Nodirbek Yakubboev, who have transformed the central Asian nation into a global powerhouse with two golds and a bronze at the past three Chess Olympiads. Javokhir Sindarov explains his brilliant victory over Hikaru Nakamura to grandmaster Maurice Ashley after their game in St Louis. “This tournament will be the hardest tournament in my life,” Sindarov said in August of his showdown with Gukesh. “I don’t know if I will get a second chance [at the world championship]. It’s hard to play 14 games against the same person in three weeks.” Tale of the tape Where do they rank internationally? Sindarov, ranked 25th in the world a year ago, has climbed to a career-best No 4 with a Fide classical rating of 2782, while Gukesh has slipped to No 26 with a rating of 2710. That makes Gukesh the lowest-ranked reigning world champion of the Elo era, which dates back to 1971, eclipsing the previous low of No 23 set by Ding in 2024. The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified in 2006. Who is the current world No 1 in chess? Magnus Carlsen holds the top position in Fide’s world rankings with a classical rating of 2823. The 35-year-old Norwegian has been at No 1 for more than 16 years uninterrupted, though that extraordinary reign is suddenly under threat after a disastrous 10-game winless streak last week in Budapest reduced his once-comfortable lead over his nearest rivals to single figures. He was considered the best player on the planet even before removing all doubt against India’s Viswanathan Anand in their 2013 world title clash. If you can name only one chess player active today, chances are it’s him. The youngest undisputed men’s classical world chess champions Carlsen bolstered his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021 when he crushed Russia’s Ian Nepomniachtchi in his fourth defense by a margin of four wins and no defeats, the most lopsided result in a world championship match since José Raúl Capablanca’s dismantling of Emanuel Lasker exactly 100 years prior. But he decided against defending it for a fifth time before the 2023 cycle, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long slog of preparation that world title matches demand. The abdication marked only the second time in history that a holder voluntarily declined to defend his title after Bobby Fischer controversially forfeited the crown ahead of his scheduled 1975 match with Karpov in Manila. Instead, Ding outlasted Nepomniachtchi in a thrilling, sometimes messy scrap for the vacant title, even if critics including Kasparov branded it an “amputated” event without the world’s best player involved. Ding’s reign lasted only 593 days before Gukesh unseated him in Singapore in 2024, taking the decisive 14th game on a catastrophic blunder to claim a 7½–6½ victory and become the first teenager to win the sport’s biggest prize. Carlsen remains active at the highest level, though he’s increasingly shifted his focus away from classical chess toward alternative formats. In February, he defeated Caruana 2½–1½ in Germany to win the Fide freestyle world championship, his eye-watering 21st world title across classical, rapid, blitz and freestyle disciplines. Also known as Fischer Random or Chess960, the variation randomizes the starting positions of the pieces on the back rank, placing a premium on creativity over rote opening preparation. (He’s also gotten married, become a father and is by all accounts pretty good at fantasy football, too.) How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up? Despite being contemporaries, they have played only three times in classical games. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. Allow and continue Gukesh’s form has largely gone off the rails since reaching the summit 23 months ago in Singapore. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad. Many of the world’s top players have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently. “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.” Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September. “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.” Who are their seconds? Neither Gukesh nor Sindarov has publicly disclosed his full team of seconds, the trusted cadre of advisers who help prepare openings and analyze the opponent. That’s not unusual: players tend to keep the identities of their seconds closely guarded before and during a match to avoid revealing clues about the direction of their preparations. But we do know a little bit. Gukesh will again work with Polish grandmaster Grzegorz Gajewski, who led a formidable backroom team during his 2024 title-winning campaign that included five other GMs and analysts from Poland, India and Germany, with additional support from Anand (acting as more of a mentor than a practical second). According to reporting from ChessBase, Sindarov is expected to be working with Ukrainian coach Roman Vidonyak, while the 22-year-old Abdusattorov, the former world rapid champion and current world No 5, revealed on a podcast that he will be in Geneva to help his compatriot prepare. Another Uzbek grandmaster, Mukhiddin Madaminov, has also been mentioned as a member of Sindarov’s team. Photograph: Europe Echecs What’s the prize money for winning the World Chess Championship? The overall prize fund is $2.5m (£1.9m), unchanged from 2024. Each player will receive $200,000 for each game won, including games won by forfeit. What’s left will be split equally between them. If the winner is decided on tiebreakers, the champion receives $1.3m with the runner-up taking home $1.2m. The same split applies if the match finishes 7½–6½ with 13 decisive games or 8–6 with 14 decisive games. Gukesh’s world ranking Each player received a $200,000 advance on their winnings one month before the first game, deducted from the prize fund. The remaining balance will be remitted to the players within 30 working days after the completion of the match. The stakes are particularly high in a sport where even the biggest stars rarely earn seven figures in annual prize money. According to a new ranking published by World Chess, no player has crossed the $1m mark in tournament winnings in 2026, with India’s Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu leading the way on $666,229. Sindarov ranks third with $589,061, while Gukesh sits 48th with just $41,500. The world championship alone will assure its winner at least $1.25m, enough to vault either player to the top of the annual earnings list. What is the schedule and how does the match work? Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played). The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours, testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter. If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023. The complete official regulations can be found here. World Chess Championship 2026 schedule How can I watch the World Chess Championship? The Guardian will provide live move-by-move commentary, expert analysis and reaction throughout the three-week match. Fans can also watch every game live on Fide’s official YouTube and Twitch channels. All games start at 3pm local time, 2pm GMT, 9am on the US east coast and 7.30pm in India. What else should I know? The World Chess Championship is typically held every two years, though this schedule has varied over time. A 1993 schism between the International Chess Federation (Fide) and the Professional Chess Association (PCA), a breakaway organization formed by Kasparov and British grandmaster Nigel Short, ushered in an era of competing world championship titles. The title was reunified in 2006 when Kramnik held off Bulgaria’s Veselin Topalov 6-6 (2½-1½) amid a bizarre cheating row over bathroom visits known as Toiletgate. Robert Sapolsky, a biologist and neuroscientist at Stanford University, says an elite chess player can burn up to 6,000 calories a day while playing in a tournament, three times what an average person consumes daily. Karpov infamously lost 22lbs (10kg) during his grueling world title encounter with Kasparov in 1984 before it was called off controversially after five months and 48 games due to concerns over player health. Chess has enjoyed a sustained pop-cultural resurgence since the pandemic, a boom that reached Broadway with last year’s reimagining of … Chess, the cult-classic Cold War musical featuring songs by Abba’s Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus. Starring Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit and Nicholas Christopher, the revival centered on a love triangle involving American and Soviet grandmasters loosely inspired by Fischer and Boris Spassky’s epochal 1972 encounter in Reykjavík (with secondary nods to Karpov and Viktor Korchnoi). Critics were less enthusiastic – the Guardian’s two-star review called it a “messy Broadway revival” that wasted its catchy songs – but the Grammy-nominated cast recording that came out in April goes dumby hard and Michele’s snub for a Tony nod was the worst blunder since Ding’s 55 Rf2?? in Singapore. That Sindarov is even playing for the world title is a historic achievement. His victory came two years after Gukesh became the youngest Candidates winner at 17, then the youngest undisputed world champion at 18. Together, they represent the youngest pairing ever to play for the world title by some distance. Sindarov will celebrate his 21st birthday on 8 December, the scheduled date of Game 12. Sindarov’s emergence is part of an extraordinary period of success for Uzbek chess. He helped the country win its first Chess Olympiad gold medal in Chennai in 2022, when Uzbekistan went unbeaten against a field of 186 teams. They followed it with a bronze in 2024 before another gold on home soil in Samarkand last year, cementing the nation’s place among the sport’s leading powers. And yes, that was him among the Uzbek fans supporting the White Wolves as they made their Fifa World Cup debut last summer in the US. The matchup also reflects the shifting geography at the top of the sport. Gukesh’s victory over Ding made him India’s second world champion after Anand and marked the first time in the competition’s 138-year history that two players from Asia had competed for the crown. Now it will happen for a second world title match in a row. The Fondation Martin Bodmer is a library and museum founded by a Swiss bibliophile who built his collection around what he considered the five pillars of world literature: the Bible, Homer, Dante, Shakespeare and Goethe. (Sounds about white.) Its 160,000 treasures include a Gutenberg Bible, Shakespeare’s First Folio and a copy of Isaac Newton’s Principia Mathematica once owned by his great rival Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Not the worst backdrop for another battle of intellects. The Guardian’s Leonard Barden has written his weekly chess column for these pages since September 1955 without missing a single week, earning a Guinness World Record for his trouble. A former British champion who once beat Fischer in blitz, the 97-year-old has chronicled the sport’s comings and goings across parts of eight decades, from Mikhail Botvinnik’s Soviet supremacy and Fischer’s Cold War apotheosis to Kasparov’s long-running dominance and the emergence of Gukesh and Sindarov. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Savannah Harrington. It has been edited for length and clarity.
Last week, I read on social media that the US Army planned to carry out controlled detonations of lead azide at a plant about 70 miles from my husband's family's home, where my husband, two babies, and I are living right now. It was scheduled for Friday, only days after I'd first heard about the detonation.
It was completely disorienting news that I didn't fully understand. No one was saying anything about what was happening or the risks of detonating the lead azide, so I started researching it for myself.
I asked what this blast would mean for my family, for the land, and for the water. I learned that lead could cause permanent damage to the brain in children under 6. My twins are 9 months old — could they be at risk living 70 miles away?
The Friday detonation was postponed to this Monday, and now it has been postponed again. We've been told it will happen Wednesday morning.
While I've felt fear rising in me, I've worked hard to lean into my faith and calm myself.
We haven't been told to evacuate
Although I understand that this is a bad situation — that the lead azide could spontaneously explode, which would have a greater impact than a controlled detonation — I don't understand why we weren't informed earlier so we could make plans to keep our families safe, or why we haven't been given enough information to make informed decisions about our families' safety.
People directly surrounding the detonation site have been told to evacuate. We have not been told to evacuate, although we've also been told that lead azide in the air could affect people as far as 100 miles away.
Local news outlets have encouraged us to stay inside, keep our windows closed, and dust surfaces to remove any dust from the detonation. But at the same time, we're told not to worry because we aren't in the evacuation zone.
There's a lot of mixed messages
Some people, like me, think it's concerning. The health impacts, especially on children, could be huge. Many people who share my concerns are considering evacuating temporarily, even though we haven't been advised to do so.
Others completely trust what we've been told on the news — that we have no need to fear the impacts of the detonated lead azide unless we've been told to evacuate, or the wind changes direction.
Some people don't even know what's happening. I met a woman today who told me her family wasn't aware of the blast.
I have no idea what our family will do because we haven't been given enough time to decide. I'm considering leaving tonight — just temporarily — but then I'd have to come back to our family's house, where the land, air, and water may have absorbed the lead azide.
The option to relocate my family permanently isn't possible when we've only been given days' notice about the blast. I can't relocate my family within a week.
I'm also thinking we might just stay in the house, close everything up, and clean really thoroughly.
I just don't know what the right thing to do is. And I feel that we haven't been given enough time to make an informed decision.

A video showing two women pleading with folded hands to stop the demolition of their house as a bulldozer demolishes tin-roofed houses is going viral on social media (here, here, and here), with the claim that it shows minority homes being demolished in Tripura and Assam. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows minority homes being demolished by a bulldozer in Tripura and Assam.
Fact: The video shows an anti-encroachment drive in the Kalshi area of Mirpur, Dhaka, Bangladesh, on 20 May 2026, during which authorities demolished illegal constructions. The demolition reportedly triggered clashes between authorities and residents, leaving several people injured. The video is unrelated to Tripura or Assam. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals. According to these reports, the video is from the Kalshi area of Mirpur in Dhaka, Bangladesh, where the administration conducted an anti-encroachment drive to remove illegal constructions on 20 May 2026. The demolition drive reportedly triggered clashes between authorities and residents, leaving several people injured.
To sum up, a video of an anti-encroachment drive in Dhaka is falsely shared, linking it to India.

The Earthly Education organization posted the video on Facebook and Instagram in November with overlaid text reading, "Reminder: this is what it will sound like 24/7 if a data center is built in your neighborhood." The post's caption accurately noted that the audio — which was captured separately from the video — was recorded in Dowagiac, Michigan, from a home located across the street from a Hyperscale Data data center.
In mid-November, the Earthly Education organization posted a video intended to raise awareness about data centers' environmental impact, as well as to urge people to act on a piece of legislation making its way through the U.S. Congress.
Earthly's website describes its purpose as aiming to "drive systemic change on the climate and ecological crisis through building awareness and mobilising communities into tangible action."
The video, posted on Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived), displayed a picturesque view of two moose crossing a stream. According to the captions, the audio featured authentic audio — recorded separately from the visuals — of data center noise in Dowagiac, Michigan.
The video was overlaid with text reading, "Reminder: this is what it will sound like 24/7 if a data center is built in your neighborhood."
The caption began, "This sound is recorded from a homeowner's porch, beside the 30-megawatt data center in Dowagiac, Michigan. Residents have already sued over the sound emissions, and yet Hyperscale Data Inc. wants to build an expansion to the current facility." The post also urged people to fight back against a bill that would reportedly accelerate the buildout of data centers.
In sum, the video's captions accurately described the authentic audio. Therefore, we rated the claim true.
Aya Miller, an independent journalist formerly with the Michigan-based MLive.com, confirmed via email that she recorded the audio on June 4 as part of video footage she posted it to TikTok days later.
Miller previously wrote about plans for Hyperscale Data to expand the 30-megawatt bitcoin mining data center into a 340-megawatt artificial intelligence computing facility. The company reportedly ceased bitcoin mining operations in early September, leading to a temporary reprieve from the constant sound from cooling fans, and planned to begin AI computing sometime in November — purportedly with less noise.
A class-action lawsuit, which Detroit attorney Laura Sheets filed in May on behalf of some homeowners, accused Alliance Cloud Services — a subsidiary of Hyperscale Data — of emitting "unreasonable and excessive noise" and "causing property damage through nuisance and negligence."
Snopes emailed a representative for Alliance Cloud Services. Additionally, we reached out to Sheets to ask what she knows about the current status of the data center site, as well as whether she wished to share a statement about the lawsuit. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Researching the rumor
A search for videos of the Dowagiac data center located reposts of a video on Facebook, Instagram and Reddit that matched the audio, including booming noises at the beginning and wind chime sounds several seconds in.
That original video displayed the hand of a person sitting on a front porch and holding a sound level meter reading about 60 decibels, with the camera tilting up to show the data center across the street. The text overlay read, "This is the sound emitted 24/7 from a 30 megawatt data center in Dowagiac, MI measured from a homeowner's porch."
One of the search results showed MLive.com posted the video on June 15. That post credited Miller, who had shared the video three days earlier on TikTok.
Miller's video shows the view from a resident's front porch on Louise Avenue in Dowagiac. Google Street View hosts 360-degree images of the same house and view.
Other videos shared online also demonstrated the noise from the same facility.
For further reading, we previously investigated whether a Meta data center introduced a rare bacterium in a Wyoming city's water.

The craze for fairness is more than skin-deep, and the trade-off can be costly. Inferior cosmetic products can end up harming your vital organs.
A 17-year-old girl in Keralam’s Malappuram developed a serious kidney ailment allegedly after using a fairness cream purchased online following its promotion by social media influencers, according to the doctors treating her.
The incident came to light after the authorities at the hospital that treated the teenager, who was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy, held a press conference on Friday. Lab tests had confirmed 1.25% mercury in the cosmetic product, according to the hospital sources.
Medical experts say that the use of fairness creams containing heavy metals such as mercury to lighten the skin is emerging as a major health hazard that can lead to serious conditions such as kidney failure if not diagnosed early.
Lack of awareness
Warning against following social media beauty trends and using topical creams seen online or bought over the counter without a prescription, M.M. Faizal, former president of the Indian Association of Dermatologists, Venereologists and Leprologists, says people lack awareness of how topical applications can enter the bloodstream.
“People are obsessed with fair skin. We have observed a rise in the number of people buying steroid creams that are easily available over the counter and applying them to their faces. Such steroid-based applications and creams containing heavy metals such as mercury can damage your kidneys easily. The government needs to bring in some mechanisms to control this,” he says.
Vulnerable group
A rise in the number of teenagers relying on spurious beauty products has forced the Keralam Drugs Control department to launch awareness campaigns targeting students in Classes XI and XII, an age group particularly vulnerable to online campaigns. Frequent inspections are carried out in marketplaces to confiscate spurious cosmetics.
State Drugs Controller K. Sujith Kumar says raising awareness about such spurious cosmetic products is the only way forward.
“We have seized cosmetics that have high mercury levels from offline markets. But there is no way to track or regulate online marketplaces,” he says.
Prolonged use of such creams can lead to kidney damage, says former secretary of the Nephrology Association of Kerala, Jayant Thomas Mathew, who has come across a few cases of kidney disorders among users. The condition could be detected early because the patients were aware of the symptoms.
“The patients had used fairness creams and noticed symptoms related to kidney disorders. They probably had membranous nephropathy, and since they sought medical help at a very early stage, treatment was possible,” says Dr. Mathew.
The symptoms
Swelling in the legs and face and frothing in the urine are some of the signs people need to be wary about, the doctor adds.
Much has changed in the beauty industry, with social media driving trends, says Liji Coleenz, a make-up artist and salon owner in Kochi with 20 years of experience.
“Even teenagers fall prey to the beauty aspirations set on social media. Our fixation with fairness is troublesome. We can never aspire to have Korean skin and need to be comfortable in our skin,” she maintains.

According to a survey by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), severe anaemia was observed in less than 2% of people in the majority of age groups. The Survey for Assessment of Markers of Population Health, Activity, Diet and Anthropometry (SAMPADA) 2023-2025 was released on Monday (November 23, 2026).
It showed that children aged 12-59 months had 42% anaemia prevalence, adolescent girls aged 10-19 years had anaemia prevalence of 46%, adolescent boys aged 10-19 years and men aged 20–59 years had 22-23% anaemia prevalence, whereas women of reproductive age had 56% prevalence.
The survey also found that mild anaemia constitutes a substantial proportion of the overall anaemia burden.
“SAMPADA provides nationally representative estimates of anaemia across children, adolescents, adults, pregnant and lactating women and older adults, together with detailed information on micronutrient deficiencies to evaluate potential causes of anaemia. It is encouraging that prevalence of anaemia is lower in SAMPADA compared to previous national surveys. The comprehensive anaemia profiling in the SAMPADA survey provides an evidence base to strengthen the ongoing national efforts towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat,” said Rajiv Bahl, secretary, Department of Health Research.
The report noted that about half of anaemic women, including pregnant and lactating women, adolescent girls, and children, have mild anaemia, indicating considerably lower risk of serious health consequences than moderate or severe anaemia. Anaemia prevalence is much lower among adolescent boys, adult and older men, and even among those affected, three-fourths have only mild anaemia, said the release issued by the Union Health Ministry.
SAMPADA represents one of the largest and most comprehensive nutrition surveys undertaken globally. The survey covered more than 2 lakh individuals from over 81,000 households across 183 districts in 35 States and Union Territories. More than 1.7 lakh blood samples were analysed for haemoglobin estimation across different age, sex, and physiological groups.
“A major strength of SAMPADA is the use of gold standard method of venous blood sampling and automated analysers for haemoglobin estimation, providing greater accuracy and reproducibility. In a sub-sample, the survey also assessed iron status, folate, vitamin B12, together with inflammatory biomarkers C-reactive protein (CRP) and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AGP) to obtain national level prevalence estimates,” the release said.
Iron deficiency accounts for about half of the anaemia cases in women, adolescent girls, and children, said the report.
The micronutrient assessment showed that although iron deficiency is the predominant contributor to anaemia in vulnerable population groups, it accounts for about half of the overall anaemia burden, highlighting the need to simultaneously address multiple nutritional and non-nutritional causes of anaemia, including infections, hemoglobinopathies, and inflammation related to chronic disease.
However, the prevalence of vitamin B12 and folate deficiency was similar in both anaemic and non-anaemic individuals across population groups, indicating a limited contribution of these micronutrient deficiencies to anaemia in India.
Iron deficiency is concentrated in specific life-stages and in moderate and severe cases of anaemia. SAMPADA findings show that iron deficiency is largely restricted to population groups including under-five children, adolescent girls, and women of reproductive age, while adolescent boys, men, and the elderly have a low prevalence of iron deficiency. Importantly, people with moderate and severe anaemia have a high prevalence of iron deficiency and need to be identified by testing for appropriate treatment and tracking till resolution as envisaged in AMB 2.0.
“These findings support more targeted, population-specific and life-course approaches to anaemia prevention and management. The evidence can contribute, while also identifying areas where further research and improved surveillance are required,” said Bharati Kulkarni, director, ICMR-NIN.

Hibernian vs Dundee; Scottish Premiership
Hibernian vs Dundee. Scottish Premiership.
Easter Road StadiumAttendance15,108.
Hibernian 2-1 Dundee: Goals from Martin Boyle and Chris Cadden secure Hibs' win at Easter Road for first time in eight months
Report as Hibernian win at Easter Road for the first time this season; Martin Boyle opened the scoring from the penalty spot; Nicky Cadden added a second; Joe Wright pulled a goal back for Dundee; Hibs move up to ninth in the Scottish Premiership; Dundee remain seventh
Tuesday 24 November 2026 22:29, UK
Hibernian ended their long wait for a Premiership home win after overcoming Dundee 2-1 at Easter Road.
Martin Boyle and Nicky Cadden - who curled home a stunning effort from outside the box - had the hosts in command before the interval.
But Dundee showed plenty of fight after the break and pulled one back through Joe Wright.

The visitors tried in vain to grab an equaliser and it was Hibs who were left satisfied by their first three points at home since beating Kilmarnock on April 4.
Despite being thrashed by Dundee United 4-0 at the weekend, Hibernian head coach Marink Reedijk decided to make only two alterations to his team, with Cadden and Thibault Klidje coming in.
Dundee manager Steven Pressley changed half of his outfield XI following the 8-0 humiliation to Hearts.
Owen Bevan was suspended and in came on-loan Bournemouth defender Matai Akinmboni for a full debut while Joe Wright, Brad Halliday, Joe Bevan and Ashley Hay started.
Hibs played on the front foot as they looked to start repairing the damage from the weekend's demoralising loss.
On a rare start, Togo international Klidje was lively and saw a header crash into the side-netting before hitting a harmless snap-shot straight at Dundee goalkeeper Owen Goodman.
From a short corner routine Hibs worked space for Cadden on the edge of the box from Josh Mulligan's lay-off and his driving effort whistled just past a post.
Dundee were desperate to keep it tight at the back but offered little going forward. Just when it looked like they were beginning to settle Hibs hit them two goals in three minutes before the break.
The first came in the 40th minute when Boyle fired a penalty past Goodman after being tripped by Ryan Finnigan.
Cadden then found the top corner with a sublime curling effort from his left foot just outside the box. It was another short corner routine that saw Miguel Chaiwa set up the wing-back.
Despite the hammer blow of losing two goals in quick succession before the break, Dundee demonstrated at the start of the second half that they were not going to roll over.
Pressley's side upped their intensity as they searched for a goal to get themselves back in the game and that arrived in the 67th minute courtesy of Wright.
Substitute Callum Jones' free-kick should have been put away by Ryan Astley but the ball broke back to Wright and he slammed the ball high into the net from six yards.
That set up a tense finish but Hibs desperately held on for a rare home victory.
What the managers said...
Hibernian head coach Marink Reedijk:
"It's always nice to win, it's a good one again in order to make sure we get confirmation that if we show our identity about intensity, aggression and proactivity and are brave, that anything can happen here.
"I hope we get another three points next match and that we go again in a way that we do the things we are good at and what our identity and what we stand for is.
"The next match against Motherwell is not at home, I know, but there will be a match at home against Rangers, where this can also come to life again. But that is far away.
"First things first, Saturday lies another challenge."
Dundee boss Steven Pressley:
"Both teams are a bit fragile and there was a lot of trepidation in the game but the one thing about us we got a degree of pride back. It's not the result but a little bit of stability and we showed a lot of courage.
"We wanted to give ourselves a foundation to build from and we gave ourselves that.
"We were much more cohesive in the second half and when you suffer the defeat we suffered on Saturday and you come here and you find yourself 2-0 down at half-time, it asks a lot of questions of you as a group and I thought they responded brilliantly.
"They showed courage and spirit and it's not been easy because there's a fragility about us. We responded in the proper manner."

The Japanese Association of Metal, Machinery and Manufacturing Workers (JAM) has decided to call for a pay scale increase of at least ¥17,000 ($107) per month in the 2027 shuntō (spring wage negotiations), sources said Tuesday.
JAM, the fifth-largest industrial labor group in trade union confederation Rengo, has about 1,900 member unions, mainly from small- and medium-sized manufacturers, with a total of some 390,000 workers.
The 2027 pay scale hike demand matches the record-high figure from the last round of negotiations, reflecting the association’s goal of reducing the pay gap between large and small companies.
Including the pay scale increase, JAM will call for total monthly pay increases of ¥21,500 or more. This compares with Rengo’s call for small unions to seek total pay hikes of at least ¥20,000.
JAM is set formally adopt its pay increase demands in January.
The association also plans to stress the need to secure funds for pay increases by appropriately raising the prices clients pay, as the business environment for small firms has become increasingly severe in part due to rising raw material and energy costs stemming from conflict in the Middle East.
